Proposal](#s4) - [4.1 The proposed form](#s4-1) - [4.2 Reasons, against the criteria](#s4-2) - [4.3 Rules for "arm lists" to add to const_for.md §5 "Fragment contexts"](#s4-3) - [4.4 Diagnostics to add to const_for.md §8 "Diagnostics and tooling"](#s4-4) - [4.5 Validation targets to add to const_for.md §9 "Validation targets for an implementation"](#s4-5) - [5. Examples](#s5) - [5.1 From a number to a variant](#s5-1) - [5.2 Structural printing](#s5-2) - [5.3 Dispatch per variant](#s5-3) - [5.4 How handwritten code changes](#s5-4) - [6. Implementation (the accompanying PR)](#s6) - [7. Anticipated questions and answers](#s7) --- ## 1. Background ### 1.1 Following #35 In #35 I raised the problem of handwritten field lists falling behind struct changes and silently going stale, and proposed `variant_name(v)` as one of a few small reflection pieces. For fields, you answered with `const for`. For variants, `const_for.md` §10 "Future work, explicitly outside v1" says "`variant_name` alone would not provide these capabilities", and leaves `variants`, field queries over payload types, and expansion into arm lists as future work. This issue proposes the whole of that const_for.md §10 item "Variants and payloads" as one design. ### 1.2 Goose today (`1e31b6d`) In this text, "the spec" means the Goose language specification (`docs/goose_spec.md`), and "const_for.md" the design document of `const for` (`docs/design/const_for.md`). A § number is a section number of that document, followed by the section's title in quotes. - **`const for` v1** (`docs/design/const_for.md`): there are three sources: `fields` (bindings ``: the field name string and the field's accessor), `types<...>` (``), and a constant list `[...]` (``). There are two fragment positions: statement lists (const_for.md §5.1 "Statement lists") and constructor initializer lists (const_for.md §5.2 "Constructor initializer lists"). Expansion into an initializer list is flattened, then receives the same checks as an ordinary constructor (const_for.md §5.2 "Constructor initializer lists"). - **Variant types**: an enum variant with a payload (`Shape.Circle`) is a "struct-like named type" (the spec §3.5 "Algebraic data types"), usable as a type of its own (the spec §8.2 "Case functions (match as an overload set)"). - **match** (the spec §8.1 "`match`"): a match over an ADT receives an exhaustiveness check. An arm names a variant and binds its payload by copy (`Circle c`) or by reference (`Circle &c`). Reference binding is allowed only on variable-mode payloads; fixed mode, and ADTs whose whole value can be reassigned, allow binding by copy only (because if the variant is replaced, a reference to the payload would see a different type). - **Case functions** (the spec §8.2 "Case functions (match as an overload set)"): functions per variant written under one name are dispatched on the tag when called with an ADT value, and exhaustiveness is checked too. - **Reference rules** (the spec §9.1 "The one rule": "a reference must … never observe its target at a wrong type"; the spec §9.2 "Roots and the depth check"): a reference must not outlive its target, and must not observe its target at a wrong type. - **What cannot be done today** (tried in practice): - `fields` is an error: `fields requires a concrete struct type, got Shape.Circle`. - Enum values cannot go in a constant list (`const for source requires a scalar or string constant`). - There is no `variants` (`const for source must be fields, types<...>, or [constants]`). - There is no `as` between enums and integers (`as requires a numeric source, got E`). ### 1.3 The problem to solve A large RPG written in Goose keeps entities and save data as integers, and writes its rules with enums and case functions. At that boundary, for dozens of enums, it has dozens each of handwritten matches from variant to number and of conversion functions from number to variant. - A match from variant to number has an exhaustiveness check, so adding a variant and forgetting to write it stops the build. - A conversion function from number to variant takes the form of an integer match with a `_`, so adding a variant and forgetting to write it passes without an error. Therefore an external test reads the matches in the source to check that every number makes the round trip. - Structural printing and per-variant processing likewise have no way but to list the variants by hand. The problem raised in #35, "handwritten lists silently go stale", remains on the variants' side. --- ## 2. Criteria These are the criteria by which the options are compared. A–H are stated in the discussion of #35, in `const_for.md`, and in the spec; P–R are added by this proposal. ### 2.1 Criteria stated in #35 and const_for.md | Criterion | Original text | Source | |---|---|---| | A. Do not add compiler built-ins per use case | "Making all of these things the compiler supports is not so great." / "This seems a somewhat specialized feature." | #35 | | B. Build on the existing mechanism (generic functions), and make the functions in the library | "it maximally piggy-backs on generic functions as the existing "macro system"." / "The library can build richer traversal functions over the v1 primitives without adding another compiler-provided visitor pattern." | #35, `const_for.md` §10 "Future work, explicitly outside v1" | | C. Use type information at compile time only; expansion generates ordinary code | "make field/type reflection something that only is possible inside compile time code" / "An expansion emits ordinary Goose operations and constants. It introduces no runtime iterator, heterogeneous container, type registry, per-object metadata, or dynamic dispatch." | #35, `const_for.md` §1 "Scope and cost model" | | D. A generated match also keeps exhaustiveness and the restrictions on payload references | "Generated matches must retain exhaustiveness and the restrictions on taking payload references." | `const_for.md` §10 "Future work, explicitly outside v1" | | E. Names and declaration order are not persistence identifiers | "Names alone do not constitute stable persistence identifiers." / "Display names should not automatically become stable type IDs or wire-format contracts." | `const_for.md` §10 "Future work, explicitly outside v1" | | F. Nothing is silently dropped; a failure is reported where it happens | "A field must never be silently omitted on failure." | `const_for.md` §8 "Diagnostics and tooling" | | G. A new fragment position states its parsing, ordering, and type-inference rules | "each needs explicit parsing, ordering, and type-inference rules" | `const_for.md` §10 "Additional fragment positions" | | H. The author states copy or reference explicitly | "Arm binders are explicit about copy vs reference, like the rest of the language" | the spec §8.1 "`match`" | ### 2.2 Criteria this proposal adds | Criterion | Meaning | |---|---| | P. Adding a variant does not let handwritten lists silently go stale | The same reason `const for` came in for in #35. A forgotten entry either stops the build, or there is no place to add one at all. | | Q. The program decides persistence numbers in one place | The meaning of the numbers written in save data must not change when variants are reordered or added. The language does not decide the numbers; the program's chosen numbers sit in one place (the same direction as [E](#axis-e)). | | R. No added runtime cost | So that programs with a limited time per frame, such as games, can use it, the result of an expansion should cost the same as a handwritten match or if (the same direction as [C](#axis-c)). | --- ## 3. Design options For each design decision, the conceivable options are listed and compared by the criteria of section 2 (○ fits, △ partly fits, × does not fit). ### 3.1 How the variants are handed over (the source) | Option | Assessment | Proposed | |---|---|---| | a. Add a source `variants` | [A](#axis-a) ○ (a source alongside `fields`, not a per-use-case built-in), [B](#axis-b) ○, [C](#axis-c) ○, [P](#axis-p) ○ (the language hands over every variant) | ◎ | | b. Allow enum values in constant lists, and list them by hand as `[E.A, E.B]` | [A](#axis-a) ○, [B](#axis-b) ○, [P](#axis-p) × (a forgotten entry passes without an error, the same as handwriting today) | | | c. A built-in "function that visits variants" (`visit_variants(v) F`) | [A](#axis-a) ×, [B](#axis-b) × (exactly "another compiler-provided visitor pattern") | | | d. Convert both ways between enums and integers with `as` | [A](#axis-a) × (a conversion built-in), [E](#axis-e) × (declaration order becomes the number). It does not solve enumerating the variants either | | ### 3.2 What the bindings of `variants` contain | Option | Assessment | Proposed | |---|---|---| | a. `` only (the variant) | [B](#axis-b) ○. But uses that need the name (printing and the like) need another means | | | b. `` (the name string and the variant) | The same shape as `` of `fields` ([B](#axis-b) ○, little to learn). `N` is a display string, not an identifier ([E](#axis-e) ○) | ◎ | | c. `` (also hand over the declaration-order number) | [E](#axis-e) × (leaves room for the declaration-order number to be used as a persistence identifier) | | | d. Limit `` to the values of variants without payload | Cannot handle variants with payloads, and does not satisfy const_for.md §10's "Variants and payloads" | | ### 3.3 What `V` stands for | Option | Assessment | Proposed | |---|---|---| | a. The variant type only (a type binding, like `U` of `types`) | Writing it as a pattern or a value needs another syntax, and there is more to learn | | | b. The same uses as a variant is written in the language today: a type (`Shape.Circle`), an arm's pattern (`Circle c`), a constructor (`Shape.Circle { r: 1 }`), and the value of a variant without payload (`Shape.Dot`) | [B](#axis-b) ○ (adds no new meaning; it only lets today's spellings be written through a binding), [G](#axis-g) ○ (each position's existing rules apply as they are) | ◎ | | c. Two bindings: the variant's "value" (only for those without payload) and its type | More bindings, and variants with payloads become awkward to handle | | ### 3.4 How a payload's fields are queried | Option | Assessment | Proposed | |---|---|---| | a. Allow variant types too as the `T` of `fields` (`fields`, `fields`) | [A](#axis-a) ○ (no new source), [B](#axis-b) ○, [C](#axis-c) ○. A variant type is a struct-like type to begin with (the spec §3.5 "Algebraic data types") | ◎ | | b. Add a new source `payload` | [A](#axis-a) △ (one more source, and one that does the same as `fields`) | | | c. Include the payload's field list in the bindings of `variants` (``) | A binding becomes a nested list, departing from v1's design of "a fixed number of bindings" | | Together with this, on which values the accessor `A` may be used: | Option | Assessment | Proposed | |---|---|---| | i. Only on values of the variant type (values bound by an arm) | [D](#axis-d) ○, the spec §9.1 "The one rule" ○ (the payload cannot be touched until the variant is settled) | ◎ | | ii. Also on ADT values, stopping at run time if the variant differs | the spec §9.1 "The one rule" × (leaves the possibility of observing at a wrong type to a runtime check), [F](#axis-f) △ | | ### 3.5 How expansion into an arm list is written | Option | Assessment | Proposed | |---|---|---| | a. Allow `const for` in a match's arm list, with an arm list as its body | [B](#axis-b) ○, [C](#axis-c) ○ (it becomes an ordinary match), [D](#axis-d) ○ (3.6), [G](#axis-g) ○ (rules in 4.3) | ◎ | | b. In statement-list expansion, a built-in that tests the tag (`is(v)`) and a chain of ifs | [A](#axis-a) × (a tag-test built-in), [D](#axis-d) × (a chain of ifs receives no exhaustiveness check) | | | c. Generate case functions generically per variant (specialize `fn f(c: V)` once per variant) | Needs expansion in declaration position. This is the part const_for.md §10 "Future work, explicitly outside v1" says "Top-level declarations and changes to overload sets require a separate design" about; a heavy change | | | d. A built-in dispatch function (the same as 3.1 c) | [A](#axis-a) ×, [B](#axis-b) × | | ### 3.6 How a generated match is checked | Option | Assessment | Proposed | |---|---|---| | a. Flatten first, then apply the same checks of the spec §8.1 "`match`" as for a written match (the same order as for initializer lists in const_for.md §5.2 "Constructor initializer lists") | [D](#axis-d) ○, [F](#axis-f) ○ (missing variants, repeated variants, and the position of `_` are found just as for written ones) | ◎ | | b. Skip the exhaustiveness check, since the expansion produces every variant | [D](#axis-d) × (breaks down when mixed with written arms or `_`) | | | c. Check each expansion within itself only | [D](#axis-d) △ (misses repeats of written arms outside it) | | ### 3.7 How reference binders in generated arms are handled | Option | Assessment | Proposed | |---|---|---| | a. The author writes `V c` or `V &c`; after flattening, the rules of the spec §8.1 "`match`" are checked per variant. Where not allowed, it is an error naming the variant | [D](#axis-d) ○, [H](#axis-h) ○, [F](#axis-f) ○ | ◎ | | b. Forbid `&` inside expansions | [D](#axis-d) ○, but variable-mode ADTs cannot be handled by reference, so it is less expressive than handwriting | | | c. When `V c` is written, use a reference where allowed and a copy where not | [H](#axis-h) × (whether it is a copy or a reference can no longer be read from the code written) | | ### 3.8 Whether expanded arms can be mixed with written arms and `_` In a match over an ADT, the expansion of `variants` makes arms for all variants. Therefore adding even one written variant arm is a repeat error under the spec §8.1 "`match`"'s "No variant is named twice". The only thing that can be mixed in without a repeat is a `_` placed last (the language today allows a `_` after all the variants, in a written match too). An integer match is different: a constant-list expansion, written constant arms that do not overlap it, and the required `_` can be mixed. If they overlap, it is the spec §8.1 "`match`"'s "earlier arms match all of its values" error (all of these are checked by the tests of the accompanying PR). | Option | Assessment | Proposed | |---|---|---| | a. Allow mixing, and leave it to the ordinary checks after flattening. What can actually be mixed in a match over an ADT is only a final `_`; in an integer match, arms that do not overlap and `_` | [B](#axis-b) ○ (initializer lists in const_for.md §5.2 "Constructor initializer lists" also leave mixing written entries and expansions to the ordinary checks), [D](#axis-d) ○, [F](#axis-f) ○ (repeats and overlaps are errors on the spot) | ◎ | | b. Do not allow mixing (a match made of expansions only) | [D](#axis-d) ○. But in an integer match it also forbids placing written arms beside an expansion, making it weaker than handwriting | | | c. Silently drop from the expansion the variants a written arm named earlier | [F](#axis-f) × (the generated arms silently change with the order written and the surrounding arms), [D](#axis-d) △ (missing ones can be checked, but what was generated cannot be seen from the text) | | | d. Choose the variants to expand with `const if` (filtering expansions) of const_for.md §10 "Future work, explicitly outside v1" | [D](#axis-d) ○, [F](#axis-f) ○, [G](#axis-g) ○. But it is a separate item of const_for.md §10 "Future work, explicitly outside v1", needing a design that decides the set of predicates. Not part of this proposal | | Leaving only some variants out of an expansion (writing the rest by hand) cannot be written within this proposal. That is the job of `const if` in const_for.md §10 "Future work, explicitly outside v1"; once that design comes in, filtered expansions and written arms can be mixed under rule a as it is. Adding `const if` later does not conflict with this proposal's rules, for three reasons. First, under this proposal, writing the same variant as an expansion in a written arm too is a repeat error, so no program that compiles today is written that way. `const if` only allows new spellings and does not change the meaning of existing programs. Second, the checks apply to the match after expansion ([3.6](#s3-6) a). If `const if` drops `Circle` from the expansion and only the `Circle` arm is written by hand, the match after expansion is an ordinary match with nothing missing or repeated, and passes under the spec §8.1 "`match`"'s rules as they are today. The rule for zero variants ([3.10](#s3-10) a) is also judged on the whole match after expansion, not per expansion, so even if filtering empties one expansion, it is not an error as long as there are other arms. Third, c (silently dropping from the expansion the variants a written arm named earlier) is also not taken because, once `const if` comes in, there would be two ways to drop a variant, and they would disagree. Note that `const if` needs a predicate that asks at compile time "is this `V` this variant". Which predicates to provide is for the design of `const if` to decide; this proposal only leaves room for it. ### 3.9 Where persistence numbers are decided | Option | Assessment | Proposed | |---|---|---| | a. The program writes one match from variant to number. The conversion from number to variant is made with a generic function running over `variants` | [A](#axis-a) ○, [B](#axis-b) ○, [E](#axis-e) ○, [P](#axis-p) ○ (the exhaustiveness check stops a forgotten entry in the match from variant to number, and the reverse direction has no place to write one at all), [Q](#axis-q) ○ | ◎ | | b. Use declaration-order numbers (`I` of 3.2 c) | [E](#axis-e) × | | | c. Write numbers in the declaration (`Town = 10`), and convert with `as` | [A](#axis-a) ×, [E](#axis-e) △ (the numbers are explicit, but the conversion becomes a built-in) | | | d. The annotations of const_for.md §10's "Defaults and annotations" (serialized names, aliases) | [E](#axis-e) ○. But it is a separate item of const_for.md §10 "Future work, explicitly outside v1", and larger than this proposal | | ### 3.10 Whether an enum with zero variants is allowed The language today allows an enum without variants (`enum Never {}`), and makes a match without arms (`match n {}`) a syntax error ("match must have at least one arm"). The expansion of `variants` makes no arms, so a match made only of that expansion is a match without arms. In statement-list or initializer-list position, the expansion simply happens zero times, with no problem. | Option | Assessment | Proposed | |---|---|---| | a. Make it an error, matching today's rule, with a message that shows the expansion made no arms | [B](#axis-b) ○ (uses today's rule as it is), [F](#axis-f) ○. As the type has no values, that match can never be reached, so nothing is lost in practice | ◎ | | b. Allow a match without arms, only for a match over an ADT without variants (unreachable) | Sound in type theory, but changes the language's rules. It also disagrees with a written `match n {}` | | | c. Make the source `variants` itself an error for an enum without variants | [B](#axis-b) △. It forbids even zero expansions in statement-list and initializer-list positions, and disagrees with `fields` allowing an empty struct (const_for.md §3.1 "Fields") | | ### 3.11 Whether a variant without payload can be bound The language today makes a binding in an arm of a variant without payload (`Dot d =>`) an error, "has no payload to bind". When a generic function writes the same arm `V v =>` for every variant, the variants without payload hit this error (found while implementing it). | Option | Assessment | Proposed | |---|---|---| | a. Allow the binding only in arms an expansion generated, binding an empty value of that variant type. Written arms remain an error as today | [B](#axis-b) ○ (a variant type is a full type to begin with, and an empty value can be made), [F](#axis-f) ○ (mistakes in written arms are stopped as today), [H](#axis-h) ○ | ◎ | | b. Allow it in every match | Removes the check that stopped mistakes in written arms, a larger change to the language's rules | | | c. Do not allow it in generated arms either | In an enum mixing variants with and without payload, one arm cannot cover every variant. `const if` of const_for.md §10 "Future work, explicitly outside v1" would be needed | | | d. In generated arms, silently drop the binding of a variant without payload | [F](#axis-f) × (if the body uses that name, it becomes a confusing error elsewhere) | | --- ## 4. Proposal ### 4.1 The proposed form For each decision of section 3, the proposed option (the same as the "Proposed" column of the tables in section 3). | Decision | Proposed option | |---|---| | [3.1 How the variants are handed over (the source)](#s3-1) | a. Add a source `variants` | | [3.2 What the bindings of `variants` contain](#s3-2) | b. `` (the name string and the variant) | | [3.3 What `V` stands for](#s3-3) | b. The same uses as a variant is written in the language today: a type (`Shape.Circle`), an arm's pattern (`Circle c`), a constructor (`Shape.Circle { r: 1 }`), and the value of a variant without payload (`Shape.Dot`) | | [3.4 How a payload's fields are queried](#s3-4) | a. Allow variant types too as the `T` of `fields` (`fields`, `fields`)
i. Only on values of the variant type (values bound by an arm) | | [3.5 How expansion into an arm list is written](#s3-5) | a. Allow `const for` in a match's arm list, with an arm list as its body | | [3.6 How a generated match is checked](#s3-6) | a. Flatten first, then apply the same checks of the spec §8.1 "`match`" as for a written match (the same order as for initializer lists in const_for.md §5.2 "Constructor initializer lists") | | [3.7 How reference binders in generated arms are handled](#s3-7) | a. The author writes `V c` or `V &c`; after flattening, the rules of the spec §8.1 "`match`" are checked per variant. Where not allowed, it is an error naming the variant | | [3.8 Whether expanded arms can be mixed with written arms and `_`](#s3-8) | a. Allow mixing, and leave it to the ordinary checks after flattening. What can actually be mixed in a match over an ADT is only a final `_`; in an integer match, arms that do not overlap and `_` | | [3.9 Where persistence numbers are decided](#s3-9) | a. The program writes one match from variant to number. The conversion from number to variant is made with a generic function running over `variants` | | [3.10 Whether an enum with zero variants is allowed](#s3-10) | a. Make it an error, matching today's rule, with a message that shows the expansion made no arms | | [3.11 Whether a variant without payload can be bound](#s3-11) | a. Allow the binding only in arms an expansion generated, binding an empty value of that variant type. Written arms remain an error as today | - **Source `variants`, bindings ``.** Hands over every variant of a concrete ADT type `E`, with or without payload, once each, in declaration order. An enum without variants gives zero. `N` is the variant name as a string constant, `V` the variant. For an instantiated generic enum, the variants of that instantiation are handed over. - **`V` is used as a variant is written today.** It can be used as a type (`V`), an arm's pattern (`V`, `V c`, `V &c`), a constructor (`V { ... }`; `V {}` for a variant without payload), and, for a variant without payload only, a value (`V`). It cannot be stored in a variable, passed as an ordinary argument, or converted to an integer (the same treatment as `A`). - **Variant types are allowed as the `T` of `fields`.** The order of fields, the meaning of `N` and `A`, and the access rules are the same as for structs. `A` may be used only on values of the variant type; using it on an ADT value is an error. Expansion into initializer lists (const_for.md §5.2 "Constructor initializer lists") works in a variant's constructor too. - **A match's arm list is added as a fragment position.** The body is an arm list, which after flattening receives the checks of the spec §8.1 "`match`". The author chooses reference binders, and they are checked per variant. Mixing with written arms and `_` is left to the ordinary checks after flattening. In a match over an ADT every variant is generated, so only a final `_` can be mixed in (3.8). Arms an expansion generated can bind variants without payload too (3.11). A pattern `V` can be used only in a match over that variant's ADT (in a match over another ADT with a variant of the same name, it is an error). A match for which the expansion makes no arms is an error (3.10). - **Persistence numbers are decided by the program's match, not by the language.** The reverse conversion is made with a generic function. ### 4.2 Reasons, against the criteria - **[A](#axis-a), [B](#axis-b)**: what is added is one source, a widening of the types `fields` accepts, and one fragment position. No conversion or dispatch built-ins are added. Conversion from number to variant and structural printing both become generic library functions. - **[C](#axis-c), [R](#axis-r)**: the result of an expansion is ordinary matches, ifs and constants; no runtime tables or type information are generated. The cost is the same as handwriting. - **[D](#axis-d), [F](#axis-f)**: a generated match receives exactly the same checks as a written match. Missing or repeated variants and disallowed reference binders are errors naming the variant. - **[E](#axis-e), [Q](#axis-q)**: the name `N` is for display, declaration order is used only for the order of expansion, and no number is handed over. The program decides the numbers in one place. - **[G](#axis-g)**: the rules for the arm position are in 4.3. - **[H](#axis-h)**: the author always states copy or reference explicitly. - **[P](#axis-p)**: when a variant is added, the exhaustiveness check stops the match from variant to number. Conversion from number to variant, printing, and dispatch have no place to add anything at all. ### 4.3 Rules for "arm lists" to add to const_for.md §5 "Fragment contexts" (the answer to [G](#axis-g)) - **Parsing**: in arm position inside a match's `{ }`, `const for in source { arm list }` may be written. The arm list is written as ordinary arms are: separated by commas, with an optional final comma. An expansion occupies one element of the enclosing list, so when an arm or another expansion follows, a comma is placed after its closing brace. Nesting is allowed. - **Ordering**: after flattening, arms are in the order written, and within an expansion in source order. In a match over an ADT every variant belongs to exactly one arm (the spec §8.1 "`match`"), so the order of arms does not change which arm is chosen. In an integer match, the spec §8.1's rule "the first arm that matches is taken" and the rule that makes a pattern earlier arms match whole an error are applied in the flattened order. - **Mixing with written arms**: left to the ordinary checks after flattening (3.8). In a match over an ADT the expansion makes every variant, so a written variant arm is a repeat error, and only a final `_` can be mixed in. In an integer match, written arms that do not overlap and the required `_` can be mixed in. - **`_`**: must be the last arm after flattening. An expansion after `_` is an error. - **Type inference**: as a flattened match, the arms' types are unified as today, and all arms infer to the same type (the spec §8.2 "Case functions (match as an overload set)"). - **Zero arms**: a match left without arms after flattening (a match made only of the expansion of an enum without variants) is an error (3.10). - **Integer matches**: arm expansion may be written, but patterns can only be constants, as today. A constant list's binding `C` can be used; `V` cannot. ### 4.4 Diagnostics to add to const_for.md §8 "Diagnostics and tooling" An error is given when: the source is not an ADT; the number of bindings is not 2; the `V` of a variant with a payload is written as a value (adding "construct it with `V { ... }`"); `V` is written in a disallowed position; `A` is used on an ADT value; a disallowed reference binder; a missing or repeated variant after flattening; an expansion after `_`; a pattern `V` is used in a match over another ADT (even if there is a variant of the same name, it is not taken as that variant); a match for which the expansion made no arms. Each names which variant (by name) of which expansion it arose from (in the PR's implementation, every diagnostic carries the expansion path, like "in const for variant Shape.Circle at …"). ### 4.5 Validation targets to add to const_for.md §9 "Validation targets for an implementation" Enums mixing variants with and without payloads, enums without variants, instantiations of generic enums, declaration order. `V c` and `V &c` in fixed mode and variable mode. Matches made only of expansions, matches mixed with written arms, nesting (`fields` inside `variants`), missing and repeat errors. Reads through `fields`, and expansion into a variant's constructor. Constant-list expansion into an integer match. Serialization and deserialization. That the generated C code has no reflection tables or runtime type information, and that a match becomes an ordinary jump table. The accompanying PR includes these as tests (section 6). --- ## 5. Examples ### 5.1 From a number to a variant ```goose // Variant → number: one per enum, as today (the only place that decides persistence numbers; exhaustiveness checked) fn number(k: Kind) -> i64 { match k { Town => 10, Catacombs => 11, Burrows => 12 } } // Number → variant: one, shared by every enum fn from_number(n: i64, fallback: E) -> E, bool { const for in variants { if number(V) == n { return V, true; } // V of a variant without payload can be used as a value } return fallback, false; } // Whether no two variants have the same number: one, shared by every enum fn numbers_distinct() -> bool { const for in variants { const for in variants { if N1 != N2 && number(V1) == number(V2) { return false; } } } true } ``` ### 5.2 Structural printing What `print` does today can be written in a library. ```goose fn show(value: T&) { match value { const for in variants { V &v => { // by reference in variable mode; in fixed mode, write V v print(N, " {"); const for in fields { print(" ", F, ": ", v.A); } print(" }"); }, } } } ``` This is also the concrete form of what I wrote in #35: "`print`'s structural printing can be written with these pieces". ### 5.3 Dispatch per variant The same as case functions do can be written generically. ```goose fn each_case(value: T) { match value { const for in variants { V c => F(N, c), } } } ``` ### 5.4 How handwritten code changes For the RPG of 1.3: | Handwritten code today | After this proposal | |---|---| | Conversion functions from number to variant (dozens) | **Gone**. One `from_number` does | | The external test that checks every number's round trip | Round-trip mismatches can no longer happen. The remaining check, "no repeated numbers", can be written inside Goose as one `numbers_distinct()` | | Matches from variant to number (dozens) | **Remain**, as the only place that decides persistence numbers (3.9 a, [E](#axis-e) and [Q](#axis-q)) | Removing the matches from variant to number as well would need const_for.md §10's "Defaults and annotations" (annotations for serialized names and numbers). It is a separate item, so it is not part of this proposal. --- ## 6. Implementation (the accompanying PR) The PR that accompanies this issue implements all of the form in 4.1 (branch `const-for-variants`, on master `1e31b6d`). It widens the implementation of `fields` (`typecheck_expansion.h`, `expansion_bind.h`, `clone.h`). const_for.md, the spec, the reference, and the tree-sitter grammar are updated in the same PR. The list of changes and how they were checked are in the PR's description. #### What was checked - `from_number` and `numbers_distinct()` of 5.1, `show` of 5.2 (`V v` in fixed mode and `V &v` in variable mode), `each_case` of 5.3, and building every variant with `fields` work (`test/typing/const_for_variants.goose`). - Each diagnostic of 4.4 is given: a variant with a payload written as a value, `A` on an ADT value, `V &c` in fixed mode, a repeat of a written arm, a variant of another ADT, an expansion after `_`, a source that is not an ADT, the number of bindings, a match without arms (the 9 files `test/errors_tc/const_for_variants_*.goose` and `test/errors/const_for_variants_arity.goose`, including one on lifetimes). - Reference lifetimes (the spec §9.2 "Roots and the depth check") work per variant just as for handwriting. In a generic function, returning a reference to a local's payload through a variable-mode `V &c` is an error, while a reference to a parameter's payload passes. Returning a reference to a field of the copy through a fixed-mode `V c` is an error, and a fixed-mode `V &c` is an error to begin with. Each is the same error message as when the same match is handwritten. - The generated C code has no variant name strings (unless `N` is used), no tables, and no runtime type information. Compared with the C of a handwritten conversion from number to variant, it was 1507 lines against 1509, differing only in the order of statements and how functions were expanded ([C](#axis-c), [R](#axis-r)). - The test suite (`run_tests.py --profile baseline --cc native --require-clang`, including the check of the reference's examples) passes entirely (audio, graphics, physics and UI are skipped, as the build does not include them). `lsp_sweep.py --quick` and tree-sitter's `build.py --check` pass too. #### What implementing it showed - **Binding a variant without payload**: that the choice of 3.11 is needed was found by implementing it. The PR implements 3.11 a. - **The owner of a pattern `V`**: in the first implementation, an arm made by `variants` of another ADT silently passed in a match over an ADT with a variant of the same name. Like `A` of `fields`, its owner is now checked; this went into 4.1 and 4.4 ([F](#axis-f)). - **A match with zero arms**: the choice of 3.10 was also found by implementing it. The PR implements 3.10 a. - **Generic type inference**: passing a variant's constructor directly, as in `show(Shape.Circle { r: 2 })`, makes `T` the variant type, and `variants` is an error. The caller passes a value of the ADT type (`let a: Shape = …; show(a)`). This is today's inference as it is, so the proposal is unchanged. - **References are not unwrapped**: passing a variable-mode value to a generic by-value parameter makes `T` a reference type (`E..&`), and `variants` is an error. In line with `fields` not unwrapping references (const_for.md §3.1 "Fields"), it is left unwrapped. The function is written `value: T&`. #### Not in the PR - **Binding resizable payloads**: binding a payload holding `u8[>..]` or the like is stopped by today's C backend with "binding a resizable ADT payload is not supported by the C backend yet". The same happens for a handwritten match; it is a separate problem from this proposal. - **Language server**: the correspondence between arms generated by an expansion and the arms of the source (hover, go to definition) is not touched. The number of arms differs from the source before expansion, so the positions of binder names in generated arms cannot be looked up correctly. --- ## 7. Anticipated questions and answers - **"Passing variant types through `fields`, can't a payload be touched before the variant is settled?"** → `A` can be used only on values of the variant type (3.4 i). Using it on an ADT value is an error. - **"Can arm expansion generate disallowed reference binders?"** → After flattening, each variant is checked as in the spec §8.1 "`match`", and it is an error naming the variant (3.7 a). The PR's tests check that it is the same error message as for handwriting. - **"A new fragment position needs rules."** → They are in 4.3. - **"`V` serving as a type, a pattern, a constructor and a value is confusing."** → It only lets today's uses of `Shape.Circle`, `Circle c`, `Shape.Circle { ... }` and `Shape.Dot` be written through a binding as they are; no new meaning is added (3.3 b). - **"Can't one just list them by hand?"** → The problem is not the effort, but that the list silently goes stale when a variant is added ([P](#axis-p); the same reason `const for` came in for fields in #35). With the form that allows enum values in constant lists and lists them by hand (3.1 b), a forgotten entry passes. - **"Doesn't this leave persistence numbers to declaration order or names?"** → It does not. The program's match decides the numbers, and the order `variants` hands over is used only for the order of expansion (3.9 a, [E](#axis-e)). - **"Isn't a linear search slow?"** → What is expanded is a sequence of comparisons with constants, a form the C compiler can turn into a table lookup. The C generated by the PR's implementation was nearly the same as for a handwritten conversion (section 6). - **"Expansions get too large."** → The limit of const_for.md §7 "Compiler integration" (100,000 nodes) applies as it is.

title: const for over enum variants and their payloads (const_for.md §10)
body: ## Contents - [1. About this PR](#s1) - [2. What changed](#s2) - [2.1 Language](#s2-1) - [2.2 Compiler](#s2-2) - [2.3 Documents](#s2-3) - [2.4 tree-sitter grammar](#s2-4) - [3. Tests and what was checked](#s3) - [4. Not included](#s4) --- ## 1. About this PR This implements issue #52. It implements the form proposed in the issue (the issue's 4.1 "The proposed form") as it is. The design's background, criteria, comparison of options, and the reasons for choosing this form are in the issue. Here are what changed, how it was checked, and what is not included. This PR implements the item "Variants and payloads" of §10 "Future work, explicitly outside v1" of `docs/design/const_for.md` (the design document of `const for`; const_for.md below), and removes that item from const_for.md §10 "Future work, explicitly outside v1". --- ## 2. What changed ### 2.1 Language - **Source `variants`**: hands over every variant of a concrete ADT type `E`, with or without payload, in declaration order, with bindings `` (the variant name string, and the variant). `V` can be written where a variant's name is written today: a type, a constructor (`V { ... }`), a match arm's pattern (`V`, `V c`, `V &c`), and, for a variant without payload only, a value. - **Variant types in `fields`**: `T` may be a variant type (`Shape.Circle`, or `V`), walking the payload's fields. The accessor `A` can be used only on values of that variant type and in that variant's constructor. - **Expansion into a match's arm list**: `const for` may be written in an arm list, its body being arms. After flattening, it receives the same checks as a written match (the spec §8.1 "`match`"). - **Binding in generated arms**: arms an expansion generated can bind variants without payload too (an empty value of that variant type). In written arms it is an error, as today. - **The owner of a pattern `V`**: using it in a match over another ADT is an error. Even if there is a variant of the same name, it is not taken as that variant. - **A match without arms**: a match for which the expansion made no arms is an error, like a written match without arms. ### 2.2 Compiler It widens the implementation of `fields`; no new mechanism is added. | File | Change | |---|---| | `src/parser.h` | Reads the source `variants<...>`. Splits a match's arm list into `ParseArms`, which reads a `const for` in arm position | | `src/ast.h` | `ES_VARIANTS`. Arm bodies in `ConstFor` (`armfragments`, `arms`). In `MatchArm`, the expansion (`expansion`) and a generated mark (`generated`). A pattern's owner (`variantowner`) | | `src/typecheck_expansion.h` | Resolving and binding `variants`, `fields`, flattening arms (`TypeCheck::ExpandArms`) | | `src/expansion_bind.h`, `src/clone.h` | When cloning arms, replaces a pattern `V` with the variant's name (`CloneArm`). The diagnostic message for `V` written as a value | | `src/typecheck_exprs.h`, `src/typecheck_flow.h`, `src/typecheck.h` | Flattens arms before a match is checked. Payload-less binding in generated arms. Checking a pattern's owner | | `src/dump.h` | Writes an arm expansion back unexpanded (round-trip tests) | ### 2.3 Documents - **const_for.md**: the table and text of §1 "Scope and cost model" (four sources, three fragment positions), the example and grammar of §2 "Syntax", §3.1 "Fields" (variant types), a new §3.4 "Variants", a new §5.3 "Match arm lists", §6 "Library use and receiver semantics", §7 "Compiler integration", §8 "Diagnostics and tooling", §9 "Validation targets for an implementation". From §10 "Future work, explicitly outside v1", the item "Variants and payloads" is removed, and "`const if` or filtering" gains the use "expanding only some variants into arms". - **The spec** (`docs/goose_spec.md`): the paragraph "Specialization-time expansion" of §6.5 "`for`", and one item on arm-list expansion in §8.1 "`match`". - **The reference** (`docs/reference.md`): `variants` in the description of position-dependent keywords. In "`const for`: expansion at specialization time", a description of `variants` and one example with its output. - `docs/index.md` (the description in the list of design documents), `docs/site/goose.xml` (highlighted words). ### 2.4 tree-sitter grammar The tree-sitter grammar has the rule that it "should never reject a program the compiler accepts", so it is updated too. `grammar.js` gains `variants` and arm expansion (`const_for_arms`), `queries/highlights.scm` gains `variants`, and `test/corpus/statements.txt` gains one example. --- ## 3. Tests and what was checked - **`test/typing/const_for_variants.goose`**: conversion from number to variant (`from_number`), checking for repeated numbers (`numbers_distinct`), structural printing by value (fixed mode) and by reference (variable mode), dispatch to case functions, building every variant with `fields`, generated arms beside a final `_`, and a constant list's arms beside written arms in an integer match. - **Error tests** (the 9 files `test/errors_tc/const_for_variants_*.goose`, `const_for_list_arm_covered.goose`, `test/errors/const_for_variants_arity.goose`): a variant with a payload written as a value, an accessor on an ADT value, `V &c` in fixed mode, a repeat of a written arm, a variant of another ADT, an expansion after `_`, a source that is not an ADT, the number of bindings, a match without arms, returning a reference to a local's payload (lifetimes), and a pattern earlier arms take in an integer match. As the error message of `fields` changed to "fields requires a concrete struct or variant type", the 2 existing tests that look for it, and 1 on the kind of source, were updated. - `python test/run_tests.py --profile baseline --cc native --require-clang` (macOS): all passed (audio, graphics, physics and UI are skipped, as the build does not include them). The check of the reference's examples (`scripts/check_doc_examples.py`) passes as part of it. - `python tree-sitter/build.py --check`: the corpus passes entirely, and all 2,713 `.goose` files in the repository parse. - `python test/lsp_sweep.py --filter const_for`: 50 `const for` test files, 11,516 requests, answered without failure. - Generated C code: the conversion from number to variant was compared written with `variants` and written by hand. Neither has variant name strings (unless `N` is used), tables, or runtime type information; they were 1,507 and 1,509 lines. --- ## 4. Not included - **Generated arms in the language server**: no work was done to tie binder names in generated arms to the source's arms for hover or go to definition. The number of arms differs from the source before expansion, so the positions of binder names in generated arms cannot be looked up correctly. That requests neither fail nor hang was checked with the `lsp_sweep.py` above. - **Binding resizable payloads**: binding a payload holding `u8[>..]` or the like is stopped by the C backend with "binding a resizable ADT payload is not supported by the C backend yet". The same happens for a handwritten match; this PR does not change it. - **The other items of const_for.md §10 "Future work, explicitly outside v1"**: `const if` (expanding only some variants), "Defaults and annotations" (annotations for serialized names and numbers), and so on are not in this PR.

Preserve CMake archive paths in cc-style response files
body:
CMake can return an archive path such as `pkg\libcmk_impl.a` in its File API link fragments. Goose currently quotes it in the generated response file only when the path contains spaces. With MinGW GCC, an unquoted backslash is consumed and linking fails looking for `pkglibcmk_impl.a`. A space in `GOOSE_HOME` hides the failure by making the writer quote the argument.

Quote and escape each cc-style response-file argument so archive paths reach GCC/Clang unchanged. Keep the existing MSVC serialization. The package fixture now exposes an interface target over its static implementation, and the focused package regression builds and runs with plain and spaced cache paths. It runs through the existing test runner, using MinGW GCC on Windows when available and cc on Unix.

Validation:
- The new regression fails on unmodified upstream `8511ae3` with the missing archive path.
- Windows 11: GCC 15.2.0 and Clang 18.1.8 both pass the plain/spaced cache cases after the fix.
- Windows/MinGW: existing AOT/JIT native rebuild, CMake options/targets/C++, and native-builder tests pass.
- Linux/WSL2 with GCC 11.4.0: package toolchain, response-file, native rebuild and native-builder checks pass, including AOT/JIT.

title: Add an API to release unused data-stack memory
body:
Long-running applications keep the peak committed memory of their data stacks after shrinking buffers or leaving a large model's scope. For example, replacing a large document with a small one makes the old storage reusable but does not return its pages to the OS.

This adds `trim_memory() -> bool` to the `os` module. It discards the complete pages above the current tops of the calling thread program's data stacks, globals and finished scratch included, using the runtime's own region registry. Live values, borrowed views, limited-array capacity and virtual reservations are preserved, later growth works normally, and other workers are not affected. `false` means an OS request failed.

**Per platform**
- Windows: `MEM_DECOMMIT`, which also returns the commit charge; the fault handler recommits on growth.
- Linux: `MADV_DONTNEED`, which drops the pages from RSS at once.
- macOS: `MADV_FREE_REUSABLE`, paired with `MADV_FREE_REUSE` when growth takes the pages back. To give growth that point, macOS data stacks now commit on fault as Windows does: regions are mapped `PROT_NONE` and the signal handler opens them 1 MB at a time.

Windows and macOS stop at a per-region commit mark, so a trim never sweeps the whole reservation.

**Behaviour change on macOS**
This applies to every macOS program, not only those that call `trim_memory()`: the first touch of each stack and each further MB of growth takes a SIGBUS that the runtime handles. The cost is small next to zero-filling the pages, but a debugger sees each fault first (lldb stops on `EXC_BAD_ACCESS` unless it is passed on to the program). Runtime C already writes stacks only in user mode (`memcpy`, `gs_bld_append`), as Windows requires, so no system call meets an unopened page. Allocation and scope exit on Windows and Linux are unchanged.

**Compiler**
A no-argument runtime call cannot see a caller's cached stack tops. The extern is therefore marked `readsalltops`: its call writes back every cached top, and every function that may reach it transitively makes its callers write back all of theirs around the call.

**Tests**
- `runtime_trim_memory.c` (native, baseline and sanitizer profiles): real decommit on Windows, residency on Linux, the commit mark and reuse interval on macOS, partial-page prefixes, separate local and global stacks, repeated trims, the guard gap, recommit on regrowth, and a trim over pages that growth skipped.
- Goose fixtures:
  - `trim_memory`: live borrowed views, retained limited-array views, transitive calls with cached tops, scratch scopes, globals.
  - `trim_memory_threads`: worker isolation.
  - `trim_memory_paths`: a static function value, a block returning through a HOF, `map`'s block, a nested function, reference parameters, a global, case-function dispatch, format hooks.
  - `trim_memory_construction`: an argument built before a trimming call, literal elements and fields, `str()` pieces, pushes in a loop, global initializers.

  `trim_memory`, `trim_memory_paths` and `trim_memory_construction` fail when the transitive write-back is disabled.

**Validation**
- Windows/MSVC: Release compiler build; the four fixtures under TinyCC JIT and as native builds at -O0, -O2 and debug; the native runtime test at /O2 and /Od; the runtime object and a standalone program built with MSVC; the runtime and stdlib fixtures under JIT.
- Linux/Fedora 44 x86_64, commit `68488e4`: Debug compiler built with GCC 16.2.1; the baseline suite passed all 4,676 checks, including native -O0/-O2, targeted `GS_DEBUG` runs, supported TinyCC JIT fixtures, the secondary Clang C-front-end check, bootstrap and samples.
- Linux sanitizers: compiler built with Clang 22.1.8 and ASan/UBSan; the sanitize profile passed all 3,967 checks with leak detection enabled, instrumenting both the compiler and generated C. All four new Goose fixtures and `runtime_trim_memory.c` passed in both profiles, including the Linux residency checks.
- Linux test setup: TinyCC needed `-DCMAKE_C_FLAGS=-DCONFIG_SELINUX=1` for this environment's executable-memory restrictions. LeakSanitizer ran outside the sandbox with `allow_addr2line=1`, allowing the repository's existing `test/lsan.supp` suppression for `cute_spirv.h` to match. No source changes were needed.
- Optional audio/gfx/physics/ui native execution was skipped because those layers were not built in; their sources were still checked and C generated. `trim_memory_threads` ran natively; TinyCC does not support the Linux threading fixtures.
- Not run locally: macOS, including the new commit-on-fault path; left to CI.

title: How to deal with the limitations of this language?
Dynamic externs: extern blocks bound from a shared library by name
body:
An `extern "lib" { ... }` block declares functions bound from a shared library by name when the program starts: no C of the program's own, no linking, and under the in-process backend no C toolchain at all.

```goose
extern "SDL2" {
    fn SDL_Init(flags: u32) -> i32;
    fn SDL_Quit();
    fn SDL_GetTicks64() -> u64;
    fn delay(ms: u32) = "SDL_Delay";
}
```

The design is in `docs/design/dynamic_externs.md` (the first commit), and the rest of the branch implements its plan one commit at a time:

- **Runtime**: `gs_dl_bind` opens each library once (`dlopen` / `LoadLibraryW`) and fills a pointer per symbol, with runtime errors naming the spelling tried. A bare name derives the platform's spelling (`SDL2.dll`, `libSDL2.dylib`, `libSDL2.so`), a dotted name is literal, and a path with a separator is relative to the program's resource directory, so a library shipped beside the program is named the same way everywhere.
- **Parser**: the block form, with members that are ordinary `extern fn`s to everything after the parser (`SFunction::dylib`), per-member recovery, the dump printing blocks back, and the tree-sitter grammar.
- **Codegen**: a member is called through a static pointer `gs_dl<N>_<symbol>`; the generated C carries the library and bind tables and calls `gs_dl_bind` in `gs_program_init` before the globals' initializers. Only a member a call reaches is bound. A package whose externs are dynamic needs no native part.
- **Sidecar**: `dylibs` lists (with the platform suffixes) map a block's name to the spelling to open, `name=spelling`; a package's are defaults, the program's win per platform; a name no block declares is an error. The generated C carries all three platforms' spellings and the runtime picks its own, so it stays portable.
- **Docs**: spec §7.10 and the grammar, reference §24 with the conventions for declaring a real library's functions under Goose's shapes (handles as `u64`, strings via a NUL and `s[0]`, `pad` where C pads, by reference, enums as `i32`), packages.md, stdlib.md, the JIT and implementation notes.
- **`ffi` module**: `cstr` and `bytes` copy memory a library owns (a `const char *` it returns, an array it keeps) into Goose storage.
- **Checker**: an extern's C symbol must be a C identifier, caught at the declaration rather than inside the generated C.
- **Syntax**: an extern's C symbol follows its signature, `fn delay(ms: u32) = "SDL_Delay";`, at the top level too; the old `extern "sym" fn` is deprecated and warns (except in packages fetched from git).
- **Review fixes**: a struct holding `pad` crosses to a shared library by reference only (its by-value calling convention differs from C's padded struct); a library named by a path finds its sibling DLLs on Windows; a package's `dylibs` may map a module the program doesn't import; the dump escapes a block's library and C symbols; the Python toolchain links `-ldl` on Linux.

**Testing.** `test/extern_dylib.py` builds a shared library with the suite's toolchain and runs a block against it through every parameter shape, under the JIT (with the C compiler pointed at a nonexistent path) and built, at -O0 and -O2; checks the generated C is deterministic and binds only the called members; covers a missing library, a missing symbol, both declared but uncalled, a bare name on the loader's path, the sidecar overrides and their four errors, and a package mixing static and dynamic externs. Syntax, recovery and checker fixtures under `test/syntax`, `test/errors` and `test/errors_tc`. The full baseline suite passes on the rebased branch.

Beyond the suite, the branch was tried against real libraries on Linux: zlib (`compress2`, `uncompress`, `crc32`), SQLite (a handle out through `u64&`, prepared statements, column text through `ffi::cstr`), SDL2 under the dummy driver (a struct of three `u8` by reference, a hidden window, rects by const reference), libcurl (reading `curl_version_info`'s struct through `ffi::bytes`), libc through the sidecar, a worker thread calling a bound function, a C host through `--header`, and an `--include` header that pulls in the library's own prototypes beside the block.

**Known limits, deferred in the design (§12):** on Linux the derived `libX.so` needs the dev symlink, so deployment to a machine with only the runtime package wants a sidecar soname line (`dylibs_linux = ["SDL2=libSDL2-2.0.so.0"]`); candidate spellings tried in order would remove that. Variadic functions cannot be bound (they happen to work on x86-64, and the docs say they are undefined). Callbacks need an adapter. A wild pointer through `ffi` is a plain segfault.

title: Time every PR against its base on the LangArena suite
body:
Adds a `Benchmark` workflow that A/B-tests each pull request against the latest commit of the branch it targets on the LangArena suite (`bench/kostya`), in time and peak memory.

## How it works
- Builds two compilers in Release: the PR's (its merge into the base) and the base's. Both compile the PR's `bench/kostya/goose/src`, so the binaries differ only in the compiler and its standard library. If the base compiler can't compile those sources, it falls back to its own and the report says so.
- `bench/kostya/ci_ab.py` runs every benchmark in its own process, base and head back to back, swapping the order each rep, best of 5. It records the benchmark's own time and the process's peak RSS (`wait4`).
- A change is marked when it exceeds 10% in time, or 10% and 1 MiB in memory, **and** holds in every rep. The geomean of the time ratios has its own 3% threshold.
- **A regression is a warning, not a failure.** A wrong checksum from the PR's build fails the job.
- The table goes to the job summary, an uploaded artifact (with raw samples) and one PR comment, which is rewritten on every push. PRs from forks get no comment, because their token can't write one, but the summary is still there.
- LangArena's `run.js` is read at a pinned commit (`LANGARENA_REF`).
- It runs only when the PR touches `src/`, `stdlib/`, `third_party/`, `cmake/`, `CMakeLists.txt`, the benchmark or its scripts, or the workflow itself. Docs, tests and samples alone don't trigger it.

## Testing
- Ran `ci_ab.py` locally with the same compiler on both sides over 4 benchmarks, 3 reps: no change flagged, deltas within ±3%, geomean 1.011.
- The workflow itself hasn't run on GitHub yet; this PR is its first run. Expect roughly 15–25 minutes on `ubuntu-latest` (the full suite takes ~53 s per run locally). `REPS` in the workflow trades time for confidence.

title: Add a pre-order delta-link row to the tree benchmark
body:
Adds one row, `bench/rust/tree_arena_fast.rs`, wired into the manifest's tree case (one Rust entry and a two-line note in the case summary).

**What it changes.** `tree_arena.rs` lays the complete tree out children-first, so `sum_tree` chases indices backwards through a ~400 MB pool at depth 24. The new row keeps the same 12-byte typed node (`v: i32` plus two u32 link fields — no whole-tree u32 storage, no unsafe, bounds checks stay on) but pushes parent-first: the DFS then visits slots in 0,1,2,...,N-1 order, exactly the order they sit in memory, so the walk is a sequential, hardware-prefetched scan; and the link fields hold slot deltas instead of absolute indices, which turns node addressing from `index*12` into an add.

**Gate.** Same seeds in the same recursive order; the row's printed checksums match the existing tree rows bit for bit at every suite depth (131071 / 2097151 / 33554431 nodes at depths 16/20/24).

**Measurement — how to read the numbers.** Each run builds the tree once and sums it eight times (the suite's workload, unchanged). Reported is processor time in milliseconds, `median / quickest`, over 10 interleaved rounds: every round runs all three rows once back to back, who goes first alternates round by round so background load can't favour anyone, and the first round is thrown away as a warm-up. Lower is better; medians repeat within ~2% between independent runs.

| depth | goose pool + typed refs | rust arena + indices | rust pre-order, 12-byte links | arena vs goose | pre-order vs goose |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 20 | 53 / 46 | 51 / 47 | 45 / 41 | **−4%** | **−15%** |
| 24 | 824 / 798 | 807 / 782 | 711 / 692 | **−2%** | **−14%** |

Percentages are median against median, with the Goose row as the baseline: e.g. at depth 20, arena vs goose is 51/53 = −4% and pre-order vs goose is 45/53 = −15%. The numbers make two points: the existing Rust arena row already tracks the Goose typed-refs row to within a few percent at the same node size, and the pre-order row is 12–15% faster than either of them — so the layout change dominates whatever small language gap there is here.

In plain terms: depth 24 is a tree of 33.5 million nodes, so one run touches ~302 million nodes (build plus the eight sums). At 711 ms that is ~2.4 ns per node touched, against ~2.7 ns for the two existing rows — merely from walking the tree in the order it is written. Peak memory is unchanged: 385.3 MB, ~33.5M nodes × the same 12-byte node. At depth 16 everything runs in milliseconds and the rows are indistinguishable.

Absolute values shift a few percent with background load; the suite's own quiet-loop protocol in `run_bench.py` reproduces this same three-row comparison, and this PR adds the row to its manifest.

title: Read scalar fields behind references once ahead of loops
body:
Codegen now reads a scalar field that a loop reads through a reference, and never stores
to, into a local before the loop. After a call, it reads the local again only if the
callee may store to the field, by a transitive store summary of the callee. The C compiler
can't do this itself: a call anywhere in the loop, however rarely it runs, or a store of
the field's type makes it reload the field at every use. A Goose store changes only memory
of its own type (spec §0), so the loop's own stores show which fields can change.

Fields the loop stores to stay in memory. The second commit says how to keep those in
locals by hand.

goose-compress's level-1 matcher at `0584d3d^` now keeps `z.fill` and `z.base` in locals
and reads them again only after `end_block`. gzip level 1 of 1 MB of JSON, 30 runs, on an
M1 Pro with Apple clang 21; every version gives the same output size, and goose-compress's
tests pass with this change:

| Version | Instructions | Cycles (3 runs) |
|---|---:|---:|
| Before | 1,123 M | 292–294 M |
| This change | 1,037 M | 284–286 M |
| [0584d3d](https://github.com/kaitk/goose-compress/commit/0584d3d), all four fields in locals by hand | 1,035 M | 281–283 M |

`test/codegen/field_reads.goose` stores to a field each way a loop or a call can, and
the runner checks the generated C of one loop (`docs/testing.md`).

title: Let packagers set TinyCC's runtime and libc paths
body:
The build hard-codes two paths for the in-process backend (TinyCC):

1. Where tcclib/ lives. CMake bakes the build directory's path into
   the binary, so building the same source in two directories gives
   two different binaries.

2. Where the C library lives. TinyCC looks under /usr (or the macOS
   SDK). On a system that keeps its C library somewhere else, every
   `goose file.goose` run fails:

       libtcc: compiling the generated C failed
       <string>:50: error: include file 'stdint.h' not found

   `goose build` is not affected, since it uses the system C compiler.

This adds three CMake options to override them. Left unset, the build
behaves exactly as it does today.

- GOOSE_TCC_LIB_PATH: where tcclib/ is installed. A tcclib/ next to
  the compiler still takes priority.
- GOOSE_TCC_SYSINCLUDEPATHS: TinyCC's include path.
- GOOSE_TCC_LIBPATHS: TinyCC's library path. This one is needed too:
  with only the include path, in-process runs of several samples
  still fail.

The second commit fixes a check in test/cli_paths.py that failed for
any compiler installed outside its build tree, such as a release. It
counted every stdlib/ in an error message, and an installed compiler
rightly lists its own stdlib/ as well as the source tree's. It now
counts only the source tree's.

We ran into all of this while packaging Goose for Nix, which builds in
a new directory every time and has no C library under /usr.

Tested on aarch64-linux, on master (94cc64d):

- Before: both problems reproduce.
- After: rebuilds give identical binaries, and test/run_tests.py
  passes in full.

title: Add CRC-32 and carry-less multiply intrinsics to std
body:
std gains crc32_u8 and crc32_u64, steps of gzip's CRC-32 (reflected, polynomial 0xedb88320, no inversion), and clmul_lo and clmul_hi, the halves of the carry-less product of two u64s, with crc32_hardware and clmul_hardware saying whether each is an instruction here. Like popcount, clz and ctz they are the runtime's (runtime_ext.h): arm64's crc32b/crc32x and PMULL where the C compiler targets them, x86-64's PCLMULQDQ inside a simd fn, and a table or shifts elsewhere, TinyCC included, with the same results on every path.

x86-64's crc32 instruction is CRC-32C, so gzip's CRC there goes through carry-less multiplication. PCLMULQDQ joins the simd fn versions' targets and their CPU check (every CPU with AVX2 has it), and each version's body is compiled with GS_SIMD_CUR set to its level, so that clmul_lo and clmul_hi are the instruction in the versions and shifts in the baseline.

test/stdlib/stdlib_crc32_clmul.goose checks both against bit-by-bit models, including inside a simd fn.

title: Mark implicit reference bindings with a `ref` inlay hint
body:
## Why

An un-annotated `let`/`var` copies a fixed-size value but binds a non-fixed lvalue by reference (§4.1). The syntax is the same either way, so this is easy to miss:

```goose
let ints = [1, 2, 3];
let ints2: i64[] = [1, 2, 3];
let x = ints;    // a copy
let y = ints2;   // a reference: y[0] = 5 changes ints2
```

Until now the editor showed the difference only as a trailing `&` in the type hint (`: i64[]&`).

## What

`InlayHints` now puts a `ref` hint before an initializer the checker bound by reference on its own:

```
let x: i64[3] = ints;
let y: i64[]& = ref ints2;
let z: i64[] = copy(ints2);      // no hint: explicit copy
let w: i64[]& .= ints2;          // no hint: explicit .=
let b: u8[>..]& = ref buf;
let name: u8[]& = ref r.name;    // a variable-size field
```

It recognizes the synthesized `&` that `AutoRef` inserts (`Unary::synth`), so `.=` and a written `&x` get no hint. In generic code it fires only when every real specialization binds by reference; exemplar clones are ignored.

## Tests

- New fixture `test/lsp/ref_hints.goose`, registered in `test/lsp_protocol.py`, covers the marked and unmarked cases. I checked that it fails when an expectation is broken.
- `python3 test/run_tests.py` passes on Linux.
- Tried by hand in Sublime Text's LSP client.

## Open questions

- The label: `ref`, `&`, or `ref:` (to match the `name:` style of parameter hints)?
- The same implicit binding also happens for untyped parameters and inferred results. Those could get the marker in a follow-up.

title: Proposal: FMA in simd builds, and an fma function in math
body:
Adding `fma` to the AVX2 and AVX-512 targets of `simd fn`, and an `fma` function to `math`, makes [goose-linalg](https://github.com/guillochon/goose-linalg)'s matrix multiply 30–34% faster from n = 100 (68 GFLOP/s at n = 400, against 50 today), with no change to what existing programs compute. One decision remains, below: what builds without hardware FMA should do.

## The change

Four small changes, all opt-in. A program that never calls `fma` compiles to exactly what it does today.

1. **Target strings.** Add `fma` to `GS_SIMD_TARGET1` (`"avx2,fma,bmi,bmi2,lzcnt,popcnt"`) and to `GS_SIMD_TARGET2`. Clang already treats AVX-512 as implying FMA, so level 2 changes in name only.
2. **Detection.** Make `gs_simd_detect` require the FMA bit (CPUID leaf 1, ECX bit 12) for level 1. Every Intel and AMD CPU with AVX2 has it, so no mainstream machine loses its AVX2 versions; the check only keeps the dispatch from trusting that.
3. **Contraction stays off.** Keep `#pragma clang fp contract(off)` and its GCC and MSVC forms. With FMA in the target, clang could otherwise fuse `a * b + c` on its own, which is what the pragma exists to stop. Only an explicit `fma` call fuses.
4. **An `fma` in `math`.** Add `fma(x, y, z)` for `f64` and `f32` next to `sqrt`, through runtime names (`gs_fma`, `gs_fmaf`) the way `sqrt` goes through `gs_sqrt`, documented as one rounding of x × y + z. Programs can already write `extern fn fma(x: f64, y: f64, z: f64) -> f64;` themselves, which is how the measurements below were taken, so this item is about documenting the semantics more than enabling anything.

The docs would need two edits: implementation.md §6.13 ("Neither includes FMA") and the `simd fn` section of the reference.

## Measurements

goose-linalg's matrix multiply, GFLOP/s:

| n | Today | `fma`, stock Goose | `fma`, target with `fma` | Speedup over today | OpenBLAS 0.3.29 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 50 | 30.9 | 2.8 | 37.3 | 1.21× | 43.1 |
| 100 | 43.7 | 2.7 | 57.1 | 1.31× | 60.2 |
| 200 | 48.5 | 2.7 | 65.0 | 1.34× | 67.7 |
| 400 | 50.4 | 2.5 | 67.6 | 1.34× | 62.5 |
| 800 | 48.1 | 2.4 | 63.8 | 1.33× | 66.7 |
| 1600 | 45.4 | 2.3 | 59.2 | 1.30× | 68.1 |

On stock Goose the same source runs 20× slower: the AVX2 version of the kernel (`gemm_block`'s `_simd1`) has 16 `call fma` and no FMA instructions. With `fma` in the target it has 32 `vfmadd` instructions and no calls.

Today and the patched target are medians of three alternating runs; the stock `fma` column is one run. OpenBLAS is NumPy 2.2.6 on one thread on the same machine, from goose-linalg's own benchmark; at n = 50 its time is mostly NumPy's call overhead.

The gain matches the hardware. Without FMA each multiply-add is two instructions sharing three ports (multiplies on ports 0 and 1, adds on 1 and 5), so a Golden Cove core tops out near 12 flops a cycle, about 56 GFLOP/s at the 4.6 GHz measured under load; today's kernel reaches 91% of that at n = 400. Two FMA ports raise the ceiling to 16 flops a cycle, about 74 GFLOP/s.

Both goose-linalg test suites pass on the patched build: 1,339 checks, and 557 that require every multithreaded result to equal the serial one bit for bit.

## Why results stay reproducible

An explicit `fma` keeps the rule that every `simd` version computes exactly what the baseline does (spec §7.12), because IEEE 754 defines `fma` as x × y + z rounded once.

- **Across levels:** the AVX2 `vfmadd`, the AVX-512 one and a correct libm `fma` on the SSE2 baseline return the same bits for the same inputs.
- **Across compilers:** clang, GCC, MSVC and TinyCC all call or inline the same operation, which C99 requires libm to round correctly, so a program's output doesn't depend on which one built it.
- **What it is not:** contraction, where the compiler decides which products to fuse. That stays off, as §6.13 explains it must. A program fuses exactly where its source says `fma`.

Results do change for code that switches from `a * b + c` to `fma`, since one rounding replaces two. That is the program author's choice, made in the source, and the same on every build.

## Open question: builds without hardware FMA

The change makes `fma` fast where it is native and correct everywhere, but slow wherever it isn't: about 20× slower in goose-linalg's kernel. That covers the SSE2 baseline (CPUs without AVX2), every MSVC build (where `simd` does nothing), and `goose run` on TinyCC. A library can't ship an `fma` kernel that is 20× slower for those users, so it needs one of these:

| Option | Goose change | Builds without hardware FMA | Reproducibility |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A. Libraries use `fma` everywhere | None beyond the above | About 20× slower in a multiply-add kernel | Same bits on every build |
| B. A built-in reporting native FMA (per `simd` version, or per backend) | One new built-in, documented as the one thing that may vary | Keep their current speed through a mul + add kernel | Results differ between machines with and without FMA |
| C. Libraries keep mul + add | None | Unchanged | Unchanged, and no gain anywhere |

B is what goose-linalg would use. It would keep its promise of deterministic results for a given build only in a narrower form: for a given build on a given class of CPU. That cuts against §7.12, which is why it's your call rather than a detail of the patch.

Not measured: whether MSVC with `/arch:AVX2` inlines `fma()` as `vfmadd`. If it does, MSVC users who already set that flag would not hit the slow path under option A.

## Reproducing

**Setup:** Intel Core i5-12600K, one performance core (logical CPU 4, pinned), Windows 11 23H2, Goose v2026.3, clang-cl 22.1.3, a plain `goose build` at `-O2`. Times are the best of at least three products and 0.5 s per size (goose-linalg's `bench/bench_matmul.goose`).

**The kernel change** in goose-linalg's `gemm_block`, inside a `simd fn`, after declaring `extern fn fma(x: f64, y: f64, z: f64) -> f64;` in the library:

```
// today
c0[j] += p0 * v0 + p1 * v1 + p2 * v2 + p3 * v3;
// with fma (and the same for c1, c2, c3)
c0[j] = fma(p3, v3, fma(p2, v2, fma(p1, v1, fma(p0, v0, c0[j]))));
```

**The patched target:** `goose build -v` names the generated C and the clang-cl command. Add `fma` to both target strings, then compile that C with the same command:

```
sed 's/target("avx2,bmi/target("avx2,fma,bmi/; s/avx512vl,avx2,bmi/avx512vl,avx2,fma,bmi/' bench_matmul.c > patched.c
```

The detection change wasn't part of the test; this CPU has FMA, so it wouldn't have changed the dispatch.

title: Add math's mul_add: x * y + z rounded once where the code has FMA
body:
Adds `mul_add(x, y, z)` to `math`, for `f64` and `f32`, as discussed in #78: `x * y + z` rounded once where the code is built for FMA, twice where it isn't. Which one you get is implementation dependent, the one exception to "every simd version computes what the baseline does" (spec §7.12).

## Where it fuses

| Build | Plain function | `simd fn` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| clang on x86-64, default | separate | fused (AVX2 and AVX-512 versions) |
| x86-64 built for AVX2 or past it (`-march=x86-64-v3`, `/arch:AVX2`) | fused | fused |
| arm64 | fused | fused |
| MSVC, default (no simd versions) | separate | separate |
| TinyCC / JIT | separate | separate |

A `*` followed by a `+` written out still never fuses: the contraction pragma stays.

## How

- **Targets:** both simd levels' target attributes include `fma`, and level 1 also requires the FMA bit (CPUID 1, ECX bit 12), which every AVX2 CPU has.
- **No compiler change for the declaration:** `mul_add` is an `extern` bound to `gs_mul_add` / `gs_mul_addf`, like `sqrt`. `runtime_ext.h` defines each as a function, and then as a macro of the same name, which every call in the generated code names, including calls through a function value (resolved at compile time). Since the code generator skips the prototype of an extern the runtime defines, nothing else changes.
- **Per call site:** the macro pastes `GS_MUL_ADD_MODE` into `gs_mul_add_fused` (`__builtin_fma`, always inlined so it is built with its caller's FMA; `fma()` under MSVC) or `gs_mul_add_separate`. `runtime.h` sets the mode to the target's (`GS_MUL_ADD_BASE`), and `EmitSimdVersions` sets it to `fused` around each version past the baseline and back afterwards.
- **Known limit, documented:** only the simd function's own body fuses, including what Goose inlined into it. A callee clang inlines into a version keeps the mode it was emitted in, so a `mul_add` in a plain helper fuses at Goose `-O2` (where Goose inlines it) and not at `-O0`. stdlib.md says so, along with how far the two roundings can differ (cancellation, intermediate overflow).

## Tests

- `test/codegen/simd_mul_add.goose`: a plain function and a simd function compute `(1 + 2^-30)^2 - (1 + 2^-29)`, which is `2^-60` rounded once and `0` rounded twice. Every build prints the same line. Given `modes`, it also prints which rounding each used.
- New runner task `clang_mul_add`: builds that test with clang at `GS_SIMD` 2, 1 and 0. It checks the fused mode is set around the AVX2 version in the C, and that each build rounds as its level, the architecture and the CPU require. The CPU is asked on Windows (`IsProcessorFeaturePresent`) and Linux (`/proc/cpuinfo`), and either answer is accepted at levels 1 and 2 where it can't be asked.
- `stdlib_math.goose`: exact cases at both widths, and the distinguishing case accepted either way.
- The full suite passes on Windows with clang-cl (`--profile baseline --cc native --require-clang`), before and after the change. I haven't run Linux, gcc, macOS or the sanitize profile; that's for CI here.
- Checked by hand: clang-cl, MSVC and TinyCC builds of the new test each round as in the table, with and without `/arch:AVX2`.

## Docs

- spec §7.12 (the exception);
- reference, `simd fn`;
- implementation §6.13 (levels now include FMA, plus how `mul_add` works);
- stdlib, `math`;
- testing.

## Effect

In goose-linalg, writing `gemm_block`'s multiply-adds as `mul_add` made its matrix multiply 1.34x faster on an i5-12600K from n = 100 to 800 (68 against 50 GFLOP/s at n = 400, ahead of OpenBLAS's 62). Its test suites pass, and its multithreaded results still equal the serial ones bit for bit.

Closes #78.

title: Add goose format, a formatter that keeps the author's line breaks
body:
Adds `goose format`, a gofmt-style formatter, and formatting in the language server.

## What it does

`goose format` rewrites files in place, normalizing:

- indentation
- the spaces between tokens
- blank lines and trailing whitespace
- the final newline
- a trailing comma in any list whose closing bracket starts a line

Line breaks stay where the author put them, and there is no configuration.

- **Inputs.** It takes files and directories. A directory means the `.goose` files under it, skipping dot-directories and build trees.
- **Standard input.** With no files, or `-`, it formats standard input to standard output.
- **`--check`.** Lists the files that are not formatted and writes nothing.
- **Exit status.** 0 when formatted, 1 when `--check` finds a file that is not, 2 on any error. A file that does not parse is left as it is.

## How it works

- **Tokens, not the AST.** It prints the file's own tokens and the comments between them, choosing the whitespace afresh. The AST dump drops comments and desugars `guard`, so it can't serve as a formatter.
- **Parser roles.** The parser says what each token is through an optional side table, `Parser::roles`. It tells a generic `<` from a comparison and a unary `-` from a binary one, and marks the brackets whose list may end in a comma. The table is null in every compile, so a normal compile only pays a null check at each hook.
- **Alignment.** A continuation line keeps its offset from the line it continues while it stays to the right of it, so hand-aligned lines stay aligned. Trailing comments move with their line, and a run of them that shared a column still does.
- **Safety check.** Every result is checked before it is written. It must have the same tokens, apart from an added comma before a closing bracket, and the same comments, apart from whitespace. It must also parse to the same AST dump and the same doc comments.
- **`--verify`.** Runs those checks plus an idempotence check in memory. Every file in `samples/`, `stdlib/`, `bench/` and `test/` passes, 2,659 in all.

## Language server

`goose lsp` answers `textDocument/formatting` for the editor's current text. The reply is edits to only the lines that change, found by a line diff, so editors keep the cursor and marks. A document that does not parse gets no edits. VS Code needs no extension change.

## Commits

1. **The formatter.** The parser roles, `src/format.h`, the CLI wiring and help, `test/format.py` and docs. The test file has golden cases, each checked as a fixed point, CLI cases and a `--verify` sweep. No `.goose` file changes.
2. **The reformat.** `samples/` and `stdlib/` reformatted, which changes six lines in two samples. A CI step checks they stay formatted, on Linux only, because a Windows checkout may have CRLF line endings. `bench/` is left alone: formatting it would undo hand-aligned columns. `test/` is left alone because its fixtures pin diagnostic columns.
3. **The language server.** `textDocument/formatting`, with a protocol test, plus format-on-save setups in `docs/editors.md` for Neovim, Helix and Emacs.

## Testing

- **Suite.** `python test/run_tests.py --profile baseline --cc native --require-clang` passes on Linux.
- **Samples.** The samples runner passes for every sample this machine can run. The gfx samples, including the reformatted `30_mini_minecraft`, were skipped because this build has no gfx layer.

struct S { tag: i64, xs: i64[>..] }
