title: Elementwise float arithmetic as whole-vector operations
body:
Rebased on master now that #79 has landed: the branch is just this PR's three commits.

Elementwise arithmetic (§6.1) on a struct or fixed array whose leaves are all floats of one width, 2, 4, 8 or 16 of them in 16, 32 or 64 bytes with no padding, becomes one operation on a vector type of the same layout where the C compiler has GCC's vector extensions. Elsewhere, and with `-DGS_VEC=0`, it stays member by member. No language change: the same programs, the same results lane by lane.

## Why

Elementwise ops are emitted member by member, and clang's SLP vectorizer has to rediscover the vectors, which it does only partly. In [goose-fft](https://github.com/guillochon/goose-fft), whose butterflies are arithmetic on structs of four `f64`, the radix-8 pass's AVX2 version had **208 two-lane operations next to 175 four-lane ones**, plus spills and shuffles. With this change it has **12 next to 261**, a third fewer spills, and no shuffles.

## How

- **Type test.** `VecShape` flattens the type (structs, nested structs, fixed arrays) and accepts one float width, 2/4/8/16 leaves, 16/32/64 bytes, and `FixedSize` equal to that (no padding).
- **Type test, cost.** `VecShape` rejects anything over 64 bytes before looking at leaves, and stops at the 17th.
- **Emission.** `GenElemwiseInto` and `GenElemwiseNegInto` emit, under `#if GS_VEC`, `GS_VST(V, &dst, GS_VLD(V, &a) OP GS_VLD(V, &b))`, with the existing member-by-member code under `#else`. The operand temps are assigned inside the `#if` too, so TinyCC pays nothing.
- **Operands.** Operands go to temps of their own type first, so a destination that is an operand works as before. So does a destination whose member a scalar operand reads (`v = v * v.x`). A scalar operand of `*` or `/` is splatted.
- **Runtime.** `runtime.h` defines the six vector types as `aligned(1)` (structs are packed) and `may_alias`, and `GS_VLD`/`GS_VST` as dereferences through them. A scalar is splatted with a vector literal. Vectors appear only inside expressions, never as a local or across a call: an earlier version's inline helpers passed 32-byte vectors between a `simd fn`'s AVX2 version and baseline code, which x86-64 Linux and macOS reject.
- **Where it's on.** `GS_VEC` is set under clang and gcc only, not MSVC or TinyCC, and `-DGS_VEC=0` turns it off.

## Effect

goose-fft, single-threaded on an i5-12600K. Same compiler and source, `/arch:AVX2`, `GS_VEC=1` against `GS_VEC=0`, run back to back pinned to one P-core:

| Transform | GS_VEC=0 | GS_VEC=1 | Speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| complex, n = 64 | 0.150 µs | 0.093 µs | 1.61× |
| complex, n = 256 | 0.624 µs | 0.414 µs | 1.51× |
| complex, n = 4096 | 12.05 µs | 9.50 µs | 1.27× |
| complex, n = 16384 | 55.6 µs | 43.2 µs | 1.29× |
| complex, n = 262144 | 1588 µs | 1372 µs | 1.16× |
| complex, n = 2²⁰ | 7879 µs | 7469 µs | 1.05× (memory-bound) |
| complex, n = 10000 | 36.1 µs | 29.5 µs | 1.22× |
| complex, n = 1009 (prime) | 16.6 µs | 14.0 µs | 1.19× |
| real, n = 1024 | 1.58 µs | 1.22 µs | 1.30× |

Every length measured is at parity or faster (the worst is 0.99×).

**A hazard to know about:** code that computes a whole struct and then immediately takes it apart member by member can get slower, because computing a vector and extracting every lane costs more than the scalars did. goose-fft had one such loop, a twiddle multiply whose result was scattered into scalar arrays, which ran 10% slower at two lengths until its multiplies were written per lane (guillochon/goose-fft@9d3b2ab). This is in implementation §6.14.

## Tests

- **New test:** `test/codegen/vec_elemwise.goose` covers all six vector types as structs, nested structs and fixed arrays, in plain functions and in `simd fn`s. It exercises every operator, a scalar on either side, compound assignment, aliasing destinations, signed zeros, infinities and NaN, alongside shapes that must stay member by member (three doubles, mixed widths, integers). Every build prints the same as the member-by-member code.
- **New runner task `clang_vec`:** checks that the C uses all six vector types and builds it with `GS_VEC` on and off. Planting vector subtraction as addition fails `clang-vec1` (on this Windows machine the runner's main native builds are MSVC, so this task is what exercises the vector path).
- **Full suite:** passes on Windows with clang-cl (`--profile baseline --cc native --require-clang`), before and after.
- **Not run:** Linux, gcc, macOS, and the sanitize profile. That's for CI here.

## Docs

- implementation §6.14 (new), and the comment on `GenElemwiseInto`;
- testing.md (the new check).

title: Polish the command line: unknown commands, a version, color, -q, completions and a man page
body:
**Stacked on #80.** This branch builds on the formatter PR: `goose format` prints its diagnostics through the new colorizer. Until #80 merges, this PR also shows #80's four commits. Only the last commit, 49b58cf1, is new here.

## What changes

- **Mistyped commands.** A first word that is no command, option or file is treated as a mistyped command. `goose biuld x.goose` now says `unknown command biuld: did you mean build?` instead of `cannot open file: biuld`. A missing `.goose` file still says it cannot open the file.
- **A compiler version.** `goose version`, and the new `goose --version`, print the compiler's version beside the runtime hash, as in `goose v2026.3-107-g5333e9a3 (runtime a5dbd11b6309)`.
  - **Where it comes from.** The build takes it from `git describe` at each build through `cmake/version.cmake`.
  - **Rebuild cost.** It lives in `src/version.cpp`, a translation unit of its own, so a new commit recompiles only that file.
  - **Releases.** A release configures `GOOSE_VERSION` with its tag, because the shallow checkout may have no tags.
- **Colored diagnostics.** Errors and warnings are colored on a terminal: the place in bold, `error:` in red, `warning:` in magenta and the caret in green.
  - **Controls.** `NO_COLOR` turns color off and `CLICOLOR_FORCE` turns it on, as do `--color never` and `--color always`.
  - **Where it never appears.** Pipes, files, the JSON diagnostics and the language server always get plain text.
  - **Windows.** The console is switched to take the escape sequences.
- **`-q` / `--quiet`.** Drops the `parsed ok`, `typechecked ok`, `bce:` and `wrote` lines, so a successful run prints only what the program prints.
- **Shell completions.** `goose completion bash|zsh|fish|powershell` prints a script that completes the commands, each command's options, help topics and `.goose` files. The scripts are generated from the help text, so they can't drift from it.
- **A man page.** `goose help --man` prints all of the help as a man page, and `package_release.py` ships it as `man/goose.1`.

## Testing

- **Suite.** The baseline suite passes on Linux (gcc and clang) and on Windows (MSVC Debug).
- **Driver tests.** The driver test now checks each change:
  - `version` and `--version`
  - the typo suggestion
  - `-q`
  - `--color always`, `NO_COLOR`, `CLICOLOR_FORCE`, and no color off a terminal
  - every shell's script
  - the man page
- **Optional tools.** Where bash, zsh and groff are installed, the test runs bash's completion for real, parses zsh's script, and checks that groff reads the man page without warnings.
- **Checked by hand.**
  - **Zsh.** Its completion function was driven with stubbed completion builtins.
  - **PowerShell.** Its completion was driven through `TabExpansion2` on Windows.
  - **Windows console.** Color switches on automatically in a real console, and `NO_COLOR` turns it off.
- **Not tested.** Fish isn't installed on either test machine, so its script has only been reviewed.

## Compatibility

- **`goose version` output.** The format changed. Nothing in the repository parsed the old `goose runtime <hash>` line except the driver test, which is updated.
- **VS Code tasks.** They now show color, since they run in a real terminal. VS Code strips escape sequences before its problem matcher reads the output, so the `$goose` matcher is unaffected.

title: Round mul_add separately under MSVC, even with /arch:AVX2
body:
Follow-up to #79: under MSVC, `mul_add` now always rounds separately, including with `/arch:AVX2`.

MSVC compiles `fma()` to a call into the C library even with `/arch:AVX2`, and the call also keeps the loop around it from vectorizing. goose-linalg's matrix multiply, whose kernel uses `mul_add`:

| Build | GFLOP/s at n = 400 |
| --- | --- |
| MSVC `/arch:AVX2`, multiply-adds separate (before `mul_add`) | 50 |
| MSVC `/arch:AVX2`, `mul_add` fused through `fma()` (master) | 18.7 |
| MSVC `/arch:AVX2`, this branch | 50 |
| clang-cl, default, AVX2 `simd` version (unchanged) | 68 |

MSVC builds no `simd` versions, so with this change no MSVC build fuses. clang-cl defines `_MSC_VER` too, but it is excluded from the check by `__clang__`, so with `/arch:AVX2` it still fuses through `__FMA__` and `__builtin_fma`.

Changes:
- `runtime.h`: `GS_MUL_ADD_BASE` is `separate` under MSVC (`_MSC_VER` without `__clang__`), with the reason in the comment. `runtime_inline.h` is regenerated.
- Docs: spec §7.12, implementation §6.13 and stdlib's `math` now say MSVC rounds twice.

Tests: the full suite passes on Windows with clang-cl (`--profile baseline --cc native --require-clang`). `test/codegen/simd_mul_add.goose` built by MSVC with `/arch:AVX2` now reports every result as separate.

title: Keep a continued chain lined up under its first operand
body:

```

title: Scan byte sets with NEON on AArch64
body:
find_any and find_pair tested one byte at a time everywhere but x86-64. This fixes that on ARM, tested on Mac.


Agent summary:
On little-endian AArch64 with clang or gcc they now run the same block loops on NEON, which every such CPU has, so there is no dispatch: the compare kinds (one to three bytes, a range, their complements) use cmeq/cmhs, and any other set is looked up in its nibble tables with TBL. TBL gives 0 for an index of 16 or more, so masking the byte with 0x8f (or its xor with 0x80) does what pshufb's high-bit rule does on x86.

NEON has no movemask, so a block's result is narrowed with shrn to a 64-bit word holding a nibble per byte. GS_BMASK, GS_BMASK_DROP and GS_BMASK_FIRST name the three steps, and the SSE2 and NEON paths share one copy of the loops. find_any on AArch64 first steps 64 bytes at a time, testing four blocks' results together: without it, a long search for one rare byte ran at about 80% of macOS's memchr.

SSH.log (73 MB), Apple M3 Max, byte loop or memchr -> NEON:
  newline, 655k matches      7.3 ->  9.1 GB/s
  "\t\n" (kind 2)            1.9 ->  7.7 GB/s
  JSON escapes (tables)      1.9 ->  3.4 GB/s
  non-printable (inverted)   1.9 ->  4.7 GB/s
  '@', no match (memchr)    40.4 -> 51.1 GB/s

test/stdlib/stdlib_byteset_blocks.goose puts every byte value at every position of searches 16 to 79 bytes long, over a filler not in the set, for sets of every kind and their complements, from two starts, and compares find_any and find_pair with plain loops (3.4M and 1.9M searches). Planted bugs in the TBL masks, the nibble mask, the tail shift, the range compare and each part of the 64-byte step all made both it and stdlib_byteset fail. Both pass on AArch64, natively, in the JIT and in a debug build, and as x86-64 under Rosetta (SSE2/SSSE3). MSVC for ARM64 and big-endian AArch64 keep the byte loop.

title: Nested growing structs
body:
In the [JSON parser sample code](https://aardappel.github.io/goose/samples/18_json.goose.html) a linked list is used to represent the children of a growing nested data structure:

    struct Node { next: Node&<u32>?, key: u8[varint], val: Json.. }

Even though the structure is a linked list it is actually used as a stack when parsing, i.e. new nodes are only added to the end of the list. This conceptually satisfies the requirements of Goose’s growing stack concept, however Goose doesn’t permit nested growing arrays.

A growing recursive struct should be possible for tasks like parsing where the child node is fully read and constructed and added to the parent before reading the next sibling node.

In the documentation and JSON sample code, node children are stored as references. The child nodes are not contained within the parent. However, there is no need for it to be a reference rather than a value, since the child will not be referenced by any other nodes in the tree.

In the case of the JSON example it could look like:

```goose
enum Json {
  Null,
  Bool { v: bool },
  Num { v: f64 },
  Str { s: u8[varint],
  Arr { children: Json..[>..] }, // Growing array of Json values
  Obj { children: Json..[>..] }
}
```

Where the `children` Json array is not an array of references but Json values, which means that new Json nodes are added directly into the space of a parent. 

In the documentation it indicates the solution for this type of thing is to add the child first, whereas the proposal is that the parent is added first with trailing growing children as contained nested values.

### Preventing prior children from growing

The main issue with this approach is the following scenario: child B is added as a sibling after child A, but child A wants to add another child under itself. In other words a previous child wants to continue to grow, but it is no longer at the end of the stack.

There needs to be some mechanism to prevent this. 

One option could be the concept of sealing/closing/freezing a value. In the previous example, once child B is added, child A is now sealed and can no longer be grown.

Consider the following scenario:

```goose
var childA .= parent.children.push(Obj{}) // create childA as a child of parent
var childB .= parent.children.push(Obj{}) // create childB as a child of parent
var childA_1 .= childA.children.push(Obj{}) // Fails - as childA was sealed after the creation of childB
```

Note that in the above example all of the *.childen.push(…) calls are utilising the same pool.

This could be extended to any nested growing structs not just recursive.

As an implementation detail Goose may need a separate stack to track which values have not yet been sealed.

title: Feature request: built-in UTF-8 rune iteration /slicing support for string (u8 [])
body:
## Feature request: built-in UTF-8 rune iteration / slicing support for string(u8[])

### Describe the feature
Goose uses `u8[]` as the string type, and string literals are stored as raw UTF-8 bytes.
Currently, slice syntax `s[a..b]` works on **bytes only**, not Unicode scalar values (runes).

It is very common to work with multi-byte text such as Chinese, Japanese, Korean and emoji.
Users need to split or take a substring by **character count**, not byte offset.
Without standard library helpers, users have to implement UTF-8 decoding logic manually every time:
- calculate rune boundary
- slice safely at UTF-8 character boundaries
- avoid splitting a multi-byte codepoint and producing invalid UTF-8 (garbled text)

I hope Goose can add built-in UTF-8 utilities in the standard library, for example:
1. `utf8.len(s: u8[]) -> usize` — count unicode runes in a UTF-8 string
2. `utf8.slice(s: u8[], start_rune: usize, end_rune: usize) -> u8[]` — slice by rune index, return valid UTF-8
3. `utf8.next(s: u8[], &offset: usize) -> Optional<u32>` — iterate runes sequentially
4. Optional: helper `utf8.take(s: u8[], n: usize) -> u8[]` take first N runes

These functions should guarantee the returned slice is always well-formed UTF-8.

### Use case
```goose
// Expected usage
let s = "你好世界abc";
let sub = utf8.slice(s, 0, 2);
print(sub); // expect "你好"

title: Seed global invariant candidates on their first write
body:
`BCE::ValidateGlobalInvariants` copied every standing candidate into `cands` and `ge0` before walking each tree, though any one tree writes only a handful. In a ~24k-line program that's 660 candidates × 2846 trees (two rounds over ~1400 global initializers, plus 32 bodies): 94 ms of BCE's ~150 ms, and 31% of the front end in a sampling profile.

Now a candidate gets its record on its first write (`CandOf`), and the inductive hypothesis is read from `gge0` directly (`Ge0`) while `seedglobals` is set. A tree that writes no candidate copies nothing.

**Same results:** the generated C (which carries every bounds-check decision) is byte for byte master's at -O0 and -O2, for all 758 programs that compile under `test/`, `samples/` and `bench/`, and for the test app's seven programs. The full suite passes.

Independent of the flow-snapshot change (#105), and they add up:
**Benchmark:** my test app, a ~24k-line program, with hyperfine (30 runs, macOS arm64). `base` is master (a108677d), `bce` is the BCE change, `flow` is the flow-snapshot change, and `both` is the two merged.

`goose -O0 --check`:

title: Walk only the narrowed globals in flow snapshots

title: Add utf8 to the standard library (#102)
body:
Implements aardappel/goose#102: UTF-8 rune iteration and slicing for `u8[]` strings.

## What

`stdlib/utf8.goose` (namespace `utf8`) decodes, validates and indexes text by code point:

| Function | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `decode(s) -> i64, i64` / `decode_last(s)` | a rune and its width; `ERROR, 0` if empty |
| `next(s, pos: i64&) -> i64, bool` | the rune at `pos`, advancing it; `false` at the end |
| `each<F>(s)` | `F(cp, start, width)` |
| `len(s) -> i64` | rune count |
| `offset(s, n)`, `slice(s, start, end)`, `take(s, n)` | indexing by rune; slices into `s`, no copy |
| `valid(s)`, `valid_rune(cp)`, `width(cp)`, `encode(out, cp)` | validation and encoding |

The decoder is Björn Höhrmann's table-driven automaton, which accepts exactly the well-formed sequences of Unicode table 3-7 (no overlongs, surrogates, values above U+10FFFF, or C0/C1/F5–FF). Both tables are `const`, so static C data. Malformed input follows Go's `unicode/utf8`: the first byte of a bad sequence is one U+FFFD rune of width 1, so every function is defined on any bytes and a slice never splits a well-formed sequence.

The issue's example works as requested: `utf8::slice("你好世界abc", 0, 2)` is `"你好"`.

On 8 MB of text, clang, Apple M5: `len` 3 ms on ASCII, 13 on mixed, 4 on CJK; `valid` 2, 10 and 9 ms.

## Tests

`test/stdlib/stdlib_utf8.goose` checks every function against a plain decoder written to table 3-7: all strings of one to three bytes (16.8 M), 20,000 random strings over the class-edge bytes at every position and prefix, and valid text damaged in one byte. Hand vectors ported from Go's `utf8_test.go`, utf8proc's `iterate.c` and Kuhn's UTF-8 stress test print as a table in the expected output. Full suite passes.

## Docs

New `utf8` section in `docs/stdlib.md`; module lists in `index.md`, `tutorial.md`, the reference's encoding note and the design doc's module map. `std`'s `each_utf8`/`push_utf8` are unchanged and documented as the lenient pair.

title: Validate UTF-8 in each_utf8; keep push_utf8 in range
body:
`each_utf8` took any byte from 0xC0 up as a lead byte and the bytes after it as its continuation, without checking them. `[0xC3, 'A']` gave one code point and swallowed the `A`, and overlong forms, surrogates and code points past U+10FFFF came through as code points, although the docs say malformed bytes give U+FFFD.

- `each_utf8` now checks each continuation byte against the ranges of Unicode table 3-7, and gives one U+FFFD per *maximal subpart* of a bad sequence (Unicode §3.9, and what the WHATWG decoder and Python's `errors="replace"` do), restarting at the byte that broke the sequence.
- `push_utf8` wrote garbage, or failed a `u8` conversion, for a code point below zero or past 0x10FFFF. It now writes U+FFFD for those. A surrogate is still written as its own three bytes, which `json` relies on for a lone `\u` escape.
- `test/stdlib/stdlib_each_utf8.goose` checks 19 malformed and boundary inputs, whose expected output is Python's `decode(errors="replace")`, and every scalar value through `push_utf8` and `each_utf8` and back.
- `docs/stdlib.md`: a paragraph on the malformed-input rule, and `push_utf8`'s range.

**Relation to #106.** #106 adds a `utf8` module and doesn't touch `std`. This PR's test file is named `stdlib_each_utf8` so the two don't collide. The two differ on malformed input: #106 follows Go and gives one U+FFFD per bad *byte*, while this gives one per bad *sequence*, so `[0xE2, 0x82, 'x']` is one U+FFFD here and two there. Either convention is fine to standardize on; if you'd rather `std` match #106, it's a small change.

title: Draw rand_int without modulo bias
body:
`rand_int` returned `rand_u64(r) % n`, which favors the low results wherever `n` doesn't divide 2^64. It barely matters for small `n`, but for `n = 3 * 2^61` the lower third of the range came up 3/4 of the time.

It now draws again while `x` is below `2^64 % n`, which leaves an equal count of `x` for each result. That bound is less than `n`, so the remainder is only computed when `x < n`, and every `x` that's kept still gives `x % n`. So a seeded sequence comes out the same as before, except where a draw is rejected, which has probability below `n / 2^64` per call. No expected output in the tests or samples changed.

`n <= 0` used to divide by zero or wrap. It's now an `assert`.

- `stdlib/std.goose`: `rand_int`.
- `test/stdlib/stdlib_std.goose`: draws 30,000 values with `n = 3 * 2^61` and checks that about 2/3 fall below 2^62. The old code fails it (about 3/4).
- `docs/stdlib.md`: `rand_int`'s line.

title: Hash floats by their bits
body:
`hash(f64)` and `hash(f32)` mixed `(x * 65536.0) as! u64`. Every value of magnitude below 1/65536 hashed as zero, and so did every value from about 2^101 up, whose scaled form is a multiple of 2^64. A dictionary keyed by such floats probed through one cluster: 10,000 keys spaced 1e-9 apart, or 1e200 apart, all took the same home slot of a 16384-slot table.

A float now hashes as its bits (`float_text::bits_of`), with the high half folded into the low half before `hash_mix`. Without the fold, a double's low bits are often all zero (52 of them for 1.0), and the multiply only carries bits upwards. Both steps are invertible, so distinct floats get distinct 64-bit hashes. `-0.0` hashes as `0.0`, which it equals, and an `f32` as the `f64` of its value.

| 10,000 keys | old | new | random hashes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `i` | 8800 | 7969 | ~7490 |
| `i * 1e-9` | 1 | 7488 | ~7490 |
| `i * 1e200` | 1 | 7468 | ~7490 |

(distinct home slots in a 16384-slot table)

- `stdlib/std.goose`: the two float overloads and the section comment.
- `test/stdlib/stdlib_std.goose`: `-0.0`/`0.0`, `f32`/`f64` agreement, and the three slot spreads above.
- `docs/stdlib.md`: one sentence on how floats hash.

The full suite passes on Linux.

title: Give math's radians, degrees, is_nan and is_inf f32 forms; add is_finite
body:
`radians` and `degrees` took only `f64`, so an `f32` angle came back as an `f64` and needed `as f32` at every call, unlike the libm functions in `math`, which come at both widths. This adds the `f32` forms, `f32` forms of `is_nan` and `is_inf` to match, and `is_finite` at both widths.

- The `f32` `radians`/`degrees` multiply by the ratio written as a literal, which rounds to `f32` once. Computing `180.0 / PI` in `f32` rounds `PI` first and gives 57.295776, where the correctly rounded ratio is 57.29578.
- `is_finite(x)` is `x - x == 0`, which is false for an infinity or a NaN.
- An `f32` already widened to `is_nan`/`is_inf` without loss, so those overloads are for consistency.

One behaviour change: a call with an integer argument, `radians(180)`, now has to name a width, as `sqrt(n as f64)` already does. Nothing in this repo or in the gfx and physics packages calls them that way.

- `stdlib/math.goose`, `test/stdlib/stdlib_math.goose`, `docs/stdlib.md`.

title: Round format_flt's exact value, at any size and number of places
body:
`format_flt` computed `(x * 10^d + 0.5) as! i64`, which goes wrong in three ways:

- It wraps once `x * 10^d` passes 2^63: `format_flt(out, 1e19, 1)` printed `776627963145224192.0`.
- From 19 places on, `10^d` no longer fits an `i64`: `3.14159` to 19 places printed `0.2969155926290448384`.
- It rounds the product rather than the value: `0.49999999999999994` to 0 places printed `1`, because adding 0.5 carries it over.

I compared it with Python's `Decimal(v).quantize(..., ROUND_HALF_UP)` on 4,870 cases (random bit patterns, random decimals near halves, and edge values at 0–25 places). The old code wrote 2,248 of them wrongly; this version writes them all correctly.

How it works:

- **Fast path, unchanged in shape.** Below 2^52, `y = x * 10^d` is off from the exact scaled value by at most `y * 2^-53`, and its fraction is exact. So unless that fraction lies within that margin of a half, its floor and fraction round the way the exact value does.
- **Exact path.** Otherwise, and for more than 18 places, `format_flt_exact` writes `x = m * 2^e` as the integer `m * 2^e`, or as `m * 5^-e / 10^-e`, in limbs of nine decimal digits. That holds every digit of any double (at most 309 before the point and 767 significant ones after it), and the digit string is then rounded half up.

Speed: one million values below 1000 at two places take 19 ms, where they took 16.

The rounding is still half up, as documented, so the only difference from C's `printf("%.*f")` is a value exactly halfway: `0.125` to 2 places is `0.13` here and `0.12` in `printf`. The docs now say so. A `-0.0` still prints without its sign, as before.

- `stdlib/std.goose`: `format_flt`, plus the new helpers `format_flt_exact` and `format_flt_mul`. It uses `float_text`'s `POW10`, `POW10_U64`, `POW5` and `bits_of`, which landed with the `parse_flt` change.
- `test/stdlib/stdlib_std.goose`: the cases above, plus the smallest subnormal to 330 places and the largest double.
- `docs/stdlib.md`: what rounding the exact value means, next to `printf`.

The full suite passes on Linux.

goose format: line up a run of declarations' types and =s, as gofmt does
body:
`goose format` now lines up a run of declarations in columns, as gofmt does:

```goose
const QUIC_FRAME_PADDING: u64 = 0x00;
const QUIC_FRAME_PING:    u64 = 0x01;
const QUIC_FRAME_ACK:     u64 = 0x02;
const QUIC_FRAME_ACK_ECN: u64 = 0x03;
```

## The rule

A line that starts with `[const|let|var|export|extern|pad] name: type [= value]` is a table row. This covers a struct's fields and a literal's `name: value` lines as well as declarations. In a run of rows:
- **Types** start one space past the longest name.
- **`=`s** start one space past the longest type, among adjacent rows that all have one.

A run ends at a blank line or a comment-only line, at a change of depth or indentation, or at different leading keywords (`let` and `var` don't mix). A row also can't span lines or leave a bracket open.

Not aligned:
- Declarations without a type, such as `const X = 1;` or a plain `let x = ...` in a function body.
- Padding the author wrote by hand. It is normalized to one space, as gofmt does.

## Implementation

The line-building loop moved out of `Layout` into a new function, `Lines`, in `src/format.h`. `Layout` calls `Lines` once to find the cells and their columns, then again with the padding. Building the lines twice keeps the output stable when it is formatted again, alongside the existing semicolon tables and aligned trailing comments.

## What it would do to this repo

Formatting `stdlib/`, `samples/`, `test/` and `bench/` with this change rewrites 470 files that are formatted today, because of the alignment. Struct fields account for most of it. CI checks that `samples/` and `stdlib/` are formatted, so the second commit reformats those 15 files (150 lines). The rest of the tree is left alone. Some excerpts:

Struct fields, with aligned trailing comments kept at their column (`stdlib/regex.goose`):

```diff
 struct Regex {
-    groups: i64,            // capture groups, group 0 being the whole match
+    groups:   i64,          // capture groups, group 0 being the whole match
     nullable: bool,         // whether the empty string matches
-    placed: bool,           // whether every group has a fixed place
-    entry: i32,             // where the program starts an anchored match
-    classes: u8[256],       // byte -> its column in the DFAs
-    skip: Skip,
-    filter: Prefilter,
+    placed:   bool,         // whether every group has a fixed place
+    entry:    i32,          // where the program starts an anchored match
+    classes:  u8[256],      // byte -> its column in the DFAs
+    skip:     Skip,
+    filter:   Prefilter,
```

A table of constants (`bench/plb/secp256k1/1.goose`):

```diff
-let P: Fe = [0xFFFFFFFEFFFFFC2F, 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF, 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF, 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF];
-let N: Big = [0xBFD25E8CD0364141, 0xBAAEDCE6AF48A03B, 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFE, 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF, 0, 0];
-let BETA: Fe = [0xc1396c28719501ee, 0x9cf0497512f58995, 0x6e64479eac3434e9, 0x7ae96a2b657c0710];
-let MINUS_B1: Big = [0x6f547fa90abfe4c3, 0xe4437ed6010e8828, 0, 0, 0, 0];
+let P:           Fe  = [0xFFFFFFFEFFFFFC2F, 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF, 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF, 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF];
+let N:           Big = [0xBFD25E8CD0364141, 0xBAAEDCE6AF48A03B, 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFE, 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF, 0, 0];
+let BETA:        Fe  = [0xc1396c28719501ee, 0x9cf0497512f58995, 0x6e64479eac3434e9, 0x7ae96a2b657c0710];
+let MINUS_B1:    Big = [0x6f547fa90abfe4c3, 0xe4437ed6010e8828, 0, 0, 0, 0];
 let PRIVATE_KEY: Big = [0xD9132D70B5BC7693, 0xB64592E3FE0AB0DA, 0x4FCA3EF970FF4D38, 0x2DEE927079283C3C, 0, 0];
```

Locals in a function body, `=` included (same file):

```diff
-    var r: Fe = [0; 4];
+    var r: Fe  = [0; 4];
     var c: u64 = 0;
```

### Rough edges to decide on

**Lines with several fields.** Only the first field on a line is a cell, so a line like this gets a gap after its first name only (`samples/31_mini_doom.goose`):

```diff
-    floor: f32, ceiling: f32, floor_pic: i64, ceiling_pic: i64,
-    light: f32, special: i64, tag: i64,
-    start_floor: f32, start_ceiling: f32,
+    floor:        f32, ceiling: f32, floor_pic: i64, ceiling_pic: i64,
+    light:        f32, special: i64, tag: i64,
+    start_floor:  f32, start_ceiling: f32,
```

The same happens in a struct literal next to a one-field line (`stdlib/regex.goose`):

```diff
         filter: Prefilter { len: 0, at1: 0, at2: 0, set1: none, set2: none }, inner: none,
-        fwd: dead, rev: dead, before: dead, places: [], prog: [Inst.Match], sets: [],
+        fwd:    dead, rev: dead, before: dead, places: [], prog: [Inst.Match], sets: [],
```

The likely fix is to leave out any line with more than one field. gofmt never meets this case, since Go puts one field per line.

**One long name widens the whole run** (`samples/31_mini_doom.goose`):

```diff
-var sides: Side[>..] = [];
-var subsectors: Subsector[>..] = [];
+var sides:           Side[>..]          = [];
+var subsectors:      Subsector[>..]     = [];
```

gofmt behaves the same way. Its answer is a blank line to split the run.

## Testing

- `test/format.py` has a new golden case covering `const` tables, `=` columns, struct fields, a struct literal, locals, and a `var` that doesn't join a `let` run. Every golden case is a fixed point: formatting it again changes nothing.

title: Fix in-process runs crashing on two large by-value structs (arm64 TinyCC)
body:
# Problem

On arm64, `goose run` crashes with SIGSEGV when a function takes two or more structs of 4096 bytes or more by value. `goose build` (clang) runs the same program correctly.

```goose
struct A { a: i64, buf: u8[..4070], tail: u8[>..] }
struct B { b: i64, buf: u8[..4070], tail: u8[>..] }
fn mk_a() -> A { var x = A { a: 7, buf: [], tail: [] }; x.tail.push(1); return x; }
fn mk_b() -> B { var x = B { b: 5, buf: [], tail: [] }; x.tail.push(2); return x; }
fn inner(a: const A&, b: const B&) -> i64 { a.a + b.b + a.tail[0] + b.tail[0] }
fn outer(a: A, b: B) -> i64 { inner(a, b) }
fn main() { print(outer(mk_a(), mk_b())); }
```

```
$ goose run -O0 repro.goose                  # exit 139
$ goose build -o r repro.goose && ./r        # 15
```

A 4070-byte buffer makes each struct exactly 4096 bytes in C; 4069 works. The generated C is sound (clean under clang -O0 with AddressSanitizer), and the bug reproduces in plain C with the TinyCC goose builds:

```c
typedef struct { long a; char buf[4088]; } Big;      /* 4096 bytes */
static long outer(Big a, Big b) { return a.a + b.a; }
int main(void) { static Big x, y; x.a = 7; y.a = 5; printf("%ld\n", outer(x, y)); return 0; }
```

```
$ build/tcc/tcc -Bbuild/tcclib -run big.c    # exit 139; clang prints 12
```

## Cause

AAPCS64 passes a struct larger than 16 bytes as a pointer to a copy in the caller's frame. TinyCC's `gfunc_call` lays the copies out one after another and takes each address with `arm64_spoff`, which for offsets of 4096 or more
emits

```c
o(ARM64_ADD_REG | ARM64_SF(1) | ARM64_RM(30) | ARM64_RN(31) | ARM64_RD(reg) | (sub << 30));
```

In ADD (shifted register), register 31 is `xzr`, not `sp`, so this is `add xN, xzr, x30`: the offset itself rather than an address in the frame. The second struct's copy is then written to a small absolute address. Offsets below 4096 use ADD (immediate), where register 31 is `sp`, which is why one large struct, or several small ones, work.

## Fix

`arm64_spoff` uses ADD/SUB (extended register, UXTX), which reads register
31 as `sp`, the form `arm64-gen.c` already uses for `sub sp, sp, x(r)`:

```c
o((sub ? 0xcb2063e0 : 0x8b2063e0) | ARM64_RM(30) | ARM64_RD(reg));
```

## Tests

`test/codegen/large_struct_args.goose` passes two and three structs of 4096
and 70 000 bytes by value, beside scalars. With the old TinyCC it crashes
(exit 139); with the fix it prints the expected output under the in-process
backend at -O0 and -O2 and natively.

`python3 test/run_tests.py -j 8` passes in full on macOS arm64 (Apple clang
21): 596 generated-C programs at -O0 and -O2, 693 TinyCC runs, the
goose_in_goose bootstrap and the samples.

title: [Windows x64] Process crashes with 0xC0000005 due to 32-byte AVX stack misalignment with MinGW GCC
Generated C differs between libc++ and libstdc++ builds of the compiler
body:
The same Goose source, compiled by the same compiler commit, gives different C depending on the C++ standard library the compiler was built with. Each build is deterministic: six runs on macOS gave byte-identical output. But a libc++ build (macOS) and a libstdc++ build (Linux) disagree.

This matters for projects that commit the generated C and check it in CI. [pedrobtz/zudiff](https://github.com/pedrobtz/zudiff) does this: its CI rebuilds the compiler at a pinned commit and fails if regenerating changes the committed C. The check passed on Linux while the source had one slice type, and failed once a second one was added.

**Versions**

- Compiler: `e76d5c9f7f0a17d83c12a405fbb2513094d03985`, Release build with cmake.
- macOS 15.7 (x86_64), Apple clang 17, libc++.
- Ubuntu 24.04, g++ 13, libstdc++. The same happens on GitHub's `ubuntu-latest` runner.

**Source**

[`tools/goose/zudiff.goose`](https://github.com/pedrobtz/zudiff/blob/3ae662055399c2ef24ed96e7dc539e88f4cf9221/tools/goose/zudiff.goose), compiled with:

```sh
goose -o zudiff_goose.c --header zudiff_goose.h zudiff.goose
```

**What differs**

Only the order of the two slice typedefs, in both the header and the C. Everything else is byte-identical.

```diff
--- libc++ (macOS)
+++ libstdc++ (Linux)
@@ header
-typedef struct { uint8_t *data; int64_t len; } sl_u8;
-
 typedef struct { int32_t *data; int64_t len; } sl_i32;
+typedef struct { uint8_t *data; int64_t len; } sl_u8;
+
```

The C file shows the same swap at the same typedefs, around line 1152.

**Where it likely comes from**

Slice typedefs are emitted lazily, the first time `CT()` meets the type (`src/codegen_types.h`, the `TY_SLICE` case after `cdefined.insert(m)`). So their order is the order in which codegen first visits each type. That order seems to come from iterating an unordered container: `codegen.h` has several `unordered_map`/`unordered_set` members keyed by strings (`mangleowners`, `mangles`, `ctypes`) or by pointers (`sinfo`, `stackcalls`, ...). libc++ and libstdc++ hash strings differently, so iteration order differs between them. I haven't confirmed which container drives this case.

**Suggestion**

Make emission order independent of hashing. For example, visit types in source or first-use order, or sort before iterating wherever iteration order reaches the output. Any embedder that checks generated C into version control and verifies it in CI would benefit from reproducible output across platforms.

Our workaround is to verify on macOS only, matching the machine that generates the C.

---
🤖 Co-authored with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

title: Take stdin's lock once per line in read_line
body:
## Why

A loop over `read_line`, as in samples/17_calc.goose, spends most of its time taking a lock. On f612e531 this program takes 1.49 s over a file of a million lines of 80 to 82 bytes (83 MB):

```goose
import std;
import os;
fn main() {
    var line: u8[>..] = [];
    var n = 0;
    loop { line.clear(); guard read_line(line) else { break; } n += line.len; }
    print(n);
}
```

`gs_os_read_line` (src/runtime/runtime_os.h) calls `fgetc` once per byte, and `fgetc` locks and unlocks the stream on every call. In C on the same file, the `fgetc` loop took 1.47 s and the same loop under one `flockfile` with `getc_unlocked` 0.20 s (measured on 64d62fc7's runtime, before the rebase). I found it in a JSON-lines tool that reads with `read_line` to hold one line at a time.

## What changed

- Runtime: `gs_os_read_line` takes stdin's lock once, reads the line with the unlocked getc, and lets go before it strips the `\r`. That is `flockfile`/`getc_unlocked`/`funlockfile` on POSIX and `_lock_file`/`_getc_nolock`/`_unlock_file` on Windows, which TinyCC's win32 stdio.h also has. The loop, the `\r` rule from 4df99ae1 (a `\r` is taken off only before a newline) and the result at end of input are unchanged.
- `src/runtime_inline.h` is regenerated with `goose --gen-runtime-header`.

## Docs changed

docs/testing.md: the `runtime_io.py` row names the two new inputs. docs/stdlib.md and docs/implementation.md §6.9 ("Output.") describe `read_line` as it still behaves.

## Tests

test/runtime_io.py reads one more input with `lines`: a line holding a NUL byte, then a 70,000-byte line ending in `\r\n`, longer than stdio's buffer, so the unlocked reads cross a refill. It passes before and after the change. The `r.ok` line in test/run_tests.py names it.

## Verification

- Rebased onto f612e531. `python test/run_tests.py --profile baseline --cc native --require-clang`: "all tests passed" on macOS 26.7.1 (M1 Max, Apple clang 17.0.0): JIT runs 855 ok, typecheck errors 1908 ok, samples 52 ok, native builds, packages and runtime I/O 13 ok.
- `goose --gen-runtime-header` run again on the branch leaves `git status` clean.
- The program above, built with `--standalone` by f612e531 and by this branch, on a file made by `awk 'BEGIN{for(i=0;i<1000000;i++) printf "{\"ts\":\"2026-10-26T12:%02d:%02dZ\",\"level\":\"info\",\"svc\":\"api-%d\",\"ms\":%d,\"path\":\"/v1/x\"}\n", i%60, i%60, i%7, i%997}'`: 1.49 s before and 0.21 s after, the median of 7 runs each under `/usr/bin/time` (1.48-1.57 s and 0.20-0.21 s). Both print 81889652. Before the rebase, on 64d62fc7, the same runs gave 1.47 s and 0.22 s.
- Not run locally: Linux and Windows; left to CI.

## Known limits

- Reading the line with `getline` on POSIX is faster again: 0.06 s on the same file. I did not use it. Windows has no `getline`, so it needs a second function and the `\r` rule would be written twice, and it allocates a buffer with `malloc` for every line.
- Each byte still goes into the builder with its own `gs_bld_append`; batching them into a 4 KB local buffer made no measurable difference.

title: Improve ASCII case conversion vectorization
Access packed memory through unaligned types, and check alignment under UBSan
Hotreloading goose leaks memory in an unnecessary way
body:
ai written report:  [REPORT.md](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/34042193/REPORT.md) (included for context)
Demo A:
https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/f40508fa-2f4d-46b4-aa93-6e4a810d745f
Demo B:
https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/da55017d-7b51-4f3d-9a21-5e7608e9df9b

In Demo A, the particles are discarded on hotreload and the data is not properly cleaned up. A is current behavior.
In Demo B, the particles are persevered between hotreload, this was achieved thru injecting c to change the runtime.

I strongly prefer B, but it is inherently unsafe but *at programming time* not after shipping final code.

the current api is:
```
void goose_init(int argc, char **argv)
static void gs_rt_init(int argc, char **argv, int64_t mainstacks, int64_t mainregions,int64_t workerregions)
```
With the following api change the user can pick between behavior A or B, and A can be improved to not leak memory:

```
memoryhandle goose_init(int argc, char **argv)
static memoryhandle gs_rt_init(int argc, char **argv, int64_t mainstacks, int64_t mainregions,int64_t workerregions)
bool can_safely_hotreload(memoryhandle)
void cleanup_rt(memoryhandle)
void goose_reinit(memoryhandle, int argc, char **argv)
```

The core thing is that rt_init needs to return something that communicates the mmaps either to reuse the memory or clean it up.

title: Apply incremental didChange edits at their range
body:
Clients with incremental sync send a range plus its fragment. The server declares textDocumentSync Full and read the fragment as the whole file, so typing (e.g. a trailing comment, one keystroke at a time) read as a one-letter program: a `top-level declaration expected` error, empty diagnostics, and no inlay hints until a full-text sync (reopen) repaired it.

Splice ranged edits into the overlay text in order; rangeless entries still replace it whole. Full-sync clients (vscode-languageclient) are unaffected.

Test: `test/lsp_protocol.py` drives an incremental insert above `basics.goose` and checks the `: Point` hint below it stands, shifted down a line; fails on the unpatched server. Docs: `docs/testing.md` item 1 covers the new case.

Verified: patched binary keeps hints through incremental typing states; full `check_lsp_protocol` passes, fails on the old binary.

title: Question: are `const` fills over 256 elements meant to be copied into each worker?

Fix read_line dropping a trailing carriage return at EOF
body:
Hi Wouter,

A second small one, in the runtime this time: a two-line fix with test coverage in `test/runtime_io.py`.

The bug: `gs_os_read_line` (in `src/runtime/runtime_os.h` and its generated copy in `src/runtime_inline.h`) removes a trailing carriage return whenever the line ends with one. The docs say the CR is removed before a newline, but the code also removes it when the input simply ends, so a final line `ab\r` with no newline comes back as `ab` and loses the CR. The CRLF case works correctly.

The fix strips the CR only when the character that ended the line is actually a newline. The runtime io test now covers a carriage return at EOF alongside the existing CRLF cases: on current master that case fails (reading `ab\r` at EOF yields `a`, `b` and loses the `13`), and with the fix the full runtime io check passes.

Verified against master (cce94b91), Release build.

Glad to reshape it if you prefer it differently.

title: NoteKill misses slice/reference field assignments and struct literals with static string slices (§5.1)
Support __wasm__ targets in the standalone C runtime (src/runtime/)
body:
Compiling C code emitted with `goose --standalone -o out.c` for `wasm32-wasi` or `wasm32-freestanding` (using `clang --target=wasm32-wasi` or `zig cc -target wasm32-wasi`) currently fails without post-processing the generated C file:

1. **64-bit default stack constants truncate on 32-bit `size_t`**:
   `GS_STACK_RESERVE` (`2048ull << 20`) and `GS_STACK_BUDGET` (`32ull << 40`) in `src/runtime/runtime.h` are passed to `gs_rt_start(..., size_t reserve, size_t gap, size_t budget, ...)`. On `wasm32` (`sizeof(size_t) == 4`), `2048ull << 20` and `32ull << 40` overflow 32-bit `size_t` and truncate to `0` unless overridden via `-D`.
2. **Unconditional POSIX headers and signal/mmap APIs in `#else /* posix */`**:
   `src/runtime/runtime_impl.h` and `src/runtime/runtime_threads.h` include `<sys/mman.h>`, `<signal.h>`, `<pthread.h>`, and `<setjmp.h>`, and call `sigaction`, `sigaltstack`, `mmap`, `mprotect`, and `pthread_*`, which are unavailable in single-threaded WASI and freestanding WebAssembly builds.

### Proposed change

Add `#if defined(__wasm__)` guards in `src/runtime/runtime.h`, `src/runtime/runtime_impl.h`, and `src/runtime/runtime_threads.h`:
- Default `GS_STACK_RESERVE`, `GS_STACK_GAP`, `GS_STACK_BUDGET`, and `GS_REGION_MIN` to 32-bit-safe sizes when `__wasm__` (or `SIZE_MAX <= 0xffffffffu`) is defined.
- Provide a `#elif defined(__wasm__)` platform section in `runtime_impl.h` and `runtime_threads.h` using `calloc`/`free` for regions (with a 64 KiB page size), no-op `gs_native_stack_init`/`gs_native_stack_free`, single-threaded mutex/condvar stubs when `GS_NEED_THREADS == 0`, and `abort()` fallback when `<setjmp.h>` is unavailable.

title: Fix: Build call-valued fields of a pushed literal in place
body:
## Bug
`ps.push(Pair { left: make(first, 1), right: make(first, 2) })`, where the field type holds relative links, corrupted memory: `goose run` aborted (exit 138) and `goose build` output was wrong.

## Cause
`FixedLitAtStk` built call-valued fields in a temporary and copied them into the pushed element, so their relative offsets were measured from the wrong slot.

## Fix
In `FixedLitAtStk`, a field whose type has relative links and is not itself a literal goes through `GenConstruct`, which builds the call (or if/match/block) at the stack top, as a pushed element is built.

## Test
`test/codegen/pushed_literal_call_fields.goose` pushes such literals and prints the fields and their links. It exits 138 before the fix and prints the expected output after. Also checked with the existing `relative_*` fixtures in `test/codegen` and `test/storage`, and `codegen_exec`, all unchanged. The full suite was not run.

title: binary reads only little-endian fields
Fix CI failing: Give packed struct members plain C scalar types
body:
## What

Struct and array members in generated C use the plain C scalar type again (`int64_t`, `double`, ...). Pointers to scalars keep the `aligned(1)` typedefs (`gs_i64 *`), which is where unaligned pointees need them.

## Why

Clang 18 miscompiles by-value passing and returning of a small packed struct when a member's type carries `aligned(1)`: the member's bytes land shifted in the register (`0x123456789abcdef0` comes back as `0x3456789abcdef0`). Clang 19, 20, 21 and GCC get it right. Since cec434a every scalar in generated C is such a typedef, so the Linux ASan+UBSan job, which uses clang 18.1.3, fails `dispatch_result_prefix` and `stdlib_regex` with garbage values. The failure needs no sanitizer and shows even at `-O0`.

Members never needed the typedef: `#pragma pack(1)` already makes their access unaligned.

## How tested

- Both programs pass under clang 18 (Ubuntu 24.04 container) at -O0/-O1/-O2, with and without ASan+UBSan.
- `run_tests.py --profile sanitize --cc clang` (clang 21) and the baseline profile: all tests pass.

title: Add c_headers to package sidecars
body:
Adds `c_headers = ["include/adapters.h"];` to package and program sidecars, using the existing `--include` placement after generated types. This lets packages supply inline C adapters without consumer flags or separate compilation. Paths are package-relative; platform suffixes are supported.

Includes documentation and tests for native builds, TinyCC, path resolution, unused externs, and header edits. Passed the Linux baseline suite with GCC, Clang checks, and TinyCC.

[goosimd](https://github.com/sstadick/goosimd) is a placeholder consumer tested through Git imports, native SSE2/AVX2 builds, and TinyCC's scalar fallback. No SIMD support is added to the compiler itself.

--

AI was used in doing this work, mostly GTP-Astra. As before, I'm happy to reproduce this without AI if that is preferred!

title: Preserve earlier tail-call argument values
body:
Hi Wouter,

I found a case where tail recursion gives a different answer with optimization on: a later argument changes a parameter after an earlier argument has read it, so a call that should keep `7` ends up keeping `10` instead.

The fix only skips saving that earlier argument when its value can't change, letting the existing temporaries preserve it otherwise or leaving the recursion in place when needed.

title: Preserve f32 source rounding in constant conversions
body:
Hi Wouter,

I found a small rounding issue with constant conversions: an `f32` holding `16777217.0` should round to `16777216`, but converting it to an integer or widening it to `f64` can bring back the original, unrounded value.

The fix rounds the value to its source `f32` precision before the optimizer copies or converts it, so those conversions agree with reading an `f32` stored at runtime.

title: No stdlib call turns os::time() into a date or reads one back
body:
## What happens

`os::time()` gives seconds since 1970-01-01 UTC as an `f64`, and `time_ns()` gives nanoseconds as an `i64`. Nothing in the stdlib turns either into a date, or reads a timestamp such as `2026-10-24T12:00:00Z` back into seconds. A program that stamps its log lines, reads timestamps out of JSON logs, or prints when a certificate expires writes the calendar arithmetic itself. Run on v2026.3; master 3cc84860 has no date or time text function in `stdlib/`, `src/runtime/` or `docs/stdlib.md` either.

## Reproduce

```goose
import std;
import os;
fn main() {
    print(time());          // seconds since the epoch: there is no call that shows the date
}
```

    $ goose now.goose
    parsed ok: 159 top-level declarations, 3 file(s)
    typechecked ok: 88 specialization(s), 2 struct/0 enum instance(s); optimized -O1: 1 inlined, 0 base case(s), 0 folded, 0 propagated, 0 tail loop(s), 0 reassociated
    bce: elided 0/0 index and 0/0 slice checks
    1793316183.291978

Writing the conversion by hand has several places to go wrong. A Gregorian year divisible by 100 is a leap year only when it is also divisible by 400, so 2100 has no February 29. Reading RFC 3339 means `+HH:MM` and `-HH:MM` offsets, an optional fraction, and second 60, which RFC 3339 §5.7 allows only at the end of a month that has a leap second, shifted by the zone offset when the time is not in `Z`. Times before 1970 need `div_euclid`, not `/` (spec §6.2).

## What the docs say

docs/design/stdlib_design.md §9 leaves it out on purpose: "Date/time formatting, directories, subprocesses, networking: `os` grows when a program needs them, one extern at a time." Directories have since come in (`list_dir`, `make_dir`, `delete_dir`). Date formatting needs no extern, though: it is arithmetic on `i64` and bytes, which is the kind of code §1 admits when the hand-written version "is easy to get wrong, as with sorting, hashing, UTF-8, float printing, and binary search".

## Options

Following #72's order, I tried it as a package first: [clintecker/goose-date](https://github.com/clintecker/goose-date), MIT, 88 lines of Goose without comments and blank lines (133 in the file), no extern. The day arithmetic is Howard Hinnant's (https://howardhinnant.github.io/date_algorithms.html). Four of my command-line programs import it at `@v1`. Its test compares `format_time` with Python's `datetime.fromtimestamp(t, timezone.utc).isoformat()` on 100,004 times in years 1 to 9999, and all are equal. The functions follow the stdlib's conventions (stdlib_design.md §2.2: text into a builder the caller passes, a parse with a trailing `bool`):

```goose
fn days_from_civil(y: i64, m: i64, d: i64) -> i64        // day 0 is 1970-01-01, any year
fn civil_from_days(z: i64) -> i64, i64, i64              // year, month, day
fn format_time(out: u8[>..]&, t: i64)                     // 2026-10-24T12:00:00Z
fn parse_time(s: const u8[:]) -> i64, bool                // RFC 3339: Z or +HH:MM, a fraction dropped,
                                                          // 23:59:60 UTC on June 30 or Dec 31 read as :59
```

1. Leave it to packages. Nothing changes here; a program imports goose-date or writes its own. Cost: each program that prints a time pins a package for what `os::time()` alone cannot show.
2. Add a `time` module to the stdlib (`import time;`), as `base64`, `csv`, `json` and `regex` were added on their own (f3f77ef2, 22325783, fb996b39, 27c70077), holding these four functions and their helpers (`days_in`, `weekday`, `date_ok`, the parse steps). It stays out of `os`, which is the layer over `src/runtime/runtime_os.h`. Cost: those 88 lines and a test, UTC only. It allocates nothing, keeps no global state for threads to share, and builds the text in the caller's builder, so it keeps "No allocator", "Threads with no shared memory" and "Everything is built in place".
3. Make goose-date a blessed package (`src/blessed.txt`), so `import date;` works without a source line. Cost: a third-party repository in the compiler's table, whose ref the compiler bumps when the package's API changes (docs/design/packages.md §4.5).

I would pick 2, or 1 if you would rather keep the stdlib to what a package cannot do. Local time and zones by name are out of scope for any of these: they need the C library's zone data, a later extern if a program needs one. Prior art: Go's `time.Format(time.RFC3339)` and `time.Parse`, and Python's `datetime.isoformat` and `fromisoformat`, are in their standard libraries. Rust's standard library has `SystemTime` only and leaves dates to the `chrono` and `time` crates. In C, `gmtime_r` and `strftime` format and `timegm` goes back, but MSVC has none of `gmtime_r`, `timegm` and `strptime`. I can send a PR for 2 with tests, a docs/stdlib.md section, and the README.md, docs/tutorial.md and stdlib_design.md §9 changes those four commits made, or leave it at the package. Which would you prefer?

title: Clarify the native-code boundary of thread isolation
body:
I've been looking at how Goose's worker isolation interacts with native adapters, and wanted to clarify one small boundary in the tutorial.

The copied globals and flat queue values already give ordinary Goose code its isolation. But a copied integer can still name the same native resource, and an extern can reach shared state outside that model. This qualifies section 14's race-freedom statements and adds a short limitation in section 18, without changing any behavior or introducing new APIs.

I kept the existing host-thread restriction in section 19 as it is. Checked the wording against the worker/global lowering and native call boundary, and checked the section link and diff whitespace.

title: Clarify the native-code boundary of thread isolation
body:
Hi Wouter,

This is just a small documentation suggestion, so please feel free to close it if you do not like it.

While working with threads, I noticed the tutorial says there is no shared mutable memory and no data races. That is true for ordinary Goose values, and the way each worker gets its own copies is a genuinely elegant design. But a reader could walk away thinking the guarantee covers everything, including native code reached through the FFI, where shared state really is possible. This change adds a short qualification in section 14 and a matching note in the limitations in section 18, so the boundary is stated in the places people will look for it.

It is wording only, with no behaviour changes. If you would like it said differently, or put somewhere else, let me know and I will happily change it to whatever suits you better.

Thank you for Goose. I use it every day, and I keep finding that the design decisions hold up.

Joshua

title: `ui::slider_float` example is wrong, and inconsistent with other ui functions.
Fix stale call hierarchy results after document edits
body:
Hi Wouter,

I found a small call hierarchy issue after editing a document. If `caller` changes from calling `a` to calling `b`, an incoming or outgoing call request made straight after the edit can still show the old relationship.

The fix includes `callHierarchy/` requests in the existing document settlement gate, so pending changes are analyzed before the saved call hierarchy item is looked up. It keeps the formatting exception and the existing refresh behavior for lenses, semantic tokens, and inlay hints.

The regression test sends each of the three affected queries immediately after an edit, without background analysis between messages. All three reproduce the stale graph on fresh master.

With a Release compiler based on master `2ed1a63d`, the regression test now passes all three cases (CTest 1/1), the full LSP protocol suite passes, and all 40 VS Code extension tests pass. The baseline suite passes 5,460 checks and the sanitizer profile passes 4,544 checks, with zero failures. The sanitizer profile instruments generated native code; the compiler itself was not sanitizer-built locally. Optional audio, graphics, physics, and UI execution tests were skipped because their packages were not built in.

If you would prefer a different approach, I am happy to adjust it.

Thank you for Goose. I use it every day, and I keep finding that the design decisions hold up.

Joshua

title: Read every width and both byte orders in binary
body:
`binary` read only `u16`, `i16` and `u32`, little-endian. External formats also need single bytes, 32- and 64-bit integers, floats, and big-endian fields (network protocols, PNG, most older file formats), and callers were assembling those from bytes by hand. This adds:

- `read_u8`, `read_i8`
- `read_i32le`, `read_u64le`, `read_i64le`, `read_f32le`, `read_f64le`
- a `be` version of every multi-byte read: `read_u16be` through `read_f64be`

Each comes at an offset and on a `Reader&`. They check ranges and fail as the existing reads do: zero and `false`, with the cursor left in place.

- Floats come from their bits through `gs_f32_from_bits` / `gs_f64_from_bits`, a `memcpy` in `runtime_ext.h`, since Goose has no bit cast of its own. A read keeps the value exactly, NaN payloads included; decoding the bits with Goose arithmetic would have lost them. `runtime_inline.h` is regenerated.
- The `Reader` forms share an `advance(r, ok, size)` helper, and the existing ones now use it too.
- `read_i8` is not in the stdlib proposal's list; it completes the signed reads.

- `stdlib/binary.goose`, `src/runtime/runtime_ext.h`, `src/runtime_inline.h`, `test/stdlib/stdlib_binary.goose`, `docs/stdlib.md`.

The full suite passes on Linux.

title: Fix tail recursion rewrite when an argument can return early
body:
Hi Wouter,

I found a bug in the tail recursion rewrite.

The rewrite changes a recursive call into a loop. The bug appears when an argument of the call can return early from the function. Example: `10 + self(argument)`. If the argument returns 100 before the call happens, the frame must not add its 10. O0 gives the correct result, 110. O1 and O2 give 120. They add a term that the program abandons.

The fix is simple. The compiler keeps the call recursive when the evaluation of an argument can return from the function or break out of the block. A break that stays inside the argument's own block or loop does not count. Safe calls still become loops.

The tests cover returns, block exits, an exit during the evaluation of a for-loop input, and the safe loop rewrites. All 40 focused checks pass, at O0, O1, and O2, with debug checks on and off. The full baseline suite passes 5,467 checks. The sanitizer suite passes 4,550 checks. There are no failures. I skipped the optional audio, graphics, physics, and UI tests because their packages are not built here.

If you prefer a different approach, I am happy to change it.

Thank you for Goose. I use it every day, and the design decisions hold up.

Joshua

title: fix: allow packaging without builtin libs and static link MinGW

﻿## Summary

It now produces a valid release containing the compiler, stdlib, tcclib, docs, samples, and vscode extension, simply omitting the `pkg/` directory when no packages are compiled in. title: Bounds-check analysis: five checks it could prove, and a defer soundness fix
Warn on an ordering comparison its operand's type decides (`u < 0`)
body:
Hi Wouter,

Comparing an unsigned value with `< 0` compiles silently, though it is always false:

```goose
import std;

fn error(e: u32) -> bool { return e < 0; }   // always false

fn main() { print(error(0), error(7)); }
```

This is easy to hit when moving ids from `i64` (with -1 meaning "none") to an index type (`u32 in nodes`): an existing `if e < 0 { return error; }` keeps compiling and never fires. Index types are unsigned, so they encourage exactly this migration.

This PR adds a warning for an ordering comparison between an integer and a constant when the integer's type alone decides it:

```
warning: comparison is always false: u32 values are 0 to 4294967295
```

- It covers `u < 0`, `0 > u`, `u >= 0`, and the same at the top of a narrow type (`b <= 255` of a `u8`, `x < -128` of an `i8`). A constant outside the type is already an error (`constant 300 does not fit u8`).
- A `u64`'s upper bound is not judged, since its range here stops at i64's.
- As with the redundant-cast warning (§6.3), code whose types differ between specializations (`InGenericCode`) is exempt: `fn negative<T>(x: T) -> bool { x < 0 }` is fine for `T = i64` and silent for `T = u32`.
- The constant may be any integer constant (`Val::ck == CK_INT`), so a named constant is caught as a literal is.

It is a small function next to `NumericBinary`, called for `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=` outside trial checks. `test/typing/decided_comparisons.goose` covers the warned cases and the ones left alone (u64 above i64, a signed `x < 0`, `e < 1`, a generic).

### Testing

On master (2ed1a63), Release build, macOS arm64: `python3 test/run_tests.py --cc native` passes all tests. No file under `test/` or `samples/` except the new fixture gets the warning, goose_in_goose and the standard library they import included.

Not run: the sanitize profile, Linux and Windows.

title: [enhancement] Mark std's scalar functions `checkfree`
body:
Hi Wouter,

A `checkfree fn` may only call `checkfree` functions, builtins or externs (§7.14), and no std function is marked. So even a function that only uses `max` or `abs` cannot be `checkfree`:

```goose
import std;

checkfree fn f(x: f64, y: f64) -> f64 { return max(abs(x), y); }

fn main() { print(f(-3.0, 1.0)); }
```
```
error: checkfree fn f calls abs, which is not checkfree: the bounds checks left in it would run inside f (§7.14)
```

This PR marks the std functions that hold no index:

- `std`: `min`, `max`, `clamp`, `abs`, `rem`, `div_euclid`, `sign`, `lerp`, `next_pow2`, `hash_mix`, the scalar `hash` overloads, `hash_combine`, and `float_text::bits_of` (which the `f64` hash calls).
- `math`: `radians`, `degrees`, `is_nan`, `is_inf`, `is_finite`.

The generic ones (`min`, `max`, `clamp`, `abs`, `rem`, `div_euclid`, `sign`) can only ever compare and compute on numbers, since `<` takes numeric operands only, so no instantiation calls user code.

`float_text::bits_of` reads its double through `bytes_of` of an `f64[1]`, and the analysis did not know that view's length. `BoundLenOf` now gives a `bytes_of` view of a fixed array of scalars its constant length (count × width), so `b[0]` … `b[7]` are proved.

`docs/stdlib.md` says which of the listed functions are `checkfree`. `test/optimizer/checkfree_std_leaves.goose` calls each of them from a `checkfree` function; it is rejected on master.

### What this leaves out

- **Functions that take a block** (`sort`, `stable_sort`, `each_split`, the heaps). They cannot be marked, because §7.14 requires a block a `checkfree` function calls to be written in a `checkfree` function. Marking `sort` rejects every ordinary `sort(xs) { a, b => a > b }`: "checkfree fn sort calls a block written in fn main, which is not checkfree". Making them usable would need a language decision, for instance judging `checkfree` per specialization, so that `sort` instantiated with a `checkfree` caller's block is checked and one with an ordinary block is not.
- **`dedup`**. Its loop indexes `xs[w - 1]` and `xs[w]` with `w <= i`, which the analysis does not infer (also not with #156).
- **`dictionary`, `slice_pool` and the rest of std**: not tried.

### Testing

On master (2ed1a63), Release build, macOS arm64: `python3 test/run_tests.py --cc native` passes all tests. The new fixture prints the same at -O0, -O1 and -O2.

Not run: the sanitize profile, Linux and Windows.

title: Proposal: contracts, abortfree/proven functions, and external provers
body:
Goose proves memory safety and, with `checkfree`, the absence of bounds checks. There is no way to state what a function computes, and no hook for handing a property the compiler cannot prove to a tool that can (Lean, Why3, Frama-C). This proposal adds contracts, two new verified-function levels, and an external-prover route. The full design note is `docs/design/proofs.md` in the draft PR linked below; this issue is the summary and the place to discuss it.

## Why Goose is a good fit

Most of what makes verifying a systems language expensive is the heap: aliasing, framing, ownership. Goose removes most of that by construction:

* no heap, so program state is a finite set of named roots;
* every reference's root is static per specialization (§9.2), so a write through `p: T&` is a functional update of a known root, as SPARK's in/out parameters are;
* effects are already summarized for bounds-check elimination (§10.5), so frame conditions can be **inferred**: no `modifies` clauses;
* integer semantics are total (§6.2): wrapping unsigned and Euclidean `%` match SMT bitvectors and Lean's `UIntN`/`Int.emod` exactly;
* grow-only arrays and index types already are a refinement type with a soundness argument (§3.11);
* no shared memory between threads, so no interleavings.

So proofs need only first-order logic over values, arrays and integers, which suits SMT and a shallow embedding in Lean.

## Levels

| Level | Written as | Guarantees |
|---|---|---|
| L0 | (always) | memory safety |
| L1 | `checkfree fn` | no bounds check left (exists today) |
| L2 | `abortfree fn` | no abort of §9.3 can fire except resource exhaustion: overflow, division by zero, `pop` on empty, lossy `as`, `assert`, callee `requires` |
| L3 | `proven fn` | L2, plus its contracts and loop invariants hold, and it terminates |

## Contracts

```goose
proven fn lower_bound(a: const i64[:], key: i64) -> i64
    requires sorted(a)
    ensures 0 <= result <= a.len
    ensures all k in 0..result: a[k] < key
    ensures all k in result..a.len: a[k] >= key
{
    var lo: i64 = 0;
    var hi = a.len;
    while lo < hi
        invariant all k in 0..lo: a[k] < key
        invariant all k in hi..a.len: a[k] >= key
        decreases hi - lo
    {
        let mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if a[mid] < key { lo = mid + 1; } else { hi = mid; }
    }
    return lo;
}
```

* `requires`, `ensures` (with `result`, or `ensures (i, ok): ...` for several results), `old(e)`, loop `invariant`, `decreases`, and `escapes` for frames crossed by `return … from`.
* Contract arithmetic is mathematical, and quantifiers are bounded (`all`/`any i in lo..hi`), so **every contract is executable**: debug builds check them with no prover installed, and release builds erase unproved ones (as with signed overflow), unless `--check-contracts` is given.
* Proved `requires`/`ensures` become entry and call-site facts for bounds-check elimination, so contracts can make code faster.
* `std.spec`: `sorted`, `is_perm`, `count`, `sum`, `distinct`, `prefix`.

## Refinements and struct invariants

`type Percent = u8 where it <= 100;` behaves exactly like an index type, which it generalizes (`u32 in a` is `u32 where it < a.len` plus the no-shrink rule). `struct Span { lo: i64, hi: i64 } where lo <= hi` must hold after every field store; an update that breaks it temporarily assigns the whole value, which in-place construction already makes cheap. No pack/unpack machinery.

## How it is checked

1. The existing difference/interval domain in `bce.h`, extended to the other aborts. This should prove most of `abortfree` with no solver.
2. SMT-LIB to z3 or cvc5 from `PATH` (not bundled), with `rlimit` instead of timeouts for reproducibility, and results cached by VC hash.
3. An external proof, or else an error in `proven` code and a run-time check elsewhere.

Failures report a counterexample in Goose terms, and `--emit-tests` can turn it into a runnable test.

## External provers and trust

* `goose prove --export lean|why3` writes the program as a shallow embedding (reference parameters become in/out values) with each unproved obligation as a `theorem … := by sorry` stub.
* `ensures … by external "proofs/Fft.lean:fft_matches_dft"` links an obligation to a theorem. The statement is hash-checked against the regenerated one, so a code change invalidates the proof instead of silently keeping it.
* `--emit-acsl` writes the contracts into the generated C for Frama-C/WP, so the C artifact can be checked too, from specs written once in Goose.
* `ghost` code and `lemma fn`s are written in Goose syntax, and erased.
* `assume(e, "reason")`, contracts on `extern fn`s and external proofs are listed by `--trust-report`, which CI can pin. That keeps a "proof" that just adds an `assume` visible in review, which matters for LLM-written code.

## Phasing

Each phase is useful without the later ones:

1. **Executable contracts**: syntax, `old`, `result`, bounded quantifiers, run-time checks. No prover.
2. **`abortfree fn`**: extend `bce.h`; no solver.
3. **SMT and `proven fn`**: VC generation, `decreases`, ghost code, lemmas, counterexamples.
4. **Refinement types and struct invariants**; index types re-expressed as one, with no change in behaviour.
5. **External provers**: Lean/Why3 export, `by external`, trust report, ACSL.

The draft PR starts on phase 1.

## Open questions

* Floats: leave them uninterpreted at phase 3 and handle them in Lean?
* Bounding data-stack use, so guard-page hits can be proved absent for non-recursive code.
* Contracts on case functions: one per overload set, or per case?
* Spelling: `all`/`any` versus `forall`/`exists`, `implies` versus `==>`.
* Whether `from_bytes` should check refinement predicates of the loaded type.

title: Executable contracts: requires, ensures and loop invariants (proofs phase 1, #160)
body:
Draft: phase 1 of the proofs proposal in #160, executable contracts, implemented in part. Opened as a draft so the syntax and the lowering can be discussed before more of it is built.

The full design note is `docs/design/proofs.md`. Its §3.3 gives the rule below, and its §17 says exactly what is in and where this differs from the proposal's text.

## The rule: a clause is an `assert`

Following the discussion on #160, a contract clause means what an `assert` at the same place means, and nothing else:

* `requires p` is `assert(p)` on entry, `ensures q` is `assert(q)` at every return, and `invariant i` is `assert(i)` at the head of every iteration.
* It is checked in every build, and the code after it may rely on it: it narrows and is a fact for bounds-check elimination. So a `requires` does what the entry `assert`s of `checkfree` functions do today.
* Where the facts already settle it, the check is removed, the same way a proved bounds check is. This applies to plain `assert`s too. Proofs only ever remove checks.

What the clauses add over `assert` is *where* a fact belongs, a function's interface, which later phases use to check callers against a `requires` and give callers a proved `ensures`.

```goose
fn lower_bound(a: const i64[:], key: i64) -> i64
    requires all i in 1..a.len: a[i - 1] <= a[i]
    ensures 0 <= result && result <= a.len
    ensures all k in 0..result: a[k] < key
{
    var lo: i64 = 0;
    var hi = a.len;
    while lo < hi
        invariant all k in 0..lo: a[k] < key
    { ... }
    return lo;
}
```

* `requires`/`ensures` on functions, with `result` and `old(e)`, and `invariant` on `while` and `for` loops.
* In contract expressions only: `implies`, and the bounded quantifiers `all`/`any i in lo..hi: p`. All of these words stay ordinary names everywhere else.

## How

* **Parser.** The parser keeps the clauses on `SFunction` and on `While`/`ForLoop`, so `--dump` prints them as written and roundtrips. A quantifier expands to the loop it means. `implies` is `!a || b`, marked so that it dumps as written.
* **Lowering.** `LowerContracts` (`src/contracts.h`) runs once, at the start of `TypeCheckProgram`, and turns each clause into a check in the body:
  * `requires` at the top of the body;
  * `ensures` before every return and at the end of the body, with `old` values bound on entry;
  * `invariant` at the top of each iteration.

  A returned variable is checked in place, and any other expression is first bound to `result` where it is built. So a nonfixed result such as `i64[>..]` is never copied.
* **The check.** A new builtin whose name contains a space, so no program can call it. It is an `assert` that aborts with `goose runtime error: ensures failed: <clause text> (file:line)`. The typechecker narrows from it and `bce.h` takes its facts, as for `assert`.
* **Removal.** `bce.h` drops an `assert` or a clause check whose condition its facts settle (`CondHolds`, `Call::nobc`). Only comparisons of integer variables, constants and lengths of named places, joined by `&&`, are judged, so the dropped condition could not abort or have effects. A clause that indexes, calls or quantifies is always checked.

## Not yet (see proofs.md §16 and §17)

* **Expensive clauses** run in every build: an unproved quantifier is a loop. §16 lists options (a per-clause `unchecked` marker, a flag, or nothing) for discussion.
* Callers do not check a `requires` yet, a failed one is reported at the clause, and a proved `ensures` is not yet a fact at call sites.
* Contract arithmetic is machine arithmetic, not mathematical.
* An `invariant` is checked at the top of each iteration's body, not on loop exit.
* No `ensures` on functions with several results, and no `escapes`, `decreases`, `spec fn` or `std.spec`.

## Tests

* `test/typing/contracts.goose` (`runtime-debug`): every form; the debug run must match the release runs.
* `test/runtime/contract_{requires,ensures,invariant}_abort.goose`: failures, in every build.
* `test/optimizer/contract_checks.goose`: a `checkfree` function that its `requires` makes check-free (without the clause it is rejected), and an `ensures` proved at every return, which `run_tests.py` confirms is gone from the generated C while a clause that indexes stays.
* `test/errors_tc/contract_*.goose`: the rejections.

`python test/run_tests.py --profile baseline --cc native --require-clang` on Windows (MSVC and clang-cl, TinyCC JIT): every section passes, including roundtrip, GS_DEBUG, JIT, goose_in_goose, samples and the C-shape checks. The exception is the native toolchain and native rebuild checks, which fail here because CMake hits the 250-character path limit inside the deep worktree path (`.claude/worktrees/...`), not because of this change.
