title: Close unused child stdin before reading process output
body:
Hi Wouter,

I found a case where RunProcess can hang: it captures a child's output without sending input, but leaves the child's stdin open. A child that waits for stdin EOF before continuing then waits forever while the parent waits for output.

This closes the unused stdin pipe just after starting the child, before reading its output. The regression checks both a child that reads stdin first and one that writes more than a pipe buffer before reading. It also keeps the test watchdog independent of the output pipe and supports the test's multiple C++ sources with MSVC.

On current master (2ed1a63dde), both scenarios pass in native and ASan/UBSan builds, for 4 scenario checks. Five existing process and toolchain checks pass across cli_paths.py, native_toolchain.py, packages_git.py, and toolchain_selection.py. Both mocked MSVC command checks pass too, for single and multiple sources.

Happy to adjust it if you'd prefer a different approach.

title: Add bounded shared storage capabilities and worker leases
body:
# Add bounded shared storage capabilities and worker leases

This proposal adds explicitly shared anonymous storage without changing Goose's
ordinary isolated-worker values. `shared_alloc` returns an opaque `SharedOwner`;
`shared_view` selects a bounded range; `shared_borrow` grants exclusive,
thread-local scalar access until `shared_release`. Disjoint ranges can be
borrowed concurrently. `memory_read<T>` and `memory_write<T>` check bounds in
all builds and support unaligned endian-aware integer access.

Only the allocating thread can close storage. Close refuses active borrows or
worker leases. Generation checks reject stale aliases, and normal/contained
worker cleanup releases abandoned accesses and leases, including descendants.
Owners and accesses cannot cross a worker boundary; direct views can. Safe
capabilities have no raw C ABI or serializable byte image.

This is a substantive language extension proposed for maintainer discussion.
File mapping, page advice, unsafe pointers, atomics, indexed arrays and byte-copy
APIs are deferred.

Validation: upstream baseline and complete candidate suite, focused GCC 14 and
Clang 23 debug/release checks, Clang ASan/UBSan lifecycle checks. Lifecycle
coverage includes stale aliases, range overlap/exclusion, disjoint borrows,
owner-only close, overflow bounds, packed capability alignment, live-worker
close, nested workers, failed native creation rollback, allocation failure,
and abort cleanup. Exact results and limits are in the readiness report.

Refreshed native validation passed: 1450 parse/typecheck checks, 693 generated C runs, 204 debug checks and 1921 typecheck rejection checks. The four reported upstream baseline failures did not reproduce.

The first Linux, macOS and Windows CI runs passed the compiler/native suite but exposed missing builtin names in the editor grammar. Added all eight substrate builtins; all 40 extension tests now pass locally. CI is rerunning.

title: Add capability-based u64 atomics in registered shared storage
body:
# Add capability-based u64 atomics in registered shared storage

Depends on https://github.com/aardappel/goose/pull/163. GitHub cannot target a
branch that exists only in the fork, so this PR targets master and includes
that prerequisite. The u64 implementation and tests remain in separate commits. The [incremental u64 diff](https://github.com/jtenner/goose/compare/upstream/shared-capability-substrate...upstream/shared-atomic-u64)
excludes the prerequisite.

Builds on the separately proposed shared capability substrate. This adds one
opaque `SharedAtomicU64` cell type with `shared_atomic_u64`,
`atomic_is_lock_free`, load, store, fetch-add and strong compare-exchange.
Atomic operations accept only that capability. Ordinary references and raw
integer addresses are rejected; no raw-address atomic interface is included.

Construction checks natural alignment, bounds and range exclusion. Atomic
bytes cannot overlap ordinary borrows or other registered cells. Worker leases
retain the allocation through the entire instruction; generation checks reject
closed/reused handles. Capability wrappers remain byte-packed while registry
metadata and atomic cells stay naturally aligned.

Orders are explicit compile-time strings. Loads, stores and both CAS orders
are validated, including the relative strength of failure order. Fetch-add
wraps modulo 2^64. Generated GCC/Clang C uses lock-free `__atomic_*` operations
and strong CAS, with explicit unsupported-backend/width diagnostics and no
mutex fallback. U32, indexed regions, exchange and other RMW operations are
deferred.

Validation: the full native suite passed; GCC 14/Clang 23 debug and release
passed the shared capability suite and 40 repeated exact-once claim runs.
All 40 load/store/RMW/CAS order cases passed. Generated C was checked at Goose
O0/O2 for explicit orders, strong CAS and lock-free gates; i486 was rejected
and x86-64 accepted. Clang ASan/UBSan and TSan fixtures passed. See the readiness
report for exact commands, baseline caveats and platform limits.

Proposed for maintainer discussion alongside the prerequisite. This branch is
stacked on `upstream/shared-capability-substrate`; the substrate must land first.

Refreshed against upstream master `2ed1a63d` on October 31. The complete
native suite passed: 1450 parse/typecheck checks, 694 generated C runs,
204 debug checks, 21 compiler/runtime/Clang checks and 1928 typecheck
rejection checks, alongside the remaining sections. The four reported upstream
baseline failures did not reproduce. Embedded JIT and unavailable multimedia
modules were skipped. Linux x86-64 is the execution-verified platform.

title: Goose batteries
body:
# Baterries for the goose

I made a library (called gslib due to lack of other ideas) here: https://github.com/SorinS/gslib.git

## The why 
I believe that goose should come with "batteries included", liike golang, odin, etc. This would provide the user with a series of solid libraries that would simplify the programming effort.  

## Layout and components
The library has the below layout:

- **gslib**
  - `compress`
  - `crypto`
    - `bignum`
    - `ssh`
    - `tls`
    - `x509`
  - `encoding`
    - `asn1`
    - `yaml`
  - `net`
    - `http`
    - `ldap`

It has: 
- a short introduction and the "import gslib, then http::get" example;
- the following components:
  - crypto/ (bignum's primitives grouped by kind, then x509, tls, ssh);
  - encoding/ (asn1, yaml);
  - net/ (http, ldap);
  - compress  (tar, zip,gzip, bzip2, xz);
  
## Build
Just  run make  in the gslib folder and it will provide the options. To build the binaries run:
make build 

and check  for 15 executables in ../bin; e.g.:
goose-http
goose-httpd
goose-ldapadd
goose-ldapcompare
goose-ldapdelete
goose-ldapmodify
goose-ldapmodrdn
goose-ldappasswd
goose-ldapsearch
goose-ldapwhoami
goose-scp
goose-sftp-server
goose-ssh

title: Warn when a function changes its copy of a struct passed to an untyped parameter
Find clang where the LLVM installer puts it on Windows
body:
On Windows the C compiler search looks for clang on PATH and in Visual Studio,
then falls back to cl through vcvars64. The official LLVM installer puts
clang.exe in `%ProgramFiles%\LLVM\bin` and leaves that off PATH unless you ask
it to, so a machine with LLVM installed, and Visual Studio without its own
clang, builds with cl.

This also looks in `%ProgramFiles%\LLVM\bin`, after PATH and Visual Studio and
before vcvars64, which is the preference the search already gives Visual
Studio's clang over cl, and names the place in the not-found message
(`src/toolchain.h`, `docs/design/packages.md`).

The no-C-compiler check in `test/run_tests.py` hides every compiler by
emptying PATH and pointing `ProgramFiles(x86)` at an empty directory. It now
also hides `ProgramFiles` and `ProgramW6432` (Windows gives a 64-bit process
its `ProgramFiles` from `ProgramW6432`, whatever its parent passed); otherwise
it finds LLVM's clang wherever LLVM is installed.

Why it matters: in a fork's cross-language benchmarks cl's code was 17–28%
slower than clang's on float-heavy work (n-body, raytrace), and `simd fn`
versions are built only under clang (`GS_SIMD`).

Checked on `master` (`2ed1a63d`), built with clang 22 on Windows 11, with LLVM
installed and not on PATH:

- `goose toolchain` now reports `clang 22.1.8, found in Program Files\LLVM`
  where it reported MSVC through vcvars64.
- With PATH, `ProgramFiles`, `ProgramW6432` and `ProgramFiles(x86)` hidden as
  the test does, it exits 1 with the not-found message, which now names
  `Program Files\LLVM`.

I didn't run the whole suite locally.

title: Touch each page before the C library's vector copies on Windows
body:
On Windows the data stacks are reserved and their pages committed by the
vectored exception handler as they are first touched (`gs_fault_filter`).
Under load, the exception that reaches the handler can carry the thread's
AVX state recorded as all zero, although the faulting instruction is in the
middle of the C library's AVX `memcpy` loop. When the handler resumes, the
copy stores the upper 128 bits of its YMM registers as zeros: 16 zero bytes
in every 32 from the newly committed page on.

**How it showed up.** In a fork of Goose
([appdoze/gust](https://github.com/appdoze/gust)), on hosted Windows CI under
load, a network test's client buffer received a 1 MB reply at full length
with zeros in it. The zeros always started 16 bytes into a commit chunk:
at offset 16, 16 KB + 16, or 64 KB + 16. The bytes were right as `recv`
handed them over, so the corruption happened in the append.

A probe built into the fault handler for the investigation showed two
things for the commit behind every corrupted byte:

- the context record's AVX state was init, meaning all zero;
- the live registers at handler entry were zero as well, so the handler
  can't restore them.

A standalone C program doing the same thing never reproduced it in millions
of faults, even with a wait before each copy: it reserves a region, commits
it from a vectored handler, and copies with AVX. So I have no small
reproducer to include.

**Fix.** Before a copy, move or fill the C library may do with 32-byte
registers, write one byte of each destination page with a scalar store
(`gs_first_touch`). Any commit fault then happens with no vector state live,
and the byte keeps its value. This covers:

- `GS_MEMCPY`, in both its TinyCC form and the other;
- the library path of `gs_memcpy`;
- `gs_memmove` and `gs_bld_append`;
- the generated code's `memmove` and non-zero `memset` calls, now `GS_MEMMOVE`
  and `GS_MEMSET`.

Two cases need nothing. Copies of a constant size that the compiler writes
out itself use 16-byte registers (32-byte ones only in a `simd fn`'s AVX
versions), and fills of zeros lose only zeros. The change is Windows-only,
and `-DGS_NO_FIRST_TOUCH` turns it off for measuring.

**Not covered.** A `simd fn`'s AVX version that itself stores 32 bytes into a
data stack's fresh top could still hit this.

**Validation.** In the fork, a stress job ran six copies of the scenario, 40
rounds each, plus the whole network test 24 times, under MSVC and clang. On
the same commit:

- without the change it corrupted
  ([run 40743479985](https://github.com/appdoze/gust/actions/runs/40743479985));
- with it, it ran clean
  ([40743489255](https://github.com/appdoze/gust/actions/runs/40743489255),
  [40744770668](https://github.com/appdoze/gust/actions/runs/40744770668));
- the handler probe's run is
  [40742991040](https://github.com/appdoze/gust/actions/runs/40742991040).

Here, on `master` (`2ed1a63d`) built with clang 22, I regenerated
`runtime_inline.h` with `--gen-runtime-header`. Then 26 fixtures from
`test/codegen` and `test/storage` that exercise appends, inserts, removals,
resizes, fills and strings gave their expected output under TinyCC, MSVC and
clang. `append_limited_queue` was left out under TinyCC, as the suite does,
because the JIT has no threads. In the fork's benchmark suite the change
cost nothing measurable beyond noise.

I didn't run the whole suite locally.

title: Add checked LSP editing and source debugging
body:
Hi Wouter!

Been exploring Goose for sometime and while building a extension for the editor I use: zed,  I noticed a couple of things Goose LSP is currently missing which this PR adds:

- **Safer editing**: checks rename and refactoring edits for accidental changes to variable bindings.
- **Nice language features**: type navigation, document highlights, range formatting, import completion, snippets, and code actions.
- **Workspace support**: indexes unopened files, watches changes, and handles unsaved buffers and workspace folders.
- **Source debugging**: maps generated native code back to Goose source lines for breakpoints and stepping.

These features work through Goose’s language server, so other editors can use them too.

title: from_bytes rejects valid index types into a global grown with `append` (stale length in the verifier)
body:
**Version:** goose v2026.3 release (`goose version`: runtime `4d3da949e563`), Linux x64.
Same result in-process (`goose file.goose`, at `-O0`, `-O2` and `--debug`) and with `goose build` (clang 21, gcc 15).

## Repro

```goose
var bytes: u8[>..] = [];
fn main() {
    bytes.append("abcd");
    let i = 2 as (u32 in bytes);          // the checked cast accepts it
    var b: (u32 in bytes)[>..] = [];
    b.push(i);
    let img = b.to_bytes();               // 4 2 0 0 0
    var rb, bok = from_bytes<(u32 in bytes)[>..]>(img);
    print("from_bytes: ", bok, " len ", rb.len);
}
```

**Observed:** `from_bytes: false len 0`

**Expected:** `from_bytes: true len 1`. Index 2 is below `bytes.len` (4), the image is the one `to_bytes` just
produced, and `from_bytes<T[>..]>(a.to_bytes())` should round-trip (`docs/design/serialization.md` §5).

## Control

The same program, with the global filled by `push` instead of `append`, prints `true`:

```goose
    for c in "abcd" { bytes.push(c); }
```

- An executed `append` breaks it whether it runs before or after `push`es. An `append` in dead code doesn't.
- `u32 upto x` (bound types) fails the same way.
- Index types into a global that was only `push`ed work, including into struct and `i32` arrays.

## Likely cause

In the generated C for `main`, after `append` the global's length lives in a local and is written back to
`GS_GL->bytes_g.len` only at the end of the function:

```c
int64_t t47 = GS_GL->bytes_g.len;
...                                   /* append: */ t47 += t0;
...
int64_t t35 = t32 ? gs_verify_u32x0(t30, t31, NULL) : -1;
...
GS_GL->bytes_g.len = t47;             /* written back at function exit */
```

while the verifier reads the global directly:

```c
static int64_t gs_verify_u32x0(const uint8_t *p, int64_t n, uint8_t *bm) {
    ... if ((uint64_t)v0 >= (uint64_t)GS_GL->bytes_g.len) return -1; ...
}
```

So it checks the index against the stale length, 0. Calls to ordinary Goose functions seem to get the
length written back first: a helper `fn seen() -> i64 { bytes.len }` reads 4. The verifier call doesn't.

## Impact and workaround

A loader that grows a pinned array with `append`, then verifies an image whose index types point into it,
rejects every valid image. Workaround: grow such arrays with `push` only. That costs a per-element loop on
load in place of one `append` (~2% of load time in our case).

Found while building https://github.com/artsensiva/symidx (`spike/bug_from_bytes_append.goose`,
`spike/bug_from_bytes_append_control.goose`).

title: Collapse short plain block comments

title: Report a case function's by-value copy held across a call into its recursive cycle
body:
Consider an enum with a variable-size variant, and case functions in a recursive cycle where only the other case calls back:

```goose
enum E { Leaf { s: u8[] }, Name { t: E..&<u32 in pool> } }
var pool: E..[>..] = [];
var outs: i64[>..<] = [];
recursive fn ev(n: E.Leaf, x: i64) { outs.push(n.s.len); }
recursive fn ev(f: E.Name&, x: i64) { ev(f.t, x); outs.push(1); }
```

And suppose `main` pushes a `Leaf` and a `Name` that points at it, and calls `ev(n, 7)`.

`goose check` accepts this. `goose build` stops with `codegen: internal: ev holds 1 data stack(s) across its call into the recursive cycle through ev (§7.8)`. This is the case #55 left open: there the variant was fixed-size, here it is not.

This is a checker gap. To give `n` its value, the dispatch in `ev(f.t, x)` copies `f.t` onto a data stack before it reads the tag, and the copy lives until the call ends (`EmitDispatch` in `codegen_calls.h`). So it is also held while the `Name` case calls back into the cycle, which §7.8 (a) forbids. The checker sees that copy only as a by-value parameter of a function in the cycle, so it reports it when the `Leaf` case itself calls back, but not when only the other case does.

Fix: `TryDispatch` in `typecheck_calls.h` now reports it. When a dispatched call is a call into the caller's cycle, each case that takes a variable-size variant by value is an error:

```text
error: ev calls into its recursive cycle through ev while case parameter n holds a by-value copy of non-fixed-size E.Leaf (§7.8): take it by reference: E.Leaf&
```

The new fixture `errors_tc/cycle_dispatch_case_by_value.goose` is the program above; without the fix it fails, as the checker accepts it. `codegen/recursive_dispatch_variable_variant_ref.goose` checks that the same cycle with `n: E.Leaf&` still compiles and runs.

Without the fix, the suite (gcc 11.5, aarch64 Linux) has one failure, the new error fixture. With it, everything passes: typecheck errors 1912 ok, generated C 692 ok, JIT 860 ok, no failures.

Prepared with the help of AI

title: Write every width and both byte orders in binary
body:
`binary` could read every width and both byte orders (#153) but write none of them, so a program producing a file header or a network message shifted bytes into an array by hand. This adds the inverse of each read, appending to the caller's `u8[>..]&`:

- `write_u8`, `write_i8`
- `write_u16le` through `write_f64le`: `u16`, `i16`, `u32`, `i32`, `u64`, `i64`, `f32`, `f64`
- a `be` version of every multi-byte write: `write_u16be` through `write_f64be`

Points for review:

- Floats give up their bits through two new runtime helpers, `gs_f32_to_bits` / `gs_f64_to_bits`: `memcpy` inverses of #153's `gs_f32_from_bits` / `gs_f64_from_bits`, next to them in `runtime_ext.h`. Goose has no bit cast, so this goes past "extern only for the OS and libm" the same way the reads did. A write followed by the read of the same name keeps the value exactly, signaling NaNs and payloads included. `runtime_inline.h` is regenerated.
- The writers are not marked `checkfree`, to match the readers. #158 can mark both together.
- There are no in-place writes (`put_u32le(data: u8[:], at, v)`) for filling in a placeholder such as a length field once it is known. That was outside the approved list; it is a likely follow-up.

Tests write mixed signed and unsigned values in both orders and check the exact bytes, read every extreme value back through a `Reader`, and round-trip four NaN bit patterns (f32 and f64, signaling and quiet with payloads) in both orders.

- `stdlib/binary.goose`, `src/runtime/runtime_ext.h`, `src/runtime_inline.h`, `test/stdlib/stdlib_binary.goose`, `docs/stdlib.md`.

The full suite passes on Linux.

title: Add split_once, the first cut of a string at a separator
body:
Parsing `key=value` pairs, headers and flags means cutting a string at its first separator. `split` builds an array for that, and `find` leaves the slice arithmetic to the caller. This adds item 1.3 of the stdlib proposal:

```goose
fn split_once(s: u8[:], sep: u8) -> const u8[:], const u8[:], bool
fn split_once(s: u8[:], sep: u8[:]) -> const u8[:], const u8[:], bool
```

It returns the part before the first `sep`, the part after, and `true`, as read-only slices into `s`; nothing is allocated. Rust's `str::split_once` and Go's `strings.Cut` do the same.

Points for review:

- When `sep` is missing it returns `s` whole, an empty slice and `false`, as `strings.Cut` does, so the first part is the whole field either way.
- **An empty `sep` is never found**: `split_once("ab", "")` gives `"ab", "", false`. That matches `split`, which treats an empty sep as absent, but differs from Rust and Go, which find it at 0 and return `"", s, true`.
- The `u8` form searches with `position`, as `split(s, u8)` does, not the `byte_set` scan.

Tests cover a single-byte and a multi-byte separator, splitting at the first occurrence only, not found, sep at the start and end, an empty `s`, an empty sep, a sep longer than `s`, and a `u8[>..]` buffer as input.

- `stdlib/std.goose`, `test/stdlib/stdlib_std.goose`, `docs/stdlib.md`.

The full suite passes on Linux.

title: Add rotations, byte swaps, ilog2, isqrt, gcd and lcm to std
body:
std had `popcount`, `clz` and `ctz` but none of the other bit and integer helpers C++20 `<bit>`, Rust and Zig provide, so programs rolled their own: an MD5 `rotl` in two benchmarks, a private `rotl` in json-serde, rotate expressions in std's own `hash`. This adds item 1.7 of the stdlib proposal:

```goose
fn rotl<N>(x: u32, n: N) -> u32      fn rotl<N>(x: u64, n: N) -> u64   // and rotr
fn byte_swap(x: u16) -> u16          // and u32, u64
fn is_pow2<T>(x: T) -> bool
fn ilog2<T>(x: T) -> i64
fn isqrt<T>(x: T) -> T
fn gcd<T>(a: T, b: T) -> T
fn lcm<T>(a: T, b: T) -> T
```

`rotl`, `rotr` and `byte_swap` are runtime functions beside `popcount`/`clz`/`ctz` in `src/runtime/runtime_ext.h`, so speed does not rest on the C compiler recognizing an idiom: MSVC's `_rotl`/`_rotr`/`_byteswap_*` intrinsics, GCC's and clang's `__builtin_bswap*`, and the masked rotate idiom `(x << s) | (x >> (-s & 31))` that GCC and clang both compile to `rol`/`ror`. TinyCC gets plain shifts. The rest are plain Goose. `hash`, `hash_lanes`, `bench/plb/json-serde/1.goose` and both mandelbrot benchmarks now call `rotl`; the benchmarks give the same output as before.

Points for review:

- **The rotate count is generic, not `i64`.** With an `i64` count, `rotl(u32, u32)` (the MD5 case) was an ambiguous call between the u32 and u64 overloads. The count is taken modulo the width, so a negative count rotates the other way, as in C++20.
- **u8 and u16 arguments need a cast** for `rotl`, `rotr` and `byte_swap`, e.g. `rotl(b as u32, 4)`, since they are ambiguous between overloads. The docs say so.
- `is_pow2` is false for x <= 0; `ilog2` is -1 for x <= 0, as positions are -1 for none.
- **`isqrt` of a negative argument fails an `assert`**, as Rust's panics. Returning -1 is the alternative.
- `gcd` and `lcm` never return a negative; `gcd(0, 0) == 0`, `lcm(x, 0) == 0`. They work on u64 magnitudes, so MIN needs no special case.
- **`gcd` and `lcm` `assert` that the result fits the type, unsigned types included** (e.g. `gcd(i64.min, 0)`, or `lcm` of the u8s 16 and 17), unlike `*`, which wraps: a wrapped divisor or multiple is meaningless.
- None are marked `checkfree`; #158 covers std's scalar functions.

Tests: `stdlib_bits` covers 0, 1, max values, MIN, counts at and past the width, negative counts and narrow types; three assert fixtures cover `gcd(i64.min, 0)`, `lcm` overflow and `isqrt` of a negative.

- `src/runtime/runtime_ext.h` (and the regenerated `src/runtime_inline.h`), `stdlib/std.goose`, `bench/plb/json-serde/1.goose`, `bench/plb/mandelbrot/1.goose`, `bench/plb/mandelbrot/1-m.goose`, `test/stdlib/stdlib_bits*.goose`, `docs/stdlib.md`, `docs/design/stdlib_design.md`.

The full suite passes on Linux.

title: Add ASCII character classes to std, in namespace ascii
body:
The repo had private copies of the same character tests: `hex_digit` in json and a sample, `is_letter` and `hex_value` in regex, and inline `'0'..'9'` range tests in json and the calculator sample. This adds item 1.8 of the stdlib proposal, in a namespace as voted:

```goose
fn ascii::is_digit(c: u8) -> bool
fn ascii::is_alpha(c: u8) -> bool
fn ascii::is_alnum(c: u8) -> bool
fn ascii::hex_value(c: u8) -> i64   // 0-15 for 0-9, a-f, A-F; -1 otherwise
```

They are ASCII only, as `<ctype.h>` in the C locale and Rust's `u8::is_ascii_*`: no byte from 0x80 up is in any class. Each range test is one wrapping `u8` subtraction and one compare, the trick base64 already uses.

Points for review:

- **The namespace lives inside `std.goose`**, declared as `fn ascii::name` the way `float_text::` already is, not as a separate `import ascii;` module. Callers write `ascii::is_digit(c)` with only `import std;`. A standalone module would be a small change if you'd rather have that.
- Callers changed: json's `hex_digit` is gone and its seven inline digit tests use `ascii::is_digit`; regex's `is_letter` and `hex_value` are gone; samples 17 (calc) and 18 (json) use the new functions.
- Left alone on purpose: the self-hosted lexer, the bench code, `is_letter` in samples 15 and 25 (lower case plus `'`, not alpha), std's base-36 `parse_int` digit decoding, and regex's frequency table.
- Not benchmarked. json's number scanning now calls `ascii::is_digit`, which should compile to the same compare.
- Possible follow-ups, not added: `is_upper`, `is_lower`, `is_hex`, and single-byte `to_upper`/`to_lower`, which regex's case folding could then use.

Tests: `stdlib_ascii` checks all 256 byte values against plain definitions, prints each class and the hex values, and probes the bytes next to each range plus high bytes such as 0xb0, 0xc1 and 0xe1, where a wrapping test would go wrong first.

- `stdlib/std.goose`, `stdlib/json.goose`, `stdlib/regex.goose`, `samples/17_calc.goose`, `samples/18_json.goose`, `test/stdlib/stdlib_ascii.goose`, `docs/stdlib.md`, `docs/design/stdlib_design.md`.

title: Add hypot, cbrt, expm1, smoothstep, wrap_angle and more to math
body:
`math` lacked several of C's `<math.h>` functions and the small shaping helpers graphics and game code reach for, so programs declared their own externs or wrote the formulas inline. This adds item 1.11 of the stdlib proposal:

- libm functions, in f64 and f32 forms: `hypot`, `cbrt`, `exp2`, `expm1`, `log1p`, `sinh`, `cosh`, `tanh`, `copysign`
- constants `E`, `INF`, `NAN`, untyped like `PI`, so `let x: f32 = INF;` works
- Goose functions, in f64 and f32 forms: `fract`, `inverse_lerp`, `smoothstep`, `wrap_angle`

Points for review:

- **`wrap_angle` maps to [-PI, PI)**, like a floored remainder: PI goes to -PI, -0.0 stays -0.0, and an infinity or NaN gives NaN. The other common choice, (-PI, PI], is Unity's `DeltaAngle`. A final fixup guards against the quotient rounding across a turn.
- **`smoothstep` with equal edges**, which GLSL leaves undefined, is 0 below the edge, 1 above it and NaN at it. Otherwise it is GLSL's: clamped t, then `t*t*(3-2t)`; reversed edges run it backwards.
- `fract(x)` is `x - floor(x)`, as in GLSL: never negative, a tiny negative x rounds to 1.0, an infinity gives NaN. `inverse_lerp(a, b, v)` is `(v - a) / (b - a)`, unclamped.
- The functions that set errno in C bind to runtime wrappers (`gs_hypot`/`gs_hypotf`, …) the way `sin` and `exp` do: 16 new `GS_LIBM` entries in `runtime_ext.h`, with `runtime_inline.h` regenerated. `copysign` never sets errno, so it binds libm directly like `floor`. For the JIT, `jit_runtime.c` and `jit_c.h` gain `exp2 expm1 log1p sinh cosh tanh copysign` (`cbrt` and `hypot` were already there).
- `NAN`'s sign is unspecified, and the docs say so.
- Additions go at the end of each section of `math.goose`, to keep conflicts with #158 small. Nothing is marked `checkfree`.

Tests extend `stdlib_math`. Values that depend on libm are checked within a tolerance; only results C's Annex F fixes are printed exactly (signed zeros through `expm1`, `log1p`, `sinh`, `tanh`, `cbrt`; `tanh(±inf)`, `cosh(-inf)`, `expm1(-inf)`, `exp2(-inf)`, `log1p(-1)`, `hypot(-inf, NAN)`), so the output should match on any libm. A NaN's sign is never printed. A 2000-point sweep checks the results stay in range at both widths.

- `stdlib/math.goose`, `src/runtime/runtime_ext.h`, `src/runtime_inline.h`, `src/jit_runtime.c`, `src/runtime/jit_c.h`, `test/stdlib/stdlib_math.goose`, `docs/stdlib.md`.

The full suite passes on Linux.

title: Add rand_range, rand_f32 and rand_gaussian to std
body:
std's random numbers gave an integer below n, a u64 and an f64 in [0, 1), so a range, an f32 or a Gaussian sample meant arithmetic at every call site. This adds item 1.12 of the stdlib proposal, with the range taking a lower bound and a size as voted:

```goose
fn rand_range(r: rng&, size: i64) -> i64            // in [0, size)
fn rand_range(r: rng&, lo: i64, size: i64) -> i64   // in [lo, lo + size)
fn rand_f32(r: rng&) -> f32                          // in [0, 1), 24 bits
fn rand_gaussian(r: rng&) -> f64                     // standard normal distribution
```

- `rand_range` asserts `size > 0` and returns `lo + rand_int(r, size)`, so it is unbiased; the caller keeps `lo + size - 1` within `i64`. The overload without `lo` starts at 0.
- `rand_f32` takes the top 24 bits the way `rand_flt` takes 53.
- `rand_gaussian` uses Marsaglia's polar method, built on `rand_flt`, `sqrt` and `log`. It is named for Gauss rather than `rand_normal` (as Java's `nextGaussian` and Python's `random.gauss` are), because in game code "normal" reads as a random unit vector.
- `rand_bool` was dropped in review: `rand_range(2)` says the same.

Points for review:

- **std reaches libm through private externs.** std imports nothing, and importing `math` would put all of libm in the global namespace of every program that imports std. So std.goose declares `extern fn rand_detail::sqrt` and `rand_detail::log`, bound to the runtime's `gs_sqrt` and `gs_log`. A program importing std, math and vec together still compiles and runs.
- **One draw per call.** The polar method produces two; keeping the second would need a field in `rng` and break `rng { seed }`, so it is dropped (documented). A seed always gives the same draws; across platforms they match only as far as libm's `log` does, which the docs also say.
- Possible follow-ups, not added: an f32 `rand_gaussian`, or one taking a mean and sigma.

Tests: fixed-seed sequences for `rand_range` and `rand_f32`, checked against an independent model of splitmix64 and `rand_int`; `rand_range(n)` matching `rand_int(n)` draw for draw; bounds (negative lo, size 1, the top of `i64`, lo = `i64.min` with size = `i64.max`, `rand_f32` on the 2^-24 grid); for `rand_gaussian`, same-seed reproducibility and, over 100000 draws, mean, variance and the share within ±1 inside tolerances, printed as true/false. An abort fixture checks `rand_range(r, 5, 0)`.

- `stdlib/std.goose`, `test/stdlib/stdlib_std.goose`, `test/stdlib/stdlib_rand_range_empty.goose`, `docs/stdlib.md`.

The full suite passes on Linux.

title: Add parse_uint for values up to u64.max
body:
`parse_int` returns an `i64`, so it cannot read a value above `i64.max`: a u64 hash, an ID or a bit mask written out in hex or decimal. This adds item 1.13 of the stdlib proposal:

```goose
fn parse_uint(s: u8[:], base: i64 = 10) -> u64, bool
```

It follows `parse_int`'s rules: the whole string is read; an optional `+` is allowed (as Rust's `from_str_radix` allows it); an empty string, a lone `+`, whitespace, underscores and `0x` prefixes are rejected. A `-` is rejected, `-0` included. Overflow is caught exactly with `v > (u64.max - d) / base` before each multiply-add, so the value never wraps. Failure gives `0, false`.

Points for review:

- **The digit decoding moved into a new `parse_digit(c: u8, base: i64) -> i64`**, which both parsers call; `parse_int` behaves exactly as before. std has no private functions, so this is a visible name, as `format_flt_mul` is. It overlaps `ascii::hex_value` from #185: whichever merges second can rename it or build it on `ascii::`.
- **Neither parser checks the base.** A base above 36 accepts every letter, and base 1 accepts only zeros. `parse_uint` keeps that so the two match; limiting both to 2–36 would be a small follow-up.
- A base below 1 returns false rather than aborting: the base is converted to u64 only after a digit has passed the `d < base` check.

Tests: `stdlib_parse_uint_range` has 43 cases: u64.max and u64.max+1 in bases 2, 8, 10, 16 and 36, i64.max and i64.max+1, values between them, leading zeros, the first digit outside each base, mixed case, base 0 and base -16, signs, the empty string, spaces, `1_000`, `0x10` and `12x`.

- `stdlib/std.goose`, `test/stdlib/stdlib_parse_uint_range.goose`, `test/stdlib/stdlib_std.goose`, `docs/stdlib.md`.

The full suite passes on Linux.

Offer UTF-8 positions to language clients that ask for them
body:
Closes the Position encoding item in docs/design/language_server.md.

What changed

goose lsp previously always negotiated UTF-16 positions. It now respects the client's general.positionEncodings capability during initialization.

Clients that support and request UTF-8 (such as Neovim 0.10+ and Helix) will now get "positionEncoding": "utf-8", with columns measured in bytes to match the compiler's native representation. All other clients, including VS Code, continue using UTF-16 as before.

Implementation
- src/lsp_rpc.h: Added a utf8_positions flag, set during initialization. Utf16Col is now ProtocolCol, and both it and ByteCol account for the negotiated encoding. UTF-8 positions that fall inside a multibyte character are normalized to the character's start.
- src/lsp.h: Reads capabilities.general.positionEncodings and responds with the selected encoding instead of always advertising UTF-16.
- src/lsp_workspace.h and src/lsp_features.h: Updated diagnostic ranges and semantic token lengths to use ProtocolCol.
- UTF-32 is not supported. Clients that only offer UTF-32 fall back to UTF-16.

Tests
- Added test/lsp/encodings.goose with identifiers and an error following é, ∑, and 🦆 to cover cases where UTF-8 and UTF-16 column offsets differ.
- Added check_position_encodings to test/lsp_protocol.py. It tests clients offering no encoding, UTF-16, UTF-32, and UTF-8 in both first and last positions.
- For each case, the test verifies the negotiated encoding, error ranges, definition, hover, references, and semantic tokens for total, using columns calculated from the source text.
- Also verifies that a UTF-8 hover request at a byte offset inside 🦆 doesn't incorrectly resolve to a name.
- The new test fails against the previous implementation and passes with this change.

Validation:

- python test/run_tests.py -j 8 — all tests passed on macOS arm64.
- test/lsp_sweep.py --quick — no failures.
- Manually tested with Neovim 0.12. The client reports offset_encoding = "utf-8", and hover, definition, references, rename, and diagnostics all resolve to the correct positions.

Documentation
- Updated docs/design/language_server.md (§4 and §10) and docs/implementation.md.

title: slice_pool: freed runs never return memory while the pool lives (measurements + a u8 page-discard prototype)
body:
## Summary

`docs/design/owning_dynamic_data.md` suggests running the open/edit/close sequence against slice pools and measuring live bytes, high water, committed bytes and copies before deciding on further work. I did that, on Windows and Linux, and I also tried the "Returning free memory" idea from the same note as a small prototype.

- With a long-lived `slice_pool<u8>` whose buffers open, grow and close in any order, the working set stays at the pool's high water (163–169 MiB) after the live data has dropped to a few MiB. The same operation sequence replayed with the C runtime's `malloc` ends at 5–11 MiB.
- The best way I found to give the memory back with today's Goose (keep the pool in a worker, compact by handing live buffers to a new worker) gets back down at the end, but costs ~50 ms pauses per compaction, a message round trip on every operation, and the main program can no longer see the bytes.
- The prototype (about 70 lines plus the regenerated `runtime_inline.h`: one runtime function and two `slice_pool<u8>` functions) returns the complete pages inside freed elements to the OS. In the same scenario its working set and per-operation cost track `malloc` closely.

Prototype branch: https://github.com/johmaru/goose/tree/slice-pool-discard-pages (commit `b218ebc8`, on top of `eadca409`)

Mainly I'd like to know whether this is something you'd want in Goose at all, and if so, in what form. The branch is there so the numbers can be checked, not as a proposal for merging as is (questions at the end).

## Why the memory stays

This is documented behaviour, not a bug; I'm only putting a number on it.

- `free_slice` / `realloc_slice` record free spans in the span tree; `items` only ever grows (`stdlib/slice_pool.goose` has no `pop`, `resize` or `clear` of `items`).
- `trim_memory()` discards pages above each data-stack top. A pool's free spans sit below `items`' top, so it cannot reach them.
- Memory is returned per owner lifetime: at scope exit (then `trim_memory()`), or when the worker owning the pool returns. A root owner cannot be reassigned, so a pool that must outlive its buffers keeps its high water.

Isolated, 64 MiB, Windows (working set / commit, MiB):

| Case | after free | after `trim_memory()` |
|---|---|---|
| plain `u8[>..]`, `clear()` | 67.9 / 67.7 | 3.9 / 0.6 |
| `slice_pool`: `free_slice` (also: freeing the last run, `realloc_slice` to 1 MiB, `recycle_all`) | 67.9 / 68.7 | 67.9 / 64.7 |
| `slice_pool` owned by a function local, after it returns | 67.9 / 68.7 | 3.9 / 0.6 |
| `slice_pool` owned by a worker, after `thread_wait` (no trim) | 3.9 / 3.6 | – |

## Scenario

Editor-style buffers in one `slice_pool<u8>`:

- up to 64 open buffers; 20,000 random steps: open 30% (4 KiB–8 MiB, log-uniform), grow 55% (256 B–512 KiB, log-uniform, `realloc_slice` to the exact new length), close 15%
- afterwards, close all but the 4 newest buffers
- working set and commit sampled every 500 steps; peak live data is 120–125 MiB
- 3 seeds; the operation sequence is written to a trace file and replayed with `malloc`/`realloc`/`free` (+ `memset`, as `alloc_slice` writes its defaults) as a baseline

Environment: Windows 11 Pro, i7-13700KF, MSVC 19.51 (UCRT). Linux: x86-64, gcc 13.3, glibc 2.39. Performance numbers were taken on `0357b1c` with the prototype applied; the branch was rebased onto `eadca409` and re-tested for correctness, not re-measured.

## Results (Windows, 3 seeds, MiB)

| | WS mean | WS peak | WS after closing all but 4 (0.6–5.5 MiB live) | open | grow | close |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `slice_pool` today | 147–154 | 163–169 | 163–169 | 93–98 µs | 71–77 µs | 0.12–0.21 µs |
| worker + compaction | 124–135 | 167–187 | 5–16 | 127–134 µs | 96–98 µs | 5.4–5.8 µs |
| **prototype** (`free_slice_discard` / `realloc_slice_discard`) | **84–91** | **117–119** | **6–11** | 296–343 µs | 173–200 µs | 101–114 µs |
| UCRT `malloc` (same trace) | 85–92 | 118–123 | 5–11 | 289–338 µs | 364–447 µs | 98–146 µs |

- Mean commit charge over all seeds: today 152, prototype 98, `malloc` 85.
- With geometric growth (capacity doubled), the prototype's mean WS is 130–146 and `malloc`'s 130–146; today's is 230–238.
- Copies done by `realloc_slice` are unchanged by the prototype (6.3–6.6 GiB per run in this scenario), since placement is the same.
- Linux shows the same pattern (seed 12345: RSS mean 152.8 → 83.0, after closing 165 → 8.4). glibc's `malloc` only gets back to a few MiB after `malloc_trim`.

The slower open/close is what returning memory costs: the close pays for the decommit/`madvise`, and the next allocation that reuses the space pays page faults. `malloc` pays the same in this scenario (blocks above ~1 MiB get their own `VirtualAlloc` region on Windows and are released on `free`).

<details>
<summary>The worker + compaction workaround, and why one worker per buffer does not work</summary>

The pool lives in a "store" worker; main sends each operation as a message and waits for an acknowledgement. When the pool's high water reaches twice the bytes the buffers occupy (and at least 16 MiB more), main spawns a new store; the old one sends every live buffer through a queue and returns, which releases its regions.

- 11–14 compactions per run, 660–859 MiB moved through queues
- each compaction pauses 47–52 ms on average (max 78 ms); almost all of it is copying bytes (old pool → queue node → new store → pool), worker start/exit is under 3 ms
- commit spikes during a handoff (old pool at high water + queued copies + new pool)
- every operation pays two thread wake-ups (close: 0.15 µs → 5.5 µs)
- main cannot read a buffer without copying it out of the store

One worker per buffer would avoid the copies, but there is one queue per message type and no way to address a particular worker, so main could not send an edit to a buffer's own worker.

</details>

## The prototype

```c
// src/runtime/runtime_os.h
GS_API uint8_t gs_discard_pages(sl_u8 s) {
#if defined(__APPLE__)
    (void)s;
    return 0;            // not tried on macOS; MADV_DONTNEED is unreliable there (see gs_trim_memory)
#else
    uintptr_t page = (uintptr_t)gs_page_size;
    if (s.len <= 0 || page == 0) return 1;
    uintptr_t start = ((uintptr_t)s.data + page - 1) / page * page;   // complete pages only:
    uintptr_t end = ((uintptr_t)s.data + (uintptr_t)s.len) / page * page;  // edges may be shared with live runs
    if (start >= end) return 1;
    size_t len = (size_t)(end - start);
#ifdef _WIN32
    return (uint8_t)(VirtualFree((void *)start, len, MEM_DECOMMIT) != 0);
#else
    return (uint8_t)(madvise((void *)start, len, MADV_DONTNEED) == 0);
#endif
#endif
}
```

`stdlib/slice_pool.goose` gets `free_slice_discard(p: slice_pool<u8>&, s)` (free, then discard the run's pages) and `realloc_slice_discard(p: slice_pool<u8>&, s, n)` (realloc, then discard the part of the old run the result does not cover: the dropped tail of a shrink, or the old place of a run that moved). Existing functions are unchanged.

- On Windows nothing else was needed: the access-fault handler already commits again on a touch anywhere in a region's usable part.
- A discarded page reads back as zeros, a valid `u8` and what `alloc_slice` writes anyway, so stale views stay type-safe. This is why it is limited to `u8`, as the design note says.
- Tests: a dedicated test (neighbours sharing edge pages keep their bytes, stale views read zeros, reuse, shrink, move) passes on Windows and Linux in release and debug builds; the full `run_tests.py` suite passes on Linux on `eadca409`. I have not run the full suite on Windows.

## Known limitations

- `u8` only.
- Windows: reading (not just writing) a discarded page commits it again, so a stale read, or a walk over the whole of `items` (e.g. `to_bytes(pool.items)`), brings the memory back. Linux maps the shared zero page and does not. I checked that placeholders plus a shared read-only zero section (`VirtualAlloc2` / `MapViewOfFile3`) avoid this (reading 64 MiB of it kept private WS at 0.3 MiB and commit at 0.7 MiB), but that would change how regions are reserved, works in 64 KiB units and splits regions into many allocations, so I left it out.
- Commit charge is somewhat higher than `malloc`'s (98 vs 85 MiB mean), probably because the fault handler commits 1 MiB chunks.
- Fragmentation and `items.len` (address space) are unchanged; only pages are returned. Pages straddling a free span's edge are kept, so up to two pages per free.
- Passing a stale view of discarded pages to the kernel (e.g. `write_file`) is untested on Windows.
- macOS: does nothing.

## Questions

The first one decides whether the rest matter:

1. Is returning memory from a live pool something you'd want Goose to support? If so, would you welcome a PR along these lines (opt-in page return for pools of zero-valid element types), or would you rather solve it another way, for example option A from the design note, or leave it to applications?

If the answer to 1 is yes, these decide what the PR would look like:

2. API shape: separate functions (as in the prototype), a per-pool setting, a size threshold (return only free spans of at least N pages, which is roughly what Windows' heap does), or deferred return (let free pages accumulate and return them once they pass a threshold, like glibc's trim threshold)? The prototype returns pages on every free, which is why its open/close cost more than the worker + compaction workaround's in total; batching might keep the memory behaviour at a lower cost. I have not measured the threshold or deferred variants yet.
3. Is there a preferred way to express "all-zero bytes are a valid value" so this could go beyond `u8` (e.g. `f32`/`f16` buffers such as an inference KV cache)?
4. Is the Windows read-recommit behaviour acceptable as a documented limitation for a first version, or would you want it fixed before merging? The fix I tested (placeholders plus a shared zero view) changes how every data-stack region is reserved, so I'd rather know before starting on it.

I'm happy to keep it at this issue if this isn't a direction you want to take.

Benchmark programs and per-seed results: https://gist.github.com/johmaru/3162203a5a10366d29e83a69e400b23a

## How this was done

I worked on this with an AI assistant (Claude), which wrote most of the benchmark and prototype code and ran the measurements. I decided what to measure and where to look, and sent it back whenever a conclusion was something I couldn't explain myself: the first numbers were Linux-only and are redone here on Windows, which I mainly use, and the reason the pool keeps its pages was narrowed down with the isolated cases above before I accepted it. I reviewed the runtime C code, and the macOS branch does nothing because neither of us can test it.

title: Reject relative references in a from_bytes grow-shrink result
body:
Hi Wouter,

I found a hole in from_bytes: loading a verified image as a T[>..<] gives the shrink scan nothing to see.

The verifier checks each link against the loaded image, and that is the last check a link ever gets. A pop of the result frees the element a link names, while the array's own elements still hold the link. The store rule that keeps references into a grow-shrink array out of storage (spec 5.2) never runs, because the verified copy is not a store. The stale link then reads and writes whatever later lands in the freed slots, and ASan sees nothing, since the data stack is a single reservation.

A short reproduction on master (40369bd1): load a six-element image of `struct N { v: i64, next: N&<u32>? }` as `N[>..<]`, pop five, and read `arr[0].next`. It prints element 5's value from freed memory; writing through the reference persists past the array's length, and the offset is whatever the image's link bytes said, so the writer picks the slot.

The fix rejects the combination at the call: a `from_bytes<T[>..<]>` whose elements hold relative references is an error naming the type. The same image loads as a `T[>..]` as before, and the grow-shrink kind keeps its coverage in test/storage with `i64` elements. The check is a type walk at the call site, so it costs nothing at run time and nothing for programs that never load into a T[>..<]. The docs list the new exclusion beside the existing ones (serialization.md section 4, reference.md section 23). Unrelated to the open index-type issues #177 and #175, which are about index fields. If you would rather keep the capability, the other shape I see is a load-provenance bit the shrink checks consult; happy to rework it that way.

With a Release build, the full baseline profile runs clean: 1912 typecheck error fixtures, 689 generated-C programs at -O0 and -O2, 857 JIT runs and 52 samples. The two expected-stderr fixtures that fail here (native_stack_overflow, render_reference_cycle) fail the same way on unpatched master on this machine, where a data stack overflows before the native one does.

The new fixture is test/errors_tc/serialize_grow_shrink_refs.goose.

title: Zero the union tail of a fixed-mode enum value
body:
Hi Wouter,

to_bytes was writing native stack bytes into save files.

A fixed-mode enum's slot is as wide as its largest variant, and a C temporary of it was declared uninitialized, so a smaller variant left a tail holding whatever the native stack held before. to_bytes writes the whole slot, so the image carried those bytes out. On this machine, saving a pool of narrow variants right after a recursion put 969 distinct pointer-shaped values in a 17 KB image, different ones each run, stack and PIE addresses both.

HasUninitSlots already covers the unused slots of a limited array, and every FixedLocal site asks it before declaring a temporary, so the fix is the one missing case: a fixed-mode enum counts as holding unwritten bytes when any variant is smaller than the slot. The same leak drops to zero across runs with the patch.

The zeroing costs one store, and only for a temporary whose enum actually has a tail: an enum whose variants are all the same width, and every non-enum type, are exactly as before. The new fixture, test/storage/serialize_adt_tail.goose, pins that an image of narrow variants has zeros in every tail byte. The baseline profile's storage tests are unchanged otherwise.

Happy to fold this into a different shape if you see a better place for the check.

title: Bound LSP frames and JSON nesting
body:
Hi Wouter,

two one-frame kills of the language server, both before any request.

A frame with Content-Length 9223372036854775807 makes body.resize throw length_error on the reader thread, which has no handler of its own, so the process aborts. A frame whose JSON nests arrays 7284 deep (2312 under ASan) recurses JsonReader::Value until the native stack is gone. Opening a deeply nested .goose file reaches the same recursion through didOpen's analysis, so an editor restoring a hostile workspace dies without any request at all; that parser and typechecker side is the same unbounded recursion as the compiler's, which I will file separately with the measurements.

The fix here is transport-level: a frame is at most 64 MiB, since an editor message is kilobytes and a bigger claim ends the stream; nesting is capped at 1000 with the parser's own diagnostic; and the reader loop can no longer throw past its frame. The cost is one comparison per frame header and one counter the parser already had room for. The normal initialize/didOpen flow is unchanged, and the CMake file API replies nest six deep at most, so the cap does not touch them.

With a Release build: the deep-array frame is rejected and the server stays up, the huge Content-Length exits cleanly, and initialize answers as before. test/lsp_protocol.py and the LSP sweep are unaffected.

Happy to adjust the limits or the diagnostic wording.

title: tutorial section "the array family" is confusing
body:
Thanks for making an interesting language. Questions I had while reading through the tutorial for the first time, I re-read "the array family" section multiple times and still had some difficultly clicking.

https://github.com/aardappel/goose/blob/eadca409f68210893f366e60d0c2f0dc29a339be/docs/tutorial.md?plain=1#L397

This is the first time `varint` occurs in the document, before it's ever defined, so this jumps out as not making sense (what is a varint? an int variable? a special integer type? must it be a constant or type varint?). Either a link to the later part of the document, or a short explanation here would be great. What does "usually" mean here? What's the maximum?

https://github.com/aardappel/goose/blob/eadca409f68210893f366e60d0c2f0dc29a339be/docs/tutorial.md?plain=1#L398

Okay, why the word "inline" here, I thought everything is stored inline? Should this say fixed capacity `k`, and the actual "active" length is stored as metadata? And why is the length "small"? Is that enforced by the compiler? Is there a limit to `k`?

https://github.com/aardappel/goose/blob/eadca409f68210893f366e60d0c2f0dc29a339be/docs/tutorial.md?plain=1#L399

Can length and capacity be more explicitly defined here? Is it equivalent to `size()` and `capacity()` on a `std::vector`, but where capacity is frozen but the "active" length is not?

https://github.com/aardappel/goose/blob/eadca409f68210893f366e60d0c2f0dc29a339be/docs/tutorial.md?plain=1#L400

Maybe it's worth marking within the table that the bottom two rows `T[>..]` and `T[>..<]` are special in that they take up the "special variable data slot" with unrestricted capacity. I know it's explained a few paragraphs later but it might be worth highlighting these two.

https://github.com/aardappel/goose/blob/eadca409f68210893f366e60d0c2f0dc29a339be/docs/tutorial.md?plain=1#L403

I immediately wondered how does alignment work if I have metadata that isn't 4- or 8-byte aligned, and I'm storing 4-byte or 8-byte values, and on a CPU that expects aligned reads/writes? Will there be padding added?

title: Proposal: whether a field has a default, in `const for ... in fields<T>`
body:
*From [Honk](https://github.com/korolenkowork/honk), a web framework written in Goose. The workarounds quoted below are in its source.*

## Summary

Let a `fields<T>` expansion ask, at specialization time, whether the
current field declares a default. This builds on the "Defaults and
annotations" item in `docs/design/const_for.md` §10, in its narrowest form:
a compile-time `bool`, with no access to the default expression and nothing
evaluated during expansion.

```goose
const for <N, A> in fields<T> {
    if !has_default(A) && !seen(N) { missing(N); }
}
```

## Motivation

A library that reads values into structs needs to know which fields the
input must supply. Honk validates JSON request bodies against plain Goose
structs, as a serde derive or Pydantic would:

```goose
struct ItemIn {
    name: u8[..32],             // must be sent
    price: f64,                 // must be sent
    tax: f64 = 0.2,             // may be left out
    discount: f64 = 0.0,        // may be left out, but Honk cannot tell
}
```

Today an expansion can see each field's *value* in `T { .. }`, but not
whether that value came from a declared default or from the type's zero.
Honk therefore guesses: a field is required when its value in `T { .. }`
is its type's zero. That guess gets `discount` wrong, and the error only
appears at run time, as a client being told `Field required`. Honk adds
`honk::Opt<T>` as an escape hatch, but users have to know the rule before
they hit it.

The same question comes up for any reader of external data: JSON, CSV,
config files, query strings, command-line flags, and the migration of old
serialized records.

## Proposed design

A specialization-time predicate on an accessor:

```goose
has_default(A) -> bool        // a constant: does this field declare `= ...`?
```

* It is valid only where an accessor from `fields<T>` is in scope, like
  `v.A`, and it folds to `true` or `false` in each expansion. Dead branches
  then fold away, as `if` on a constant already does.
* It does not evaluate the default. §10 notes that "defaults may contain
  runtime work and must not be executed during expansion". The predicate
  only asks whether the declaration has a `= ...`. The value is still
  obtained as today, through `T { .. }`, at run time.
* A variant payload's fields (`fields<V>`) answer the same way.

### Alternative spellings

* A third binding `<N, A, D>`, where `D` is a `bool` constant. This
  overlaps with the type binding `<N, A, U>` that §10 already considers,
  and binding counts are exact in v1, so it would need its own rule.
* A source filter, `fields_with_default<T>` / `fields_without_default<T>`.
  It needs no new expression form, but splits one loop into two.

The predicate keeps v1's two bindings unchanged and composes with a future
`U` binding.

## What it removes in Honk

```goose
// today (honk/model.goose): a guess, with five overloads for the guess
fn required_field(v: i64, k: i64) -> bool { v == 0 }
fn required_field(v: f64, k: i64) -> bool { v == 0.0 }
fn required_field(v: bool, k: i64) -> bool { false }
...

// with the proposal
if !has_default(A) && !seen[i] { add_error(e, "missing", loc, "Field required", ""); }
```

The generated OpenAPI `required` lists would become exact as well.

## Compatibility and cost

* Purely additive: no existing program changes meaning. `has_default` is a
  contextual name, like `fields` and `types`.
* No runtime cost, since the answer is a constant per expansion. Compile
  time grows by one flag read per field.
* The compiler already knows, at every struct literal, which fields have
  defaults, because `T { .. }` and missing-field errors depend on it.

## Open questions

* Should a field whose type has a default of its own (a nested struct whose
  fields all have defaults) count as having one? This proposal says no:
  only a written `= ...` counts, which is what users can see in the
  declaration.
* Generic structs: `has_default` answers for the instantiation, which is
  the same for every instantiation because defaults are written once.

title: Proposal: a field's type in `fields<T>`, and size parameters
body:
*From [Honk](https://github.com/korolenkowork/honk), a web framework written in Goose. The workarounds quoted below are in its source.*

## Summary

Two related changes, each useful alone, that let generic code handle every
member of the array family without enumerating sizes:

1. **The field-type binding** `const for <N, A, U> in fields<T>` from
   `docs/design/const_for.md` §10, with `U` bound to the field's read type.
2. **Size parameters** on generic functions, `fn f<let K>(s: u8[..K])`, so
   that one overload covers `u8[..K]` for every `K`. Today the spec says
   "there are no size parameters (`fn f<N>(a: i64[N])` is an error)" (§3.3).

## Motivation

Honk's model code walks a struct's fields and picks a reader, writer or
JSON Schema writer for each field through overload resolution:

```goose
const for <N, A> in fields<T> { read_value(r, dst.A, e, loc, BY_TYPE); }
```

Two things make that harder than it should be.

**There is no way to say "any other type is a model".** An overload set
needs a catch-all for nested structs, but a generic `T` parameter ranks the
same as `T[:]`, so arrays become ambiguous. Honk works around this with a
dispatch token: every specific overload takes `k: i64`, the catch-all takes
`k: f64`, and each call passes an `i64`. That works only because an
integer-to-float conversion is the candidate the compiler tries last
(§7.1). The trick is correct but obscure, and it repeats through nine
overload sets. With `U` bound, the library could dispatch on the type
itself, by `types<...>` membership or by passing `U` explicitly.

**Limited arrays need one overload per capacity.** A request field
`name: u8[..32]` must be read by an overload whose parameter is exactly
`u8[..32]&`, since a `u8[:]` cannot grow and a generic `T&` cannot append.
Honk therefore lists ten capacities (8 to 4096) in each of four overload
sets. Any other capacity fails to compile with an error about `fields`,
which confuses users:

```goose
fn read_value(r: json::Reader&, dst: u8[..8]&, ...)    { read_limited(r, dst, 8, ...); }
fn read_value(r: json::Reader&, dst: u8[..16]&, ...)   { read_limited(r, dst, 16, ...); }
// ... eight more, in four overload sets
```

With size parameters this becomes one overload:

```goose
fn read_value<let K>(r: json::Reader&, dst: u8[..K]&, ...) { read_limited(r, dst, K, ...); }
```

## Proposed design

### 1. `<N, A, U>`

As sketched in §10. `U` is the field's **read type**: the type `v.A` has as
an expression. For a `varint` field that is `i64`. For a resizable or
variable-size field it is the field's declared type, usable only where
that type is legal (as a reference parameter's pointee, say), which matches
§10's warning that "not every storage type is legal as an ordinary function
result".

`U` behaves as a type parameter inside the fragment, so it composes with
what exists today:

```goose
const for <N, A, U> in fields<T> {
    read_into<U>(r, dst.A);          // dispatch on U explicitly
}
```

### 2. Size parameters

* Syntax `<let K>` in a function's generic list, to mark a constant rather
  than a type. `let` already means "an immutable binding", and `let` globals
  already serve as compile-time sizes.
* `K` is inferred from an argument's type (`u8[..32]` binds `K = 32`), and
  may be given explicitly (`f<32>(...)`).
* Inside the body `K` is an `i64` constant, usable wherever an array size
  or a `const for` constant is today.
* Each distinct `K` is its own specialization, as each type is now, so
  there is no runtime cost and code size grows per size used.
* Overload ranking: binding a size is a generic exact match, the same rank
  as binding a type. `u8[..K]&` therefore beats a coercion to `u8[:]`, as
  `T[>..]&` does today.

## What it removes in Honk

The 40 capacity overloads, the dispatch-token parameter on nine overload sets,
and the "capacities 8 to 4096" limit in the docs. The error users see for
an unsupported field type would name their field type instead of
`fields requires a concrete struct`.

## Compatibility and cost

* Both are additive. `<let K>` is new syntax in a generic list where `let`
  is not legal today. A third binding in `fields` is new, and the existing
  two-binding form is unchanged.
* Specialization per size follows the existing model. The compiler already
  tracks array sizes as part of types.

## Open questions

* Should size parameters also be allowed on structs (`struct Buf<let K> {
  data: u8[..K] }`)? Useful, but larger: it touches type identity and
  serialization. This proposal is functions only.
* `T[k]` fixed arrays would benefit too (`fn sum<T, let K>(a: T[K])`),
  although slices already cover most read-only uses.

title: Proposal: generic `thread_fn`, and replies to one worker
body:
*From [Honk](https://github.com/korolenkowork/honk), a web framework written in Goose. The workarounds quoted below are in its source.*

## Summary

Two additions to the concurrency surface, in the spirit of open item 9 of
the spec's Appendix B ("queue fairness/capacity, select, worker-local
init"):

1. **Generic `thread_fn`**, instantiated per spawn site like any generic
   function, so a library can start workers that run code its caller names.
2. **Addressed replies**: a way for one worker to send a value that only a
   chosen worker receives, so request and reply between threads needs no
   code outside Goose.

## Motivation

Honk runs a web server on N workers. Each worker accepts connections on a
shared socket and answers them with the app's routes.

**1. The app has to write the worker.** A `thread_fn` cannot be generic,
so Honk cannot provide "a worker that serves app". Every app writes one:

```goose
let CONFIG = honk::Config { port: 8000, .. };
thread_fn worker(fd: i64, id: i64) { honk::serve_on(fd, id, CONFIG, app); }
fn main() { honk::serve_threads(CONFIG, 0, worker); }
```

instead of

```goose
fn main() { honk::serve_threads(honk::Config { port: 8000, .. }, app); }
```

Besides the boilerplate, `Config` must become a `let` global, because the
worker can only read flat or static globals and `Config` holds slices.

**2. Replies need C.** Shared state lives in one store thread. Handlers on
any worker send it a command and wait for the answer. Queues are one per
type for the whole process, so a reply put on `Reply`'s queue goes to
whichever worker takes it first, not the one that asked. Honk solves this
with about 100 lines of C ([`honk/src/honk_mail.c`](https://github.com/korolenkowork/honk/blob/main/honk/src/honk_mail.c)): a mailbox per worker
id, guarded by a mutex and a condition variable, holding the reply as a
`to_bytes` image with a sequence number. It works, but it steps outside
the language's guarantees for something the language is close to
offering.

## Proposed design

### 1. Generic `thread_fn`

```goose
thread_fn serve_worker<App>(fd: i64, id: i64) { accept_loop(fd, id, App); }

fn serve_threads<App>(n: i64) {
    for i in n { thread_spawn(serve_worker<App>, fd, i + 1); }
}
```

* A generic `thread_fn` is instantiated at each `thread_spawn` that names
  it with concrete arguments, and each instantiation is a separate worker
  program, exactly as a non-generic `thread_fn` is now. Spawn sites are
  static (§11.2 already lets `thread_spawn(W, ...)` take a function
  parameter bound to a `thread_fn`), so the set of worker programs remains
  known at compile time.
* Type and function-value parameters are compile-time entities and never
  cross the thread boundary, so the "flat arguments" rule (§11.2) applies
  to value parameters only, unchanged.
* `thread_spawn(serve_worker<App>, ...)` needs the existing explicit form
  `f<...>` to be accepted as a function value in argument position. Today
  `spawn_all<worker<handle>>(3)` reports `unknown type: worker`.

### 2. Addressed replies

The smallest addition that removes the C:

```goose
fn thread_id() -> i64                    // this worker's id; 0 on main
fn qput_to(id: i64, v) -> bool           // a queue of v's type that only worker `id` reads
fn qget_mine<T>() -> T                   // takes the next T addressed to this worker
fn qget_mine<T>(ms: i64) -> T, bool      // with a timeout
```

* Each worker gets one private queue per type, created lazily, and the
  existing shared queues are unchanged.
* Values must be flat, as for every queue.
* With these, Honk's `ask` becomes plain Goose:

```goose
fn ask<Req, Resp>(req: Req) -> Resp {
    qput(Call<Req> { from: thread_id(), req: req });
    let reply, ok = qget_mine<Resp>(ask_timeout_ms);
    ...
}
```

A per-worker queue also gives a natural shape to worker-local init and to
`select`, both already named in item 9.

## Compatibility and cost

* Generic `thread_fn` relaxes an error into a feature: every program that
  compiles today means the same.
* Addressed queues are new builtins. Their cost is a per-worker table of
  queues, paid only by programs that call them.

## Open questions

* Should `thread_id()` be the spawn id `thread_spawn` returns? That is
  simplest for a supervisor, which already holds those ids.
* Ordering between `qput_to` and shared `qput` from the same sender: this
  proposal guarantees order per queue only, as today.

title: Add read_stdin(out, max), which reads stdin in pieces
body:
## Why

Closes #118, as option 1 there. `read_stdin(out)` holds the whole stream before a program can work on any of it, so a program that sums 3 GB piped from `head -c 3000000000 /dev/zero` needs `--stack-reserve 8G` and peaks at 2.86 GB resident. Read 64 KB at a time with this overload, it prints the same `3000000000 0` and peaks at 1.6 MB, with no `--stack-reserve`.

binji asked whether this has to be specific to stdin unless Goose gets file handles. I think it does for now: stdin has no path, so `read_file` cannot reach it, and mmap cannot map a pipe. If file handles come out of #115, stdin can be one of them, and this overload becomes a thin call on that API, as `resource_dir()` is over `resource_dir(out)`.

It keeps the README's goals as `read_stdin(out)` does: the bytes go into the caller's builder, with no allocator and no handle to close, and it adds no state for threads to share.

## What changed

- Stdlib: `extern fn read_stdin(out: u8[>..]&, max: i64) -> bool` in stdlib/os.goose, beside `read_stdin(out)`. It appends up to `max` bytes to `out` and waits until it has them or input ends, like `fread`. It returns false, having appended nothing, when no bytes were left or `max` is 0 or less. As with `read_stdin(out)`, a read error looks the same as the end of input.
- Runtime: `gs_os_read_stdin_max` in src/runtime/runtime_os.h, the same `fread` loop through a 64 KB buffer as `gs_os_read_stdin`, stopping at `max`; declared in runtime_ext.h.
- `src/runtime_inline.h` is regenerated with `goose --gen-runtime-header`.

## Docs changed

docs/stdlib.md: the `os` listing has the overload, and the paragraph on `read_stdin` and `read_line` says what it appends and when it returns false. docs/testing.md: the `runtime_io.py` row names the new cases.

## Tests

test/runtime_io.py adds a `pieces <max>` mode, which calls `read_stdin(got, max)` until it returns false and prints `got.len` after each call, and four inputs: 7 bytes with a max of 3 (3, 6, 7), empty stdin, a max of 0, and 150,000 bytes with a max of 100,000, which crosses the 64 KB buffer inside one call.

## Verification

- On eadca409. `python test/run_tests.py --profile baseline --cc native --require-clang`: "all tests passed" on macOS 26.7.1 (M1 Max, Apple clang 17.0.0): JIT runs 860 ok, typecheck errors 1911 ok, samples 52 ok, native builds, packages and runtime I/O 13 ok.
- `goose --gen-runtime-header` run again on the branch leaves `git status` clean.
- The two programs, built by this branch: over `head -c 3000000000 /dev/zero`, `read_stdin(out)` (built with `--stack-reserve 8G`) took 1.17-2.53 s at 2.86 GB peak resident, and `read_stdin(buf, 65536)` took 0.76-1.57 s at 1.6 MB, 3 runs each under `/usr/bin/time -l`. On 0, 1, 65535, 65536, 65537 and 1000003 random bytes they print the same length and sum.
- Not run locally: Linux and Windows; left to CI.

## Known limits

- It reads into a 64 KB buffer on the C stack and appends it to `out`, the same copy `read_stdin(out)` and `read_file` make.
- It waits for `max` bytes or the end of input, so it does not suit interactive input; `read_line` stays the way to read lines as they are typed.

In-process run: `extern fn` to libm functions outside a fixed table fails to link (nextafter, expm1, log1p, fma, ...)
body:
**Goose:** eadca40, and current main 369c7a2c built from source (same result). Linux aarch64, Ubuntu 24.04, glibc 2.39.

```goose
extern fn nextafter(x: f64, y: f64) -> f64;
fn main() { print(nextafter(1.0, 2.0)); }
```

`goose x.goose`:

```
libtcc: relocating the generated C failed
tcc: error: unresolved reference to 'nextafter'
```

`goose build x.goose && ./x` prints `1.0000000000000002`.

The in-process backend registers a fixed table of libm symbols in `src/jit_runtime.c` (`sqrt` … `cbrt`, `hypot`, `ldexp`, `frexp`, each with its `f` form). Every other `<math.h>` function fails to link. I checked `nextafter`, `nextafterf`, `expm1`, `log1p`, `erf`, `tgamma`, `copysign`, `remainder` and `fma`. With `fma`, TinyCC also prints `warning: implicit declaration of function 'fma'`, so the in-process `math.h` does not declare it either.

**Expected:** these resolve as they do in a build. libm is already loaded in the compiler's process, so a lookup for names missing from the table would do, as would registering the rest of C99 `<math.h>`. Otherwise this limit could be listed with the others in command_line.md ("What a run cannot do, a build can": threads, optimization, `resource_dir`). The reference's `extern fn` section uses libm functions (`cbrt`, `hypot`) as its examples, and those two happen to be in the table.

**Workaround:** `goose build`.

title: Out-of-tree build cannot find the standard library, though the docs say it is found in the source tree
body:
**Goose:** current main 369c7a2c (`goose v2026.3-267-g369c7a2c`), built from source. Linux aarch64, Ubuntu 24.04, cmake with gcc 13.3.

A build directory that is not inside the source tree, or is more than three levels below its root, gives a `goose` that cannot find `stdlib/`:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/aardappel/goose ~/x/goose
cmake -S ~/x/goose -B ~/x/build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build ~/x/build -j
cd ~/x/work
printf 'import std;\nfn main() { print(sqrt(2.0)); }\n' > a.goose
~/x/build/goose a.goose
```

Output (paths renamed, `GOOSE_STDLIB` unset):

```
a.goose:1: error: cannot find the module std, looked for
    /home/me/x/work/std.goose
and found no standard library, looking in
    /home/me/x/build/stdlib/
    /home/me/x/stdlib/
    /home/me/stdlib/
    /home/stdlib/
    /home/me/x/work/stdlib/
set --stdlib or GOOSE_STDLIB to its directory
```

A program that imports nothing runs fine from the same build, because TinyCC's directory is compiled in (`GOOSE_TCC_LIB_PATH`).

**Expected:** several docs say the compiler finds the standard library in the source tree it was built from: README ("it finds the standard library in the source tree it was built from"), stdlib.md ("The compiler locates the library in its source tree") and spec §11.1 ("else the `stdlib/` of the source tree the compiler was built in"). `StdlibDirs` in `src/main.cpp` searches next to the executable and up to three parents, as command_line.md §12 describes. One fix is a compiled-in last fallback, `${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/stdlib`, that a packager can override as with `GOOSE_TCC_LIB_PATH`. The other is to change the three docs to match.

**Workaround:** `GOOSE_STDLIB=~/x/goose/stdlib` or `--stdlib`.

math: sin and cos of one value are not combined into sincos (about 1.4x slower than the C equivalent)

Plain-text warnings give no column: a redundant-cast warning on a line with two casts is ambiguous
Stop deeply nested code at the compile stack's floor
body:
Hi Wouter,

Deeply nested code crashed the compiler with a native stack overflow. This version drops the count from the first draft and uses the floor `CheckSpecBody` already checks for the call path, wherever a pass recurses with the program's nesting. It is three commits, and each one passes the suite on its own.

1. **Run the language server and the formatter on the compile thread.** Both ran on the main thread, which on Linux gets whatever `ulimit -s` gives (usually 8 MB) and has no floor.
2. **Stop the parser and the checker at the floor.** The parser checks in `Sub` and `ParseType`, which every recursion of the parse goes through. The checker checks in `Descend` and in constant folding, and `Clone` checks too, since the checker runs it from anywhere on the call path. The checker still names the call path when that is what took the stack, and the nesting otherwise. The parser's error is an exception of its own, so statement recovery doesn't resume at the same depth. A function whose body is too deep stands as broken, as with any statement error, so its callers don't cascade.
3. **Stop the passes after the parse at the floor.** A long `a + b + ...`, `x.f().g()...` or `T[:][:]...` parses in a loop, so the parser never sees its depth, and some later passes use more stack per level than the parser or the checker. The expansion binder, type name resolution, type substitution and validation, and the code generator stop with the same error. The dump writes `...` past the floor, which the formatter's self-check reports as the error, and the server's index and features leave the rest out.

On a clang -O3 build:

| input | master | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| `x + 1 + 1 + ...` | crashes past 37,400 terms | checks up to 35,000, then an error |
| `if ... else if ...` | crashes past 16,200 arms | checks up to 15,200, then an error |
| guards in one function | crashes past 7,800 | checks up to 7,300, then an error |
| a million parentheses, or a million-term sum | crash | error |
| a million nested slice types, in a parameter, a field or an alias | crash | error |
| an array size written as a 100,000-term sum | crash | error |
| `goose format` on 20,000 nested parentheses | crash (8 MB main thread) | formats |
| language server, 100,000-term sum | crash in the index | diagnostic, and the server keeps running |

How deep a program can go still depends on the build, as it already does for the call path. A fixed bound would make it the same everywhere, but to keep accepting what a release build checks today it would have to sit above about 45,000 levels, and the passes without a check of their own would then need room for that in every build. The expansion binder alone takes 224 bytes per level at -O3 and 3.6 KB in an ASan Debug build, which comes to over 160 MB.

Tests: `run_tests.py` checks that a 1,500-term sum, 1,500 `else if` arms and 1,000 guards check and generate C. It also checks that a million parentheses, a million-term sum, a million nested slice types (in a parameter and in an alias) and a 100,000-term array size report the error. `format.py` and `lsp_protocol.py` cover the formatter and the server on such files, including a function too deep to parse, whose caller then raises nothing more. Each commit passes the baseline suite on a clang Release build here with `ulimit -s 8192`, and the last one also passes the sanitize profile on the CI sanitizer configuration. This machine defaults to an unlimited stack, where `native_stack_overflow` and `render_reference_cycle` fail their expected-stderr checks on master as well.

A few related things are left out, filed with measurements as #226, #227 and #228:
- Generated C nests as deep as the source. clang rejects the C for a 1,500-term sum ("bracket nesting level exceeded maximum of 2048"). `goose run` on Linux crashes in TinyCC on a 5,000-term sum, since the JIT compiles on the 8 MB main thread. Master does the same.
- The formatter's output grows with the square of the nesting depth, since every level is indented: 20,000 nested parentheses format to 1.6 GB.
- Checking time: nested calls and nested `defer` take exponential time (each extra level doubles it), nested `while` loops quadratic, and checking a call that passes a 5,000-deep slice type takes 88 seconds.

title: Reject a stack frame past 2 GiB in the TinyCC backend
body:
Hi Wouter,

`goose run` with a function whose fixed locals give it a C frame of 2 GiB or more dies inside the compiler process, and not by running out of memory.

On master (40369bd1), two 1 GiB fixed arrays as locals of a recursive function make the TinyCC x86_64 epilog wrap the int it subtracts from rsp, skip __chkstk, and emit `sub rsp, 0xffffffff80000040`: rsp moves up by 2 GiB and the next store faults 2.5 GB above the stack. Release SIGSEGVs, --debug SIGBUSes, and 1023 MiB of locals is clean while 1024 is not, so the array size picks the displacement. The same shape is #120 on arm64, which is large by-value structs rather than locals.

The fix makes both x86_64 epilog variants report a wrapped frame as too large instead of emitting the broken subtraction, so the same program now fails with `stack frame of 2147483696 bytes too large` and nothing runs. Frames past 4 GiB wrap before the check and stay unsupported, as in upstream TinyCC; I can push the guard upstream too if that is where you would rather carry it.

Verified with a Release build: the reproduction above errors cleanly, and the storage and serialize fixtures run as before.
