Add src_file() and src_line(), the source location of a call
body:
## Summary
- `src_file()` and `src_line()` read the file and line the parser already stores on the call, and codegen emits them as constants. The names leave `file` and `line` free as parameters.
- A default that calls either builtin is stamped when the checker resolves it to the builtin, so `fn info(text: u8[:], file: u8[:] = src_file(), row: i64 = src_line())` sees the caller. An argument the caller writes is kept. A function of the same spelling is not restamped.
- The design is in `docs/design/call_location.md`. `src_file()` is the file's last path segment, on purpose: an abort prints the path the compiler loaded, and a log line must not embed that directory. The column stays in the compiler.

## Test plan
- [x] `test/codegen/call_location.goose` prints the file name, the direct `src_line()` call, a defaulted call, an explicit file and row, and a `src_file()`/`src_line()` call inside the callee.
- [x] `python scripts/check_doc_examples.py docs/reference.md --line 3741` compiles the reference signature.
- [x] `python test/run_tests.py --profile baseline --cc native --require-clang` on a build of this branch.

title: Feature request: a verified, zero-copy view over foreign bytes (e.g. an mmap)
body:
Thanks for Goose. `from_bytes` is the nicest serialization story I've used: one call, a verifier
generated from the type, and a corrupt file is a `false` rather than a wild reference. This request is
about the one place where it costs a lot, serving memory, with measurements from a small comparison project.

## Context

[symidx](https://github.com/artsensiva/symidx) is a code-symbol index (name → kind, file, line) built three
ways with byte-identical output: Goose, idiomatic Rust (serde + bincode), and "expert" Rust (rkyv 0.8 over
an mmap, bytecheck plus an explicit validation pass). The Goose image is the most compact of the three,
thanks to inline `u8[varint]` names and `varint` fields. While building it we also hit #177
(`from_bytes` and `append`).

The full write-up is in `bench/REPORT.md` there. The main problem is **serving memory**: a long-running
tool (a language server, an index) keeps the loaded data resident for its whole life, and with `from_bytes`
that costs about twice the image.

| Peak RSS while serving one selective query | Goose (`read_file` + `from_bytes`) | Rust (rkyv over mmap) |
|---|---|---|
| 3 MB image, Linux | 11.4 MB | 5.6 MB |
| 39 MB image, Linux | 116 MB | 44 MB |
| 3 MB image, macOS (CI VM) | 10.6 MB | 3.5 MB |

So serving memory is 2.0–3.1× higher, although Goose's image is 1.1–1.2× smaller. Load time follows the
same cause. With a warm page cache:

| Load, warm cache | Goose | Rust (rkyv over mmap) |
|---|---|---|
| 3 MB image | 12.2 ms | 1.3 ms |
| 39 MB image | 134 ms | 5.3 ms |

That's 10–25× slower. For completeness, with a cold cache (3 MB image, CI runners, 3 runs) reading from
storage dominates both: 18.4 vs 9.3 ms on Linux (2×) and 122 vs 120 ms on a macOS VM (parity). Cold load
isn't the problem; resident memory and warm restarts are.

## Where the cost comes from

Profiling the 3 MB case with a warm cache (`SYMIDX_PROFILE=1` in `goose/symidx.goose`):

- `from_bytes` copies the payload into the result, so the read buffer and the copy are resident at once.
  Serving costs at least about 2× the image.
- About half of the `from_bytes` time is first-touch page faults on the destination. The same call into
  already-faulted memory is 2× faster. The verify walk itself runs at about 1 GB/s, which is fine.
- `read_file` alone on the 39 MB image (27 ms) is 5× rkyv's whole load. Nothing after the read can win that back.

The verifier isn't the problem. The copy, and the lack of any way to point at bytes the program
didn't allocate, are.

## Proposal

A sibling of `from_bytes` that verifies and then returns a view instead of a copy:

```goose
fn view_bytes<T[>..]>(bytes: const u8[:]) -> const T[:], bool   // verified in place; [] and false if not
```

- **Semantics:** the same verifier as `from_bytes`, and the same framing. The result is a read-only slice
  rooted at `bytes`' root, so the existing root rules keep it from outliving the bytes. Nothing is copied,
  and it is never writable, like a `bytes_of` view today.
- **Alignment:** Goose layouts are packed, so a view needs no alignment fix-ups. That's simpler than in rkyv,
  where alignment is a recurring source of errors.
- **Foreign memory:** a view only helps if the bytes needn't be copied in first. Something like
  `os::map_file(path) -> const u8[:], bool`, owned by the variable it's bound to and unmapped at scope exit,
  would make an mmap an ordinary root. `read_file` into a buffer would also work, and still saves one of
  the two copies.
- **Index types:** this is the part that needs real design, and I may well be missing a simpler answer.
  `u32 in files` names a global array, but a view's indices would point into another view. Options:
  - allow `in` to name a global `const T[:]` that was itself produced by `view_bytes`, and verify the
    dependent view after it (the order is the program's, as it is for `from_bytes` today);
  - or allow index types relative to a view parameter, checked at `view_bytes` time.

  Without either, views would still serve images whose links are self-relative, and that's already
  most of the serialization chapter's examples.

## Possible extension: segmented verification

For very large images, verification could optionally be deferred per segment. Measured on the Rust side,
validating 1024-entry chunks only when a query first touches them cut peak RSS for a selective query on
the 39 MB image from 43 MB to 12 MB. The price is that "loaded" no longer means "fully verified". This is
optional, and separable from the main proposal.

## Why it matters

The pitch in the tutorial ("your data is already a file format") is exactly what a fast-starting tool
wants: a language server, an index, a cache. With a verified view, Goose would keep its compactness and
safety and match zero-copy loaders on serving memory and warm start-up time. Today it loses the comparison
on those two metrics, so we went with Rust for the larger project. I'd be glad to test a prototype against this
benchmark.

title: Generic `format` overload isn't being used by `print` or `str`
Proposal: `import c "x.h"`, a C header's declarations without writing them twice
body:
> **Update:** the prototype is now draft PR #224, with the open points of
> the first version addressed, one commit each. This text describes it as
> it is now.

Every C library a Goose program uses needs its interface written twice: in
C, by the library, and in Goose, as `extern fn` declarations in the shapes
of §7.10 and reference §24. Where a function does not fit those shapes,
there is a third copy, an adapter in C. Typical adapter jobs are:

- turning a pointer into a `u64`;
- copying a slice into a NUL-terminated string;
- returning a string as a length plus a copy;
- turning a Goose function into a callback;
- calling a variadic function.

Nothing checks that the hand-written signatures agree with the header.

The compiler already contains a C parser, TinyCC, so it can read the header
itself. The prototype is draft PR #224 (branch
<https://github.com/francescoalemanno/goose/tree/c-import>), and its design
note is `docs/design/c_import.md`.

```goose
import ffi;
import c "sqlite3.h";      // beside this file, or in the sidecar's c_include

fn main() {
    var db = sqlite3 {};
    if sqlite3_open_v2(":memory:", db, SQLITE_OPEN_READWRITE, null) != SQLITE_OK {
        print(ffi::cstr(sqlite3_errmsg(db)));
    }
    sqlite3_close(db);
}
```

## What it does

The compiler reads the header with TinyCC and writes a Goose module, which
goes through the normal pipeline (`goose --c-import x.h` prints it). The
module declares:

- **functions** as `extern fn`, variadic ones with `...`;
- **handles** for structs the header never completes, or that a function
  hands out: `extern struct sqlite3 { p: u64 = 0 }`, named by the
  header's pointer typedef where it has one (`XML_Parser`);
- **complete structs** as `extern struct`s, with `pad` where C pads;
- **constants**: enum constants and constant macros as `let`s, evaluated by
  TinyCC in the header's scope, so `((sqlite3_destructor_type)-1)` works;
- **typedefs** as aliases, so signatures read as the header does
  (`sqlite3_int64`, `HPDF_Page`);
- **macros that wrap a function** as Goose functions of untyped parameters:
  zlib's `deflateInit(strm, level)` calls
  `deflateInit_(strm, level, "1.3.2", 112)`.

What has no Goose shape is left out (variables, `va_list` functions,
unions by value). Using one is an error saying why, only where it is used,
as with Zig's translate-c:
`cis_take: not imported from x.h (parameter 1, a union by value)`.

## The language part

Where §24 needed an adapter, the boundary gains a shape, usable in
hand-written externs too:

1. **`cstr`**: any `const u8[:]` or `null`, copied with a NUL for the
   call.
2. **`T?` crosses as a pointer that may be NULL**, and at an extern it also
   takes a slice of `T`, as its elements' address. An empty slice has one
   too, so `(const int *p, size_t n)` takes `(v, v.len as u64)`.
3. **`cptr`** for `void *`: a `u64`, `null`, a reference, a slice, or other
   storage by reference.
4. **Callbacks**: a parameter `fn(P...) -> R` takes `cfn(f)`, the C wrapper
   of an `export fn f` of that signature. Function values stay
   compile-time only.
5. **`extern struct`**: its pads must put each field where C does, and it
   crosses by value as C's own struct, so `{ f32, pad 4, f64 }` arrives in
   the float registers.
6. **`...`** for variadic C functions, specialized per call by the
   arguments' types.

## Checks

- The generated C asserts what the module assumed of the target
  (`sizeof(long)`).
- A package's native part compiles a generated file that includes the
  header and asserts every struct's size and offsets, with the program's
  own compiler. A cross build therefore stops where TinyCC's view is wrong,
  without shipping every target's C library headers as Zig does.

## Measurements (macOS arm64)

| Header | Functions bound | Constants | Left out |
|---|---|---|---|
| sqlite3.h 3.53 | 295 | 511 | 6 (3 `va_list`, 3 variables) |
| zlib.h 1.3.2 | 87 | 42 | 1 `va_list` |
| expat.h 2.7.5 | 67 | 89 | 0 |
| hpdf.h (libharu) | 532 | 947 | 0 |
| SDL3/SDL.h | 1224 | 2233 | 23 (16 static inline, 7 `va_list`) |

The header checks of all five (604 asserts) hold with clang.

**A SQLite wrapper rewritten on `import c`.** The wrapper (connections,
statements, binding, columns, backup) comes from a larger program. It lost
its 118-line C adapter and its 22 hand-written externs, and the program's
tests pass unchanged.

## Still open

1. **Returned memory**: borrowed or owned cannot be told from a header.
2. **Function pointers in struct fields**, or returned by C, stay `u64`.
3. **Linux and Windows** are untried.
4. **Where the import is written**: in the source, or as a sidecar list, as
   Zig moved its C translation into the build system.

The PR's commits stand on their own, so they can be taken one at a time:
for example the boundary shapes (`cstr`, `T?`, `cptr`, callbacks,
`extern struct`, `...`) first, since they serve hand-written externs as
well.

title: [enhancement] import c: a C header's declarations as a Goose module
body:
Prototype for issue #223, opened as a draft for discussion. It is a series
of commits on master, one per piece, so that any of them can be taken or
left. Each builds and passes the tests on its own.

The first three are the original prototype:

1. **TinyCC: read the declarations of a C header.**
   - `third_party/tinycc/tcc_cdecl.c` includes `libtcc.c` and parses a
     header without generating code.
   - It reports every declared name through a plain C API (`tcc_cdecl.h`).
2. **import c: a C header's declarations as a Goose module.**
   - `src/cimport.h` translates by the rules of reference §24.
   - The loader feeds the text in as a module of the importing package.
   - It adds `cstr` and `T?` at the boundary.
3. **import c: tests and documentation.**

The rest closes the open points of that version, taking Zig's C
translation as a reference where it applies:

4. **The system's headers before goose's minimal ones.** goose's minimal
   `stdint.h` hid the macOS SDK's, so SDL3 could not be read. Linux system
   directories are added.
5. **Using a name the module left out says why**, where it is used (as Zig's
   `@compileError` stubs do).
6. **A JIT library names only the imported functions called**, so a header
   declaring functions the library was built without still links.
7. **`cptr`, and slices where C wants a pointer.**
   - A slice passes its elements' address at an extern's `T?`, an empty
     slice's too.
   - `void *` is `cptr`.
8. **C function pointers and `cfn(f)` for callbacks.**
   - A parameter `fn(P...) -> R` takes the C wrapper of an `export fn` of
     that signature.
   - C may call it back during any extern call, on the data stacks above
     the caller's.
9. **TinyCC: x86-64 structs mixing integer and float eightbytes.**
  - **The bug:** TinyCC classified a struct of up to 16 bytes with one class
    for all its fields. So `{ i64, f64 }` went to C in two integer
    registers, where System V puts the double in an SSE one.
  - **Who it hit:** this was already wrong for any extern called by value
    under the JIT on x86-64 (a build was right). CI found it with
    the next commit's test.
  - **The fix:** the struct is now classified per eightbyte, both ways.
    `pkg_float_abi` covers it, and I checked it against clang's code on
    x86_64-linux-gnu.
10. **`extern struct`**: a struct whose pads must put each field where C
   does. It crosses by value as a C struct of the natural layout, so the
   calling convention is C's.
11. **Variadic functions with `...`.** The further arguments are
    specialized per call, as untyped parameters are.
12. **Wrapper macros as functions, handles named by their typedef.**
    zlib's `deflateInit` becomes a function; expat's handle is `XML_Parser`.
13. **Typedef names, from a small TinyCC hook (optional).** `CType` gets an
    `int tdef` in what was padding, and signatures read as the header does
    (`sqlite3_int64`, `HPDF_Page`). It can be dropped; only the header
    check of 14 reads its aliases.
14. **Check the module's layouts against the header.** A package's native
    part compiles a generated file that includes the header and asserts
    every struct's size and offsets. It is compiled by the program's own
    compiler, so a cross build stops where TinyCC's view is wrong.
15. **The design note** (`docs/design/c_import.md`), with the measurements,
    a comparison with Zig, and what is still open.
16. **Generated checks that MSVC's C accepts.** The asserts go through
    `GS_CHECK`, which is `_Static_assert` where the compiler has it and a
    negative-size array where it does not (MSVC without `/std:c11`).

## Testing

- `python test/run_tests.py --profile baseline --cc native --require-clang`
  on macOS arm64: the same results as master, plus the new fixtures.
  - The package `pkg_c_import` covers every rule, built at -O0 and -O2 and
    under the JIT.
  - Each new error has a rejection test.
- `scripts/check_doc_examples.py docs/reference.md`: 0 failures.
- Every commit was built and tested on its own, in a clean clone.
- **Five real headers** (sqlite3, zlib, expat, libharu, SDL3) import, and
  their header checks (604 asserts) hold with clang.
- **A SQLite wrapper of a larger program** was rewritten on it. Its 118
  lines of C adapter and 22 hand-written externs are gone, and its tests
  pass unchanged.
- **Linux and Windows:** CI on the first push found three portability
  bugs:
  - `_Static_assert` with MSVC;
  - a missing `<stdint.h>` in the test's C;
  - a leak of the variadic instances under ASan.

  They are fixed in the commits they belong to, and in 16.
- **A second CI run** found the TinyCC x86-64 bug above, under the JIT on
  Ubuntu.

title: fix: compare relative reference targets in equality
body:
Relative references inside structs, arrays, and enums could compare by their stored offsets instead of their targets. Two fields pointing to the same object could compare unequal, while matching offsets at different addresses could compare equal.

This fixes structural equality to resolve relative references from each field's original address and compare their targets. It also preserves those addresses when evaluating equality operands and keeps self-relative and pool-relative equality helpers distinct through arrays and generic types.

The four new regression tests cover fixed and variable-length layouts, nested composites, arrays, enums, generic helper caching, null references, and zero offsets. The existing equality tests provide coverage for ordinary values too.

Validation on Linux x86-64 with GCC 14.2:
- Release compiler build passed.
- All 8 focused equality fixtures passed.
- All 168 codegen fixtures passed natively at O0/O2.
- TinyCC passed 167 codegen fixtures at O0/O2. The queue fixture is unsupported by TinyCC and was skipped there; it passed natively.
- All 62 marked GS_DEBUG cases passed on both backends.

title: Nested calls and nested `defer` take exponential time to check
body:
On master (335fddc1), a clang -O3 build, `goose check` takes time that doubles with each level of a nested call:

| levels | 14 | 18 | 22 | 26 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `g(g(...g(x)...))` | 0.04 s | 0.49 s | 7.8 s | over 2 minutes |
| `x.g().g()...` | 0.04 s | 0.51 s | 8.0 s | over 2 minutes |

```goose
fn g(x: i64) -> i64 { x }
fn f(x: i64) -> i64 { g(g(g(g(g(g(g(g(g(g(g(g(g(g(g(g(g(g(g(g(g(g(x)))))))))))))))))))))) }
fn main() { print(f(1)); }
```

Nested `defer` blocks double too: 20 levels take 0.14 s, 26 take 8.1 s, and 100 don't finish in two minutes.

```goose
fn f() { defer { defer { defer { print(1); } } } }  // and so on, n deep
```

Two other shapes grow polynomially:
- Nested `while` loops are quadratic: 1,000 take 0.17 s, 2,000 take 0.70 s and 4,000 take 2.9 s.
- A call that passes a deeply nested slice type grows roughly with the cube: `fn g(y: i64[:][:]...)` called as `g(x)` from a function whose `x` has the same type takes 0.7 s at 1,000 levels, 5.8 s at 2,000 and 89 s at 5,000.

title: Generated C nests as deep as the source, and the JIT builds it on the main thread
body:
A long sum `x + 1 + 1 + ...` becomes a single C expression with one `gs_add_i64(...)` around the rest for every term, so the C nests as deep as the source. On Linux with master (335fddc1):

- clang 22 rejects the C for 1,500 terms with "bracket nesting level exceeded maximum of 2048", after warning that its stack is nearly exhausted.
- `goose run` crashes inside TinyCC (`unary`, `expr_eq`, `gexpr`) at 5,000 terms. The in-process build runs on the main thread, whose stack on Linux is the `ulimit -s` limit, usually 8 MB, and with `ulimit -s 65536` the same program runs.

With #214 the compiler itself checks such a sum up to about 35,000 terms on a clang -O3 build, so the C becomes the limit well before that.

Two changes could work together. Building with TinyCC on the compile thread (`RunOnCompilerStack`) would give it the same 64 MB on every platform. Splitting an expression into temporaries past some depth, in the code generator, would keep the C within what clang and MSVC accept.

title: `goose format` output grows with the square of the nesting depth
body:
The formatter puts each level of a nested expression on its own line, indented one step further, so the formatted text grows with the square of the depth. Formatting a function whose body is n lines of `(`, then `1`, then n lines of `)`, with a clang -O3 build:

| n | formatted text | peak memory |
|---|---|---|
| 5,000 | 100 MB | 0.29 GB |
| 10,000 | 400 MB | 1.1 GB |
| 20,000 | 1.6 GB | 5.0 GB |
| 30,000 | 3.6 GB | 11.2 GB |

On Linux, where the main thread usually gets 8 MB, master (335fddc1) crashes on the stack before 20,000, so the last two rows come from #214, which runs the formatter on the compile thread. The language server needs as much memory to answer a formatting request for such a file.

Capping the indentation at some depth would keep the output linear in the input, at the cost of the layout past that depth.

title: [fix] Keep json::format_number within POW10 just below 1e37
`std::copy_into`'s name doesn't make sense with method-style calls
body:
The stdlib function copy_into can be called `copy_into(dst, src)`.
This matches memcpy's argument order (I assume that was the motivation).
However with UFCS the function can also be called `dst.copy_into(src)`,
which really looks like it should copy from `dst` into `src`. Two ways
we could resolve this confusion are

- rename to `copy_from`, so that we write `copy_from(dst, src)` or `dst.copy_from(src)`
- reorder the arguments, so that we write `copy_into(src, dst)` or `src.copy_into(dst)`

Of the two, the first seems less hostile since we can leave a deprecated `copy_into`
in the stdlib for a while

title: Calling exported functions from host threads: what would be needed, and should it be supported?
Recursive cycle: a reference inside a by-value parameter cannot be stored, even when it points into a pool owned outside the cycle
Data Parallelism with shared reads and disjoint slice writes
body:
`thread_fn` and `thread_spawn` + `qput`/`qget` work well when threads run independently of the caller's scope, since copying data in and out through queues avoids lifetime and aliasing
 issues.

   For data-parallel loops where the caller just wants to split work across $N$ threads and wait for them to finish before moving on (like `samples/22_image_filters.goose`, or analytical
 scans/joins), the copy boundary becomes the bottleneck:

   - The main thread has to slice and copy inputs into `qput` messages and copy `qget` results back into the destination array on a single core.
   - Shared read-only data (like a lookup table, hash table, or the full source image for stencil halo rows) has to be copied to each worker instead of read in place.
   - Spawning per pass maps and unmaps worker Data Stacks every time, and even with persistent `thread_spawn` workers reading from a queue, all input/output bytes still go through `malloc`
 + `memcpy` in the queue.

   Some numbers on 8 cores (`-O2`):

   - **`samples/22_image_filters.goose` scaled to 4K (`3840x2160`, 20 ping-pong blur passes + Sobel):**
     - 1 core: 78 ms
     - 8 persistent `thread_spawn` workers + `qput`/`qget`: 38 ms
     - 8 pooled workers reading `src` in place (`const u8[:]`) and writing to disjoint output slices (`u8[:]`): 10 ms

   - **128 MB `i64` array transform with an 8 MB lookup table (20 passes):**
     - 1 core: 151 ms
     - 8 persistent `thread_spawn` workers + `qput`/`qget`: 418 ms (slower than 1 core due to main-thread queue copies)
     - 8 pooled workers reading the input/table in place and writing to disjoint output slices: 50 ms

   Because the caller blocks until all tasks in a pass finish, it seems like the compiler already has what it needs to check this safely without lifetime annotations:

   1. Caller variables stay alive and can't be mutated by the caller while the pass is running.
   2. Shared inputs passed as `const T[:]` or `const T&` (for flat `T`) can be read concurrently in place.
   3. Mutations are isolated if each task writes to a disjoint slice `T[:]` of the output array (or pushes variable-sized output to its own `T[>..]&`), as long as the output array's root
 doesn't alias any of the shared `const` arguments.
   4. Reusable worker threads can keep their Data Stack regions mapped across passes and reset their stack watermarks between tasks.

   The main workload we're trying to unlock with this is an analytical query engine in Goose (columnar scans, filters, hash joins, and group-by aggregations). A typical query runs a
 sequence of memory-bound parallel phases over large columns:
   - scanning and filtering input columns in place (`const T[:]`) into per-worker filtered outputs;
   - radix-partitioning build rows and constructing $P$ disjoint partitions of a hash table in parallel (`HashSlot[:]`);
   - probing that hash table as a shared read-only slice (`const HashSlot[:]`) from all workers at once while writing matched rows into disjoint slices of the output array;
   - merging per-worker aggregation states.

   With queues, copying gigabytes of columns and hash tables between main and workers dominates query time; being able to read shared columns/tables in place and write into disjoint output
 slices makes all of those phases run at memory bandwidth across cores.

title: Header-backed `extern "<header.h>"`, fixed-length slice windows `s[lo..+N]`, and `target_has`
[fix] Get master's CI green again: libm calls on macOS, extern_libm's cbrt on Linux
body:
Since 1420008, CI on master has been failing on three of its four jobs. Windows passes. There are two separate causes, and this PR has one commit for each.

**macOS: `libm calls` fails with "calls pow".** On Apple targets, symbols take a leading underscore. So clang emits `__asm__("_pow")` as the literal IR name `"\01_pow"`, and LLVM no longer knows that function as libm's `pow`:

```
declare double @"\01_pow"(double noundef, double noundef) local_unnamed_addr #4
```

As a result, `pow(x, 2.0)` stays a call, and `sin` and `cos` of one value stay two calls. The fix: under clang on Apple, each runtime name now forwards to libm's own name, redeclared `const`, as gcc already does. With that, Apple clang 21 turns `pow(x, 2.0)` into a multiply and combines `sin`/`cos` and `sinf`/`cosf` into `__sincos_stret`/`__sincosf_stret`. Where symbols take no prefix (Linux, Windows x64), clang keeps the asm labels.

**Linux: `extern_libm.goose` fails.** Three tests fail: `cgen-output-differs-by-O`, `expected-output jit` and, in the sanitize job, `expected-output` at -O2. The cause is that glibc's `cbrt(27.0)` returns `3.0000000000000004`, one ulp above 3.0, while gcc folds the call to `3.0` at -O2. `cbrt` and `cbrtf` are now compared with 3.0 within a tolerance, as `tgamma` already is.

**Checks.** On macOS arm64 with Apple clang 21:
- `goose format --check samples stdlib` passes;
- `test/run_tests.py --profile baseline --cc native --require-clang` passes, including `libm calls`.

There was no Linux machine at hand, so Linux is left to this PR's CI.

title: TinyCC: x86-64 struct passing (mixed eightbytes, unaligned fields)
body:
Two fixes to TinyCC's x86-64 System V calling convention, one commit each. Both made a JIT run pass a struct by value to C in the wrong place, while a `goose build` of the same program was right.

## 1. Structs mixing integer and float eightbytes

On x86-64 System V, a struct of up to 16 bytes is classified one eightbyte at a time, so `{ i64, f64 }` travels in one integer register and one SSE register. TinyCC merged all the fields into a single class (integer), and passed and returned such a struct in two integer registers. Code compiled by another compiler then read the double from the wrong register.

In Goose this showed up under the JIT: an extern call passing or returning such a struct by value got garbage, while a `goose build` of the same program was right. It affects any extern, on Linux and macOS x86-64. Windows x64 and arm64 have their own code and are unchanged.

## The fix (`x86_64-gen.c`, `tccgen.c`)

- `classify_x86_64_eightbytes` classifies each eightbyte, and a struct of 9 to 16 bytes whose eightbytes are one INTEGER and one SSE gets a new mode, `x86_64_mode_mixed`.
- A call passes it in the next register of each class, or on the stack when either class has run out. A function receives it the same way.
- Such a struct is returned in RAX and XMM0: `gfunc_sret_mixed`, used where tccgen reads a call's result and where it makes a return.
- `va_arg` of such a struct still reads it from the stack; that path is unchanged.

## 2. Structs with a field off its alignment

The convention passes and returns an aggregate in memory when a field sits at an offset that is not a multiple of its alignment. TinyCC classified such a struct by its fields' types alone, and passed a packed `{ int; double }` in two integer registers, where clang puts it on the stack. Goose emits its structs packed (`#pragma pack(1)`), so a Goose `{ i32, f64 }` passed by value to C under the JIT reached the C (compiled by clang with the same packed layout) in the wrong place.

`classify_x86_64_unaligned` looks for such a field through nested structs and arrays, leaving out bitfields as other compilers do; the struct then goes in memory both ways.

## Testing

- `pkg_float_abi` now passes and returns `{ i64, f64 }` and `{ f64, i64 }`, and a packed `{ i32, f64 }` and `{ u8, i32 }`, between C compiled natively and Goose under the JIT.
- I compared a cross TinyCC's output for x86_64-linux-gnu with clang's: arguments, parameters, results and returns agree. The cases covered integer+double, double+integer, a 12-byte struct, packed structs with unaligned fields, the callee side and `return`.
- The full suite passes on macOS arm64 on current master.
- The first commit, with a test that failed on Ubuntu x86-64 before it, also ran green in CI on all four jobs (Ubuntu, ASan + UBSan, Windows, macOS) as part of #224. The second is checked on x86-64 only by this PR's CI.

title: The defer example on the official website throws an error.
Add trim for slice_pool<u8>, returning free spans to the OS
body:
For #191.

Adds `trim(p: slice_pool<u8>&) -> bool`, as discussed in the issue. It walks the free-span tree and discards the whole pages inside each free span. They read back as zeros, which is what `alloc_slice` gives them anyway. `alloc_slice` and `free_slice` are unchanged, so nothing happens unless `trim` is called.

- The page discard moves out of `gs_trim_memory` into `gs_discard_pages` (runtime_impl.h). `gs_trim_memory` and the new `gs_slice_pool_trim` both use it.
- The walk checks node numbers, counts and visits the same way the other `gs_spc_*` functions do, and aborts on a corrupt tree. Two of the new tests corrupt the tree on purpose.
- `elem` is a parameter so plain scalar pools can use the same C function later. For now only `u8` calls it, with 1.

Measurements, 64 MiB freed and then trimmed:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| Linux RSS | 65.8 MiB | 1.8 MiB |
| Windows working set / commit | 68.3 / 67.7 MiB | 4.3 / 3.6 MiB |

With 10000 runs of 6000 bytes: Linux 59.1 → 1.9 MiB, Windows 61.8 / 62.7 → 4.5 / 4.6 MiB. The virtual size stays the same, since the address range stays reserved.

Stale views on Windows: passing an untouched view of a trimmed run straight to `write_file` returns false and leaves a 0-byte file, without crashing. After the view is read from Goose (which commits the pages again), `write_file` works. On Linux the same call writes zeros and returns true. stdlib.md mentions this.

Testing: the full `run_tests.py` passes on Linux and on Windows (`--profile baseline --cc native`; that machine has no clang, so cgen-clang was skipped). I can't test macOS. Its branch is the `MAP_FIXED` code moved unchanged from `gs_trim_memory`. There's no test for the false return, because I couldn't find a way to make decommit or `madvise` fail on a mapped, page-aligned range.

Two notes:
- Naming: std already has `trim(s: u8[:])` for strings. They don't clash (a program importing both builds and picks the right one), but if you'd prefer a different name like `trim_free`, I'm happy to rename it.
- The fault handler committing a whole `GS_COMMIT_CHUNK`: I'll look at that in a separate PR, after measuring.

## How this was done

As with the issue, I worked on this with Claude, which wrote most of the code and ran the tests and measurements. I chose the approach, reviewed the changes, and had it fix what looked wrong to me, such as the docs first saying only that the memory goes back to the OS, not that the reservation stays. The C follows the style of the code around it.

title: Reusable thread_pool and pool.apply(chunks(...), fn, args...)
32-bit embedded support
body:
Goose promises memory safety, fast execution, and low memory usage. These are desirable attributes for embedded applications in resource constrained environments like small single board computers and microcontrollers. Additionally, the fact that Goose generates C code makes cross compilation and custom toolchain usage easy.

Most of these targets (e.g. Raspberry Pi, ESP32, etc.) are 32-bit. Microcontrollers often lack a MMU that enables paging of anonymous mmap memory. RTOS'es like Zephyr provide only partial POSIX compatibility. We'll also include WASM since it shares many qualities with the other listed embedded targets.

I wanted to see how feasible it was to use Goose on an embedded device so I put together the following fork with experimental 32-bit support for these embedded targets:

https://github.com/mogenson/goose#experimental-32-bit--embeddedwasm-support---m32

The main changes are:

Data stack size reduction and carving data stacks from a single static buffer. With 32-bit addressing we cannot have 2 GB data stacks because an entire 32-bit user space is 2-3 GB. However even with data stacks capped to the range of a few kilobytes we can run all of the (non-GUI) Goose samples and benchmarks. If we have the Goose compiler select heterogeneous sizes for each fixed size stack, we can tightly pack them into a single slice of pre-reserved memory. Although pre-allocating all memory for a program can seem wasteful at first, this is a common practice for embedded applications that make use of arena allocators to avoid ever causing system memory exhaustion.

Next, we reduce the size of int64 members like slice length to 32 bits and add stack overflow checks on bumps.

Finally we gate the use of some POSIX APIs behind a flag so we can create an application that only depends on libc (where needed).

I've put these changes behind a `-m32` command line arguement. We keep the actual Goose compiler 64-bit for host builds, it just emits 32-bit compatible code.

The result is we can build and run all of the Goose sample and benchmark programs in both a WASM runtime and a Zephyr ARM Cortex M3 emulator.

Let me know if embedded 32-bit support is something you'd be interested in for Goose and if these design decisions are something worth exploring.

title: Cap formatter indentation for deeply nested input
body:
Fixes #228.

The formatter currently keeps increasing display indentation for every nested
line. For line-per-bracket input that makes the number of emitted spaces
quadratic in nesting depth.

This change caps display indentation at 256 columns. It does not reject or
truncate input and does not change token order; only the horizontal layout
past that display depth is capped.

A regression test checks the cap, a linear output bound, and formatter
idempotence on deeply nested input.

Measured on a clang Release build after rebasing onto 6c1fbc788f6eb1f17db4cab998353d7540ed825d:

| nesting depth | master output | patched output |
| ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 5,000 | 100,060,024 bytes | 2,564,148 bytes |
| 10,000 | 400,120,024 bytes | 5,144,148 bytes |
| 20,000 | — | 10,304,148 bytes |

Patched output scales 2.006x from 5k -> 10k and 2.003x from 10k -> 20k,
with a measured maximum indentation of 256 columns.

Validation:
- `test/format.py`: pass
- `goose format --verify .`: 2940 files verified, 76 intentionally skipped
- 5k formatted output is idempotent
- full `test/run_tests.py` suite: pass

This is intentionally separate from #214: it addresses output-size growth,
not compiler stack handling.

title: flat_map::erase aliases a value cell to a surviving key after backward-shift
body:
`flat_map::erase` (src/flat_map.h:91–110) pushes the erased key's value cell to `freecells` at line 98, then the backward-shift loop (lines 102–108) may move a surviving key into the slot just vacated, carrying its own `index`. If the surviving key's `index` happens to equal the just-freed cell, two live keys end up pointing at the same value cell: a write through one silently corrupts the other.

**Reproduction sketch** (isolated C++ test, ~300k-key churn):

```cpp
goose::flat_map<Node*, Val> m;   // the checker's nodevals pattern
// fill 300k keys, erase 150k, re-insert 150k with distinct markers
// verify every live key still reads its own marker
```

The collision is hash-dependent: it fires when `Home(k)` of the shifted key and the erased slot land in the same probe window. Under the checker's real key distribution (AST node pointers) this has been observed to fire under heavy erase/insert churn.

**Consequence:** the typechecker's `nodevals` table can alias two distinct `Node*` entries to one `Val` storage. A write into one node's recorded value silently corrupts the other's, so the checker may miss an error it was about to report — wrong diagnostics, not a crash.

**Suggested fix:** only push the cell to `freecells` if the backward-shift loop did not place a survivor into the vacated slot; equivalently, check `slots[i].index != freecells.back()` after the shift before pushing, or reset the cell's `index` to a tombstone value and reassign it when `operator[]` takes it from `freecells`.

**Test to add:** a focused unit test that drives `flat_map` through the churn pattern and asserts that no two live keys read each other's values.

title: LSP JSON-RPC: large integer request ids above 2^53 are silently rounded, breaking cancel and response correlation
body:
`src/json.h:210` stores JSON numbers in a `double` field (`Json::num`). `strtod` silently rounds any 64-bit integer above 2^53 (e.g. a uint64 counter, an id, a byte offset) to the nearest representable double. There is no bigint path and no overflow flag.

**Consequence in the LSP:**

- `lsp_rpc.h:48–59`: the echoed request id is mangled for large integer ids.
- `lsp_rpc.h:127,130`: `$cancelRequest` ids are mangled, so cancellation matching fails.
- `lsp_rpc.h:53–56`: `JsonText` renders numbers via `if (v.num == floor(v.num) && fabs(v.num) < 1e15) to_string((int64_t)v.num)` — the `1e15` cutoff is not the int64 boundary, so a value like 4e15 (an exact double, within int64) does NOT go through the integer path and instead renders through `Append(s, v.num)`, producing a floating-point string. The same logical value renders two different ways depending on magnitude.

**Trigger:** send a request with `"id": 4000000000000000000` (4e18, above 2^53).

**Suggested fix:**
- Parse JSON integers as `int64_t` (or keep the original digit string) instead of a `double`.
- Fix the `JsonText` cutoff to the int64 representable bound (~9.2e18), or better, track whether the value was originally an integer and render it as such.

**Test to add:** LSP round-trip with a 64-bit integer id above 2^53; assert the echoed id matches exactly.

title: JSON-RPC Content-Length framing desyncs on a malformed value
body:
`src/lsp_rpc.h:101–102`:

```cpp
length = strtoull(line.c_str() + 15, nullptr, 10);
```

There is no validation of the parsed value:

(a) A non-numeric suffix such as `Content-Length: 12abc` causes `strtoull` to read `12` and silently drop `"abc"`. Only 12 body bytes are read, the stream desynchronizes, and the next header block is misparsed.

(b) There is no ERANGE check on `strtoull` overflow. It saturates to `ULLONG_MAX`. The 64 MB cap at line 108 (`if (length > (64u << 20)) return false;`) prevents a buffer overflow, but the residual defect is the framing desync in (a).

**Consequence:** one malformed header desyncs the reader; subsequent frames are garbage. `ParseJson` throws `CompileError`, caught in `ReadAll` (lsp_rpc.h:121–124), the frame is dropped, and the stream is left misaligned — the LSP server silently stops servicing until the client reconnects.

**Suggested fix:** validate that the value is all-digits and that `strtoull` did not hit ERANGE before reading the body; reject the frame rather than desync.

**Test to add:** feed `Content-Length: 12abc\r\n\r\n` then 12 bytes; assert the server does not desync (it should reject or resync, not silently drop subsequent valid frames).

title: JSON \u escape: lone UTF-16 surrogate emits invalid UTF-8, skewing all LSP column calculations on that line
body:
`src/json.h:134–141`: when decoding a `\\uXXXX` escape, the code combines a high surrogate with a *following* low surrogate only when the next two characters are `\\u`. A lone high surrogate (e.g. `\\uD800` at the end of a string, or `\\uD800x`) falls through to `Utf8(s, cp)` with `cp` in `[0xD800, 0xDC00)`.

`Utf8`'s `cp < 0x10000` branch encodes this as a 3-byte UTF-8 sequence of an *unpaired surrogate*, which is **invalid UTF-8** (RFC 3629 §3).

Additionally, the low surrogate value `lo` is not range-checked against `[0xDC00, 0xE000)`.

**Consequence in the LSP:**

Editor document text (`didOpen`/`didChange`) containing a lone `\\uD800` escape becomes invalid UTF-8. Downstream, every UTF-8 column calculation (`Utf8Len` at lsp_rpc.h:241, `Utf16Col`/`ByteCol` at lsp_rpc.h:245–265) miscounts that character: a 3-byte surrogate is treated as a valid 3-byte UTF-8 unit, so LSP ranges, carets, and name lookups on that line point at the wrong byte offset. Silent mis-rendering of diagnostics.

**Trigger:** `didOpen` with text containing the 6-byte sequence `\\uD800`.

**Suggested fix:** reject an unpaired surrogate (fail the string parse with a clear diagnostic) instead of emitting a 3-byte encoding of `[0xD800, 0xE000)`. Range-check the low surrogate against `[0xDC00, 0xE000)` when combining.

**Test to add:** parse a JSON string containing `\\uD800`; assert the parser either rejects it or substitutes U+FFFD, and does not emit bytes `ED A0 80` (the 3-byte encoding of the unpaired surrogate).

title: MakeUnknown in resolve.h dereferences adt->struc->st without a null guard
body:
`src/resolve.h:217–236`: the variant-lookup loop reaches `MakeUnknown(t, t->var, cat(adt->struc->st->name, ".", t->var->name))` at line 221 after testing only `adt->struc->st->unknown`. A `TY_VARIANT` node with a `TY_STRUCT` ADT detail whose `st` field is `nullptr` (the constructor default of `TypeStruct::st`) would dereference null and abort.

No parser path currently builds such a node — every `TY_STRUCT` `TypeExpr` created in `resolve.h` (lines 55, 72) and in `ast.ConstOf` copies one that has `st`. However, the guard is missing exactly where the code admits "this may not be the variant we expected", and it is one deref away from a real crash if a future pass (e.g. a new `Ast::VariantOf` variant) creates a struct variant with an unset detail.

**Trigger today:** not reachable from `.goose` input. Reachable by adding a `TY_VARIANT` whose `adt` is a `TY_STRUCT` with `st == nullptr` and running `ResolveTypeNames` — compiler crash (null dereference, abort).

**Suggested fix:** add a null guard:

```cpp
if (adt->struc->st)
    MakeUnknown(t, t->var, cat(adt->struc->st->name, ".", t->var->name));
```

**Test to add:** a unit test that constructs a `TY_VARIANT` with `st == nullptr` and asserts `ResolveTypeNames` does not crash.

title: JIT: a crash in generated code kills the whole compiler process, with no symbolic stack trace
body:
JIT mode compiles the generated C in-process via TinyCC and calls `main` directly. A segfault in the generated code (dangling pointer, OOB write, stack overflow) is not caught — it terminates the entire compiler process.

This is documented as a known limitation in `docs/design/jit_backend.md:154–160`:
> "A crash inside generated code therefore takes the compiler process down with no symbolic stack."

**Mitigation direction (not yet implemented):** enable TinyCC's own stack backtrace and bounds checking for the ELF/Mach-O targets. TinyCC's `TCC_OUTPUT_MEMORY` cannot catch SIGSEGV, but the compiler can install a signal handler that prints a symbolized backtrace before the process dies.

On Linux, the main thread stack is not reserved at link time (Windows/macOS link a 64 MB main thread stack; Linux uses `ulimit -s`, typically 8 MB), so deep recursion in generated code can overflow the main thread stack and kill the compiler even before TinyCC's own backtrace would help.

**Suggested fix:**
1. Install a SIGSEGV handler that prints a symbolized backtrace of the generated C's call stack (using TinyCC's DWARF or `backtrace()`).
2. On Linux, either run the JIT execution path on a dedicated thread with a large stack, or document the `ulimit -s` requirement.
3. Add `#line "file.goose" N` directives in the generated C (at least for debug builds) so TinyCC diagnostics and backtraces carry Goose source locations.

**Test to add:** a test that generates a deliberate segfault and asserts the compiler prints a backtrace before dying (or, in a non-JIT test mode, that the diagnostic includes the Goose source line).

title: TypeChecker: failed struct/enum instances are never evicted from the specialization cache, silently disabling the checker for that type
body:
When a type error interrupts the construction of a struct or enum instance, `Checkpoint::Restore` (typecheck.h:2965) marks the instance as `failed`:

```cpp
for (auto i = structinsts; i < tc.ast.structinsts.size(); i++)
    if (!tc.ast.structinsts[i]->validated) tc.ast.structinsts[i]->failed = true;
```

The cache `t->struc->inst` and `st->insts` still points at this failed instance. On the next call to `GetStructInst` for the same generic type, `Reused` throws `Abandoned`:

```cpp
if (t->struc->inst) return Reused(t->struc->inst);   // -> Abandoned
```

`Abandoned` is caught by `CheckRoot` (typecheck.h:2989–2990) and the root ends silently. The cache is never corrected to point at a valid instance, so **all** subsequent roots using the same generic type throw `Abandoned` again with no new diagnostic.

**Consequence:** after a first error in a function using `S<i32>`, all other functions using `S<i32>` are no longer typechecked. No broken C code is generated (codegen never sees the failed instance), but the checker is effectively disabled for that type for the rest of the program. This is a silent semantic weakening.

**Trigger:**
```goose
struct S<T> { a: T; b: u32; }
fn f1() { var x: S<i32>; x.a = 3.14; }  // error, S<i32> marked failed
fn f2() { var y: S<i32>; y.a = "bad"; }  // silently skipped, no error reported
```

**Suggested fix:** in `Reused`, when it detects a failed instance, remove it from `st->insts` and `t->struc->inst` so that the next call rebuilds it.

**Test to add:** two functions using the same generic type where the first has an error and the second has a *different* error — the second error must be reported.

title: JIT runtime global state has no re-entrance guard: nested RunJit calls overwrite gs_jit_jump, causing undefined behavior
body:
`src/jit_runtime.c:8-27`: `gs_jit_jump`, `gs_jit_status`, and `gs_jit_resource_dir` are global `static` variables (not thread-local). `goose_jit_run` sets `gs_thread_cap = INT64_MAX` at entry, overwriting the runtime's initial value.

If generated code calls back into `RunJit` (via an `extern fn` that a host C package provides), the global `gs_jit_jump` is overwritten. A subsequent `longjmp` then targets the wrong `setjmp` location, causing undefined behavior.

**Risk assessment:** the current call path is single-threaded and serial, so the risk is low today. However, the API has no guard, and the `--header` library embedding scenario could introduce re-entrance.

**Suggested fix:** add a re-entrance detection flag (`static int gs_jit_running = 0;`). At the top of `goose_jit_run`, if `gs_jit_running` is already set, `abort()` with a clear diagnostic. Set it before `setjmp`, clear it on the normal exit path.

**Test to add:** a test that calls `RunJit` from within a JIT-compiled `extern fn` and asserts the re-entrance guard fires.

title: Linux main thread stack is not reserved for JIT execution, deep recursion in generated code overflows the compiler stack
RunProcess has no timeout: a hung CMake or C compiler blocks goose forever, and SIGINT is not propagated
body:
`src/process.cpp:33-76` (`RunProcess`): after spawning a child process (CMake configure/build, or the C compiler), the driver loops reading stdout/stderr until EOF with **no timeout**.

**Consequences:**

1. A package whose `CMakeLists.txt` contains `execute_process(COMMAND sleep 3600)` hangs goose forever.
2. A CMake package that does a network fetch on a slow or dead network hangs indefinitely.
3. `CC` pointing to a script that never exits hangs goose.
4. `SIGINT` (Ctrl-C) is not propagated to the child process — `subprocess_destroy` is not called on the interrupt path, so the child may become an orphan.

**Risk assessment:** the design assumes build tools respond normally; a hung package is a known attack surface for malicious CMake packages. The OOM path is defended (64 MB cap on the LSP framing), but the hang path in the build system is not.

**Suggested fix:**
- Add an optional timeout parameter to `RunProcess` (based on `poll` or `setitimer`), defaulting to 0 (no limit) for backward compatibility.
- In `Builder::Run` (`src/build.h:79-97`), catch `SIGINT` and send `SIGTERM` to the child process, wait 5 seconds, then `SIGKILL`.
- Document that CI environments should use `--offline` and a package allow-list.

**Test to add:** a unit test that asserts a child process that sleeps is killed after the timeout expires (with a short timeout value).

title: Package cachekey from .build sidecar can contain .. or an absolute path, escaping the Goose build directory
body:
`src/native.h:51-57` (`NativeBuildDir`) builds the package build directory as:

```cpp
if (!p.cachekey.empty()) return cat(GooseHome(), "/build/pkg/", p.cachekey, "/", b.tc.id);
```

`p.cachekey` comes from the package's `.build` sidecar file, which is fully under the package author's control. If `cachekey` contains `..` segments or an absolute path, the build directory can escape `GooseHome()/build/pkg/` and write to any directory the user can write to.

**Trigger examples:**

1. **Symlink attack:** a `.build` file with `cache_key` that resolves to a path under a symlink whose target is outside `~/.goose` → writes to the symlink target.
2. **Directory traversal:** `.build` file with `cache_key = "../../../"` → build directory lands above `GooseHome/build/`.

`WriteFileMakingDirs` (`src/toolchain.h:133-141`) uses `fopen(path, "wb")` with no `O_NOFOLLOW`, so a symlink at the final path segment writes to the symlink target.

Additionally, `BuildCMakePart` (`native.h:295-371`) passes the package root into CMake's `-S` argument; a malicious `CMakeLists.txt` with `execute_process(COMMAND ...)` or `file(WRITE ...)` can write to arbitrary paths. This is a design consequence of supporting native CMake packages, but the directory traversal via `cachekey` is an unintended attack surface.

**Risk assessment:** `GooseHome` defaults to `~/.goose` (user-writable), so the symlink attack surface is limited to the `~/.goose` subtree under default settings. However, if a user sets `GOOSE_HOME` to a shared directory (e.g. in CI), the risk expands.

**Suggested fix:**
- Validate `cachekey` in `NativeBuildDir`: reject any value containing `..` segments or starting with `/` (absolute path).
- Use `O_NOFOLLOW` (POSIX) or the equivalent in `WriteFileMakingDirs` to prevent symlink-following writes.
- Document that CMake packages execute arbitrary CMake code and recommend a package allow-list for CI environments.

**Test to add:** a unit test that asserts `NativeBuildDir` rejects or sanitizes `cachekey` values containing `..` or absolute paths.

title: IntStr(INT32_MIN) generates "(-2147483647 - 1)", which is formally undefined behavior in C

body:
`src/process.cpp` (RunProcess): after launching a child (CMake configure/build, the C compiler), the driver reads its output until EOF with no timeout. A child that hangs (deadlock, network fetch, an infinite loop in a generated CMake file) blocks goose forever.

- A network package: `git clone` on a slow network with no timeout.
- `CC=gcc` pointing at a hanging script.

**Assessment:** `subprocess.h` has no built-in timeout API. The design assumes build tools respond normally; a hung package is a known attack surface for a malicious CMake package.

Document that CI environments should use `--offline` and a package allow-list.

title: JIT runtime: global state (gs_jit_jump, gs_jit_status) has no reentrancy guard, nested RunJit calls cause undefined behavior
body:
`src/jit_runtime.c` lines 8-27: `gs_jit_jump`, `gs_jit_status`, and `gs_jit_resource_dir` are global `static` variables (not thread-local). `goose_jit_run` uses `setjmp`/`longjmp` to intercept `exit()`.

**The bug:** `gs_thread_cap` is set to `INT64_MAX` at the top of `goose_jit_run` (line 111), overriding the runtime's initial value. If generated code calls back into `RunJit` (via an `extern fn` callback), the global `gs_jit_jump` is overwritten, and the `longjmp` target becomes wrong, causing undefined behavior.

**Also:** `gs_rt_release()` (`runtime_impl.h` lines 1536-1541) frees the main region and uninstalls the fault handler, but does not reset the `gs_regions`-related global variables. If the generated code causes `goose_jit_run` to return early via a mechanism other than `exit()` (e.g. `abort`), `gs_jit_resource_dir` is set to `NULL` (line 120) but the regions may not be released.

**Trigger:**
- A package callback `extern fn` calls `RunJit` (requires the host to provide this feature), or two consecutive JIT runs without cleaning up the previous region.

**Assessment:** The current `RunJit` is a single-threaded serial call, so the reentrancy risk is low. But the API has no protection; future extensions (e.g. `--header` library embedding) could introduce this.

**Suggested fix:** Add a reentrancy detection flag (global `gs_jit_running`); if reentrancy is detected, `abort()` and report it. In the `--header` library embedding scenario, evaluate the caller-side constraints.

title: for-loop range tail parsed with stmt_level cleared: a block-ended tail is misdiagnosed and the tail value dropped
Match pattern: negated u64.max is silently accepted as 1, contradicting spec §6.2
body:
In `src/parser.h` `ParsePatternBound` (around line 1445), a negated u64 literal that is not exactly `2^63` is silently accepted instead of being rejected.

**The bug:**

```cpp
auto val = neg ? (int64_t)(0u - (uint64_t)lex.ival) : lex.ival;
```

For `-18446744073709551615` (`-u64.max`), the two's-complement wrap gives `1`. The error at line 1454 fires only when `lex.ival != INT64_MIN`, and `ival` for `u64.max` is `-1` (whereas `INT64_MIN` is `-9223372036854775808`), so the guard does not fire. Spec §6.2 allows only `-(2^63)` as a negated u64 pattern constant; every other negation of a u64 constant must be a parse-time error.

**Consequence:** the match arm's table is built from `1`, the intended `-u64.max` arm is silently reinterpreted as `1`, and no diagnostic is produced. This is wrong codegen with no error.

**Reproduction:**

```goose
fn main() {
    var x: u64[2] = [0, 1];
    match 1 {
        -18446744073709551615 => print("matched u64.max negation"),
        _ => print("default"),
    }
}
```

Expected (per §6.2, matching the existing test `negated_u64_literal.goose`): a parse-time error "negated literal too large for i64".
Actual: compiles and prints `"default"` (the arm constant is `1`, so the arm would match `1`; the `u64.max`-negation spelling is silently reinterpreted).

The expression path (`ParsePrimary` → `Unary(T_MINUS, IntLit)`) is caught later by the checker, but the pattern path builds the constant at parse time, so the guard must be there.

**Suggested fix:** mirror the guard at `parser.h:1454` to the `iuns` case:

```cpp
if (neg && lex.iuns && (uint64_t)lex.ival != (uint64_t)(INT64_MIN))
    Error("negated literal too large for i64");
```

i.e. reject every u64 negation except the one that is exactly `i64.min` (`-(2^63)`).

**Test to add:** a match arm with `-18446744073709551615` as the pattern constant; assert a parse-time error.

title: JSON-RPC: large integer values above 2^53 are silently rounded when stored in a double
body:
`src/json.h` stores JSON numbers in a `double` field. `strtod` silently rounds any 64-bit integer above 2^53 (e.g. a `uint64` counter, an id, a byte offset) to the nearest representable double. There is no bigint path, no overflow flag, no `ERANGE`/`errno` check.

**Consequence in the LSP:**

- `lsp_rpc.h:48-59`: the echoed request id and `$cancelRequest` ids (`lsp_rpc.h:127,130`, via `JsonText` at `lsp_rpc.h:48`) are mangled for large integer ids: the id stored in the cancelled set and the id written back into the reply differ, so cancellation matching and response correlation fail.
- `JsonText` number rendering (`lsp_rpc.h:53-56`): the `fabs(v.num) < 1e15` guard is not the int64 boundary. For any value in `[1e15, 9.22e18)` the cast `(int64_t)v.num` is out of the safe range; combined with the rounding in the parse, large ids in `[1e15, 9.2e18)` are inconsistent.

**Trigger:** send a request with `"id": 4000000000000000000` (4e18, above 2^53).

**Suggested fix:**
- Parse JSON integers as `int64_t` (or keep the original digit string) instead of a `double`.
- Fix the `JsonText` cutoff to the int64 representable bound (~9.2e18), or track whether the value was originally an integer and render it as such.

**Test to add:** LSP round-trip with a 64-bit integer id above 2^53; assert the echoed id matches exactly.

Fix indefinite hang on std next_pow2, increase its performance, and expand its tests.
body:
Prevent process hang on signed 64-bit / i64 integer overflow with an assertion within std next_pow2.
Increase performance from O(log x) (looping for up to 62 iterations), to a single O(1) constant time operation, with the new function being ~4 CPU instructions compared to a max of ~188 instructions with previous looping implementation.
The new implementation utilises clz (hardware count-leading-zeros lzcnt on x86, clz on ARM), with modern CPUs executing clz in a single clock cycle.
Added tests for negative input numbers, 64-bit boundaries, and the new number overflow assert for std next_pow2.

title: Implement par for, chunk(k, n) and chunk_at(bounds, k) (child_threads.md §4-§5)
Windows: a fault in a trimmed slice_pool page commits a whole 1 MiB chunk
body:
Follow-up to #191 and #241.

`gs_fault_filter` commits `GS_COMMIT_CHUNK` on every fault. After `trim`, one touch of a decommitted page brings back up to 256 decommitted pages around it.

Proposal: for a read fault below `r->committed`, commit just that page. Only `trim` leaves holes below `committed`, and writes keep the chunk, so growth and reuse are unchanged. The full `run_tests.py` passes on Windows.

```c
size_t n = page < r->committed && ep->ExceptionRecord->ExceptionInformation[0] == 0
               ? gs_page_size : GS_COMMIT_CHUNK;
```

64 MiB run freed and trimmed, then (Windows, MSVC, two runs each):

| | now | proposal | 1 page, any fault | 64 KiB |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A: read 1 byte through a stale view | +1028 KiB | +8 KiB | +8 KiB | +68 KiB |
| B: `alloc_slice(4096)` into the span | +1024 KiB | +1024 KiB | +4 KiB | +64 KiB |
| C: reuse the whole 64 MiB | 12 ms | 12 ms | 42 ms | 20 ms |
| D: grow by 64 MiB | 11 ms | 11 ms | 11 ms | 11 ms |

A and B are commit charge. "Any fault" fixes B but makes C 3.5x slower.

I also tried fixing B in `alloc_slice`, committing the reused part of a run before writing it once the pool has been trimmed. B drops to +4 KiB, and pools that never trim are unaffected, but 100k allocations of 64 B after a trim went from 2 ms to 51–55 ms, one `VirtualAlloc` each. So I left it out.

OK to send a PR with the proposal?

## How this was done

As with #191, Claude wrote the benchmark and the variants and ran the measurements; I chose what to compare and checked the results.

title: format_flt drops the sign of -0.0
Cap AST dump indentation for linear format self-checks
body:
# Cap AST dump indentation so `goose format` self-checks stay linear

## Summary

`goose format` verifies its work by parsing both the input and the formatted
text and comparing their full `Ast::Dump` output. `Indent` in `src/dump.h`
wrote four spaces per nesting level with no cap, so dumping `n` nested blocks
wrote about `4·n²` bytes. At `n = 20,000` that is a 1.6 GB dump, and
`goose format --check` peaked at ~1.4 GB RSS for a 40 KB input.

This caps dump indentation at 256 columns — the same display cap the
formatter itself received in #250 (64 levels at four spaces each). Whitespace
is not part of the program, so the dump stays parseable, and `--dump`,
`--dump-file` and `--roundtrip` still produce identical text for the same AST.

## Changes

- `src/dump.h`: `Indent` now stops after `DUMPINDENTMAX = 256 / 4` levels.
  This bounds `--dump`, `--dump-file`, `--roundtrip`, and the formatter's
  internal `CheckSame` dump.
- `test/format.py`: new `check_deep_block_dump` regression test. It formats a
  file with 10,000 nested blocks, checks that `goose check --dump` stays
  linear (`≤ 2·n·(256+16)+4096` bytes), and checks that `goose format`
  succeeds on the same file.

## Results

20,000 nested blocks (`fn main() { ` + 20,000 `{` + 20,000 `}` + ` }`), a
40,015-byte input, on macOS 26.5.2 arm64 with Apple clang 21:

| Measurement                      |          Before |        After |
| -------------------------------- | --------------: | -----------: |
| `goose check --dump` output      | 1,600,160,014 B | 10,303,886 B |
| `goose format --check` wall time |          1.97 s |       0.02 s |
| `goose format --check` max RSS   |         1.47 GB |      57.6 MB |
| `goose check --dump` max RSS     |          944 MB |      36.8 MB |
| Maximum dump line width          | ~80,000 columns |  257 columns |

The before values were measured on `master` at `e0b12259` before the change;
the after values are from the same machine and input after the change.

`goose check --roundtrip --parse` on the same file exits 0, so the capped dump
still reparses and redumps identically.

## Test plan

- [x] `python3 test/run_tests.py --exe build/goose --nocgen -j 10` — all tests passed
- [x] `goose format --verify` over `samples`, `stdlib`, `bench` and `test` — 2,943 files verified, 76 skipped
- [x] `goose check --roundtrip --parse build/scratch/blocks_20000.goose` — exit 0
- [x] `test/format.py` including the new deep-block regression case

The regression test bounds a 10,000-block dump at ~5.5 MB. An uncapped dump of
that input is about 400 MB (the measured 20,000-block dump was 1.6 GB), so the
old behavior fails the new check by a wide margin.

Related: #228, #250.

## Summary

Adds support for underscores as digit separators in numeric literals to improve readability, similar to Python and Rust.

For example:

```goose
let million = 1_000_000;
let hex = 0xFF_AA;
let pi = 3.141_592;
```

## Changes

- Updated `lexer.h` to recognise underscores between digits and remove them before numeric conversion.
- Added validation to reject incorrectly placed separators, such as `1__000` and `100_`.
- Updated the Tree-sitter grammar to recognise numeric literals containing underscores.
- Added regression tests for valid and invalid numeric separators.

## Testing

- Verified decimal integers, hexadecimal integers, decimal floats, scientific notation, and hexadecimal floats.
- New regression tests pass.
- Ran the full Goose test suite. One unrelated failure remains (`libm calls`), which I also reproduced on a fresh, unmodified clone of the upstream repository.

## Notes

Numeric separators are purely syntactic and do not change the underlying numeric values.

In TypeCheck::NoteBreak, 'sc.hasbreak = true;' was assigned before checking 'if (!reachable) return;'.
If a break is unreachable, for example when an expression is evaluated as part of the break returns from the enclosing function,
the break does not properly function. 
Moving 'sc.hasbreak = true;' below the '!reachable' check ensures only breaks that can actually be executed mark the scope as having exited via break.

```
fn foo() -> i64 {
	loop {
		break block {
			return 42;
		};
	};
}

fn main() {
	print(foo());
}
```

Before fix: `error: function foo can fall off the end without returning value(s)`

After fix: `42`

title: Resolve imports from unsaved editor buffers
body:
Import lookup checks whether a file exists on disk before choosing it, even when the editor has supplied its contents through `SourceProvider`. This can leave a new unsaved module unresolved or select a standard-library module instead of the local buffer.

This change checks `SourceProvider` before disk when resolving imports. Unsaved files follow the same precedence and package-name conflict rules as saved files, including empty buffers.

Validation:

- Reproduced the failure against unmodified upstream.
- Added six LSP regression cases covering new modules, standard-library and bundled-package precedence, library search paths, empty buffers, and package-name conflicts.
- Full LSP protocol suite and existing package-import fixture pass.

title: Skip dead remainder loop in blocked loops (fixes #210)
body:
## Skip dead remainder loop in blocked sums (fixes #210)

### Problem
`CodeGen::GenBlocked` always emits a loop for the iterations left over after the blocks of k. When a loop counts from 0 to a constant multiple of k, that remainder loop can never run. gcc 13 at `-O2` still warns about it (`iteration 2305843009213693952 invokes undefined behavior [-Waggressive-loop-optimizations]`). The C was correct; only the warning was wrong. Both shapes that `GenBlocked` emits are affected: the in-order float sum and the strip-mined `i % k` loop.

### Fix
As suggested in the analysis on #210:
- `GenBlocked` gets a `tail` flag and leaves out the remainder loop when it's false.
- Both call sites in `ForLoop::CgStmt` compute the flag:
  - **Count/range site:** the start is 0 (the existing `fromzero`) and the end is a non-`uns` `IntLit` that's a multiple of k. For the issue's `let n = 1000; for i in n`, constant propagation has already turned the end into a literal.
  - **Array site:** the array is fixed (`fixedarr`) and `ArrSize` is a multiple of k. The length comes from the type, not from BCE.

No pragmas and no warning suppression.

### Tests
- `test/optimizer/loop_shapes.goose` gets `shape_sum_whole` (count 64), `shape_sum_ragged` (count 61) and `shape_sum_fixed` (`f64[16]&`). Each is compared against a reference loop and is also called from `again()` so -O1 keeps it out of line.
- `check_loop_shapes` in `run_tests.py` now also checks whether each function's C has a remainder loop:
  - none for `shape_sum_whole` and `shape_sum_fixed`;
  - one for `shape_sum_ragged`, `shape_sum_count` (runtime count), `shape_sum_dot` (slice) and `shape_strip_fixed` (fixed `i64[37]`, strip-mined by 4).
- `test/expected/loop_shapes.out` gets two new lines from `again()`; the existing 41 are unchanged.
- I ran the checker against the C from the compiler without the fix. It fails on exactly `shape_sum_whole` and `shape_sum_fixed`, and passes with the fix.
- Full `run_tests.py` on Windows (MSVC 19.44, Release, `-DGOOSE_BUILTIN_LIBS=all`): every section's count matches master at f4637bf, including the -O0/-O2 builds, TinyCC runs and the goose_in_goose bootstrap. The one failure, "packages from git", fails on master too. It's caused by `safe.bareRepository=explicit` in the environment I tested in, not by this change.

### gcc before / after
gcc 13.3.0 (Ubuntu 24.04, WSL) on the C that `goose -O2` emits, compiled with `gcc -O2 -Wall -c`:

| Program | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Issue repro, `n = 1000`, sum | warns (`-Waggressive-loop-optimizations`) | no warning, no remainder loop |
| Same, strip-mined `lanes[i % 4]` | warns | no warning, no remainder loop |
| `n = 1001` (control) | no warning | no warning, remainder kept |
| Sum over a fixed `f64[16]` | no warning (dead remainder loop) | dead remainder loop gone |

Before, on the issue's program:
```
In function 'main_g',
    inlined from 'main' at before.c:1722:5:
before.c:1690:56: warning: iteration 2305843009213693952 invokes undefined behavior [-Waggressive-loop-optimizations]
 1690 |         s_g = (s_g + ((((gs_f64 *)((GS_GL->xs_g.base)))[i_g_2])));
before.c:1689:18: note: within this loop
 1689 |     for (; i_g_2 < t4; i_g_2++) {
```
After: nothing. The program still prints `499500.0`.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

title: Keep wrap_angle in [-PI, PI) for large inputs
body:
# Keep `wrap_angle` in `[-PI, PI)` for large inputs

## Summary

`wrap_angle` computed `x - TAU * floor((x + PI) / TAU)`. For large `x` the quotient rounds, so the remainder can be off by many turns and the single correction step only adjusts by one. `wrap_angle(1e18)` returned `121.7168146928204`, and the f32 form of `1e9` returned `-57.716816`, both outside the documented range.

This repeats the reduction while the remainder is out of range. It only runs when the first result was already wrong, so every input that master handled correctly keeps its exact result, and the common case stays one reduction. `-0.0` still stays `-0.0`, and infinity and NaN still give NaN. For a huge input the result is in range, but is not promised to match an exact modulo.

## Changes

- `stdlib/math.goose`: both `wrap_angle` overloads repeat the reduction until the result is in `[-PI, PI)`, and the comment explains why. The `fmod` approach from the earlier revision is gone.
- `test/stdlib/stdlib_math.goose`: f64 cases `1e18` and `1.1319666049798702e17`, f32 cases `1e9` and `210858020.0`, each checked against `[-PI, PI)`; small-negative passthrough and `PI`-boundary cases. Expected output updated.

## Results

Before, on master at `f4637bfb`:

- `wrap_angle(1e18)` = `121.7168146928204` (out of range)
- `wrap_angle(1e9 as f32)` = `-57.716816` (out of range)

After:

- `wrap_angle(1e18)` = `2.3362938564082754`, in range
- `wrap_angle(1.1319666049798702e17)` = `2.8495559215387587`, in range
- `wrap_angle(1e9 as f32)` = `-1.1681442`, in range
- `wrap_angle(210858020.0 as f32)` = `2.849556`, in range

Inputs that master already wrapped correctly are unchanged: `wrap_angle(1e10)` is still `-0.5092315673828125`, and `wrap_angle(-1e-20)` is still `-1e-20`.

## Test plan

- [x] `python3 test/run_tests.py --profile baseline --cc native --require-clang --exe build/goose -j 8` — all tests passed
- [x] `goose run test/stdlib/stdlib_math.goose` matches `test/expected/stdlib_math.out`
- [x] `goose check test/stdlib/stdlib_math.goose` — exit 0
- [x] `goose format --check stdlib` — clean

title: Print unsigned index values unsigned in bounds diagnostics
body:
# Print unsigned index values unsigned in bounds diagnostics

## Summary

A u64 index above `i64.max` was bounds-checked correctly (the comparison is unsigned) but reported as a negative value when it failed. `GS_IDX` cast the failing index to `int64_t` and `gs_idxfail` printed it with `%lld`, so `index 18446744073709551615` came out as `index -1`.

This adds an unsigned form of the check, `GS_IDXU`/`gs_idxufail`, and has codegen choose it when the index expression's type is unsigned. Signed index types keep the existing signed diagnostic, so `index -2` and `index -9223372036854775808` are unchanged.

## Changes

- `src/ast.h`: new `IsUnsignedT(TypeExpr *)`.
- `src/runtime/runtime.h` and `src/runtime_inline.h`: declare `gs_idxufail` and add `GS_IDXU`, which compares unsigned and prints the failing value with `%llu`.
- `src/runtime/runtime_impl.h`: native definition of `gs_idxufail`.
- `src/codegen_emit.h`: `IndexTypeCheck` uses `GS_IDXU`/`gs_idxufail` for unsigned `in`/`upto` index types.
- `src/codegen_values.h`: `IndexLoc` and `EmitHoistedCheck` use `GS_IDXU` for unsigned index expressions.
- `src/codegen_builtins.h`: `free` uses `GS_IDXU` for an unsigned index argument.
- `test/runtime/index_u64.goose` (new) and expected files: a u64 out-of-bounds array index.
- `test/expected/free_u64.stderr`: now expects `index 18446744073709551615`.

## Results

Before, on master at `f4637bfb`:

- `let i: u64 = 18446744073709551615; a[i]` → `index -1 out of bounds (length 10)`
- `let i: u64 = 9223372036854775808; a[i]` → `index -9223372036854775808 out of bounds (length 10)`
- `pool.free(18446744073709551615 as u64)` → `index -1 out of bounds (length 1)`

After:

- `index 18446744073709551615 out of bounds (length 10)`
- `index 9223372036854775808 out of bounds (length 10)`
- `index 18446744073709551615 out of bounds (length 1)`

Signed regressions still print signed values: `bce_negative_mask` (`-2`), `bce_large_step` (`-9223372036854775808`), `bce_wrapped_offset` (`-5`), `bce_global_initializers` (`-4`), `bce_effectful_range` (`-1`), `bce_receiver_push` (`-1`), `bce_range_shift` (`-1`), and `bound_type_abort` (`4`).

## Test plan

- [x] `goose run test/runtime/index_u64.goose` and its native build print the unsigned message

title: Reject bases outside 2..36 in the parse and format functions
body:
# Reject bases outside 2..36 in the parse and format functions

## Summary

The formatting docs give the base as `2..36`, but nothing validated it. `parse_int`/`parse_uint` treated any larger base as unbounded: `parse_int("10", 37)` returned `37 true` and `parse_uint("10", 64)` returned `64 true`. `format_uint` cast the base to `u64` and used it directly, so base 0 aborted with `division by zero`, base 1 exhausted its 64-byte digit buffer, and bases above 36 emitted non-digit bytes (`format_uint(36, 37)` wrote `{`, and base 64 wrote `0x96`).

This checks the base once in each function. `parse_int`/`parse_uint` return `0, false` for a base outside `2..36`, matching their existing bad-input result. `format_int`/`format_uint` abort with `<function>: base out of range`, as the design doc's §8.3 already describes for an unknown base.

## Changes

- `stdlib/std.goose`: `parse_int`, `parse_uint`, `format_uint` and `format_int` reject a base outside `2..36`; the stale `parse_uint` comment about bases below 1 is removed.
- `docs/stdlib.md`: parse signatures say false outside `2..36`; the strings section says the format functions abort outside it.
- `docs/design/stdlib_design.md`: §8.3 names both format functions.
- `test/stdlib/stdlib_parse_int_range.goose` and `stdlib_parse_uint_range.goose`: bases 0, 1, 37, 64 and -1 return `0 false`; base 36 still parses `ff` as 555.
- `test/stdlib/stdlib_format_uint_base_37.goose` (new): an invalid base aborts with `format_uint: base out of range`.
- `test/stdlib/stdlib_format_int_base_37.goose` (new): an invalid base aborts with `format_int: base out of range`.

## Results

Before, on master at `f4637bfb`:

- `parse_int("10", 37)` → `37 true`; `parse_uint("10", 64)` → `64 true`
- `format_uint(out, 36, 37, ...)` → one byte `{` (0x7B)
- `format_uint(out, 63, 64, ...)` → one byte 0x96, not valid UTF-8
- `format_uint(out, 5, 0, ...)` → `goose runtime error: division by zero`
- `format_uint(out, 5, 1, ...)` → `goose runtime error: limited array capacity exceeded`
- `format_uint(out, 255, -1, ...)` → one byte `V`

After:

- `parse_int("10", 37)` and `parse_uint("10", 64)` → `0 false`
- every invalid format base aborts with `goose runtime error: format_uint: base out of range` (or `format_int: ...`)
- base 2, 10, 16 and 36 output is unchanged; `format_uint(255, 36)` is `73` and `parse_int("ff", 36)` is `555 true`

## Test plan

- [x] `python3 test/run_tests.py --profile baseline --cc native --require-clang --exe build/goose -j 8` — all tests passed
- [x] new format abort tests pass in JIT and native C at -O0/-O2
- [x] parse range tests pass in JIT and native C, with expected output updated
- [x] valid bases 2, 10, 16 and 36 produce unchanged output

title: Potential Bug: Returning Optional Growable Arrays (u8[>..]?)
Numeric separators are undocumented (follow-up to #292)
body:
### Summary

Commit `32a4f445` ("Feature/numeric seperators (#292)") added `_` separators to
integer and float literals in the lexer and the tree-sitter grammar, with tests,
but did not document them. Neither the reference's lexical-structure section
(`docs/reference.md` §1) nor the spec (`docs/goose_spec.md` §2 lexical section)
mentions that underscores may appear in literals.

### What works today (undocumented)

```goose
fn main() {
    print(1_000_000);       // 1000000
    print(0xFF_AA);         // 65450
    print(3.141_592);       // 3.141592
    print(1_000e3);         // 1000000.0
    print(0x1.A_Bp3);       // 13.34375
    print(1e1_0);           // 10000000000.0
}
```

Rules the lexer enforces (also undocumented):

- a separator must sit between two digits of the same digit run
  (`1__0`, `1_`, `0x_1`, `0x1_`, `1e_1`, `1.0_`, `0x1.8_p3` are all
  `invalid numeric separator` / a parse error);
- separators are allowed in the integer part, fraction, and exponent,
  including a hex float's binary exponent (`0x1.8p1_0` = 1536.0);
- the formatter preserves the author's separators (`goose format` leaves
  `1_000_000`, `3.141_592`, `0x1.A_Bp3` untouched).

### Suggested fix

In `docs/reference.md` §1, extend the integer/float literal paragraphs with the
`_` rule and one example. In `docs/goose_spec.md`, add the same to the literal
grammar. Mention that the formatter preserves the spelling.

<sup>Goose v2026.4-20-gd5ae5bbd, macOS 26.5.2 arm64, clang 21.0.0.</sup>

title: Commit one page for a read fault below the commit mark

Closes #287.

**Short version:** as discussed in #287, a read fault below the commit mark now commits only one page. It's a local optimization, but there are real cases where it matters.

- `gs_region::committed` comment and spec C.4: pages below the mark can be uncommitted.

title: Assert index bounds in std insert_at
body:
# Assert index bounds in std insert_at

## Summary

insert_at shifts elements from index i upwards after pushing the new element. Previously, passing an index outside 0..xs.len caused the function to push the element first, followed by an out-of-bounds read at xs[-1] (when i < 0) or an out-of-bounds write at xs[i] (when i > xs.len). This left the array in a partially shifted or mutated state.

Adding assert(i >= 0 && i <= xs.len); at function entry ensures invalid indices fail immediately before any mutation occurs, matching the safety model of remove_at and swap_remove.

## Changes

- stdlib/std.goose: assert i >= 0 && i <= xs.len at entry in insert_at.
- docs/stdlib.md: document that insert_at asserts 0 <= i <= xs.len.
- docs/design/stdlib_design.md: document that insert_at asserts 0 <= i <= xs.len.
- test/stdlib/stdlib_std.goose: test insertions at index 0, in the middle, and at xs.len on growable arrays.
- test/expected/stdlib_std.out: update expected output.
- test/stdlib/stdlib_insert_at_bounds.goose: add abort test for negative index.
- test/expected/stdlib_insert_at_bounds.{aborts,out,stderr}: add expected abort fixtures.

## Results

Before:
- Calling insert_at(xs, -1, v) pushed v, shifted existing elements, and failed deep in xs[0] .= xs[-1], leaving xs corrupted.
- Calling insert_at(xs, 10, v) pushed v onto xs before failing on xs[10] .= v.

After:
- Calling insert_at with an index outside 0..xs.len fails the assertion immediately at entry, leaving xs untouched.
- Insertions at valid indices (0 through xs.len) continue to work properly.

## Test plan

- [x] Ran python3 test/run_tests.py (all tests passed).
- [x] Verified stdlib_insert_at_bounds.goose aborts cleanly on invalid bounds.
- [x] Verified stdlib_std.goose passes with additional edge case insertions.
