title: Liveness of a function's variables; hand large fixed values over at last use
body:
A fixed value above `NATIVE_VALUE_LIMIT` (4096 bytes) goes to a call as a pointer to a copy the caller makes for it, whatever the argument. When the argument is a variable the caller never reads again, that copy is all cost: the callee can have the variable's own storage. This adds the analysis that says when, and uses it there.

**`src/liveness.h`** finds the last uses of a function's variables on its final (optimized, inlined) tree:

- Backward liveness over the tree: children in evaluation order, loops to a fixpoint, and `break`, `continue`, `return` and an inlined body's `return` taking the live set of where they go. A whole assignment is a definition, so `x = f(x)` hands `x` over.
- A read through a reference that may point into a variable is a read of it, by the same provenance `MayReachLocal` uses.
- Not tracked: variables a nested function, a function value or a deferred body reads, anything those may point into, pools and root components.
- An element, a slice or a reference argument is read through an address taken before later operands run. So a use counts only where nothing else in its full expression (the statement, or the whole value of a `let`, `return`, `break` or `match` arm) names the variable or a reference into it.
- Children whose order isn't certain (a literal's fields, a builtin's arguments) see each other's reads as later.
- Loops nested too deep to stay cheap give no last uses.

**`CodeGen::MovableArg`** (`src/codegen_calls.h`) hands over a local or a parameter at its last use. The variable must not be global, captured, bound to a writable reference, or reached by another argument of the same call. A callee that builds its result in place (`NeedsResultLocation`) still gets a copy, since that result may land in the argument it is reading.

On master this only helps programs passing structs over 4096 bytes by value, which is rare. It's mainly the base for the next PR, which passes structs over 256 bytes by pointer and uses this for their hand-offs.

**Tests.** `test/codegen/last_use_moves.goose` covers both kinds of case:

- **Must copy:** read after; in a loop it is declared outside of; on another branch; through a reference; twice in one call; a global; `&&`; `defer`; past a `break`; through an index, slice or reference argument in the same expression; a reference read by a deferred body or a nested function.
- **Needn't copy:** at a last use in a `match` arm or a `block`'s `break`.

Its expected output is master's. run_tests.py also checks the C for which calls hand the variable over.

The suite passes on Windows (MSVC) and Linux (gcc, also the JIT). The only failure is `libm calls` on Linux, which fails on master too with this machine's gcc.

**Cost.** The analysis only runs for functions with calls passing such structs. For goose_imgui (structs over 256 bytes, with the next PR) it is 9 ms of the 610 ms spent producing C. Programs passing no large structs pay nothing. A synthetic function of 6,000 statements costs 6 ms.

title: Pass fixed structs over 256 bytes by pointer, and leave out the copies nothing can tell
body:
A struct of a few hundred bytes passed or returned by value is copied through memory at every call the C compiler doesn't inline: into the parameter, into the return temporary, and into the destination. gcc does it with a `memcpy` call above 256 bytes. In goose_imgui, with its 535-byte `Desc`, that was 114 MB a frame in 179,000 calls under gcc. The only remedy was to shrink the struct. The language doesn't change: an argument is still a copy (§7.2), and a result still arrives when the call is done (§7.3). Only the generated C changes, where nothing can tell.

This replaces the earlier version of this PR and #309. Following the review, the liveness analysis is gone, and so is `AliasParam`. One commit, 374 lines of compiler change.

**The convention.** A fixed value over 256 bytes (`PtrAbi`) is passed as a pointer and returned through an out-pointer, as values over 4096 bytes already were. Values still live on a data stack only above 4096. Export wrappers keep their by-value C signatures. Dispatch, thread spawn and user `format` overloads use the new convention.

**The copies left out:**

- **Fresh destinations.** A result is built straight into a fresh destination (`Dst::fresh`): a temporary, a variable being declared, or an out-pointer, which callers point only at such storage. Any other destination gets a temporary and a copy afterwards. A struct literal is built in place.
- **Arguments that die at the call** (`DiesAtCall`: a call's result, an inlined body's value, a literal) are handed over without a snapshot.
- **A variable's only use** (`SingleUses`, the rule from the review): an Ident that is the only one naming its variable in the function, outside any loop the variable isn't declared in and outside deferred bodies and nested functions, hands the variable over (`MovableArg`). It doesn't depend on operand order: there is no other use to order against, and no reference to the variable can exist without naming it. Since the variable is named nowhere else, it can't be another argument or the call's destination either. A read-only parameter handed so to one that changes it is consumed (`ConsumedParam`), so its callers give it a copy of its own.
- **Read-only parameters by pointer.** A parameter the callee never writes (`ParamUnwritten`) is given the caller's own variable, provided nothing else can write that variable during the call (`StableArg`). `EmitArg` now returns whether it lent a variable this way, and only then do non-fresh results go through a temporary. The `stableptrarg`/`callargs` member state is gone. Dispatch reads its arguments before the switch (`later`), so it never lends; it asserts that.
- **Inlined named results.** An inlined body's named result is bound at its fresh destination (`OpenIbFixed`), so a chain of inlined setters works in one variable. Not where the body defers anything or returns past itself (`return … from`).

Not here: `AliasParam` (the setter returning its own parameter, sharing storage with its argument). At -O2 it changed no generated C, since `OpenIbFixed` does the same job once setters are inlined. It only helped -O0 builder chains, so it can come back as its own small PR if -O0 speed of that idiom matters. Last uses after earlier uses, on one branch, or in a `match` arm aren't found either. If a measured program needs them, the full analysis can come back with that program as its benchmark.

**Results.** goose_imgui at d29163d (still with the 535-byte `Desc`), `bench/scenes.goose` from 146ab1e. Measured on an i9-13900KF, Arch Linux in WSL2, master (d5ae5bbd) against this PR. C compilers: **gcc 16.2.1** and **clang 23.1.4**, each at goose's default flags.

Copies a frame at `rows 1000` (`memcpy`/`memmove`/`memset` calls, counted by an `LD_PRELOAD` shim):

| | master | this PR |
|---|---:|---:|
| gcc | 179,109 calls, 113.6 MB | 94,073 calls, 64.5 MB |
| clang | 85,844 calls, 20.7 MB | 99,847 calls, 28.5 MB |

The gcc numbers match the earlier version of this PR exactly. clang already removes most of these copies on master. With this PR it makes more library calls than before. I haven't traced which ones; the likely source is the snapshot an argument passed by pointer still takes where it can't be lent or handed over, which clang could fold into a by-value call. It is still a little faster (below).

ms a frame of record + layout + after + walk, the smallest of five rounds, master and this PR alternating, pinned to one core:

| scene | gcc master | gcc PR | | clang master | clang PR | |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| rows 250 | 0.89 | 0.73 | -18% | 0.67 | 0.64 | -4% |
| rows 1000 | 4.07 | 3.33 | -18% | 3.09 | 2.95 | -5% |
| rows 4000 | 23.97 | 22.05 | -8% | 21.38 | 21.14 | -1% |
| windows 50 | 1.23 | 1.03 | -16% | 0.97 | 0.93 | -4% |
| windows 200 | 6.52 | 5.68 | -13% | 5.57 | 5.45 | -2% |
| docked 32 | 0.66 | 0.54 | -18% | 0.51 | 0.48 | -6% |
| tree 500 | 0.89 | 0.77 | -13% | 0.78 | 0.74 | -5% |
| moving 500 | 0.24 | 0.20 | -17% | 0.19 | 0.19 | 0% |
| grids 500 | 0.35 | 0.30 | -14% | 0.29 | 0.29 | 0% |
| rich 200 | 0.42 | 0.41 | -2% | 0.40 | 0.40 | 0% |

So the 2x is gcc's, as the review found. With clang (the default on Windows and macOS) it is a few percent.

**Tests.**
- `test/codegen/fixed_pointer_abi.goose`: 64 cases of aliasing between arguments, destinations, globals and references, for every mechanism above and the cases where each must not apply. Among them `defer`, `return … from`, recursion, dispatch, a `format` overload, and sizes either side of 256 bytes. Its expected output is master's.
- `test/codegen/last_use_moves.goose`: the cases where a hand-over must not happen (read after, in a loop, on another branch, through a reference, twice in one call, a global, `&&`, `defer`, past a `break`, through an index, slice or reference argument, a reference read by a deferred body or a nested function), and those where the single-use rule makes one. Its expected output is master's. run_tests.py checks the C for which calls hand the variable over.
- `test/codegen/export.goose`: exports taking and returning a 336-byte struct.
- `test/threads/medium_fixed_thread.goose`: a 300-byte thread argument.

The suite passes on Windows and on Linux (gcc, also the JIT). The only failure is `libm calls` on Linux, which fails on master too with this machine's gcc.

**Not covered.** A literal of a type with uninitialized slots built in place has no test. goose's own `bench/` wasn't run; structs at or under 256 bytes keep their convention.

title: slice_pool: reading `items` after `trim` recommits freed pages
body:
`docs/stdlib.md` defines `items.len` as the high-water length, and this proposal changes that. If you want to keep it, feel free to close this.

## Problem
`trim` discards the pages of free spans, but `items.len` stays at its high-water value. To save a whole pool to a file with every run at its index, a program reads all of `items`. On Windows `write_file` can't read decommitted pages (it returns false, as measured in #241), so the program copies `items` first, and the copy commits every trimmed page again.

Repro: 4096 runs of 64 KiB, free the last 90%, `trim`, `os::trim_memory`, then `copy.append(p.items[..])`.

## Proposal
In `gs_slice_pool_trim`, when the last free span ends at `items.len`, remove it from the tree and lower `len` and the stack top to the span's start. `trim_pages` takes `items` as `u8[>..]&`, so generated code reloads the top after the call.

Prototype: https://github.com/johmaru/goose/tree/slice-pool-trim-tail

Measured on Windows against `d5ae5bbd`:

| | Today | With the change |
|---|---|---|
| `items.len` after `trim` | 256.0 MiB | 25.6 MiB |
| Copy time | 93-166 ms | 7-8 ms |
| Committed inside `items`, before -> after copy | 25.6 -> 257.0 MiB | 25.6 -> 25.6 MiB |
| Commit charge, before -> after copy | 32.0 -> 521.4 MiB | 32.1 -> 59.2 MiB |

The copy is faster because it copies 25.6 MiB instead of 256 MiB. Without the copy, memory after `trim` is the same in both. This only covers free space at the end: holes between live runs still come back on a copy.

## Open questions
- A stale view of the cut part now fails `range_index`. Is that acceptable?
- After `os::trim_memory`, the cut part sits above the commit mark, so a stale read there still commits 1 MiB with #305 (+1028 KiB, against +8 KiB without `os::trim_memory`). Dropping the mark condition, so every read fault commits one page and writes keep the chunk, fixes that. Reuse (C in #287) stays at 11-15 ms as with #305, and the full `run_tests.py` passes. Should I fold that into #305?
- The copy reads free runs too, which stdlib.md calls an application error. Their bytes don't matter here, only where the live runs sit, so the docs may need to tell a stale view apart from reading `items` as a whole.

title: [BUG] Inlined call with a narrower result type loses its implicit widening as the left operand (u16 * u32 computed at 16 bits at -O1/-O2)
body:
model-id: claude-fable-5-2
effort: medium
prompt: (none asking for a bug — it surfaced as a wrong result while writing a Goose program; the model then reduced it to the repro below and checked it against main)

## Summary

When a call to a small function that returns a narrower integer is the **left** operand of a mixed-width binary operation, the operation is carried out at the narrower width at `-O1` and `-O2`. At `-O0`, or with the same value held in a variable, it is carried out at the wider width as the reference describes (a `u16` converts to `u32` implicitly).

## Reproduction

```goose
import std;
import os;

var regs: u16[8] = [0; 8];

fn reg(i: u8) -> u16 { return regs[i & 7]; }

fn main() {
    regs[0] = (arg_count() + 0xFFFE) as! u16;      // 0xFFFF at run time, not a constant
    let wide: u32 = regs[0];
    let a: u16 = reg(0);
    print(reg(0) * wide, " ", a * wide, " ", wide * reg(0));
}
```

Expected: `4294836225 4294836225 4294836225`

| Build | Output |
|---|---|
| `goose build -O0` | `4294836225 4294836225 4294836225` |
| `goose build -O1` | `1 4294836225 4294836225` |
| `goose build -O2` (default) | `1 4294836225 4294836225` |

`goose run` and `goose build --debug` give the same wrong first value as `-O2`.

## What the generated C shows

`goose -O0 -o out.c`:

```c
int64_t t3 = gs_fmt_i64(t11, (int64_t)(gs_mul_u32((gs_u32)(t4), wide_g)));
```

`goose -O2 -o out.c`:

```c
int64_t t2 = gs_fmt_i64(t7, (int64_t)(gs_mul_u16((gs_u16)(GS_GL->regs_g.e[0]), wide_g)));
```

After inlining, the multiply is emitted as `gs_mul_u16` instead of `gs_mul_u32`. The other two expressions in the same program stay `gs_mul_u32` at both levels.

## Scope observed

With the narrow call on the left:

| Expression | Got | Expected |
|---|---|---|
| `u16 call * u32` | 1 | 4294836225 |
| `u16 call + u32` | 65534 | 131070 |
| `u8 call * u16` | 1 | 65025 |
| `u16 call * u64` | 1 | 281470681677825 |
| `let x: u32 = u16 call * u32;` | 1 | 4294836225 |

Not affected: the narrow call as the **right** operand (`u32 * u16 call`), and a narrow **variable** on either side.

A function that returns a constant (`fn narrow() -> u16 { return 0xFFFF; }`) shows the same behaviour, so it does not depend on the callee reading memory.

## Workaround

Bind the call to a typed local before mixing widths: `let a: u32 = reg(0);`.

## Environment

- Goose v2026.4 release (macos-arm64), and `main` at d5ae5bb built from source
- macOS on Apple Silicon, Apple clang 21.0.0

title: Highlight numeric separators in the VS Code grammar
body:
# Highlight numeric separators in the VS Code grammar

## Summary

The numeric-separator change (#292) updated the lexer and the tree-sitter grammar, but the VS Code TextMate grammar still assumed literals contained no `_`. Because `_` is a word character, the trailing `\b` in each numeric pattern could not match inside a literal: `1_000` and `0xFF_AA` were not scoped as numbers at all, and `3.141_592` / `0x1.A_Bp3` were split into a numeric prefix and an identifier-like remainder.

This mirrors the tree-sitter patterns in the TextMate grammar, allowing separators in the integer part, fraction and exponent of decimal and hex literals, and drops the trailing `\b` so the whole literal matches. Invalid spellings are still left to the compiler; the grammar only decides text scopes.

## Changes

- `vscode/syntaxes/goose.tmLanguage.json`: the four `#numbers` patterns accept `_` between digits in decimal and hex integers, fractions and exponents; the trailing `\b` anchors are removed so a separator cannot prevent the match.
- `vscode/test/grammar.test.js`: a new test tokenizes `1_000`, `0xFF_AA`, `3.141_592`, `1_000e3`, `0x1.A_Bp3`, `0x1.8p1_0`, `1e1_0` and `1_0..2_0`, asserting each literal is one token with the right numeric scope and that the range operator still wins.

## Results

Before, on master at `d5ae5bbd`, tokenizing `let a = 1_000; let b = 0xFF_AA; let c = 3.141_592; let d = 0x1.A_Bp3;` gave:

- `1_000` — no numeric scope
- `0xFF_AA` — no numeric scope
- `3.141_592` — `3` as `constant.numeric.integer`, `141_592` unscoped
- `0x1.A_Bp3` — `0x1` as `constant.numeric.integer.hex`, `A_Bp3` as `entity.name.type`

After:

- `1_000` → `constant.numeric.integer.goose`
- `0xFF_AA` → `constant.numeric.integer.hex.goose`
- `3.141_592` → `constant.numeric.float.goose`
- `0x1.A_Bp3` → `constant.numeric.float.hex.goose`

The new grammar test fails on `master` at the first `1_000` assertion and passes with the change.

## Test plan

- [x] `cd vscode && npm ci --no-audit --no-fund`
- [x] `GOOSE_TEST_COMPILER=$PWD/../build/goose npm test` — 41/41 passed
- [x] new grammar test against `master`'s `goose.tmLanguage.json` — fails as expected (`1_000` has no numeric scope)
- [x] `python3 test/run_tests.py --profile baseline --cc native --require-clang --exe build/goose -j 8` — all tests passed

title: Read inf, -inf and nan back in std parse_flt
body:
# Read `inf`, `-inf` and `nan` back in std `parse_flt`

## Summary

`parse_flt` scanned only digits, `.` and an exponent, but `print`, `format` and `format_flt` write the non-finite values as `inf`, `-inf` and `nan`. The docs promise that `parse_flt` gives the double nearest to the decimal "as C's `strtod` does, so a float's text from `print` or `format` reads back as the same value", and `strtod` accepts `inf`, `infinity` and `nan` case-insensitively with an optional sign. On master, `parse_flt(str(1.0 / 0.0))` returned `0.0 false`, and so did `"inf"`, `"-inf"`, `"nan"`, `"Infinity"`, `"NaN"` and `"+inf"`.

`parse_flt` now recognizes `inf`, `infinity` and `nan` after the optional sign, in either case, and `nan(...)` with `strtod`'s parenthesized n-char-sequence (letters, digits and underscores). The whole string must be consumed, as for the decimal forms. Negative infinity keeps its sign, and a NaN is `0.0 / 0.0`.

## Changes

Six files:

- `stdlib/std.goose`: `parse_flt` checks for the non-finite spellings between the sign and the digit scan; new `float_text::equals_ignore_case` and `float_text::nan_at` helpers.

title: Keep implicit numeric widening when the inliner unwraps a call
body:
# Keep implicit numeric widening when the inliner unwraps a call

## Summary

An inlined call that returns a narrower numeric type than its call site checked it at lost that widening when the optimizer unwrapped the callee's tail expression. `TryInline` accepted any tail with the same `TypeExpr::kind` as the call (except references and enums), while `RetypeOperand` had set the call's `exprtype` to the operands' common type. `Binary::CgX` takes an operator's type from `left->exprtype`, and `Binary::Opt` folds at `IntTypeOf(left)`, so a narrow call on the left of `+ - * / % & | ^`, any comparison, or an integer constant fold was computed at the callee's narrow width. An `f32` return widened to `f64` was computed at f32 precision.

Only the left operand was affected: a variable holding the same value, a call on the right, assignment, argument passing and `return` already converted at their destination. Shifts were unaffected because they take the left operand's type by definition.

Fixes #313.

## Changes

Three files:

- `src/optimize.h`: `TryInline` still unwraps a same-type tail. Otherwise it restores the call site's implicit conversion, but only for conversions the checker performs implicitly (§6.3): integer widening, checked with `TypeCheck::ImplicitInt`, and f32 to f64. Integer and float literals are retyped at the call-site type so `Binary::Opt` still folds them at the right width and signedness; other convertible tails get an `AsCast`, and anything else keeps its `InlineBlock`. Inlining itself is never disabled.
- `test/optimizer/inline_mixed_width.goose`: runtime and constant-returning callees on the left of every affected operator, f32/f64 arithmetic and comparison, shifts and a call on the right as controls.
- `test/expected/inline_mixed_width.out`: expected output.

## Results

Before, on master `96b84548`, the new fixture at `-O2` (native and JIT agree):

```
arith false false false false false
bit true false false false
cmp false false false false false false
mirror true
shift true true
f32 false false false false
f32cmp false
cfold false false false true true
cfbit false false false
cfcmp false false false false true true
cff32 false
```

The `true`s are the unmixed cases (`mirror`, `shift`) and the folds whose narrow result happens to coincide (`/`, `%`, `==`, `!=`). After:

```
arith true true true true true
bit true true true true
cmp true true true true true true
mirror true
shift true true
f32 true true true true
f32cmp true
cfold true true true true true
cfbit true true true
cfcmp true true true true true true
cff32 true
```

`-O0` and `-O2` produce the same output natively and through the TinyCC JIT. Constant folding after inlining is preserved: the issue's constant-returning reproduction still folds at `-O2` (70 folds, against 56 when convertible tails are left as `InlineBlock`s).

## Test plan

- [x] `python3 test/run_tests.py --profile baseline --cc native --require-clang --exe build/goose -j 8` — all tests passed
- [x] `goose build -O0`/`-O2` and `goose run` on `test/optimizer/inline_mixed_width.goose` match the expected output
- [x] `GS_DEBUG=1` native and JIT runs match (the fixture is marked `runtime-debug`)
- [x] `goose format --check test/optimizer/inline_mixed_width.goose` — clean
- [x] the same fixture at `-O2` with master's compiler fails as shown above

title: Add mat and quat: matrices and quaternions for 2D and 3D transforms
body:
Two new global stdlib modules for 2D and 3D game transforms, alongside `vec`. Names follow GLSL, or glm where GLSL has nothing (quaternions, projections).

## `mat`
- `float2x2`…`float4x4` and `double2x2`…`double4x4` are fixed arrays of column vectors (`type float4x4 = float4[4]`).
  - As in GLSL, `m[i]` is column `i`, and a 4x4's bytes are a std140/std430 `mat4`.
  - The functions are generic over `vec4<T>[4]` etc., since Goose has no generic type aliases.
- `mul` for matrix·matrix, matrix·vector (GLSL `m * v`) and vector·matrix (GLSL `v * m`); `transpose`, `determinant`, `inverse`, `outer_product`, `row`, and the size conversions `to2x2`/`to3x3`/`to4x4`.
- 3D builders: `translate`, `scale`, `rotate(axis, angle)`, `rotate_x/y/z`.
- Cameras: `perspective`, `ortho`, and a four-argument `ortho` for 2D, plus `look_at`.
  - They use gfx's conventions (right-handed, y up, depth 0..1), so they match `gfx`'s functions term for term.
- 2D homogeneous 3x3 builders, and `transform_point`/`transform_vector` for both sizes.

## `quat`
`quat` imports `mat` for the conversions.
- `quat<T>` with the aliases `floatq`/`doubleq`.
- `mul`, `rotate(q, v)`, `angle_axis`, `to_angle_axis`, `rotation(from, to)`, `quat_look_at`, `slerp`, `nlerp`, `from_euler`, `euler_angles`, `mat3_cast`/`mat4_cast`/`quat_cast`, `conjugate`, `inverse`.
- `compose(t, q, s)` builds the model matrix of a position, rotation and scale.

## Design notes
- **There is no operator overloading, so `a * b` of two matrices or two quaternions is elementwise** (the language's §6.1 rule, which is GLSL's `matrixCompMult`). The products are `mul`, as in `gfx`. `+`, `-` and scalar `*` behave as in GLSL. The docs call this out.
- **The type comes from the arguments, never from the destination.** An all-literal call is `f64`, as with `math`. The docs show `radians(60.0 as f32)` for an f32 projection.
- **The four-argument `ortho` is the six-argument one with near −1 and far 1,** so a 2D scene's z = 0 lands at depth 0.5. glm's version is built for GL's −1..1 depth range and would clip z > 0 under gfx.
- **`euler_angles` always rebuilds the rotation it was given,** including at yaw ±π/2. It solves pitch and yaw after roll. glm's version double-counts the turn at gimbal lock.
- **`to_angle_axis` and `rotation` use the numerically stable forms:** `atan2` of the vector part's length, and the half-vector construction. They keep small angles and stay unit length near opposite directions, including in f32.
- **Everything except `row` is `checkfree`.** `stdlib_checkfree` now covers the new modules.

## Tests
- `test/stdlib/stdlib_mat.goose` and `test/stdlib/stdlib_quat.goose` check inverse round trips, a 4x4 determinant against numpy, the builders and cameras, and quaternion/matrix agreement.
- They also cover each conversion branch, slerp against nlerp at t = 0.25, Euler round trips at gimbal lock in f32 and f64, and small-angle and nearly-opposite cases in f32.
- `run_tests.py` results, on a desktop:
  - Windows (MSVC): all tests pass.
  - Arch Linux: one failure, `libm calls`. The test expects gcc to fold `pow(x, 2.0)` into a multiply, and the gcc 20260810 snapshot there doesn't. It doesn't involve these modules.

title: Reserve 8 MB of native stack for worker threads
body:
model-id: claude-opus-5-5
effort: high
prompt: gslib's goose-httpd overflows its native stack on macOS worker threads; draft a runtime fix

A worker thread got the system's default native stack: 512 KB on macOS, 1 MB on Windows, 8 MB on Linux. A few frames holding large fixed values exhaust the smaller ones; a TLS server handshake on a worker (gslib's goose-httpd, a thread a connection) overflowed on macOS on the first request. Workers now reserve GS_THREAD_STACK (8 MB, -D to change), as much as a main thread gets, where the system's default is less. It is address space, committed as the stack grows.

title: [BUG] An `export fn` called back from C overwrites its callers' data-stack locals
body:
<!--
If you used AI to find this bug, fill in the below fields.
If purely human authored, use model-id `human`, no effort/prompt needed :)

NOTE: please use "frontier" LLMs at high effort when you can. If you don't you cause the
maintainers more work in review.
-->

model-id: claude-opus-5-5
effort: high
prompt: (None, it found while working on a goose program)

<!--
The rest of your issue description starts here.
-->

When a Goose program calls a C function, and that C function calls an `export fn` of the same program before it returns, anything the callback allocates (a `str(...)`, a growable array) can land on top of live strings and arrays of the Goose functions further up the call chain. The callers then see corrupted values or crash once the call returns. It happens with `goose run` and with `goose build` alike.

C libraries do this routinely: a GUI toolkit calling a model's `data()` or a paint handler, a signal delivered while it is being emitted, a `qsort`-style comparator. I ran into it while writing a Qt binding for Goose, where every override handler is an exported function that Qt calls from inside its own calls.

### Environment

- goose v2026.4-17-gf4637bfb (runtime d521138194f1), at f4637bfb
- Linux x86_64, gcc 13.3.0; the TinyCC JIT shows the same thing

### Reproduction

Three files, no dependencies.

`include/cb.h`
```c
#include <stdint.h>
__attribute__((weak)) int64_t on_callback(int64_t n);
static inline int64_t call_back(int64_t n) { return on_callback ? on_callback(n) : -1; }
```

`reentry.build`
```
c_headers = ["include/cb.h"];
```

`reentry.goose`
```goose
extern fn call_back(n: i64) -> i64;

export "on_callback" fn on_callback(n: i64) -> i64 {
    let s = str("callback temporary number ", n, " with some padding to fill the stack");
    let t = str(s, s, s);
    return t.len;
}

fn main() {
    let keys: const u8[:][] = ["alpha", "beta", "gamma", "delta"];
    let local = str("main local ", 42);
    var total = 0;
    for k in keys {
        total += call_back(k.len);
        if local != "main local 42" { print("CORRUPTED local: ", local.len); }
        print(k, " ", local);
    }
    print("total ", total);
}
```

**Expected**

```
alpha main local 42
beta main local 42
gamma main local 42
delta main local 42
total 756
```

**Actual**, with both `goose run reentry.goose` and `goose build reentry.goose -o reentry && ./reentry`

```
CORRUPTED local: 13
alpha callback temp
CORRUPTED local: 13
Segmentation fault (exit 139)
```

`local` now holds the callback's temporary string, and `keys` is overwritten so that the loop crashes.

The callback doesn't have to be called from `main`. The same thing happens when the C call is made from a function that `main` calls, which corrupts both that function's locals and `main`'s; and when a callback calls back into C, which calls the export again.

### Cause

As far as I can tell, this comes from stack-top caching (implementation.md §6.10). `main_g` keeps the tops of the data stacks it grows in C locals. It writes them back only before calls that `SyncReach` says can reach those stacks. An `extern fn` reaches nothing unless it takes a builder or is `gs_trim_memory`, so in the generated C, `main_g` calls `call_back(...)` with its cached tops still unwritten.

The export wrapper then calls `on_callback_g(..., 0)`, so the callback starts at `GS(0)->top` as read from memory. That is still the top from before `main` grew the stack, which is where `keys` and `local` live, and the callback bumps over them.

A frame up the chain that called a Goose function has the same problem: its own stacks aren't part of what that callee reaches, so its tops stay cached too.

### Proposed fix

`SFunction::readsalltops` already does what is needed for `gs_trim_memory`. The caller of such an extern, and transitively every caller of that caller, writes back all its cached tops before the call and reads them again after it. Setting it on every non-stdlib `extern fn` of a program that has an `export fn` fixes all the cases above. A program without exports compiles exactly as before, and so do calls to the runtime's own externs, which never call back.

```diff
--- a/src/codegen_frames.h
+++ b/src/codegen_frames.h
@@ -319,6 +319,18 @@
 inline void CodeGen::CollectSpecs() {
     for (auto sp : ast.fnspecs)
         if (sp->live && sp->body) livespecs.push_back(sp);
+    // In a program with an `export fn`, C the program calls may call back
+    // into Goose before it returns (a GUI toolkit calling a handler, qsort
+    // calling a comparator). The export runs at gs_sp 0 and reads the tops
+    // from memory, so every frame up the chain must have published its
+    // cached tops first, or the callback allocates over their live data.
+    // That is what readsalltops does for gs_trim_memory; the runtime's own
+    // externs never call back.
+    bool exports = false;
+    for (auto sf : ast.functions) exports |= sf->isexport;
+    if (exports)
+        for (auto sf : ast.functions)
+            if (sf->isextern && !ast.StdlibFile(sf->line.fileidx)) sf->readsalltops = true;
     // Names: suffix whenever the goose name maps to more than one live
     // spec (overloads or multiple specializations).
     map<string_view, int> namecount;
```

With this change:

- `reentry.goose` prints the expected output under `goose run` and native.
- A second test (callback reached through an intermediate function, a callback that calls back into C, a callback that pushes to a global) passes too.
- `test/run_tests.py` passes in full (baseline profile, gcc 13.3 and TinyCC).
- In a program that calls into C in tight loops (12–150 ns a call), the extra write-backs make no measurable difference.

I'm happy to open a PR with this and the second program as a regression test, or to leave the fix to you if you'd rather solve it another way (for example by having export wrappers start above the stacks in use).

### Not covered by the fix

Loop-invariant views of a global array (`hoistrefs` / `hoistfields`) aren't reloaded after an extern call either. A callback that shrinks or clears a global its caller is looping over leaves the caller reading the old length. The memory stays inside the region, so this reads stale data rather than being unsafe, but the same flag could be used to drop those hoists across such calls.

title: Omit the dead remainder loop when a blocked loop's count is an exact multiple
body:
# Omit the dead remainder loop when a blocked loop's count is an exact multiple

## Summary

`CodeGen::GenBlocked` always emits a block loop followed by a scalar remainder loop:

```c
while (t4 - i_g_2 >= 8) { /* k iterations */ }
for (; i_g_2 < t4; i_g_2++) { /* tail */ }   // dead when t4 % 8 == 0
```

When a loop starts at zero and its count is a constant multiple of the block size, the tail can never run. GCC 13.3 still diagnoses that dead `for` as `-Waggressive-loop-optimizations`; the C is correct, but the warning is alarming and the unreachable code is unnecessary.

`ForLoop::CgStmt` now computes `exact` when the range starts at zero and its end is a non-negative `IntLit` multiple of `k`, and passes it to `GenBlocked`. `GenBlocked` leaves out the `ctr < hi` tail only in that case. A count that is not a constant multiple, a runtime count, or a `u64` value above `i64` max keeps the tail. The array-element blocked loop passes `false`: its length is a runtime read.

Fixes #210.

## Changes

- `src/codegen_stmts.h`: `GenBlocked` takes a final `exact` flag and skips the remainder loop when it is set. The `OpenLoop`/`CloseLoop` scope, block loop, labels and divisor hoisting are untouched.
- `src/codegen.h`: forwarding declaration.
- `src/codegen_nodes.h`: `ForLoop::CgStmt` computes `exact` from `fromzero` and a non-negative `IntLit` end; the array-element caller passes `false`.
- `test/optimizer/loop_shapes.goose`: constant-count sum and strip-mined functions with counts 1000, 1001, 8, 4 and 0, plus `0..1000`/`0..1001` range variants, each checked against a hand-written `while` reference.
- `test/run_tests.py`: `check_loop_shapes` asserts the block `while` shape is present and, for the exact-multiple counts, that no `for (; ...)` tail follows; 1001 and 4 must keep theirs.
- `test/expected/loop_shapes.out`: the fixture's new output lines.

## Results

`build/analysis/issue210.goose` at `-O2`, the issue's reproduction:

| loop             | master `855f1037` | this branch |
| ---------------- | ----------------- | ----------- |
| `for i in 1000`  | tail present      | tail absent |
| `for i in 1001`  | tail present      | tail present |
| `for i in 8`     | tail present      | tail absent |
| `for i in 4`     | tail present      | tail present |
| `for i in 0`     | tail present      | tail absent |

Both compilers emit the same program behavior: the repro prints `499500.0`, and every new fixture result matches its `while` reference at `-O0` and `-O2`. A `gcc-16.2` build of the repro runs warning-free; the only C that could trigger GCC 13.3's warning is the tail this branch removes.

The new runner checks fail on master for exactly the 1000/8/0 cases and pass on this branch.

## Test plan

- [x] `python3 test/run_tests.py --exe build/goose -j 8` — all tests passed (baseline, 3,900+ checks)
- [x] `goose format --verify stdlib test docs` — 2,818 files verified, 77 skipped
- [x] issue repro through `goose -o` on master and this branch — before/after C differs only in the dead tail, both print `499500.0`
- [x] new `loop_shapes` fixtures at `-O0` and `-O2` — same output, all reference checks pass
- [x] `gcc-16.2` build of the repro — clean compile, runtime output `499500.0`

title: Add file-local namespace aliases: namespace g = target;
body:
`namespace g = goose_gfx2d;`, written before a file's declarations, lets that file write `g::Sprite` for `goose_gfx2d::Sprite`. Until now `docs/design/namespaces.md` listed aliases as unsupported, so long names (often a package's namespace) had to be written out at every use.

```goose
import goose_gfx2d;
namespace g = goose_gfx2d;

fn main() {
    let s = g::Sprite { ... };
    g::draw(s);
}
```

## Rules
- An alias works in every kind of qualified name: expressions, types, variants, pools, match-pattern constants and `return ... from`.
- **It holds in the file that declares it alone.** Neither the files it imports nor its importers see it. So a library's aliases can't collide with its users' names, and an alias may even take the name of another namespace without affecting any other file.
- The target must be a namespace some file declares with `namespace x;`, even one that declares nothing in it.
- These are errors:
  - an alias in a declaration's own name (`fn g::f`), so where a declaration lives never depends on one file;
  - an alias of an alias, or of itself;
  - an alias with the name of the file's own namespace;
  - an alias declared twice, or after a declaration.

## Design notes
- **This is a standalone directive, not `import x as g`.** An import loads a file, while a namespace can span several files and a file can declare none. So an import alias would suggest a file-scoped module that Goose doesn't have. Opening a namespace (`use x;`) was also left out, since it would mean merging overload sets across namespaces.
- **The parser does all the work.** `ParseQualifiedName` replaces an aliased qualifier with its target, so lookup, the type checker, codegen and C symbol names are unchanged. `--dump` prints the target and reparses to the same program.
- **Error messages name the target** (`unknown type: goose_gfx2d::Nope`), but the underline covers the name as written (`TypeName::written`).
- **The "unknown namespace" check runs once every file is parsed, and is skipped if an earlier error was reported.** A file that failed to load or parse might be the one that declares the target.
- **The language server** takes a qualified name's spelling from the source text, so hover, definition, references, rename and highlighting work on `g::x`. Completion after `g::` lists the target's names. A name written with spaces around `::` is skipped instead of being given the wrong range.
- **Editors:** the tree-sitter grammar and the VS Code highlighting know the directive.

## Tests
- `test/syntax/namespace_aliases.goose` uses an alias in every kind of qualified name. Its import `ns/alias_user.goose` declares its own `im` alias for a different namespace and a `terrain` alias, which the importer also uses as a namespace. It also aliases `ns/hollow.goose`, a namespace with no declarations.
- `test/errors/ns_alias_*.goose` covers each error, including that an imported file can't use the importer's alias.
- `test/lsp/ns_alias.goose`, run from `lsp_protocol.py`, covers the language server cases.
- `run_tests.py` passes on Windows and in Arch Linux (WSL2). The one Linux failure, `libm calls`, fails the same way on `master` with that machine's gcc 20260810, which calls `pow` where the test expects a multiply.
- `tree-sitter/build.py --check` passes. The VS Code grammar test was added but not run here.

title: Square a constant 2 in pow under gcc 16
body:
gcc 16 turns `pow(x, 2.0)` into `x * x` only with `-fno-math-errno`, since the call would set errno on overflow. Goose builds at plain `-O2`, so on Linux with gcc 16, `test/libm_calls.py` failed: `squares()` kept its call to `pow`. A plain `#include <math.h>` file shows the same thing, so the cause is the compiler, not goose.

Goose has no errno, so in the gcc branch of `runtime_ext.h`, `gs_pow` and `gs_powf` now square a constant 2 themselves (guarded by `__builtin_constant_p`) and call libm otherwise. The clang and TinyCC branches are unchanged. Comparing gcc 16 with and without `-fno-math-errno` on other `pow` cases (x⁰, x¹, x³, x⁻¹, x^0.5, 2^x, constant arguments), squaring was the only result that changed; `sincos` and constant folding are unaffected.

**Older gcc:** gcc 7 through 15 already folded `pow(x, 2.0)` to `x * x` with errno on, so the new code compiles the same as before there (checked on Compiler Explorer with gcc 7.1, 9.5, 12.2, 13.2, 14.2 and 15.1). At `-O0` the guard is false and the call goes to libm, as before.

**Testing:** the full `run_tests.py` passes on Arch Linux with gcc 16.2.1 and clang 22, libm calls check included. A program comparing `-O0` (libm) with `-O2` (folded) on ±0, ±1e200, 1e-200, NaN and ±inf printed the same output from both.

title: Remove false sharing on private heap when access to gs_gl/gs_stks data.
body:
model-id: GLM-5.3 Flash
effort: Max

# Remove false sharing on private heap when accessing `gs_gl`/`gs_stks`

Every worker thread gets its own private heap state: a globals instance (`gs_gl`, what the thread-local pointer aims at) and its stack block (`gs_stks`). Threads share no mutable data (goose_spec.md 11.2), but plain `calloc` can place two workers' small chunks in the same 64-byte cache line — each worker's stores then invalidate the line its neighbour is writing, and a threaded program pays coherency traffic for data nobody actually shares. On the new `false_sharing` benchmark the fix roughly halves wall time at 4 and 8 worker threads (up to 2.3x), with no change at 2 threads.

## What changed

- **`src/runtime/runtime.h`** — add `gs_aligned_calloc` / `gs_aligned_free`. Chunks are handed out 64-byte (cache-line) aligned, with the request rounded up to whole lines: `aligned_alloc`'s C11 contract wants a size that is a multiple of the alignment, and whole lines keep a chunk's last line its own whatever the allocator packs beside it. Windows uses the CRT's `_aligned_malloc` / `_aligned_free` (msvcrt exports both; tcc declares neither, so runtime.h declares them for tcc); elsewhere C11 `aligned_alloc`, taken back by `free`. Zeroing is done explicitly with `memset`.
- Workers' private structures now come from the aligned allocator: the stack block (`gs_stack_block`), each worker's globals instance (emitted in `EmitThreadThunk`), and the release paths (`gs_thread_release`, `goose_exit`, `gs_jit_cleanup`).
- **`src/jit_runtime.c`** — export the aligned allocator to JIT-compiled code via the `gs_jit_symbols` table; **`src/runtime_inline.h`** regenerated for the JIT-inline variant of the same runtime code.
- **`test/threads/runtime_threads_lifecycle.c`** — the aborting worker allocates its `gs_gl` through the new path.

## How these numbers were taken

- Base = `master` (`855f1037`), optimized = this branch (`798ec075`). Both compilers freshly built in Release with no optional native packages, run back to back on the same machine (Ryzen 7 7840HS, Windows 11), nothing else running.
- `python bench/run_bench.py --only false_sharing --no-jit --out …` — best of 3 whole-process runs after two discarded warm-ups. JIT rows are skipped: the TinyCC backend does not support threads yet. Checksums agree across Goose, C++ and Rust in both runs.
- The generated C for the Goose rows is **identical between the two compilers except for the three allocation sites above**, so the delta measures the allocator change alone.

## Results

Wall time in ms (best of 3); MB is peak working set at the large size. MSVC 19.52 (`v145`) and clang-cl 22.1.3 build the Goose and C++ rows; rustc 1.100.0 builds the Rust row.

| Benchmark    | Size   | Toolchain | Base (ms) | Optimized (ms) | Δ time    | MB base → opt |
|--------------|--------|-----------|----------:|---------------:|----------:|---------------|
| goose threads | small  | v145   | 86.1  | 85.2  | -1.0%     | 3.9 → 3.9 |
| goose threads | small  | clang  | 56.4  | 57.1  | +1.2%     | 3.9 → 3.9 |
| cpp threads   | small  | v145   | 680.6 | 202.8 | (noise)   | 4.0 → 4.0 |
| cpp threads   | small  | clang  | 337.1 | 334.6 | -0.7%     | 4.0 → 4.0 |
| rust threads  | small  | rustc  | 144.3 | 143.5 | -0.6%     | 4.3 → 4.3 |
| goose threads | medium | v145   | 171.3 | 90.2  | **-47.3%** | 3.9 → 3.9 |
| goose threads | medium | clang  | 221.7 | 60.7  | **-72.6%** | 3.9 → 3.9 |
| cpp threads   | medium | v145   | 221.0 | 717.2 | (noise)   | 4.0 → 4.0 |
| cpp threads   | medium | clang  | 349.6 | 352.6 | +0.9%     | 4.0 → 4.0 |
| rust threads  | medium | rustc  | 153.7 | 154.0 | +0.2%     | 4.3 → 4.3 |
| goose threads | large  | v145   | 253.4 | 126.9 | **-49.9%** | 3.9 → 3.9 |
| goose threads | large  | clang  | 206.4 | 88.9  | **-56.9%** | 3.9 → 3.9 |
| cpp threads   | large  | v145   | 856.2 | 819.0 | -4.3%     | 4.0 → 4.0 |
| cpp threads   | large  | clang  | 670.5 | 686.1 | +2.3%     | 4.0 → 4.0 |
| rust threads  | large  | rustc  | 561.3 | 582.4 | +3.8%     | 4.3 → 4.3 |

At the large size the report's aggregate has Goose 6.45x / 7.72x faster than the
C++ row and 4.59x / 6.55x faster than the Rust row (v145 / clang) on this
branch, against 3.38x / 3.25x and 2.22x / 2.72x on master.

### Takeaways

- **Goose workers stop paying for each other.** At 2 threads the row is flat (±1%) — `calloc` happened not to place the two chunks adversarially. At 4 and 8 threads the fix removes 47-50% (v145) and 57-73% (clang) of wall time. The improvement is consistent across both backends and both sizes, which is what makes it signal against this row's noise.
- **The Rust baseline is stable (±4%), as it should be** — same source, same compiler on both sides; the change does not touch it.
- **The C++ row swings far more than Rust between runs of identical source**: 680.6 vs 202.8 ms at small/v145, and the direction is inconsistent across sizes. Its `thread_local` blocks come from the same kind of unaligned allocation, so a placement lottery of its own is the likely cause; the fixed harness policy (best of 3) does not control for it. Read C++ deltas as noise, not as regressions.
- **Peak RSS is resolved.** The scratch/sink trim in `798ec075` brings every row to 3.9-4.3 MB (the previous iteration measured 845-955 MB and left an open +32-38% question in the draft). The aligned allocation adds at most 63 bytes per chunk, which is invisible at this scale; Goose now uses slightly less memory than C++ (1.04x) and Rust (1.12x) at the large size.

<!--

-->
A call giving an ADT, and an integer where a float is declared, to an overload taking the whole ADT passed `goose check` and then wrote C that no compiler accepts:

    enum E { A }
    fn f(k: E, v: f64) {}
    fn main() { f(E.A, 3); }

A candidate converting an integer to a float ranks after tag dispatch (§7.1), so TryDispatch ran first and took f(E, f64) as every variant's case, since a variant matches a parameter of its own ADT. The dispatch then handed each case the variant's payload where f takes the ADT: clang says "passing 'E_g_A_p' to parameter of incompatible type 'E_g'", TinyCC "cannot convert". `3.0` built, as it resolves before dispatch.

A case takes the variant or a reference to it (§8.2). An overload taking the ADT at the dispatch position is now no case, so such a call finds none, and the ordinary candidate takes it as the integer-to-float last resort: f(E.A, 3) is f(E.A, 3.0). Case functions, a generic f<T> (which binds T to each variant) and a case set beside a whole-ADT overload (typing/int_float_conversions' `scale`) resolve as before. The spec's §8.2 says that an overload taking the ADT is an ordinary candidate.

codegen/dispatch_whole_adt_int_float runs each shape that failed: a payload-less variant constant, a value of the ADT, an integer variable, the ADT after the float, an f32, a variable-mode parameter, a call as a statement and an ADT with payloads. Without the change it fails to build.

title: [BUG] Assigning a nested call's u8[>..] result to a u8[..N] stores an empty string at -O1/-O2
body:
<!--
If you used AI to find this bug, fill in the below fields.
If purely human authored, use model-id `human`, no effort/prompt needed :)
-->

model-id: claude-opus-5-5
effort: low
prompt: none for the bug itself; it showed up while the model was writing a command-line tool in Goose, and the repro was then cut down by hand

<!--
The rest of your issue description starts here.
-->

## Summary

When a function's `u8[>..]` result comes through three levels of calls and is assigned to a limited array (`u8[..N]`), the destination ends up **empty**. There is no error and no abort. Binding the result to a `let` first and then assigning gives the right text. It happens at `-O1` and `-O2` (the default), in `goose run` and `goose build` alike, and not at `-O0`, so it looks like an inlining problem.

## Repro

```goose
import std;

fn norm(p: const u8[:]) -> u8[>..] {
    var parts: const u8[:][>..] = [];
    each_split(p, '/') { parts.push(it); };
    var out: u8[>..] = [];
    for part in parts { out.append(part); }
    return out;
}

fn join(a: const u8[:], b: const u8[:]) -> u8[>..] {
    var s: u8[>..] = [];
    s.append(a);
    s.append(b);
    return norm(s);
}

fn mk() -> u8[>..] { return join("x/", "y"); }
fn mk2() -> u8[>..] { return join("p/", "q"); }

fn main() {
    var d: u8[..64] = "";
    d = mk();
    print("[", d, "]");           // expected [xy]
    d = mk2();
    print("[", d, "]");           // expected [pq]
    let t = mk();
    d = t;
    print("[", d, "]");           // [xy]: binding the result first works
}
```

Expected:

```
[xy]
[pq]
[xy]
```

Actual, with `goose run repro.goose`:

```
[]
[]
[xy]
```

| Compiler | `run` (-O2) | `run -O1` | `run -O0` | `build` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| v2026.4 (runtime dce889723a23) | `[] [] [xy]` | `[] [] [xy]` | `[xy] [pq] [xy]` | `[] [] [xy]` |
| main at d92c431 (runtime d521138194f1) | `[] [] [xy]` | `[] [] [xy]` | `[xy] [pq] [xy]` | `[] [] [xy]` |

## What it takes to trigger

Cutting the repro down further:

* **The `each_split` (a block-taking call) in the innermost function matters.** Replace `norm`'s body with `out.append(p)`, or with pushing `p` into `parts` without `each_split`, and the output is correct.
* **The three call levels matter.** Assigning `join(...)` directly (no `mk` layer) is correct.
* **Two call sites matter.** With only `mk` (no `mk2`), `d = mk()` is correct.
* **The kind of destination does not matter.** A `u8[..N]` local and a `u8[..N]` struct field both fail. A struct field was where it first appeared, as `n.dir = mk()` with `dir: u8[..1024]`.

## Why this looks like a bug, not a rule

Spec §4.4 says a limited array is assignable "if the new length fits capacity" (here 2 bytes into 64). §4.3 covers this exact receiver: "A limited-capacity receiver must establish that the complete live result fits before writing outside its available slots", and it allows a temporary for that check. Neither allows the value to be dropped. The only valid outcomes are the right string or an abort for capacity. The fact that adding an unrelated function or changing `-O` changes the result points the same way.

## Workaround

Bind the call's result before assigning it to the limited array (`let t = mk(); d = t;`), or pass it through a parameter.

## Environment

Linux x86_64, gcc 16.2.1 for `goose build`; the JIT behaves the same.

title: help --man fails groff 1.25 -ww: a mid-line ellipsis trips the new style warning
body:
`test/run_tests.py`'s check "help --man is a man page groff reads without warnings" fails with GNU groff 1.25.0:

```
$ goose help --man > goose.1 && groff -man -ww -z goose.1
troff:goose.1:32: warning: end of sentence detected before end of text line [-w style]
troff:goose.1:317: warning: end of sentence detected before end of text line [-w style]
```

**Why:** groff 1.25 adds a warning category, `style` (its NEWS: "The formatter supports a new warning category, "style""), and `-ww` turns it on. Two lines of the help text put an ellipsis before more text on the same line, and troff reads the period followed by spaces as the end of a sentence:

```
  -- args...      What follows is the program's arguments.
  --multi-test file...  Compile each file as a run of its own would, ending what
```

**Fix (checked):** write `\&` after a mid-line ellipsis in the man output (`args...\&`, `file...\&`). With that, `groff -man -ww -z` prints nothing on groff 1.25.0, and `man -l` renders the two lines exactly as before. (Running the check with `-ww -Wstyle` would also silence it, but the escape keeps the page clean for every groff.)

Seen on Debian sid (groff 1.25.0) at d92c4315; both help lines are unchanged in `src/main.cpp` at bbede669. The same suite run is otherwise clean on gcc 16.2.0 and clang 24.0.0 apart from `libm calls` on gcc 16, which is #326.

title: Let std contains search arrays of variable-size elements
body:
<!--
If you are using AI to make this PR, fill in the below fields.
If purely human authored, use model-id `human`, no effort/prompt needed :)

NOTE: please use "frontier" LLMs at high effort only. If you don't you cause the

-->

model-id: claude-opus-5-5
effort: max

<!--
The rest of your PR description starts here.
-->

std's `contains` fails to check on an array of variable-size elements, such as strings, while `position` takes the same arguments without complaint:

```goose
import std;

fn main() {
    let words: u8[][>..] = ["bb", "a", "ccc"];
    print(position(words, "ccc"));   // 2
    print(contains(words, "ccc"));   // error
}
```

```
error: v is not fixed-size and is not copied implicitly (§4.1): pass copy(v) for a copy, or bind it by reference
    print(contains(words, "ccc"));
          ^
  while checking this standard library expression
  in fn contains(u8[][:], u8[]) instantiated from ...
```

A struct holding a `u8[]` fails the same way.

**Cause.** `contains` was `position(xs, v) >= 0`, which passes its own parameter `v` on to `position`'s by-value `v: T`. For a non-fixed `T` that is an lvalue at a value-typed destination, which §4.1 rejects. The caller's argument is fine (a literal is an rvalue), so the error comes from inside std and nothing at the call site avoids it: `copy(w)`, `&w` and an explicit type argument all fail too.

**Fix.** `contains` is now `any(xs) { it == v }`, which compares each element in place and copies nothing, so its result is the same as before for every element type that already worked. The diagnostic's suggestion, `position(xs, copy(v)) >= 0`, would instead break arrays of references, where `copy(v)` is the pointee; the new test covers that case.

**Tests.** `test/stdlib/stdlib_contains_variable.goose` covers strings (by function and method call, on the array and on a slice of it, with a literal and with `copy`), nested arrays, a struct holding a string and an empty array, plus fixed-size elements and references, whose results are unchanged. It fails on master and passes with the change at -O0 and -O2, with `--debug`, and in a native gcc build.

- `python test/run_tests.py --profile baseline --cc native --require-clang` passes on Ubuntu 26.04 (WSL2, gcc 15.2, clang 21.1), as it does on master. That build has no builtin gfx/physics/ui, so `test/physics/physics_bodies.goose`, the one other test calling `contains` (on physics handles), was run on its own with the package fetched: its output still matches `physics_bodies.out` at -O0 and -O2.
- `goose format --check samples stdlib` is clean.

Fixes #313.

## Cause
`TryInline` unwraps a trivial inlined result to its plain expression when the value's type has the same *kind* as the call's (`unwrapok`). When the call is the narrower operand of a mixed-width operation, the checker has retyped the call node to the wider type (`RetypeOperand` sets `exprtype = ct`). Unwrapping replaced it with the body's expression, which still has the narrow type, so `reg(0) * wide` (`u16` call, `u32` variable) was emitted as `gs_mul_u16` at -O1/-O2.

## Fix
For `TY_INT` and `TY_FLT`, `unwrapok` now requires the same type, so the `InlineBlock`, whose `exprtype` records the type the value converts to, is kept, as already happens for references and ADTs. Retyping the unwrapped node in place was not an option: if it is itself an operation (`a + b` on `u16`), that would change the width it computes at.

## Test
`test/optimizer/inline_widened_operand.goose` covers the cases from the issue (`u16 call * u32`, `+`, `u8 call * u16`, `* u64`, a typed `let`, a constant-returning callee) plus an `f32` call added to an `f64`. On master at -O2 it prints `1 4294836225 4294836225`, `65534`, `1`, …; with the fix, -O0/-O1/-O2 agree.

<!--
The rest of your PR description starts here.
-->

Fixes #332.

## Cause
Storing a call's result in a static-capacity limited array relies on the checker typing that call as the limited array itself: then `EmitSpecCall` returns a value and the copy and capacity check follow. A call that an inlined body returns (`d = mk()` with `fn mk() -> u8[>..] { return join(...); }`) keeps its callee's type, `u8[>..]`. For a bytes-typed result `Call::CgAny` assumes it was written in place, so the result was built on the data stack and dropped: the destination kept its old value (empty in the issue), and no capacity check ran. The same happens when the `InlineBlock` is not unwrapped (a body with other statements, or two `return join(...)`s), so this is a codegen fix, not one in `TryInline`.

## Fix
`Call::CgAny` sends a `DK_LVALUE` destination through `GenIntoLimited`, which `LeafAny` already uses for every other node. It copies a result of another array representation into the limited array under its capacity check, and does nothing when the types already agree, so the direct-call path is unchanged.

## Tests
- `test/optimizer/inline_call_into_limited.goose`: the issue's shape, a `var` initializer, a block body, two returns, a struct field and an array element as destinations. On master at -O2 every line prints `[]`.

<!--

When `from` and `to` point almost opposite ways in f32, quat's `rotation(from, to)` does not turn `from` onto `to`:

    import math;
    import vec;
    import quat;

    fn main() {
        let from = float3 { 1.0, 2.0, 3.0 };
        let to = float3 { -1.0, -2.0, -3.00001 };   // 1.6e-6 rad from opposite
        let q = rotation(from, to);
        let got = rotate(q, normalize(from));
        let want = normalize(to);
        print(got.x, " ", got.y, " ", got.z);       // -0.29127046 -0.5825409 -0.7588195
        print(want.x, " ", want.y, " ", want.z);    // -0.26726067 -0.53452134 -0.8017847
        print(q.w);                                 // -0.034380704
    }

The result is about 4 degrees from `to`, and the negative w means it went the long way round, past PI, where the doc comment and docs/stdlib.md promise the shortest arc. Over a million random f32 pairs near opposite, the miss reached 0.38.

w is `dot(a, h)`, where `a` and `b` are the inputs normalized and `h = normalize(a + b)` is the half vector. Expanded, a · h = |a + b| / 2 + (|a|² − |b|²) / (2 |a + b|). The second term is zero for exact unit vectors, but `normalize` leaves `a` and `b` an ulp or so off unit length, and near opposite |a + b| is tiny, so that term dominates w. The opposite-case branch only starts below |a + b| = 1e-6.

This PR takes w as `length(sum) * 0.5`. |a + b| / 2 equals a · h for unit vectors, and a + b of nearly opposite vectors comes out without cancellation error, so it keeps its precision. The same rounding leaves `a × h` a little short of unit length, so the quaternion is normalized. The opposite-case branch is unchanged.

Worst error |rotate(q, normalize(from)) − normalize(to)| over 1,000,000 random pairs each, with lengths from 0.01 to 100; for the near-opposite rows, `to` is `-from` plus a random offset of relative size 1e-7 to 1e-2 (f32) or 1e-16 to 1e-2 (f64), log-uniform:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| f32, nearly opposite | 0.38 | 1.2e-6 (7.4e-7 outside the opposite-case branch) |
| f32, any directions | 3.1e-5 | 6.6e-7 |
| f64, nearly opposite, outside the opposite-case branch | 6.3e-10 | 1.3e-15 |
| f64, any directions | 1.3e-13 | 1.3e-15 |

Outside the opposite-case branch, w is now never negative; before, it was negative for 236,000 of the million near-opposite f32 pairs. `rotation(x, x)` still gives the identity.

Not changed: the opposite-case branch still takes over below |a + b|² = 1e-12. In f32 that costs little, since the rotated `from` lands within about 1e-6 either way. In f64 it turns directions up to about 1e-6 rad from opposite about an arbitrary perpendicular axis, missing `to` by up to 1e-6, while the new w alone would be good to about 1e-15 there (the near-opposite f64 row above leaves those inputs out). Whether f64 should get a smaller cutoff is your call.

Checks:
- New `test/stdlib/stdlib_quat_rotation_opposite`: the pair above and the pair that missed by the most in the random run. For each, it prints the rotated `from` and `normalize(to)`, rounded, then whether they are within 1e-5 and whether w ≥ 0. On master it prints `false false` and `false true`.
- `stdlib_quat`, `stdlib_mat`, `stdlib_checkfree` and `stdlib_vec` keep their expected output. No sample calls quat's `rotation`.
- The fixture and the random comparison print the same under `goose run` at -O0, -O2 and --debug and under `goose build` with gcc 15 and clang 21, with and without --debug. The table comes from a copy of the new code, and the patched `rotation` matched it bit for bit on all 4,000,000 pairs.
- `python3 test/run_tests.py --profile baseline --cc native --require-clang` on Ubuntu under WSL (gcc 15.2, clang 21.1): all tests passed, with the same skips as master there (the audio, gfx, physics and ui layers, which that build leaves out, the tests TinyCC can't run yet, and the Windows-only commit limit).
- `goose format --check samples stdlib` is clean.

title: Let format_uleb and parse_uleb carry the full 64-bit range under --debug
body:
<!--
If you are using AI to make this PR, fill in the below fields.
If purely human authored, use model-id `human`, no effort/prompt needed :)

NOTE: please use "frontier" LLMs at high effort only. If you don't you cause the
maintainers more work having to review/redo. Report an issue instead if you
don't have access to these.
-->

model-id: claude-opus-5-5
effort: max

<!--
The rest of your PR description starts here.
-->

Under `--debug` (GS_DEBUG), std's ULEB128 helpers abort on values their docs cover. `format_uleb` aborts on any negative value:

```goose
import std;

fn main() {
    var out: u8[>..] = [];
    format_uleb(out, -1);
    print(out.len);   // 10
}
```

```
goose runtime error: as conversion out of range (debug): -1 as u64 (uleb_format.goose:5)
```

`parse_uleb` aborts on a well-formed ten-byte encoding carrying bit 63:

```goose
import std;

fn main() {
    let v, k = parse_uleb([0x80, 0x80, 0x80, 0x80, 0x80, 0x80, 0x80, 0x80, 0x80, 0x01]);
    print(v, " ", k);   // -9223372036854775808 10
}
```

```
goose runtime error: as conversion out of range (debug): 9223372036854775808 as i64 (uleb_parse.goose:4)
```

At -O0 and -O2 both programs print the commented values. Release builds wrap, so `format_uleb(out, -1)` writes ten bytes that `parse_uleb` reads back as `-1 10`.

**Cause.** `format_uleb` converted its `i64` with `v as u64`, and `parse_uleb` returned `v as i64`. A plain `as` is range-checked in debug builds (spec §6.3), so the first aborts on any negative `v` and the second on any value of 2^63 or more. The docs put those values in range. §3.6 gives varints "1–10 bytes; full 64-bit range", and `docs/stdlib.md` lists `format_uleb` as writing 1-10 bytes, where only a negative `i64` takes ten. Apart from unterminated input, `parse_uleb`'s comment refuses only what is "past the 64-bit range", and its check `shift == 63 && (b & 0x7e) != 0` lets a tenth byte carry bit 63 on purpose.

**Fix.** Both conversions are now `as!`, which wraps in every build, so a debug build computes what a release build already did. Release output is unchanged. This is also how the runtime's `gs_uleb_write` and `gs_uleb_read` convert (`(uint64_t)` going out, `(int64_t)` coming back), and b534f9b8 made the same change for `hash(i64)`. A sentence in each function's comment says why.

You might prefer that a ULEB never stand for a negative value. In that case `parse_uleb` would return `0, 0` for 2^63 and up (its tenth-byte test `b & 0x7e` becomes `b & 0x7f`), and `format_uleb` would assert that `v` is not negative. Encodings would then stop at nine bytes, so `docs/stdlib.md` and both comments would change too. I can switch the PR to that if you prefer it.

**Tests.** `test/stdlib/stdlib_uleb_range.goose` carries the `runtime-debug` marker, so the suite also runs it under GS_DEBUG. It round-trips 0, i64.max, -1 and i64.min, checking each encoding byte for byte. It also parses the ten-byte -1 (`-1 10`), a tenth byte past bit 63 (`0 0`) and an eleven-byte encoding (`0 0`). On master it aborts at -1 under `--debug`. With the change it passes at -O0, -O2 and `--debug`, and in native gcc and clang builds, both release and `--debug`.

- `python3 test/run_tests.py --exe build/goose --profile baseline --cc native --require-clang -j 10` passes on Ubuntu 26.04 (WSL2, gcc 15.2, clang 21.1), with the same skips as on master: audio/gfx/physics/ui, the JIT tests TinyCC cannot run yet, and a Windows-only test.
- The existing callers print the same as before. `samples/25_serialize.goose` and `test/stdlib/stdlib_regex.goose` (through `stdlib/regex.goose`) were checked at -O0, -O2 and `--debug`, and `test/storage/serialize.goose` at -O0 and -O2. Under `--debug`, that last fixture matches through its ULEB line, then stops at an overflow in its own digest (`digest * 3`, line 460), as it does on master. It has no `runtime-debug` marker, so CI does not run it that way.
- `goose format --check samples stdlib` is clean.

effort: high
prompt: While fixing other issues you hit a build failure from a `#` in the checkout path; fix it as a PR.

<!--
The rest of your PR description starts here.
-->

## Problem
In a checkout whose path holds a `#` (here `~/Documents/# Swift/...`), the build fails:

```
build/generated/builtin_packages.h:26: error: use of undeclared identifier 'GOOSE_BUILTIN_RSPDIR_physics'
```

CMake drops a `-D` definition whose value holds a `#` ("Preprocessor definitions containing '#' may not be passed on the compiler command line because many compilers do not support it"). Four definitions carry paths:

- `GOOSE_BUILTIN_RSPDIR_<pkg>`: `builtin_packages.h` then does not compile (with `-DGOOSE_BUILTIN_LIBS=all`).
- `GOOSE_STDLIB_PATH` and `GOOSE_TCC_LIB_PATH`: they sit behind `#ifdef`s, so they go missing silently. A compiler built in a build directory outside the source tree then cannot find the standard library.

## Fix
- The paths are now C string literals in generated headers instead of `-D` values:
  - `build_paths.h` (new, next to `builtin_packages.h`) defines `GOOSE_STDLIB_PATH` and `GOOSE_TCC_LIB_PATH`. `main.cpp` and `jit.h` include it, and their `#ifdef`s are unchanged.
  - `builtin_packages.h`, which already spells each package's source directory as a literal, spells its response-file directory the same way. Only the configuration's name stays on the command line (`GOOSE_BUILD_CONFIG="$<CONFIG>"`), concatenated as `"<rspdir>/" GOOSE_BUILD_CONFIG`, so multi-config generators keep working.
- `goose_c_string` escapes a backslash or a quote in these literals (the `-D` values were not escaped either).
- `test/lsp_protocol.py`: `uri_of` now escapes a path the way the server's `UriOfPath` (`src/lsp_rpc.h`) does. A raw `#` (or space) in a test's URI never matched the URI the server published diagnostics for, so the language server checks waited out their timeouts.

## Checked (macOS, Apple clang 21)
- In `/Users/.../goose-#hash` with Ninja, Release, `-DGOOSE_BUILTIN_LIBS=all`: configure prints no `#` warnings, the build succeeds, and `test/run_tests.py --profile baseline --cc native` passes apart from the groff check fixed in #335.
- Ninja Multi-Config, Debug, in the same path: builds, and the Debug compiler links a program that imports `gfx` through `pkg/gfx/Debug`.

Not tested on Windows/MSVC.

title: Publish cached data-stack tops around extern calls when a program has export fns (#322)
body:
<!--
If you are using AI to make this PR, fill in the below fields.
If purely human authored, use model-id `human`, no effort/prompt needed :)

NOTE: please use "frontier" LLMs at high effort only. If you don't you cause the
maintainers more work having to review/redo. Report an issue instead if you
don't have access to these.
-->

model-id: grok-4.7
effort: high
prompt: Fix the bug where an export fn called back from C overwrites its callers' data-stack locals, and add a regression test.

<!--
The rest of your PR description starts here.
-->

Fixes #322.

An `export fn` wrapper enters the Goose function at `gs_sp` 0 and reads data-stack tops from memory. Callers keep the tops of stacks they grow in C locals, and write them back only before a call that `SyncReach` says can reach those stacks. An `extern fn` reaches nothing unless it is handed a builder or is `gs_trim_memory`, so a call into C left the cached tops unpublished. The callback then allocated at those stale tops, on top of the callers' live strings and arrays. A frame further up had the same hole: its stacks are not part of what its callee reaches, so they stayed cached too.

`SFunction::readsalltops` already makes a caller, and transitively every caller of that caller, publish every cached top around the call and read them back afterwards. In a program that has an `export fn`, every extern declared outside the standard library is marked that way. The runtime's own externs are not: they never call back. A program with no export compiles as before.

`test/codegen/export_callback.goose` calls the export wrappers from `main`, from a function `main` calls, and from a callback that calls back into C, and has a callback push onto a global array. Before the fix, `goose run` corrupted `main`'s string and segfaulted. After it, `goose run` and native builds at `-O0` and `-O2` print the expected output. `goose format --check samples stdlib` passes, and `python test/run_tests.py --exe build/goose --profile baseline --cc native --require-clang` passes (gcc 13.3 and TinyCC).

Loop-invariant views of a global (`hoistrefs` / `hoistfields`) are still not dropped across such a call. A callback that shrinks a global its caller is looping over leaves the old length. That stays inside the region; it is the case the issue leaves out.

model-id: grok-4.7
effort: high
prompt: Rename the standard-library copy_into function to copy_from, keep the old name working, and warn when it is used. Update callers, documentation, samples, and tests.

<!--
The rest of your PR description starts here.
-->

Closes #230

`copy_into(dst, src)` follows memcpy's argument order, but `dst.copy_into(src)` reads as a copy from `dst` into `src`. The call does the opposite. `copy_from` keeps that argument order and reads correctly both ways: `copy_from(dst, src)` and `dst.copy_from(src)`. `copy_into` stays, with the same arguments, and a call warns.

Goose had no way to mark a function deprecated. `deprecated`, optionally followed by a string, is a qualifier only in that position, in the same way `inline` and `checkfree` are. A direct call warns, and so does naming the function as a value. A later call through that value does not warn again. The standard library writes `deprecated "use copy_from" fn copy_into`, so the warning is `copy_into is deprecated: use copy_from`.

The implementation of the copy is `copy_from`. `copy_into` calls it. Library, sample, benchmark, and test callers of the standard-library function now use `copy_from`. Local functions that were already named `copy_into` are unchanged. Spec §7.15, the reference, and `docs/stdlib.md` describe the qualifier and the rename. The tree-sitter grammar and the VS Code grammar recognize `deprecated`. Regenerating the checked-in parser also writes back the namespace-alias rules from #325, which grammar.js already had and `tree-sitter/src/parser.c` did not.

`python test/run_tests.py --exe build/goose --profile baseline --cc native --require-clang` passed (108s, 4 jobs). `build/goose format --check samples stdlib` passed. The tree-sitter corpus passed (29/29), and `npm test` in `vscode` passed (42/42).

title: Windows: cryptographic random bytes with ProcessPrng
body:
## The Problem

`os` has no source of random bytes safe for keys, nonces, or tokens.
`random_seed()` is meant for seeding `std`'s RNG; on POSIX it reads
`/dev/urandom`, but on Windows it is a mix of the clocks, the process id and
an address, which is predictable.

A program that needs real entropy today has to call the OS itself through
`extern "c" { fn getentropy(p: u8&, n: u64) -> i32; }`, which opens the C
library at startup. Windows has neither that library nor `getentropy`, so
such a program stops before `main`:

```
cannot load c (c.dll): Windows error 126
```

Extern blocks are bound at startup, and there is no platform switch, so one
source cannot name `getentropy` on POSIX and `ProcessPrng` on Windows. The
runtime is the place for it.

## Fix

```goose
// Fills out with cryptographically secure random bytes from the OS, for
// keys and nonces: getentropy(3), or ProcessPrng on Windows. False if the OS
// gives none, and then out is not to be used.
extern fn random_bytes(out: u8[:]) -> bool = "gs_os_random_bytes";
```

- **Windows:** `ProcessPrng` (`bcryptprimitives.dll`, Windows 10 and later,
  as Go 1.22+ and Rust's std use), else `RtlGenRandom` (`advapi32.dll`
  `SystemFunction036`) in parts of at most 2^30 bytes. Both are looked up
  once with `LoadLibraryW`/`GetProcAddress` and cached, so programs link
  nothing new and TinyCC builds keep working.
- **macOS, Linux, the BSDs:** `getentropy(3)` in 256-byte calls (its limit),
  else `/dev/urandom` (Linux kernels before 3.17).
- It returns false only if the OS gives nothing, like the rest of `os`;
  callers that want to abort assert on it.
- `random_seed` now draws its 8 bytes from the same source and keeps the
  clock mix only as a last resort, so it is no longer predictable on Windows.

Files:

- `src/runtime/runtime_ext.h`: the `GS_API` declaration of
  `gs_os_random_bytes` (which also puts it in the JIT's symbol table).
- `src/runtime/runtime_os.h`: `gs_os_entropy`, `gs_os_random_bytes`, and
  `gs_os_random_u64` on top of them.
- `src/runtime_inline.h`: regenerated with `goose --gen-runtime-header`.
- `stdlib/os.goose`: `random_bytes`.
- `docs/stdlib.md`, `docs/design/stdlib_design.md`: the signature, its
  sources and when it fails.
- `test/stdlib/stdlib_os.goose`, `test/expected/stdlib_os.out`: 1000 bytes
  (several getentropy calls) come back true and filled in every 250-byte
  part, a second draw differs, and an empty slice is true.

## Testing

The patch applies unchanged to `d92c4315`, `bbede669` and `3a0aa2eb`.

- **macOS arm64 (Apple clang 21), on `d92c4315`:**
  `python3 test/run_tests.py -j 8`: all tests passed (919 JIT runs,
  1958 typecheck errors, 81 parse errors, 52 samples, goose_in_goose
  bootstrap). `stdlib_os` matches under `goose run` at -O2, -O0 and
  --debug, and under `goose build`.
- **Windows Server 2022 x64, on `3a0aa2eb`:** goose built with MSVC 19.44
  (VS 2022 Build Tools, Release). `python test/run_tests.py --cc msvc`:
  all tests passed (745 generated-C programs at -O0 and -O2, 217 GS_DEBUG
  programs, 922 JIT runs, 1958 typecheck errors, 52 samples).
  `stdlib_os` matches under `goose run` at -O2, -O0 and --debug, and
  `goose build --cc X` of `stdlib_os` and of the program below runs and
  prints the expected output for each of:
  - `msvc` (19.44),
  - `clang-cl` and `clang` (LLVM 23.1.5),
  - `gcc` (MinGW-w64 GCC 16.2.0, UCRT).
  On `bbede669`, a 113-check package suite (JIT and native builds) that
  takes all its key material from `random_bytes` also passed with each
  compiler.
- **Linux x86_64 (glibc 2.31):** verified on the earlier base `cfd2f489`,
  where `stdlib_os` passed under `goose run` and `goose build`.

A minimal program, before and after:

```goose
import os;

fn main() {
    var b: u8[32] = [0; 32];
    print(random_bytes(b));     // true
    var zero = true;
    for x in b { if x != 0 { zero = false; } }
    print(!zero);               // true
}
```

title: Collect every byte-set hit in one scan with find_all
body:
## Summary

Adds `find_all(s: const u8[:], set: const ByteSet&, out: i64[:]) -> i64` to the stdlib, backed by a new `gs_scan_collect` in the runtime.

`find_any` answers where the *next* hit is, so a caller that wants all of them pays the extern call, its kind dispatch and its byte-set setup once per hit — the motivating parser (a drainrs port at haydenflinner/drainrs-goose) came out ~2x *slower* calling `find_any` per separator than its scalar loop, and ~19% faster once the scan was batched. `find_all` writes every hit index into `out` in one call.

This is the "where" primitive of APL's `⍸`, K's `&` and NumPy's `flatnonzero` — returning indexes, but into a caller's buffer so nothing allocates.

**Depends on #99** — this shares the SIMD scan machinery it adds (the diff here will shrink to the last two commits once that lands; on x86 it uses the SSE2 paths that already exist upstream).

## Semantics

- Writes hit indexes ascending, up to `out.len`.
- Returns the count **written** (≤ `out.len`), not the count that exists. A `strlcpy`-style total would force a full scan even when `out` fills early, which makes the chunked form quadratic; a return of `out.len` says more may follow, collected by a call on what is left past the last written index.
- `cap <= 0` or empty input → 0.

## Implementation

- `GS_COLLECT_LOOP` shares the find_any block loops over the compare kinds and nibble-table sets; new `GS_BMASK_NEXT` steps a block's mask to its next hit (bit-clear on SSE2, nibble-clear on NEON). Scalar fallback for short inputs and all other targets.
- `src/codegen.h`: emits the `sl_i64` typedef wherever `runtime_ext.h` is spliced in, as it already does for `sl_u8`. Any `runtime_ext.h` helper naming a slice type other than `u8` would otherwise break every program's generated C.
- `src/runtime_inline.h` regenerated.

## Testing and benchmark

- `test/stdlib/stdlib_byteset.goose` now cross-checks `find_all` against a byte loop over every set kind, all starts and lengths covering block, tail and scalar paths, with `out` both large enough and deliberately short: 23,040 searches, 0 wrong. Full `run_tests.py` suite passes (clang backend, TinyCC JIT).

title: Raise the Linux main-thread stack limit to 64 MB at process start (#271)
body:
<!--

If purely human authored, use model-id `human`, no effort/prompt needed :)

NOTE: please use "frontier" LLMs at high effort only. If you don't you cause the
