model-id: grok-4.7
effort: high
prompt: Raise the Linux soft RLIMIT_STACK to 64 MB at process start for goose and built programs.

<!--
The rest of your PR description starts here.
-->

Fixes #271

On Linux the main thread grows up to the soft RLIMIT_STACK. A process often starts with 8 MB, and no link option raises it. Windows and macOS already reserve 64 MB for that thread at link time. A recursion of about 12 MB then stops with `goose runtime error: native call stack overflow`, under `goose run` and in a built executable.

`gs_raise_main_stack` raises the soft limit to that same 64 MB when the hard limit allows a raise that far, and leaves a soft limit that is already higher. The program's `main` calls it before `gs_program_init`. `gs_rt_start` calls it again immediately before `gs_native_stack_init` records the bounds the overflow guard uses; on Linux those bounds come from that soft limit (`pthread_getattr_np`). goose's own `main` calls it at process start, so `goose run` and `goose format` have the same stack as a built program. The kernel checks the limit as the main stack grows. A worker's stack is unchanged: glibc takes its default size at startup, and the runtime still reserves 8 MB where that is smaller.

`test/main_stack.py` starts the process with the soft limit at 8 MB (`ulimit -S -s 8192`, so the hard limit stays where it was) and runs a 3000-deep recursion, about 12 MB of frames. `goose run` and the built executable both print `3000`.

The suite's deep-block format test, 10,000 nested blocks, already exits 0 at that 8 MB soft limit. Formatting 40,000 nested blocks segfaulted there before this change (`goose check --dump` and `goose format`) and now exits 0.

`python test/run_tests.py --exe build/goose --profile baseline --cc native --require-clang`, soft stack 8192: all tests passed (gcc 13.3.0 and TinyCC, with the clang checks).

title: Test the conditions copy elision relies on; add --no-copy-elision
body:
#310 leaves out copies of fixed structs over 256 bytes where the code generator finds nothing can tell. #341 found three of its conditions that no test needed, and #342 added fixtures for those. This PR checks all the rest, adds the tests that were missing, and adds a way to catch the next one.

**Dropping each condition.** I removed each of the 60 conditions in `StableArg`, `MovableArg`, `SingleUses`, `ParamUnwritten`, `ConsumedParam`, `OpenIbFixed`, `DiesAtCall`, `EmitSpecCall`'s destination check and `LeafAny`'s in-place literal, one at a time, and ran the full suite on each:

| | conditions |
|---|---|
| a test failed before #342 | 10 (`fixed_pointer_abi`, `last_use_moves` and its C shapes, `large_fixed_values`) |
| #342's fixtures fail | 3: #341's three |
| only the new tests fail | 3: `captured` in `StableArg` and in `MovableArg`, `refwrite` in `StableArg` |
| `isglobal` and `ownerspec`, each enough alone | fail together: in `StableArg` the suite catches it (`writes_global`), in `MovableArg` only the new tests do |
| no test fails | the rest, listed in each function's comment |

**Tests.**
- `test/codegen/copy_elision_guards.goose`: a case for each of the last three, and for the `MovableArg` pair: `captured_lent`, `captured_moved` (a block passed to a generic function writes the variable; its body belongs to the callee's specialization, so the caller names the variable only once), `ref_lent`, `global_once`.
- `--no-copy-elision` (a hidden option, under `goose help internals`) makes every copy: no fresh destinations, hand-overs or lending. `test/copy_elision.py` generates programs from the call shapes the conditions guard and checks that each prints the same at -O0 and -O2, with and without the option. On its own it catches 10 of the 16 caught conditions and both pairs, #341's three among them. The suite runs eight seeds (built where there is a C compiler). `python test/copy_elision.py --seeds 0-499` runs a wider sweep, and `--print SEED` prints a program.

**Comments.** Each condition's comment now names the case that fails without it, or says that none does. For some there is a reason:
- `ParamUnwritten`'s check for writes matters alone only for a parameter an optimizer rewrite writes, which no test makes. `isvar` covers a `var` parameter, and the two together fail `fixed_pointer_abi`.
- `ConsumedParam`, and `SingleUses`' `declloop`s for match binders and for-loop variables, only cost copies when wrong.
- `BuildsAtLocation` and `refwrite` in `MovableArg`: a destination or a writable reference names the variable a second time, which `SingleUses` already declines.

The others are left as they were, with no test: the type and storage-kind checks (`reusable`, `istemp`, `resulttemp`, the type, `fvptr`, `splitroots`, `refalias`), `OpenIbFixed`'s `pool`, `NeedsResultLocation`, `ibfixed`, `refalias`, `reusable` and `defer` checks, and `DiesAtCall`'s. Dropping each group at once still fails no test. So either no program reaches them, or they're redundant with the checks around them. I haven't found which. `fixed_pointer_abi`'s `pick_deferred` was written for the `defer` check, but passes without it.

**docs/testing.md** has a new section asking for the same of the next such change: drop each condition, see a test fail, name the test at the condition.

**Run** (rebased on master, 9412b80f):
- The full suite passes on Windows (MSVC) and on Linux (gcc 16). The copy-elision check runs in both, built with the native C compiler.
- 500 generated programs agree on Linux (JIT) before the rebase, and 200 after; 8 built with MSVC and 100 in the JIT agree on Windows.

title: Define whether parse_uleb accepts non-canonical encodings
Embedded NUL silently truncates Goose source
body:
## Bug

An embedded NUL byte is treated as end-of-file, so later source bytes are silently ignored.

Verified on upstream master 3a0aa2e with goose v2026.4-43-g3a0aa2eb.

## Minimal reproduction

Create a file containing these exact bytes:

    66 6e 20 6d 61 69 6e 28 29 7b 7d 00 40
    fn main(){}\x00@

Then run:

    goose check nul.goose
    goose run nul.goose

Expected: rejection because the @ after U+0000 is not valid Goose syntax. The language reference defines a source file as UTF-8 text; U+0000 is not an EOF marker.

Actual: both commands exit 0 with no stdout or stderr. Everything after the NUL is ignored.

## Likely defect location

- src/lexer.h Lexer constructor receives only a NUL-terminated pointer, without the source length.
- src/lexer.h zero-byte token branch unconditionally emits T_EOF.
- src/utils.h LoadFile preserves the complete file in a sized std::string, but src/main.cpp ParseProgram passes only c_str().

A complete fix likely needs a consistent end pointer/length across file parsing, formatter/build-file scanning, package scanning, recovery loops, and unsaved LSP source providers; a file-load-only rejection would not cover every source path.

title: Invalid source UTF-8 is copied into diagnostics JSON
body:
## Bug

A source file containing an invalid Unicode scalar sequence causes --diagnostics json to emit bytes that are themselves invalid UTF-8, so strict JSON clients cannot decode the diagnostic.

Verified on upstream master 3a0aa2e with goose v2026.4-43-g3a0aa2eb.

## Minimal reproduction

Create a source file containing exactly the three bytes ED A0 80, the illegal UTF-8 encoding of surrogate U+D800, then run:

    goose check --diagnostics json bad_utf8.goose

Expected: exit 1 with an illegal-source-character diagnostic encoded as valid UTF-8 JSON.

Actual: exit 1, but stdout includes ED A0 80 in both message and text. Strict UTF-8 decoding fails at output byte 58.

This is distinct from closed issue #261, which concerned decoding surrogate escapes in inbound JSON. Here the invalid bytes originate in source text and are copied into outbound diagnostics JSON.

## Likely defect locations

- src/lexer.h Utf8CharAt validates lead/continuation shape but not overlong sequences, surrogate code points, or the U+10FFFF ceiling.
- QuotedCharAt consequently copies the invalid bytes into the message.
- src/utils.h RenderDiagnostic independently copies the raw source line into text.
- src/json.h JsonQuote assumes input is already valid UTF-8 and passes non-control bytes through.

A complete fix needs both scalar-valid decoding and a defined replacement or escaping policy for raw diagnostic text; changing only one path leaves the other invalid.

Treat bare CR as a source line ending across compiler tooling
body:
## Bug

A source file using bare carriage returns as line endings does not terminate // comments. The language reference says line endings are read as newline regardless of convention.

Verified on upstream master 3a0aa2e.

## Minimal reproduction

Create a file containing these exact bytes:

    2f 2f 0d 66 6e 20 6d 61 69 6e 28 29 7b 7d 0d
    //\rfn main(){}\r

Run:

    goose run cr.goose

Expected: the CR ends the comment, main is parsed, and the program exits 0.

Actual: the lexer treats the whole file as a comment and exits 1 with:

    program needs exactly one global fn main()

LF and CRLF controls work.

## Likely scope

A correct change is broader than the line-comment loop alone. Source newline handling is currently duplicated across:

- src/lexer.h scanning, recovery, comments, raw strings, and diagnostics
- src/utils.h diagnostic rendering
- src/format.h and src/dump.h source rendering
- src/lsp_rpc.h and src/lsp_features.h line indexing

A prototype that unified LF, CRLF, and bare-CR behavior needed coordinated changes in all of these paths plus documentation-comment and JSON-diagnostic regression coverage. Fixing only // comments would leave line numbers, carets, formatting, raw strings, and LSP positions inconsistent.

title: Adapt bit-not constants in constant expressions
body:
## Bug

An adaptable bit-not constant is rejected when constant evaluation unifies it with a narrow typed operand.

Minimal repro:

    let N: u8 = 1;
    fn main() {
        let a: u8[N & ~0] = [0];
    }

Expected: the extent is 1. The language rules make ~c adapt at the typed operands width when c fits; the identical runtime expression N & ~0 evaluates to 1.

Actual before this change:

    ~0 does not fit u8: 0 does not

## Change

Use the pre-complement adaptable range already stored in Val::notconst when checking whether the constant fits the other operands type. Existing fit checking remains in force; for example ~300 still does not fit u8.

The bit-not constant fixture now covers unsigned and signed 8-bit operands in compile-time array extents.

## Tests

- focused JIT exact-output runs at O0 and O2
- existing ~300 no-fit diagnostic control
- full baseline harness with GCC O0/O2 and TinyCC: all tests passed (170 seconds)
- git diff --check

title: Narrow optional field accesses after short-circuit and while checks
Views of a handle may not be used after release
body:
<!--
If you are using AI to make this PR, fill in the below fields.
If purely human authored, use model-id `human`, no effort/prompt needed :)

NOTE: please use "frontier" LLMs at high effort only. If you don't you cause the
maintainers more work having to review/redo. Report an issue instead if you
don't have access to these.

model-id: glm-5.3-flash
effort: max
prompt:
> This repo is the impl of the goose language.
> Read @docs/goose_spec.md and @docs/implementation.md
> Currently, a borrow of an own can outlive its consumption:
>
> ```
> let i = [7, 7, 7];
> trusted fn make() -> own i64[:] { i[..] }
> trusted fn consume(_: own i64[:]) { }
>
> fn main() {
>     let a = make();
>     let b = a[..];
>     consume(a);
>     // no compile error but
>     // b is usable here even though a isn't
> ```
>
> The case of a slice_pool sets the precedent that the claim of ownership implies the
> owner may deallocate the memory, such that any subsequent access to the slice by
> borrows is undefined behavior. Assemble a plan for implementing release-is-a-shrink

I also did an hour or so of manual review and cleanup of the result

<!--
The rest of your PR description starts here.
-->
Section 4.8 of docs/design/ownership.md: a plain view read out of an own handle (`let r: u8[:] = s`), directly or through a borrow of what it points at, must not be used after the handle is consumed. Consuming the handle -- release, a defer's claim at an exit, a move out by take or replace -- refuses any such view that is still used, at the consume, naming it, the way a shrink of a grown array is checked against the views that name it (UsedAfter, ShrinkScanVars).

The handle names the views it spawned as they are read (RefProvOf) and as their bindings take it (BindProv, rebinds included): one field on the provenance, no place (§9.2) -- the roots keep the pointee's real provenance, the pool and its slots unchanged -- so no rule that asks roots for a place moves. A view lives in a variable of its own, is passed down or returned, and is never stored into a field, an element, a global or any other holder, as for a shrinkable array's views (§5.2); the store rule refuses one (FitsAt, CheckBindingRoot, a literal's field), and a return that hands a view of a claimed handle up to the caller is refused where it hands it (CheckReturn). A rebinding of the view's variable to another handle ends what it answered to, and each binding names one handle.

Nine rejection fixtures and four that stay legal go with it, the spec says the rule next to §5.5's obligation, the reference shows it, and the design note's status records what is built. The other runs are the checker's; nothing in codegen, the runtime or the pools moves.

body:
<!--
If you are using AI to make this PR, fill in the below fields.
If purely human authored, use model-id `human`, no effort/prompt needed :)

NOTE: please use "frontier" LLMs at high effort only. If you don't you cause the
maintainers more work having to review/redo. Report an issue instead if you
don't have access to these.

model-id: glm-5.3-flash
effort: max
prompt:
```
Add support for inherited function valued arguments. These are declared with other generic parameters:
```goose
fn foo<inherited bar: fn()>() { bar() }
```
They are used within the body of the function which declares them identically to other function valued parameters.

The difference is in how they are supplied to the function. They are drawn by name from the scope of the function call:
```goose
fn bar() { print("foobar"); }
foo(); // at this call site we find a function named `bar` in scope and the call to `foo` inherits it through the `bar` argument
```

This is a preliminary to sketching HOF-as-coroutines, discussed
- [on discord](https://discord.com/channels/1559977219663732797/1570210456793260032/1571176244500893740)
- [in goose-resume-conditions](https://github.com/bkietz/goose-resume-conditions/issues/1)

HOF-style-coroutines without this feature will be required to pass their (potentially many) suspend operations as regular arguments, which will lead to lots of unnecessary repetition. Additionally, the type of a suspended coroutine (which must include the suspend operations as well as the root coroutine itself) becomes difficult to spell.

Before:
```goose
suspend fn a<suspend_op_0, suspend_op_1, suspend_op_2, ...>() {
  b(suspend_op_0, suspend_op_1, suspend_op_2, ...);
  b(suspend_op_0, suspend_op_1, suspend_op_2, ...);
  b(suspend_op_0, suspend_op_1, suspend_op_2, ...);
}
suspend fn b<suspend_op_0, suspend_op_1, suspend_op_2, ...>() {...}

// ...
type Task = suspend<a, suspend_op_0, suspend_op_1, suspend_op_2, ...>;
```

After:
```goose
suspend fn a<inherited suspend_op_0, inherited suspend_op_1, inherited suspend_op_2, ...>() {
  b(); b(); b();
}
suspend fn b<inherited suspend_op_0, inherited suspend_op_1, inherited suspend_op_2, ...>() {...}

// ...
type Task = suspend<a>;
```

title: Write one C function for specializations whose C is the same
body:
<!--
If you are using AI to make this PR, fill in the below fields.
-->

model-id: claude-opus-5-5
effort: xhigh
prompt:

I started with a session to investigate the issue when I discovered the issue, went over potential solutions and prototyped something. This the prompt supplied to the implementing agent. I followed it up using claude's code-review skill on xhigh settings, with the fixes incorporated into this PR.

>Goose specializes a function per root class of each slice or reference argument, so a non-generic function called with both a global and a local slice is written out twice even when its C is identical. Make codegen write one C function per group of specializations whose C is the same up to references: blank each function’s own name, the specializations it calls and its return ... from numbers (each standing for its target), group by blanked text, and split until every reference points into the same group, so copies of a recursion merge too. Keep one function per group, point every reference at it and renumber return-from targets to the kept copy’s; if the compiler’s own reasoning about non-local returns says that renumbering is unsound, stop and report. Checking stays per specialization. Add tests that fail without the change, keep the suite passing, and measure lines of C, not compile times.

<!--
The rest of your PR description starts here.
-->

## Write one C function for specializations whose C is the same

Goose checks a function once per specialization, and the key includes the root class of each
reference or slice argument. So a non-generic function called once with a global slice and once
with a local one is written out twice, even though the two C functions are the same apart from
their names, the names of the specializations they call, and their `return ... from` numbers.

`CodeGen::MergeSpecs` (new `src/codegen_merge.h`) runs after codegen has written all the C and
keeps one function per group of such copies:

- Only copies of one function merge (an element-run twin only with twins), so only functions
  written more than once are read. A program with none pays for a count of its functions and
  gets the same C as before. Distinct functions whose C happens to be the same, such as two empty
  methods, stay apart.
- A copy's references are read from its text: the C names of the copies (which `Unique` keeps
  apart from every other C name), and their target numbers (in `gs_lret/gs_fdst/gs_fval_K_J` and
  as what `gs_rf` is compared with or set to), each standing for the function that catches it.
  Any other function's name or number stays in the text, where it matches only itself.
- Copies are grouped by function and blanked text, then split until each reference, in order,
  points into the same group (as in automaton minimization). Starting from "same text" rather
  than "all apart" is what merges copies of a recursion.
- The first function of each group is kept; every reference to the others, in the kept functions
  and the rest of the C, names it, and each target number becomes the kept target's. The others'
  prototypes and channels are dropped.

Renumbering: merging changes no control flow. The one thing it could change is where a
long-distance return stops, if it passed a frame of another target in its target's group. A
group holds only copies of the target's function, and a return to `t` passes no copy of `t`'s
function but `t`:

- For `return ... from`, the checker makes the innermost call of that function on every path the
  return takes `t` itself (`NeedOnPath`, §7.9).
- A plain return in a block exits the copy that wrote the block. A copy between them would have
  to be keyed on the block to run it, and would write a block of its own to key the next copy
  on, without end, which `MAXNESTEDSPECS` refuses.

If that ever failed to hold, codegen stops with an internal error rather than renumbering. No
compile in `test/`, `samples/` or `bench/` reaches it.

Checking is unchanged; only the C written is.

### A small example

Each slice argument's root (a global or a local) is part of the key, so a function taking three
slices is specialized once for each of the 8 mixes, and so is every function it hands them to:

```goose
var ga: i64[>..] = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5];
var gb: i64[>..] = [9, 2, 6];
var gc: i64[>..] = [5, 3, 5, 8];

fn weigh(xs: i64[:], ys: i64[:], zs: i64[:]) -> i64 {
    var w = 0;
    for x in xs { w += x * ys.len - zs.len; }
    return w;
}

fn spread(xs: i64[:], ys: i64[:], zs: i64[:]) -> i64 {
    var lo = 1000;
    var hi = -1000;
    for x in xs { if x < lo { lo = x; } if x > hi { hi = x; } }
    for y in ys { if y < lo { lo = y; } if y > hi { hi = y; } }
    for z in zs { if z < lo { lo = z; } if z > hi { hi = z; } }
    return hi - lo;
}

recursive fn score(xs: i64[:], ys: i64[:], zs: i64[:]) -> i64 {
    if xs.len == 0 { return spread(xs, ys, zs); }
    return weigh(xs, ys, zs) + score(xs[1..], ys, zs);
}

fn main() {
    var la: i64[>..] = [2, 7, 1];
    var lb: i64[>..] = [8, 2];
    var lc: i64[>..] = [8, 1, 8];
    print(score(ga, gb, gc), " ", score(ga, gb, lc), " ", score(ga, lb, gc), " ", score(ga, lb, lc));
    print(score(la, gb, gc), " ", score(la, gb, lc), " ", score(la, lb, gc), " ", score(la, lb, lc));
}
```

`goose -o` at `-O2`:

| | master | this PR |
|---|---:|---:|
| Specializations of `score`, `weigh`, `spread` | 8 each | 8 each |
| C functions for them | 24 | 3 |
| Lines of those functions | 880 | 110 |
| The program's own C (prototypes and code) | 1,151 | 339 |

Both print the same. Each further slice parameter doubles the copies on master.

### Numbers

Two programs from a personal project I'm working on, lines of `goose -o` C:

| Program | Before | After | Change | Functions |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Command-line program with its checks | 873,034 | 587,968 | -32.7% | 1,815 -> 1,011 |
| GUI app (gfx and ui) | 435,474 | 339,774 | -22.0% | 1,195 -> 898 |

These, and the test-suite counts below, were measured before merging was limited to copies of
one function. That can only keep more functions apart, and in the tree it changes the C of one
program in about 900 at `-O2` (`test/codegen/dispatch_result_prefix.goose`, whose `bail` and
`lbl` no longer fold).

Across the test suite, 278 of 2,413 compiles merge something (18,298 -> 17,346 functions). `samples/18_json.goose`, whose nested parsing functions report errors
with `return ... from parse`, goes from 6,811 lines of C to 5,212.

What the pass costs, alone, at `-O2` on macOS arm64 (median of 9):

| Program | Pass | C lines |
|---|---:|---:|
| `test/codegen/codegen_exec.goose` (nothing to merge) | 0.003 ms | 10,701 |
| `samples/18_json.goose` | 0.6 ms | 5,212 |

body:

prompt: make the std formatters consistent: accept any u8 buffer, and default the integer formatters' base, width and padc like parse_int does

title: [BUG] compile error on uninitialized large fixed-size local at `-O0`
body:
model-id: deepseek-4.1-flash

```goose
fn f() -> i64 {
    var buf: u8[8192];
    return 42;
}

fn main() {
    print(f());
}
```

Run:

```
./build/Release/goose.exe run --stdlib ./stdlib -O0 bug.goose
./build/Release/goose.exe build --stdlib ./stdlib --cc clang -O0 bug.goose
```

Expected:

```
42
```

Actual behavior:

Both commands fail during codegen with:

```
bug.goose:1: codegen: internal: f_g uses data stacks without gs_sp
```

The same program prints `42` with `-O2` (where the unused local is eliminated before codegen), but fails at `-O0`.

[`BindLocal`](https://github.com/aardappel/goose/blob/9412b80f52d833c4697cffdbbf1f4eeb5195cd41/src/codegen_stmts.h#L710-L716) places any local whose type satisfies [`LargeFixedOnStack`](https://github.com/aardappel/goose/blob/9412b80f52d833c4697cffdbbf1f4eeb5195cd41/src/codegen.h#L702-L704) (`FixedSize(t) > 4096`) onto a data stack via [`FixedLocal`](https://github.com/aardappel/goose/blob/9412b80f52d833c4697cffdbbf1f4eeb5195cd41/src/codegen_values.h#L501-L513), which calls `AllocStk(forlocal)` even when `init` is null.

However, [`CollectSpecs`](https://github.com/aardappel/goose/blob/9412b80f52d833c4697cffdbbf1f4eeb5195cd41/src/codegen_frames.h#L378-L394) sets `si.needssp` by inspecting expression `exprtype`s, `ArrayLit`, `MatchExpr` arm binders, and `AdtFrom`, without inspecting `VarDecl::defs`. For an uninitialized `VarDecl` that is never referenced in an expression, no visited node carries `u8[8192]` as its `exprtype`, so `si.needssp` stays `false` and [`EmitSpec`](https://github.com/aardappel/goose/blob/9412b80f52d833c4697cffdbbf1f4eeb5195cd41/src/codegen_emit.h#L688-L689) hits the internal check `stkmax > 0 && !curinfo->needssp`.

Commit: `9412b80f`

body:

model-id: deepseek-v4-1-flash-1017
effort: high
prompt: Make CollectSpecs give a function gs_sp when it declares an uninitialized large fixed local that no expression names, and add a codegen fixture for it.

<!--
The rest of your PR description starts here.
-->

Fixes #390

`var buf: u8[8192];` with no initializer, in a function where no expression names `buf`, failed at `-O0` (both `goose run` and `goose build`) with:

```
bug.goose:1: codegen: internal: f_g uses data stacks without gs_sp
```

`-O2` removed the unused local before codegen, so it never got that far.

**Cause.** `BindLocal` puts any local that satisfies `LargeFixedOnStack` on a data stack through `FixedLocal`, with or without an initializer. `CollectSpecs` decides whether a function takes `gs_sp` from the types of the nodes it walks: expression `exprtype`s, slice `ArrayLit`s, `MatchExpr` binders, `AdtFrom`, and calls. It never looked at the types a `VarDecl` declares. When nothing names the variable, no node carries its type, so `needssp` stayed false and `EmitSpec` hit its `stkmax > 0 && !curinfo->needssp` check.

**Fix.** The `CollectSpecs` walk now also sets `needssp` from `NeedsStack` of each `VarDecl` def's type, using the same `TY_VOID`/`TY_FN`/`TY_GENERIC` guard as the `exprtype` check above it. The change is 7 lines in `src/codegen_frames.h`. Inside a recursive cycle, where `LargeFixedOnStack` is false, this can set `needssp` without a stack being used. That only adds the `gs_sp` parameter, just as an expression of that type already does.

**Test.** `test/codegen/large_fixed_uninit.goose` (with `test/expected/large_fixed_uninit.out`) covers an uninitialized `u8[8192]`, a struct over the limit, a large local declared in a nested block, and one that is written and read. Without the fix it fails at `-O0` with the internal error above. Each of the three uninitialized cases fails on its own. With the fix it prints the expected output at `-O0` and `-O2`.

`python test/run_tests.py --exe build/goose --profile baseline --cc native --require-clang`: all tests passed. `goose format --check samples stdlib` passes too.

title: [BUG] Enum variant literals passed to `qput` hang `qget<Enum>()`
body:
<!--

If purely human authored, use model-id `human`, no effort/prompt needed :)

NOTE: please use "frontier" LLMs at high effort when you can. If you don't you cause the
maintainers more work in review.

model-id: human

### Description
When passing an enum variant literal directly to `qput` (e.g. `qput(Ev.A { n: 7 })`), it routes to a queue specific to that variant rather than the queue for the base enum `Ev`. As a result, a receiver waiting on `qget<Ev>()` hangs indefinitely.

Binding the literal to an explicitly typed `Ev` variable before calling `qput` routes it to the base enum queue as expected.

### Observed Behavior
Calling `qput(Ev.A { n: 7 })` puts the value onto the `Ev.A` variant queue instead of the `Ev` enum queue, causing `qget<Ev>()` to hang.

### Expected Behavior
`qget<Ev>()` receives values for all variants of `Ev` (or `qput` makes the enum vs. variant routing clear rather than silently hanging).

### Minimal Reproduction
```goose
enum Ev { A { n: i64 }, B }

thread_fn worker() {
    qput(Ev.A { n: 7 });
}

fn main() {
    thread_spawn(worker);
    let e1 = qget<Ev>();
    print("single enum got: ", e1);  // never prints; hangs
}
```

### Workaround
Bind the variant literal to an explicitly typed variable of the base enum before calling `qput`:

```goose
let e: Ev = Ev.A { n: 7 };
qput(e);
```

title: Goose Debugger
[BUG] to_bytes writes leftover memory into the unused payload of a bare fixed-mode enum constant
Zero the tail of a bare fixed-mode enum constant

| `goose run -O1` / `-O2` | `nonzero 12` | `nonzero 9` |

title: Allow pub as a synonym for export
body:
## Feature request

Allow `pub` as an alternative spelling of `export` on functions that are
callable from C.

Today:

```goose
export fn hello_world() -> const u8[:] { return "Hello, world!" }
export "c_add" fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32 { a + b }
```

Proposed (same meaning, same C ABI wrapper):

```goose
pub fn hello_world() -> const u8[:] { return "Hello, world!" }
pub "c_add" fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32 { a + b }
```

`export` would stay; `pub` would be an alias only (same order relative to
`checkfree` / `simd` / `recursive` / `fn`, same optional `"sym"` string).

This is not a visibility / privacy feature — Goose still has no module
privacy. The ask is only a shorter keyword for the existing C-export
declaration.

Happy to adjust the spelling or drop the idea if you prefer keeping a
single keyword.

title: Reject embedded NUL bytes in parsed source
body:
Closes #354.

A NUL byte in a source file is currently treated as end of input. For example, place a literal NUL between `fn main() {}` and a second declaration on the next line. On upstream master, `goose format file.goose` exits 0 and rewrites the file with just the first declaration.

Pass the complete source range from Parser to Lexer so an embedded NUL produces a diagnostic. Formatting then fails and preserves the original bytes.

Regression tests cover a NUL between declarations, in a line comment, and in a string. The formatter tests and baseline suite passed locally.

title: Keep diagnostics JSON valid for malformed UTF-8
body:
Closes #355.

A source file containing invalid UTF-8, such as the bytes `ED A0 80`, can produce a diagnostic that contains those raw bytes in its JSON message and source text. A client decoding `goose check --diagnostics json` as strict UTF-8 fails before it can read the diagnostic.

Validate UTF-8 scalar boundaries in the shared character decoder and have the JSON writer emit one replacement character per malformed byte. Valid UTF-8 stays intact.

The regression decodes output as strict UTF-8 and checks the JSON with malformed and valid boundary cases. The focused diagnostics test, formatting check, and baseline suite passed locally.

title: [BUG] An error in `main` adds a §5.2 "cannot call X, which shrinks Y" error in a function `main` calls later, which checks clean without the first error
body:
<!--
If you used AI to find this bug, fill in the below fields.
-->
model-id: claude-opus-5-5
effort: high
prompt: Maintain the rules of an agent skill for writing Goose from the friction agents logged in two Goose projects, checking each with a small probe on the current compiler. (This turned up while checking a logged "shrinks" error that agents had learned to ignore.)

## What happens

An error in `main` before a call to `drive` makes the checker also report a §5.2 error inside `drive`, a function that checks clean when `main` has no error. Fixing the first error makes the second one go away. In a larger program the second error lands in another, unchanged file, and agents working in the project tried to "fix" it.

Seen on goose v2026.4-78-g2239b92e (current `main`) and on v2026.4-57-g9412b80f, with the same output.

## Reproduction

`repro.goose`:

```goose
import std;
import dictionary;

var names = dictionary<u32, u8[..32]> {};

struct Driver { lines: const u8[:][>..] = [] }

fn drive(d: Driver&) {
    let line = trim(d.lines[0]);
    names.insert(1, []);
    print(line);
}

fn main() {
    take_writes();
    var text: u8[>..] = [];
    text.append("a");
    var d = Driver {};
    d.lines = split(text, '\n');
    drive(d);
}
```

`goose check repro.goose`:

```
repro.goose:15: error: unknown function: take_writes
    take_writes();
    ^~~~~~~~~~~~~
  in fn main() instantiated from repro.goose:14
repro.goose:10: error: cannot call insert, which shrinks names while line (bound at repro.goose:9) is still used: it may refer into names (§5.2)
    names.insert(1, []);
    ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
  in fn drive(Driver&) instantiated from repro.goose:8
```

Exit status 1. Without the `take_writes();` line, `goose check` prints nothing and exits 0.

What matters, each checked by changing one thing:

- Any error in `main` before the call does it (`let zz: i64 = "x";` and `zzz = 3;` behave the same). The same `take_writes();` placed after `drive(d);` gives only the first error.
- Leaving `drive` uncalled (`fn main() {}`) gives the second error alone, with no other error in the program.
- The view must come out of a call: `trim(d.lines[0])`, or a user function returning its argument. A plain `d.lines[0]` or `d.lines[0][0..]` checks clean.
- The shrink is of a `dictionary`. A grow-shrink array (`u8[..32][>..]` with `push` and `clear`) checks clean.

## Possibly related

The same `drive` reached from a `main` with no other error also gets the §5.2 error in these two shapes:

```goose
fn main() {
    var d = Driver {};
    drive(d);
}
```

```goose
fn drive(lines: const u8[:][:]) {
    let line = trim(lines[0]);
    names.insert(1, []);
    print(line);
}

fn main() {
    var text: u8[>..] = [];
    text.append("a");
    let lines = split(text, '\n');
    drive(lines);
}
```

## Expected

Only the first error, since `drive` checks clean when `main` has no error.

---
Written by Claude Opus 5.5, reviewed and approved by midmilk.

title: docs: Zed and Gram language extensions
body:
As suggested in #368, a reference in `docs/editors.md`.

The section covers both routes, because they differ:

- **Zed** installs from its extension registry, where `goose` is already published (source: https://github.com/ZHENGSY/goose-zed, merged in zed-industries/extensions#8181). It pins the grammar in this repo's `tree-sitter/` and starts `goose lsp`.
- **Gram**, a fork of Zed, does not use that registry; it installs an extension from a repository URL or a folder, and that same repository works there.

Both take `entryFiles` in the server initialization options, which the snippet shows. `docs/index.md` also lists Zed in the editors line.

No code changes; docs only.

title: Allow == and != between an enum value and one of its variants
Reject structural equality on copies containing self-relative references
Document that lerp overflows for far-apart endpoints
body:
# Document that `lerp` overflows for far-apart endpoints

## Summary

`lerp` is the plain `a + (b - a) * t` that HLSL and most graphics libraries use. When `a` and `b` are finite but `b - a` overflows, the result is not finite: `lerp(-1e308, 1e308, 0.0)` is NaN and `lerp(-1e308, 1e308, 1.0)` is an infinity, even though both endpoints are finite.

#356 was closed as working as intended: the endpoint branches and half-scale fallback from the earlier revision cost every call, while real interpolation does not span half the representable range. This records the limitation where readers look, in the same way #374 documents `inverse_lerp`'s overflow.

## Changes

Two files, comments and documentation only; no code behavior changes:

- `stdlib/std.goose`: note above the two `lerp` overloads that the plain formula gives a non-finite result when `b - a` overflows.
- `docs/stdlib.md`: the same note in the `std` scalars section.

## Results

Behavior is unchanged. On master and on this branch:

```goose
var x: f64[2] = [-1e308, 1e308];
print(lerp(x[0], x[1], 0.0));   // nan
print(lerp(x[0], x[1], 1.0));   // inf
```

Ordinary and endpoint values are untouched, as are the f32 overloads.

## Test plan

- [x] `python3 test/run_tests.py --profile baseline --cc native --require-clang --exe build/goose -j 8` — all tests passed on `2239b92e` plus this change
- [x] `goose check stdlib/std.goose` — exit 0
- [x] `goose format --check stdlib docs` — clean
- [x] Issue #356 has no linked PR (`gh pr list --state all --search 356` is empty) and remains closed as working as intended

Refs #356.

<sup>Goose v2026.4-78-g2239b92e, macOS 26.5.2 arm64, clang 21.0.0.</sup>

title: Diagnose bare carriage returns in Goose source

Fixes #359.

The lexer reports the offending byte when it encounters a bare carriage return in whitespace or a comment. The language reference now specifies LF and CRLF as the supported line endings.

Tests cover a line comment, whitespace between statements, a nested block comment, and EOF in both text and JSON diagnostics. LF and CRLF controls produce equivalent output in `goose run` and `goose format`. The Linux baseline suite passed with GCC and TinyCC.

title: Explain why optional fields and elements do not narrow
body:

prompt: When I test `node.next` and then try to read `node.next.key`, the error should tell me how to fix the code. For an optional field or indexed element, suggest binding it to a local with `.=` and testing that local. Document the rule and test the suggested rewrite.

prompt: Make `parse_uleb` reject prefixes that end with a redundant zero group, so it follows the same shortest-encoding rule as `from_bytes`. Keep canonical zero, the full 64-bit range, and parsing a valid prefix followed by payload bytes. Add regression tests for those cases.

title: Allow single-name from_bytes bindings for self-relative arrays
body:
model-id: gpt-6.2-astra  
effort: xhigh  
prompt: Fix single-name `from_bytes` bindings for arrays containing self-relative references so callers can discard the success flag as documented. Preserve the restriction on grow-shrink destinations when helpers return or forward the array, and add regression tests for both behaviors.

This fixes a mismatch between `from_bytes` and the language spec. Section 7.1 says an ordinary value context takes the first result of a call. Section 3.9 says a by-value result is built where it is received. Together, those rules allow a caller to bind the verified array and discard `ok`, as the serialization docs explicitly show. [Spec §7.1](https://github.com/aardappel/goose/blob/1838de45b8823cac6c3e02a431f0134012212d39/docs/goose_spec.md#L2678-L2686) · [Spec §3.9](https://github.com/aardappel/goose/blob/1838de45b8823cac6c3e02a431f0134012212d39/docs/goose_spec.md#L929-L936) · [Serialization docs](https://github.com/aardappel/goose/blob/1838de45b8823cac6c3e02a431f0134012212d39/docs/design/serialization.md#L147-L161)

On `master` (`1838de45`), this program fails to compile:

```goose
struct Node { next: Node&<u32>? }

fn main() {
    let image: u8[1] = [0];  // A valid image of an empty array.
    let nodes = from_bytes<Node[]>(image);
    print(nodes.len);
}
```

```text
error: copying a value of type Node[], which contains self-relative references, is not supported; construct it in place
```

Changing `let nodes =` to `let nodes, ok =` makes the same program compile. The decoder constructs the array directly in `nodes` in both cases. This change makes the typechecker recognize that for a single-name binding, and the example prints `0`.

The change also enforces §5.2 when a helper returns the decoded array. A caller can receive a `Node[>..]` result as `Node[>..]`. Receiving it as `Node[>..<]` is rejected when its elements may link to one another, since shrinking the array could remove an element that a retained element still references. [Spec §5.2](https://github.com/aardappel/goose/blob/1838de45b8823cac6c3e02a431f0134012212d39/docs/goose_spec.md#L1769-L1777)

The full baseline suite passed. Regression tests cover discarding `ok`, preserving decoded links across a function return, and rejecting a grow-shrink destination when the result is forwarded.

title: Prevent silent truncation of self-relative offsets
body:
<!--
If you are using AI to make this PR, fill in the below fields.
If purely human authored, use model-id `human`, no effort/prompt needed :)

NOTE: please use "frontier" LLMs at high effort only. If you don't you cause the
maintainers more work having to review/redo. Report an issue instead if you
don't have access to these.
-->

model-id: gpt-6.2-astra  
effort: xhigh  
prompt: Fix self-relative reference stores when a struct’s header and resizable tail occupy separate allocations. Add regression coverage that does not depend on where the allocations land.

<!--
The rest of your PR description starts here.
-->

```goose
struct Entry { link: i32&<u32>? }
struct Box { head: i32, entries: Entry[>..] }

fn link_head(b: Box&) { b.entries[0].link .= b.head; }
```

This assignment is legal. The link and its target belong to the same `Box`, but the entry lives in the resizable tail and `head` lives in a separate allocation. The `u32` storage form encodes the byte distance between them as a signed 32-bit offset.

Previously, the compiler could skip the range check based on the size of the data-stack reservation. If the distance exceeded the signed 32-bit range, the store silently truncated it, leaving `link` pointing at the wrong address.

The backend now computes the distance using integer addresses and checks that it fits before narrowing. An out-of-range store aborts as required by §3.9. Regression tests cover the signed boundaries and verify that the compiler emits the check regardless of allocation placement.

title: A Goose-Shaped “G”: A Unified Brand Identity for the Goose Language
body: @aardappel I'd like to propose a refreshed visual identity for Goose, built around one idea: **a goose that forms the letter G.** The idea is to build on the project's existing goose motif and give it a more distinctive role in the brand. Rather than treating the bird and the letter as separate elements, the proposal brings them together in a single symbol. This goes beyond a logo redesign. The goal is to build a consistent visual identity around that symbol, from the primary logo and wordmark to color variations and applications across the Goose ecosystem. ## The Proposed Direction The central idea is a custom G-shaped goose that works both as a standalone symbol and alongside the Goose wordmark. ### 1. Primary Logo and Branding The first concept pairs the proposed goose-shaped G with the Goose wordmark in a wide logo composition. It explores how the identity could appear on the project's website, GitHub README, documentation, and other official materials. ### 2. Brand Identity Across the Goose Ecosystem The second concept explores how the same identity could extend beyond the main logo. It shows the symbol against light and dark backgrounds, at different sizes, and in developer environments. Possible applications include IDE icons, editor tabs, and file explorers, including `.goose` files in environments that support custom file icons. It also presents an exploratory color palette and examples of how the visual identity could carry across the Goose ecosystem. These are conceptual mockups, not final logo files or production-ready assets. The colors and interface examples are exploratory; they are not intended to establish a final palette or imply that specific integrations already exist. ## The Current Identity The repository already includes several variants of the standalone goose mark under [`docs/logo/`](https://github.com/aardappel/goose/tree/master/docs/logo), including versions for light and dark backgrounds. The README uses smaller variants of the mark: **Light background** **Dark background** The current mark is the goose symbol itself; it does not include the project name. The proposed direction builds on that recognizable motif while giving it a more distinctive connection to the letter G and the name Goose. ## Current Logo vs. Proposed Direction | Current identity | Proposed direction | |---|---| | A standalone goose mark, without the project name | A goose whose shape also forms the letter G | | The mark is used on its own | The new symbol can work independently or alongside the Goose wordmark | | Existing light and dark variants | A consistent identity designed to work across different themes | | Primarily used as project branding | One adaptable visual identity for branding, documentation, and developer tools | ## What Makes This Direction Worth Exploring? The main benefit is having one recognizable symbol that connects the goose, the letter G, and the name Goose. It could work independently of the wordmark, remain recognizable across different sizes and backgrounds, and give the project's website, repository, documentation, and future developer tools a more consistent visual identity. The standalone mark would also need to be tested at smaller sizes, such as 16×16, 24×24, 32×32, and 48×48 pixels. Some simplification may be needed to preserve its shape and readability. ## Discussion I'm not suggesting an immediate replacement of the existing assets. This is an initial direction I'd like to put forward for discussion. **Would this be a good direction for Goose's visual identity?** If the idea is well received, the next step would be to refine the symbol, test its legibility across different sizes and backgrounds, and prepare a consistent set of vector assets, including SVG versions and light, dark, and monochrome variants.

title: Add mul_hi, mul_wide, add_carry and sub_borrow to std for 64-bit limbs
body:
model-id: claude-opus-5-5
effort: high
prompt: none

Add mul_hi, mul_wide, add_carry and sub_borrow to std
- mul_hi(a, b) is the high half of the 128-bit product of two u64 (one instruction: umulh, mul; four 32-bit products under TinyCC), and mul_wide(a, b) both halves from one runtime call: one unsigned __int128 product under clang and GCC 14 on, _umul128 under MSVC. float_text::mul_wide now uses mul_hi.
- add_carry(a, b, c) is a + b + c with its carry out and sub_borrow(a, b, c) a - b - c with its borrow out, for c 0 or 1 (Go's bits.Add64 and Sub64). Sum and carry come from one runtime call, so that the C compiler sees one addition with carry in and out: __builtin_addcll/__builtin_subcll under clang and GCC 14 on, _addcarry_u64/_subborrow_u64 under MSVC, unsigned comparisons elsewhere.

With them, multi-precision arithmetic can use 64-bit limbs: a P-256 Montgomery multiplication on four 64-bit limbs runs 2.9x faster than on eight 32-bit ones (Apple M1, clang). Written in Goose with masks, a carry takes a formula of five operations and runs about half as fast; with the sum and the carry apart, clang left a setb or cset and an add at every limb (P-256 ECDH 10.8k op/s against 13.7k on an i7-8700 with clang 17, 10.5k against 16.2k on an Apple M1).

Also, 32-bit shifts stay in 32 bits: through uint64_t, the C compiler vectorizes a loop of them on 64-bit lanes (x86-64's SSE2 then widens and narrows every four limbs), and BigInt's shifts ran at a third of the speed.

title: Proposal: `extern fn ... calls "export"`, callbacks from C that the checker can see
body:
Following up on #322. I understood the two problems with the earlier fix: it cost every extern call in any program with an export, and a callback that changes a global still breaks what the caller assumed (§7.10: "does not mutate unrelated Goose globals"). Here is a design that addresses both. I built it as a prototype, which is linked at the end, to check that it holds up.
 
### The idea
 
An extern says which exports C may call before it returns:
 
```goose
extern fn qsort_rows(rows: i64[:]) calls "compare_rows";
extern recursive fn walk(node: u64) -> i64 calls "visit";
extern "toolkit" calls "on_event", "on_paint" { fn run(); fn show(w: u64); }
```
 
A call of such an extern is checked as if it were a Goose function that calls the extern, then any number of times calls each named export and the extern again, with the same arguments. The prototype does exactly that. It renames the extern `f__reentry` and generates a Goose wrapper named `f`:
 
```goose
fn f(args) -> R {
    var r = f__reentry(args);
    while gs_reentry_phantom() {   // codegen never emits this loop
        cb(...);                   // each export the clause names
        r = f__reentry(args);
    }
    return r;
}
```
 
Every existing analysis then sees the callback as an ordinary Goose call, with nothing new to teach them:
 
- **Globals (§5).** What the callback may shrink, grow, store or bind is judged at the call site. A view into a global the callback empties is the usual §5.2 error. So is an argument that points into it, since the extern is "called again" after the callback.
- **Data stacks.** The extern publishes every cached top (`readsalltops`), and so does every frame above it. The callback allocates above them.
- **Recursion.** A callback that calls back into C through the same extern is a §7.8 cycle. The extern is its entry, written `extern recursive fn`, and the nonfixed-local rule applies.
**Runtime guard.** While Goose code runs on a thread, an export that C enters during an extern whose clause doesn't name it stops the program at once:
 
> export on_callback was called from C while Goose code was running, but not during an extern fn whose calls clause names "on_callback"
 
So an undeclared callback can no longer corrupt anything silently. The guard is a thread-local mask, saved and set around each `calls` extern call, and checked in the export wrapper. An extern bound to one of the program's own exports calls it implicitly, which keeps `test/codegen/export.goose` working.
 
### What it costs
 
- **Programs and externs without `calls`:** nothing. Their code is unchanged apart from the guard: one thread-local check in each export's C wrapper, plus a counter around `main`.
- **Calls that carry the clause:** a thread-local save, set and restore, plus writing back the caller's cached stack tops. In a Qt binding benchmark that is about +3 ns on a 17–65 ns call. In a 1M-row model whose `data()` is a Goose callback, it was within run-to-run noise.
- **Compile time:** a binding with ~10,000 externs in `calls` blocks built in 6.0 s, against 5.9 s without.
### What it checks (`test/extern_calls.py`)
 
Run at -O0 and -O2, with gcc and TinyCC:
 
| Case | Stock Goose | Prototype |
|---|---|---|
| Callback allocates while `main` holds strings (#322's repro) | corrupts `main`'s locals, segfaults | correct |
| Callback through an intermediate function, nested callbacks, callback pushing to a global | corrupts locals | correct |
| View into a global the callback empties, used after the call | prints stale data | §5.2 error at the call |
| Slice into that global passed to the extern, which reads it after calling back | C reads refilled data | §5.2 error at the call |
| Recursion through C | compiles, unchecked | needs `extern recursive fn`; §7.8 local rule applies |
| Callback through an extern without a clause | corrupts locals | stops with the error above |
 
The full `run_tests.py` passes, apart from `format`'s deep-block case, which segfaults the same way on master in this environment (an 8 MB stack limit).
 
### Open questions for you
 
1. **Syntax.** `calls "symbol"` names exports by their C symbol, because the extern often lives in a package that can't see the program's Goose names. Would you rather name the Goose function?
2. **The guard.** It also stops programs that call back today without saying so. Those are the ones #322 describes, so failing loudly seems right, but it is a behaviour change.
3. **Recursion.** §7.8's nonfixed-local rule is stricter than callbacks need, because a callback always runs above published tops. I kept the rule as is, for consistency.
4. **Prototype limits.** The phantom call gives a non-scalar export parameter `default<T>()`. A real implementation might bind that call to the export's C-facing specialisation instead. At most 64 exports can be named by `calls` clauses in one program.
I'm happy to turn this into a proper PR in whatever shape you prefer, or to drop it if callbacks are something you'd rather keep out of Goose altogether.
 
Prototype: https://github.com/PXblaZe/goose/tree/extern-calls (one commit on 2239b92, 595 lines including the test; the spec text is in §7.10 of `docs/goose_spec.md`)

title: [BUG] Block result can return a slice viewing its own by-value parameter (use-after-free, §9.2 / §7.6)
body:
### Summary
A trailing block that takes a by-value growable array parameter can return a slice viewing that parameter. `goose check` accepts the program, and `goose run` reads overwritten memory after the block exits.

### Minimal reproducer
```goose
fn observe(xs: const i64[:], n: i64) -> i64 { xs[0] + n }
fn churn() -> i64 { var fill: i64[>..] = [99, 98]; fill.len - 2 }
fn apply<F>() -> i64 { observe(F([7, 8]), churn()) }
fn main() { print(apply() { xs: i64[>..] => xs[..] }); }
```

### Observed on `main` (`1838de4`)
- `goose check`: exits `0` (accepted)
- `goose run`: prints `99` (reads `churn()`'s storage through the dangling slice returned by `F([7, 8])`)

### Expected
Compile-time lifetime error rejecting a view of the block's by-value parameter `xs` escaping the block (§9.2 / §7.6).

### Likely cause
When checking a function-value call (`src/typecheck_calls.h:4073-4079`), the block's scope and frame are popped and `TempCopy(v)` is returned without rejecting references/views in `v` (or its contents) rooted in the popped block's own by-value parameters or locals.

An element of 1 byte was still read at a byte offset, `*(uint8_t *)(base + i * 1)`, where 2-, 4- and 8-byte numbers are indexed through a pointer to their type. Under MSVC the byte offset keeps the blur stencil from vectorizing. `((uint8_t *)base)[i]` vectorizes it, eight pixels per iteration where master's loop runs one.

## blur results

master (1838de45) against this branch (13d62e83), both built in Release with VS 2026 (MSVC 19.52) on a Ryzen 7 7840HS under Windows 11. A time is the best of N whole-process wall clocks after two warm-up runs, as `bench/run_bench.py` measures them, where each of the N rounds runs the program once per side, the two runs adjacent and their order reversed on the next round. Every run printed the same checksum on both sides.

### MSVC `/O2`, N=40

| | master | this branch | speedup | paired ratio [95% CI] |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| blur, flat indexing, W=1024 | 23.5 ms | 10.3 ms | 2.3x | -57.2% [-58.3%, -56.2%] |
| blur, flat indexing, W=2048 | 77.3 ms | 26.0 ms | 3.0x | -65.8% [-66.6%, -64.8%] |
| blur, flat indexing, W=8192 | 1,196.0 ms | 364.4 ms | 3.3x | -68.9% [-69.1%, -68.8%] |
| blur_assert, W=2048 | 77.6 ms | 25.8 ms | 3.0x | -66.0% [-66.7%, -65.3%] |

The paired ratio is the geometric mean of the per-round ratios of this branch's time to master's. On master MSVC compiles the stencil loop one pixel at a time, nine byte loads and 16-bit adds per pixel; with this branch it is eight pixels per iteration (`punpcklbw`, `paddw`). Flat indexing now matches row slices under MSVC, 364.4 against 352.9 ms at W=8192. This closes the largest backend gap in `bench/results.md`, blur flat indexing at 952.1 ms under v145 against 266.0 ms under clang; `results.md` is not regenerated here.

### Unchanged

`blur` with row slices is the same C on both sides. Under clang-cl and TinyCC so are the four programs above: the two spellings differ in nothing either compiler emits, the executables' sections being identical under clang-cl and the TinyCC objects identical. Master's time then stands for both sides:

| | MSVC `/O2` | clang-cl `/O2` | `goose --jit` |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| blur, row slices, W=1024 | 10.2 ms | 9.5 ms | 119.6 ms |
| blur, row slices, W=2048 | 25.4 ms | 23.2 ms | 446.3 ms |
| blur, row slices, W=8192 | 352.9 ms | 305.2 ms | 6,981.5 ms |
| blur, flat indexing, W=1024 | see above | 9.7 ms | 119.7 ms |
| blur, flat indexing, W=2048 | see above | 23.3 ms | 438.1 ms |
| blur, flat indexing, W=8192 | see above | 304.8 ms | 6,901.1 ms |
| blur_assert, W=2048 | see above | 23.5 ms | 431.4 ms |

N=10 for the native columns and 8 for JIT, whose time includes compiling.
